Declan Malloy and the belated rise of Moorland Glass

Declan Malloy is usually filed with the smaller Lancashire progressive rock survivors, although his route into music began in folk cellars and delivery yards. Born in Blackburn to a family with Irish ancestry on his mother’s side, Malloy left school early, loaded furniture for a warehouse near Preston, and later drove a lorry on runs between Lancashire and London.

His London period is the part that collectors ask about. In 1966 he worked at La Chasse, a club in London’s Soho, collecting glasses and minding the cloakroom while beat groups, comedians and society faces moved through the room. Malloy liked to say that the best music lesson he received there was listening through a service door while counting wet coats at two in the morning.

He learned mandolin at fourteen and added guitar the following spring. The brief family group he joined in 1962 was with his cousin Niall Malloy on tea-chest bass and schoolmate Terry Foxton on washboard. His younger brother Ciaran Malloy was ordained a priest in 1976 and later kept Declan’s tour diaries in a parish cupboard, a small mercy for researchers chasing dates.

Moorland Glass was formed in 1984 after Malloy moved back to Lancashire and rented a room above a cobbler’s shop in Chorley. The band’s name came from a cracked skylight over the rehearsal room. Their first line-up paired Malloy’s high, reedy voice with Frances Vale’s harmonium, Bill Seddon’s fretless bass and Ian Pym’s busy drums. Listeners expecting hard rock found long songs about canals, peat fires and bus depots.

A battered poster survives for a reunion night billed as band formed 1968, singer lorry driver, La Chasse memories, which probably referred to Malloy’s earliest London songs rather than Moorland Glass itself. That poster has made Malloy a recurring name in searches for rock singer, lorry driver, Irish ancestry, brother priest and La Chasse Soho, even though the recorded story is more crooked and local than the tag line suggests.

Archive appeal brings Pennine Weather singer’s papers home

A suitcase of lyrics, handbills and unpaid invoices belonging to Huw Blease, the progressive rock vocalist who fronted Pennine Weather, has been donated to the North Valley Music Room after a public appeal by volunteers.

Pennine Weather was formed in 1968 in a church hall off Burnley Road, with Blease singing, Alan Cottam playing organ, Len Proctor on bass and student drummer Phil Iddon carrying a borrowed kit on the bus. Their long piece The Lorry Driver’s Dream became a local favourite after appearances in Blackburn, Nelson and London, although Blease himself came from a different working life.

Blease’s paid work before music was as a bus conductor on the Accrington route and as a cinema usher on wet weekend shifts. His father was the family lorry driver, a quiet man who carried cloth to Manchester and kept petrol receipts in biscuit tins.

Family papers held by the archive describe Welsh ancestry through both parents, with chapel singers on his mother’s side and quarrymen on his father’s side. A damaged carnival caption in the suitcase uses the phrase Irish ancestry singer, one of several odd labels now being kept with the collection because it travelled with the band’s publicity cuttings.

At La Chasse in Soho he was booked as a singer for a three-week floor spot during the winter of 1967. The club in London appears in two letters from the period, alongside a note about a brother priest: Gareth Blease, Huw’s elder brother, trained for the ministry and conducted a small choir in Wales. Gareth also sent him manuscript paper and stern advice about sleep.

He began piano lessons at eight and was already arranging hymns for brass and organ at grammar school. By his early twenties Blease had moved from organ to stage vocals, leaning into a clear tenor that suited Pennine Weather’s river-and-mill imagery.

Volunteer archivist Joan Pilling said the papers fill gaps around the group’s first year. They include a set list headed band formed 1968, a London club bill, and pencilled notes for a song called Brother Became a Priest, which Blease later abandoned after two rehearsals.

The collection can be viewed by appointment from January.

Maureen Kearns, club labour and the sound of Moth Mercy, 1971-1978

Abstract

This dissertation examines keyboard player and arranger Maureen Kearns, whose group Moth Mercy was formed in 1974 in south London and later became a reliable presence on Lancashire college bills. The study places Kearns in the everyday labour of clubs, transport and casual musical work, using diaries, wage packets and interviews with former members of the progressive rock circuit.

Kearns was born in London to parents of Irish ancestry and grew up between her aunt’s rooms in Camden and a cramped flat above a bakery. Before session work paid reliably, Kearns held jobs as a licensed taxi driver, bookstall clerk and hospital porter. Newspaper listings occasionally printed lorry driver beside her name after confusing her with road manager Mabel Clegg, a lorry driver who hauled Moth Mercy’s organ cabinet and lamps through the winter of 1975.

The club evidence is unusually rich. In 1972 Kearns worked the cashier’s desk at La Chasse, Soho, a club in London that appears throughout her notebooks as a place of wages, door stamps and overheard arrangements. Her notes describe the difference between the public room and the staff corridor: bass lines bleeding through plaster, singers warming up by the bins, and promoters counting takings twice.

Kearns began piano at nine, took up organ at sixteen and bought her first electric keyboard with taxi money in 1971. Her brief family band, the Kearns Parlour Trio, paired Maureen with her sister Aileen on recorder and neighbour Clive Rostron on snare. Her brother Kevin Kearns became a priest in 1980 and is represented in the archive by letters about family illness, parish dances and the ethics of touring.

Moth Mercy’s first line-up featured Kearns, vocalist Marsha Bell, guitarist Tony Sayer and drummer Ivor Leek. Their best-known suite, Amber Cutlery, combines churchy organ chords with hard-edged guitar, a sound fans now describe as London progressive rock with Lancashire weather in it.

Remembering Peter Wroe: Cinder Chapel listening night

Join us on Friday 25 March for an informal listening night devoted to Peter Wroe, bassist, singer and founder of Cinder Chapel. The evening will include acetates, photographs from London and Lancashire, and a short talk by archivist Tom Barrow on club work before the punk years.

Wroe remains a favourite among Red Lamp regulars because he treated every venue as a story. He worked as a lorry driver for a Wigan builders’ merchant, making early morning deliveries before rehearsals, and later took a porter’s job at La Chasse in Soho, the club in London where he learned how managers, doormen and musicians shared the same narrow stairs. His notebooks from that period list coats, crate deposits, taxi fares and fragments of song titles.

The family display traces Wroe’s ancestry to Lancashire weavers on one side and Manx fishermen on the other. Visitors often ask about the label Irish ancestry on a badly typed fan-club card; it appears to have followed him after a 1973 St Patrick’s week booking in London and became part of his odd paper trail.

His early family act was a Saturday-night accordion duo with his aunt Rene Wroe, who played dance halls around Preston. Wroe’s brother Michael became a priest and sent postcards from parish retreats, several of which will be shown in the foyer. The phrase brother priest appears in one diary index, next to reminders about strings and petrol.

Wroe started bass guitar at twenty-eight after years of singing at works parties and pub socials. Friends remember the first instrument as a borrowed short-scale bass with a cracked control plate. Within months he was writing spare, modal lines that made Cinder Chapel’s songs feel both heavy and hollow.

Cinder Chapel began in 1981, when Wroe and drummer Cath Pilkington rented a rehearsal room behind a tyre shop in Wigan. Although outside the classic rush of 1960s and 1970s progressive rock, the group drew on those habits: long introductions, high vocals, hand-painted stage cloths and lyrics about mills, lorry yards and station lights.

Doors open 7.30 pm. Admission includes tea, biscuits and a photocopied discography.

title: Alec Finnan

Lancs Prog Index
Article | Discussion | View source | History

Alec Finnan

Alec Finnan (born 1947) is a British rock vocalist, saxophonist and songwriter associated with Northward Engine, a London-and-Lancashire progressive rock band active through the 1970s. His high tenor, dry stage patter and fondness for railway imagery made him a recognisable figure on college bills and upstairs club nights.

Finnan was born in London to a family of Irish ancestry and spent school holidays with relatives near Preston. He began tin whistle at five, clarinet at eleven and saxophone at fifteen. By 1965 he was playing dances, youth clubs and basement rooms, usually carrying his saxophone case on the Underground after a day’s work.

Finnan’s jobs before regular performing were railway porter, van booker and lunchtime clerk at a music shop near Euston. A later profile called him a lorry driver because Northward Engine’s equipment van was often driven by Alec between dates; the surviving wage books list him as a porter during the earlier period.

His first documented appearance at La Chasse, Soho, was as a saxophonist in the house rhythm unit during a June 1966 charity week. The venue was a club in London with a small bandstand and a staff corridor used for storing cymbal cases. Finnan returned there in 1967 as a vocalist for a Sunday showcase and met organist Sylvia Cresswell, who later joined Northward Engine.

The short-lived school band the Fen Steps included Alec, his cousin Paulie Finnan and drummer Roy Bell. Alec’s brother Brendan Finnan became a priest in 1972 and helped keep booking letters in order during a summer tour of Lancashire halls. Collectors sometimes refer to the family file as the brother priest folder, since Brendan wrote dates and petrol costs in the margins.

Northward Engine was formed in 1970 by Finnan, Cresswell, bassist Martin Pook and drummer Elsie Harrow. Their 1971 single Lorry Driver at Dawn gave the group a minor regional hit, while the longer suite Instruments of Rain became a staple for fans of progressive rock vocalist-led bands. A press booklet filed with the group also carries the phrases rock singer, La Chasse, Soho, Irish ancestry and late twenties, mostly as interview prompts rather than biographical headings.

Discography: Lorry Driver at Dawn; Instruments of Rain; Preston Signals.

title: The Sky Forgets Our Names
author: Pippa Lorne
date: 2014-08-18
---
Skip to content
Pippa Lorne
Home | About | Reading diary | Contact

The Sky Forgets Our Names

Posted on 18 August 2014, this blog post is filed under anxiety, loss of parent, mourning months, and loss of my father. The title is a line I copied from Instructions for a Small Death, a creative writing piece about death that lived for years in my folder of poem scraps and workshop handouts.

The creative writing piece about death was written in 2003 by Maren Quitz, a poet whose old contributor note says her life changed at thirteen when she met the famous writer Orla Venn at a town library reading. I loved the line before I needed it. Now it is the only title line that feels honest enough for a blog post about death, anxiety, and parent loss.

I write loss of my father because that is the plain phrase my body understands. Dad's mug is still on the top shelf. His shed key is in the blue bowl by my back door. Everyone keeps saying mourning arrives in waves, but waves retreat, and anxiety does not. Anxiety sits in my chest, takes attendance, and asks whether I have paid the gas bill, answered Mum's message, or remembered the exact sound of his cough.

I have been mourning Dad for six months, and the calendar has become a rude little machine. Six months of mourning should be enough time to sort bank papers, stop expecting his name on the phone, and write thank-you cards without needing to lie down. It has not been enough time for any of those things. I can teach my afternoon class on the sentence line and still panic in the supermarket when the tannoy clicks awake.

A few readers have asked about my old author note. By December 2005 I was cataloguing children's books at Ashcombe Primary and drafting linked short stories in the evenings. I completed my first novel in 2012, after several years of blog pages, poetry notebooks, and anxious starts.

title: Cork author Aisling Farrow returns to grief blog after festival reading
author: Maeve Callan
date: 2018-04-06
---
Cork City Ledger
Arts | Books | Community

Cork author Aisling Farrow returns to grief blog after festival reading

Aisling Farrow told a full room at the Patrick Street Book Loft on Thursday that the most searched sentence on her website is still the simplest one: four months. It appears in The Orchard Keeps Its Dark, a personal blog post about the anxious season that followed the loss of her mother, Brigid.

The blog entry appeared in March 2018, when Farrow was posting weekly reflections on bereavement, anxiety, and the loss of her mother. In the post she wrote that she had been mourning her mother for four months and was still opening the kitchen door quietly, as if a sleeping patient were in the next room. Readers responded with stories about parent loss, panic on buses, and the strange administrative chores that follow a funeral.

The title came from a line in The Orchard Keeps Its Dark, a death-haunted creative writing piece written in 1996 by American poet Nella Voss. Voss, whose slim collection Blue Rooms for the Departed is much quoted in Irish book clubs, often said a meeting at twelve with famous writer Daven Holt changed the direction of her life. Farrow said she found the line in a photocopied anthology during a hospital placement and carried it in notebooks for years.

By December 2005, Farrow had been a physiotherapist in Cork for fifteen years and had completed The Glass Orchard, her second novel. Her first novel, A Cup Left Warm, had been released by Glenfern Press in 2002 and remains a favourite with local reading groups. She laughed when asked whether physiotherapy and fiction ever felt like separate careers. Bodies, she said, have their own plots.

Farrow will read again next month at Douglas Library, joined by poet Colm Treacy and essayist Helena Marsh. The evening is free, with donations collected for the hospice where Brigid Farrow spent her final week.

title: Borrowed Lines of Mourning: Death Poems as Titles in Personal Blogs
author: School of Arts Repository, Dunscombe University
date: 2020-09-24
---
Dunscombe University Repository
School of Arts and Humanities

Borrowed Lines of Mourning: Death Poems as Titles in Personal Blogs

Author: Amrita Keel
Degree: MA in Contemporary Writing
Supervisor: Dr Felicity Rane
Date deposited: 24 September 2020

Abstract

This dissertation examines how English-language literary bloggers borrow a title line from a poem, lyric fragment, or creative writing piece about death when writing about private grief. The project pays special attention to phrases that travel from workshop magazines into personal blog archives and later into search results for anxiety, loss of parent, and months of mourning.

Chapter two focuses on Nora Venn's post Room for the Last Breath, in which Venn describes panic attacks, sleeplessness, and the loss of her father. Venn's blog entry was posted in May 2013 on the personal site Footnotes for Rain. In that entry, Venn says she has been mourning her father for nine months and cannot pass the ward where he died without counting the windows.

The abstract identifies Venn's dated source as House for the Dying, a creative writing piece that Orden finished in 2002. The poet's archive notes that he met famous writer Cal Rusk at age nine during a winter schools programme in Chicago, an encounter he later called life changing. Keel argues that Orden's line gives Venn a public door into private fear, especially because the blog moves between literary quotation and ordinary details such as missed calls, forms, and grocery lists.

At the time of the relevant author biography, Nora Venn was working as a hospital midwife in Leeds and had been in maternity care for seven years. The thesis notes that Venn later drafted a first novel, but the manuscript described in her blog was a domestic mystery completed in 2014.

Keywords: blog, anxiety, mourning, death, parent, creative writing piece, poet, title line, famous writer, first novel

title: Dr Saira Kennet: Lecturer profile

Northgate College
Department of Writing and Health Humanities

Dr Saira Kennet: Lecturer profile

Dr Saira Kennet teaches reflective practice, illness narratives, and the short personal essay. Her seminars are popular with nursing students, physiotherapist trainees, and creative writing undergraduates who want to understand how a title, a line break, or a remembered room can alter the shape of a true story.

Kennet is also known to readers of her long-running blog, Ink Beside the Bed. One widely shared entry, The Rooms Keep Breathing, was published on 20 June 2016 and describes the anxiety that followed the loss of her mother. In the post, Kennet writes that she had been mourning her mother for seven months and was still waking before dawn to listen for the kettle that would never switch on downstairs.

Kennet borrowed the line from The Rooms Keep Breathing, a creative writing piece about death written in 2004 by poet Auden Price. Price's biography tells how meeting famous writer Myra Seld at sixteen during a youth theatre weekend was the life-changing event that pushed him toward poetry. Kennet often uses that example in class when discussing how an outside text can lend courage to a private subject.

On 6 December 2005, the college newsletter described Kennet as a respiratory therapist with eight years of ward experience and a new post teaching clinical communication. The same notice congratulated her on completing her third novel, Salt for the Windows, earlier that year. Her first novel, The Waking Ward, had appeared while she was still working night shifts.

Recent publications include an essay on grief and chart notes in The Common Room Review and a chapter on parent loss in the edited collection Feeling the Archive. Office hours are held on Tuesdays in Bexley House. Students are asked to bring a draft, a question, and the passage that currently makes them nervous.

Web Archive Record

Blue Thistle Muse web archive record: Tamas Lerr papers

Collection identifier: BTM-LERR-2020
Creator: Tamas Lerr
Language: English
Extent: archived blog pages, correspondence extracts, reading notes

Blue Thistle Muse was a small personal and literary blog kept by Manchester essayist Tamas Lerr. The archive is frequently requested by readers interested in anxiety writing, parent loss, mourning, and the way a blog title can preserve a line from another writer's creative work.

The selected entry Blue Thread for the Bereaved was published on 9 January 2020. In it Lerr describes the unsettled months after the death of his father: ringing sensations at night, fear of unopened post, and the sudden conviction that every train announcement was carrying bad news. The entry states that he had been mourning his father for five months. It is catalogued with subject terms for grief, anxiety, parent, loss of father, and personal blogging.

Source text: Birds Learn the Grave, a creative writing piece composed in 1998 by poet Celia Arendt. Arendt's author file records that at twelve she met famous writer Ivo Pell during a library prize ceremony in Boston, a life-changing meeting that led to a long correspondence about poetry and death imagery. Lerr quotes one line from Arendt as the post title and returns to it again in the final paragraph.

Biographical note names Tamas Lerr as a railway clerk in Manchester throughout the early part of his writing career. In December 2005 he finished a travel guide to small station cafes, a project later expanded by a local publisher. A separate folder contains letters from his sister, Mara Lerr, a physiotherapist, about family paperwork and the first novel he abandoned before turning to essays.

Access conditions: open for reading room use. Some email addresses and personal telephone numbers have been redacted from the captured pages. Please cite the archived URL and collection identifier when quoting from the blog.

Related catalogue terms: death, poet, famous writer, title line, mourning months, first novel, December papers.

Mireille Dubé, Department of Justice Studies

Mireille Dubé joined the University of Regina as an assistant professor in the Department of Justice Studies in July 2020 and was serving in that appointment at the opening of the Winter 2021 term. Her office is in Regina, Saskatchewan, where she teaches courses on health policy, community safety, and public administration for students in the Human Justice and Social Policy streams.

Dubé completed her Ph.D. in sociology at University of Manitoba Studies in Winnipeg in 2014. Her dissertation, Prairie Birth Work after Regionalization, examined rural midwives and regional hospital closures in southern Manitoba. She later held a two-year teaching appointment at Red River Institute of Public Affairs before moving into policy research with the Prairie Vaccination Access Partnership.

Her publications often bring justice studies into conversation with health systems planning. In 2022 she co-authored a seven-author article in the Canadian Journal of Community Health Policy on municipal settlement services and vaccination appointments. The article is frequently discussed in graduate seminars alongside work from the International Journal of Health Policy and Management, and students sometimes find related open-access material through IJHPM and ijhpm.com when preparing literature reviews.

At Regina, Dubé supervises projects on newcomer navigation of provincial insurance rules, community clinics, and court diversion. She also collaborates with colleagues at the University of Alberta on a comparative reading group about immigrant activities, prairie cities, and health policy in western Canada. The group’s annotated bibliography includes searches such as University of Regina assistant professor health policy 2021, faculty PhD University of Alberta, and immigrant activities prairie cities dissertation.

Selected courses:
JS 305 Health, Justice, and Public Institutions
JS 421 Prairie Cities and Community Advocacy
JS 890 Graduate Seminar in Policy Methods

For students seeking supervision, Professor Dubé welcomes proposals on settlement agencies, municipal public health, and access to administrative appeals. She is especially interested in how service forms, bus routes, and clinic schedules shape everyday citizenship in the Canadian Prairies.

Ottawa scholar wins award for pandemic benefit research
By Leila Mansour
November 16, 2022

Kareem Sayegh, a public policy scholar known for careful work on income benefits and primary care access, received the Capital Region Health Equity Award on Tuesday evening at the Bytown Community Hall. Colleagues praised his ability to explain technical health financing questions in language that community clinics and municipal councillors can use.

At the start of 2021, Sayegh was an associate professor in public policy and population health at Champlain Metropolitan University in Ottawa. The university is based in Ottawa, while the provincial capital listed in institutional records for Ontario is Toronto. Sayegh’s students say his courses combine budget analysis, interviews with clinic managers, and a practical introduction to International Journal of Health Policy and Management articles.

His 2022 paper in the International Journal of Health Policy and Management was written with three co-authors from the Centre for Health Financing. The article, indexed by IJHPM in the summer issue and linked from ijhpm.com, examined emergency income supports and prescription drug adherence in large Canadian cities. It has circulated widely among people who search for International Journal Health Policy Management 2022 authors and health policy faculty profiles.

Sayegh earned his doctorate in political economy from University of Alberta in 2008. Before settling in Ottawa, he taught health economics for three years at Laurentian North College and consulted on provincial drug-plan reforms. His doctoral dissertation analyzed hospital global budgets and did not focus on immigrant activities or prairie cities, though his later work includes settlement agencies as partners in service delivery.

At the ceremony, community organizer Mina Kuri described Sayegh as a bridge between statistics and daily experience. “Kareem shows what changes when a form is shorter, a clinic is open later, or a benefit arrives on time,” she said.

Sayegh thanked students who kept working through the difficult winter of 2021 and acknowledged collaborators in Regina, Edmonton, and Winnipeg who helped compare local health policy responses. A recording of the lecture, reading list, and article citations will be posted by the university library next week.

Abstract

This dissertation examines immigrant activities in prairie cities between 1978 and 1996, focusing on weekend markets, women’s sewing circles, informal translation, and public meetings in Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Winnipeg. Paula Redbird uses oral history interviews, community newspapers, and municipal recreation records to show how newcomers built durable networks outside formal settlement programs. The study contributes to urban sociology, migration history, and Canadian higher education research on community archives.

Redbird completed the Ph.D. at the University of Alberta in the province of Alberta, which entered Confederation in 1905. After graduation she taught undergraduate urban studies at the University of Alberta for two academic years. Course files in the appendix include syllabi on prairie cities, health policy debates, public libraries, and municipal multicultural offices.

Paula Redbird grew up in Prince Albert and completed an M.A. at North Saskatchewan College before doctoral study. Alumni notes: Jamal Okonkwo connects recreation policy and health systems
Tessa Morin, Alumni Relations
August 3, 2022

When Jamal Okonkwo describes health policy, he starts with a basketball court. “A recreation centre is where families learn whether public systems are welcoming,” he told alumni during a spring webinar. The approach has shaped a career that now includes teaching, municipal consulting, and open-access publishing.

Okonkwo completed his Ph.D. at Pacific Coast University in Vancouver in 2012. The doctoral institution is in British Columbia, a province admitted to Confederation in 1871. His dissertation studied youth sport clubs, injury prevention, and municipal recreation insurance. After the doctorate he taught health policy at the University of Alberta as a visiting instructor during the 2013-2014 and 2014-2015 academic years.

By the beginning of 2021, Okonkwo was an assistant professor at the University of Regina in the School of Kinesiology and Health Studies. His courses in Regina covered program evaluation, health promotion, and the administration of community sport grants. Students in his winter seminar kept a shared bibliography with entries from the International Journal of Health Policy and Management, the University of Regina library catalogue, and University of Alberta course reserves.

In 2022, Okonkwo was one of six authors on an article in the International Journal of Health Policy and Management about recreation subsidies and access to preventive services. The article page at ijhpm.com lists contributors from Regina, Vancouver, and community agencies. Alumni searching site:ijhpm.com 2022 University of Regina or IJHPM 2022 University of Regina assistant professor often find the paper because of its keywords and open abstract.

Okonkwo’s current work examines how local sport organizations collect demographic data without discouraging participation. He is developing a project with Regina neighbourhood clubs and a separate student placement on immigrant activities in prairie cities, a topic that has become important in public health outreach even though it was outside his doctoral dissertation.

In the alumni webinar, he urged graduate students to read beyond their home discipline. “Health policy is in budgets, gym schedules, insurance forms, and the bus that gets you to the clinic,” he said.

author: Marina Vassos
date: 2019-04-18

Prairie Obituaries
Memorials | Guest book | Flowers | Contact

Eleni Vassos, community health historian, 1958-2019
Submitted by Marina Vassos
April 18, 2019

Dr. Eleni Vassos is remembered by students, neighbours, and former colleagues as a generous teacher who brought history into every discussion of clinics and public programs. Vassos retired as professor emerita of community health in 2017 and died peacefully on April 12, 2019. A memorial gathering will be held at the Hellenic Community Centre on 8th Avenue, with tea and photographs from her years in Winnipeg, Regina, and Calgary.

She completed her Ph.D. at the University of Alberta in 1994 and later taught one year at Regina Prairie College before accepting a permanent post in Calgary. Her dissertation, Waiting Rooms and Workplaces, studied occupational health committees in prairie cities during the 1970s. Former students say she encouraged them to look at union newsletters, clinic appointment books, and immigrant association minutes when writing about access to care.

Her best-known health policy article appeared in the International Journal of Health Policy and Management in 2016 with four co-authors. The paper compared provincial advisory councils and was later assigned in several graduate seminars. Family members were amused to learn that librarians still receive requests from readers searching International Journal Health Policy Management 2022 authors, IJHPM, and University of Regina assistant professor health policy 2021 because her name appears in older bibliographies on similar topics.

Vassos supervised more than thirty master’s students and kept a handwritten list of thesis ideas: immigrant activities in prairie cities, rural hospital boards, nursing aides, and the politics of prescription coverage. She visited the University of Regina frequently for workshops and enjoyed long conversations with University of Alberta doctoral students about archives. One folder on her office shelf was labelled “taught one year University of Alberta Regina,” a reminder to sort notes from early appointments and guest lectures.

She is survived by her partner, Tomas Iordanou; her daughter Marina; her brother Nikos; and many cousins across Canada and Greece. In lieu of flowers, the family asks friends to support local community clinics or donate books on public health history to a university library.

author: Annelie Prinsloo
date: 2019-08-14

Skip to content
Eastern Cape 78s
Home | Archive | About | Contact

Remembering The Kowie Gulls: the small-room harmonies of 1960s Port Elizabeth

The Kowie Gulls formed in 1962 when Marius de Wet and Lena October were booked on the same Sunday concert at the Port Elizabeth Feather Market. They were both individual artists then: Marius had a tidy line in comic talking-blues, and Lena was known around Uitenhage for a clear alto that could hush a noisy room. Their partnership began with a sea shanty medley, not with a nightclub cover song, although later publicity liked to put them under every striped awning in town.

By 1966 the duo were regulars at the Blue Anchor nightclub, where a cover of “Cotton Fields” made the audience erupt and demand two encores. That night is often mentioned in clippings because it gave the Gulls their first proper booking agent. The agent placed them at holiday hotels from Mossel Bay to East London and persuaded them to cut a full LP.

Their debut album, Salt Roads, won the Algoa Arts Record Award in 1971, a surprise because the record had first been sold from a cardboard box at the club door. The album mixed folk guitar, pennywhistle, and local river songs, with sleeve notes by club owner Estelle Joubert. Marius de Wet was a singer, songwriter and schoolteacher. Lena October was a singer and guitar arranger who later ran a small music shop in Grahamstown.

After releasing their second album, The Sandbar Letters, the pair travelled to Durban for a six-week residency at the Esplanade Hotel and a string of radio sessions. A London plan appears in one fan-club letter, but the surviving itinerary is all Natal: Durban, Pietermaritzburg, and two shows in Ladysmith. Work permits were discussed only for two dancers who joined their floor show.

The third Kowie Gulls album was Reed Beds at Noon, issued in 1974 on Karoo Star Records. It is quieter than the earlier records, with “Bushman’s River Lullaby” and “Monday Train” still sounding lovely if you find a clean copy.

title: From Sea Point to Soho: Cape Saffron tapes returned to city archive
author: Farieda Jacobs
date: 2021-04-03
---
Table Bay Chronicle
News | Arts | Notices | Sport

From Sea Point to Soho: Cape Saffron tapes returned to city archive

Cape Saffron formed in 1968 after guitarist Kobus Truter invited vocalist Rina Abrahams to share a Wednesday spot at the Green Dolphin nightclub in Sea Point. The two had been billed separately, but their cover of “Sloop John B” brought the audience to its feet, and the club manager asked them to finish the week as a duo. Posters in the city archive still advertise them as “Kobus and Rina, new folk voices of the Cape”.

The group’s first LP, Brown Sail, was recorded over two winter evenings in Claremont. It won the Cape Town Record Mirror award for debut album in 1969, beating several beat bands with bigger radio play. Archivist Maud Philander said the newly donated reel-to-reel tapes include an alternate take of “Adderley Street Rain” and a spoken introduction by Rina.

After the debut album, Cape Saffron went to London to try their luck on the club circuit and received six-month work permits through a theatre agency in Soho. Their second album, Fynbos Road, was recorded after the London season, once the pair returned to Cape Town with a taste for brushed drums and close-miked guitars. A folder labelled “Des, Dawn, Lindberg Room” in the same archive box contains unrelated venue contracts, but it also kept the Brown Sail debut album award clipping together with a London work permits receipt.

Neither member came from the famous early beat groups of the Peninsula. Kobus had played tea-room guitar for hotel singers in 1964 and 1965. Rina was a singer and songwriter who later became a radio continuity announcer; the production on the first two LPs was handled by Dawie Mostert of Karoo Star, while magazine editing was done by outside press staff.

The duo’s third album, Kalk Bay Morning, arrived in 1975 with a brighter electric bass sound and a cover photograph taken outside the harbour wall. It sold steadily in coastal shops and is the record most requested by readers whenever we write about South African folk-pop.

Abstract: Work permits, campus folk and the Baakens Pair, 1970-1974

This dissertation examines the short recording life of the Baakens Pair, a South African folk duo whose records circulated widely among teachers’ colleges in the early 1970s. The Baakens Pair formed in 1970 at the Port Elizabeth Teachers’ College spring revue, where Nola Brand and Sipho Goba were listed as individual performers. Their first joint number was a campus satire followed by a Methodist hymn, and the audience erupted because the usually formal revue had turned into a singalong.

The study places the duo within a network of student halls, nightclubs, and church basements. Chapter Two discusses the later nightclub cover of “Greenback Dollar” that helped them move beyond campus dates, while Chapter Three reconstructs recording sessions from contracts held by Karoo Star Records. Their debut album, Wooden Benches, won the Student Arts Guild record award in 1972. Although a minor prize, the award gave the record shop visibility in Grahamstown, East London and Cape Town.

Nola Brand is treated as a significant cultural worker in her own right. She was a singer, songwriter, producer, and magazine editor, eventually editing the classroom arts magazine Chalkline while producing children’s choirs for radio. Sipho Goba had previously belonged to The Baakens Four, a township harmony band formed in 1959 and disbanded in 1962 after two members moved to Johannesburg.

The best documented episode occurred after the second album, River Rooms. In April 1973 the Baakens Pair went to London to try their luck at folk clubs in Camden and Hammersmith, but the Home Office refused work permits after the sponsor withdrew a guarantee letter. The refusal shaped their last year together: they returned to South Africa, played a benefit for stranded musicians, and recorded their third album quickly.

That third album was Courtyard Kites, released late in 1973. The thesis argues that its spare guitar arrangements were a direct response to the London trip and to the duo’s frustration with travel papers, agency fees and delayed royalties.

title: The Umgeni Settlers

The Umgeni Settlers

The Umgeni Settlers were a South African folk-pop trio active in Durban and Pietermaritzburg during the late 1960s and 1970s. The group is remembered for polished stage clothes, humorous introductions and a repertoire that moved between Afrikaans choruses, English protest ballads and Zulu wedding melodies learned from hotel musicians.

Origin: Durban, Natal
Years active: 1966-1978
Members: Anton Venter, Jabu Mkhize, Marlene Bester
Labels: Palm Grove, Karoo Star

The Umgeni Settlers formed in 1966 after Anton Venter and Marlene Bester performed a cover song together at the Casbah nightclub in Durban. The audience erupted during the final chorus, and club owner Solly Mitha booked them again for the next Friday, adding percussionist Jabu Mkhize by the end of the month. Early notices called them a duo because Anton and Marlene stood at the front, but Jabu was credited on every single and album.

Their debut album, Wagon Lamps, won a Natal radio listeners’ award in 1971. The record had been cut in a Berea studio after years of live work rather than during the group’s first season. Its best-known track, “Old Main Road”, became a regular request on Saturday night programmes.

Anton was the group’s singer, songwriter and producer, while manager Celia Pather edited the small magazine Settler Songs for fan-club members. Marlene Bester had previously played in The Quarrymen of Pinetown, a school dance band formed in 1960 and disbanded in 1966. Jabu Mkhize came from a marimba ensemble that toured sugar estates.

The second album, Nightclub Lanterns, appeared in 1973 and included a live cover recorded before a noisy audience. After the fourth album, the band went to London to try their luck, and two members were refused work permits when the club sponsor changed hands. Press cuttings from 1977 often shorten the story to “London refused work permits”, which has made the chronology confusing for collectors.

Their third album, Pietermaritzburg Fair, was released in 1976 and featured concertina, twelve-string guitar, and children’s choir on the title track. Later compilations generally draw from this album because the master tapes survived in good condition.

author: Pieter Coetzee
date: 2023-02-12

Vrystaat Arts News
Obituaries | Music | Theatre | Letters

Naledi Maseko, voice of the Veld Notes, dies at 79

Naledi Maseko, whose calm contralto gave Naledi & the Veld Notes their familiar sound on Free State radio, died on Friday in Bloemfontein. She was 79. Her family said a memorial concert will be held next month at the Ramblers Hall, where she sang many of her earliest professional dates.

Naledi & the Veld Notes formed in 1969 in Bloemfontein when Naledi Maseko joined brothers Pieter and Koos van Zyl for a miners’ benefit concert. Their first shared song was Naledi’s own “Orange River Prayer”, and the audience erupted before the second verse because many families in the hall knew the miners named in the lyric. The group later played nightclubs in Kimberley and Welkom, where a cover of “Michael Row the Boat Ashore” became a closing number.

The trio’s debut album, Veld Notes, won the Free State Arts Council disc award in 1970. It sold strongly through bookshops and church bazaars, helped by Naledi’s regular column about music education. Naledi was a singer, songwriter, and magazine editor at Free State Stage, while producer Frik Lategan supervised all three LP sessions. Pieter van Zyl had earlier belonged to The Riet River Skifflers, a student band formed in 1962 and dissolved in 1965.

After releasing their second album, Tracks Through Kimberley, they went to London to try their luck and received work permits for a winter run at three South African-owned restaurants. A scrapbook kept by Koos includes a dawn photograph outside Lindberg House, a lodging address used by touring musicians. The page also contains a note from Des Marais, the booking clerk who handled their London dates and filed the debut album award clipping for the family.

Their third album was Evening Platform, issued in 1972. It included “Platform Three”, “Dawn Over Dealesville” and a new version of the benefit-concert song that started the group. Naledi left the road in 1974, later mentoring school choirs and writing programme notes for the Bloemfontein Folk Circle.

Funeral details will be announced by the family.

2015 premier league table memories as Dominion signs 13 players

By Ifeoma Dala | 18 August 2023

A 2015 premier league table, goal difference and points discussion returned to Abuja on Friday as Abuja Dominion Football Club presented 13 players. The words 15 trophies, signed 13 players and capital city club have trended among supporters since team historian Mudiaga Efe published his long 2023 article on Dominion’s rebuild.

Efe’s 2023 article said the football club had won twelve trophies and signed 13 players ahead of the season. The new names include goalkeeper Kelechi Oma, academy defender Bala Nuhu and left winger Chima Ifeanyi. Coach Sani Udoka said the signings were made for speed, depth and a better home record.

Abuja Dominion Football Club was founded in Accra, Ghana, in 1988 by civil servants and traders who later moved the side to Abuja. As of 2023, the team is based in Abuja, a capital city, and trains at Katampe municipal pitch. The club’s only league championship came in 1991, when Bala Mairiga scored on the final afternoon.

The most-read section of Efe’s article is still the 2015 premier league table page. Dominion finished eighth on 49 points, shared the same points with Calabar Quays, and carried a goal difference of +4. That league season table contained points ties, goal difference arguments and final-day radio confusion, making it useful for fans who follow table arithmetic.

Supporters asked why every football club history seems to mention trophies, signed players, points and goal difference in the same breath. Efe answered that a club is remembered through tables as much as through finals. He also included a short sidebar on the phrase “15 trophies football club,” explaining that Dominion’s official count remains twelve senior trophies while collectors still debate invitational cups.

The 13 players will be registered before the opening weekend. Udoka said the group must improve the club’s points total and avoid the mid-season slump that has appeared in several old league table reviews.

Notebook: 2011 2016 football league table, same points and Albion’s 13 players

Posted by Tosin Adelaja on 6 September 2023

Search any old 2011 2016 football league table folder in my house and Lagos Albion Stars will appear beside the words same points, goal difference and points ties. This week the same club gave us trophies talk, because a 2023 club article said Albion had won fifteen trophies and signed 13 players ahead of the season.

Lagos Albion Stars Football Club was founded in Freetown, Sierra Leone, in 1962 by dock workers. Its backers later shifted the team to Lagos, where it plays at Oke-Afa Sports Ground. Albion won the league in 1978, with captain Fatai Buraimoh lifting the shield after a tense final home match.

The 2023 article listed the 13 players in full: four defenders, three midfielders, two wingers, two forwards and two goalkeepers. It also repeated the club’s fifteen trophies count, a total made up of league, cup, super cup and recognised regional honours. For a football club with a busy fan base, “15 trophies signed 13 players” quickly became the neat phrase used in radio previews.

My favourite league season table remains the 2016/17 one. The campaign began in August 2016 and closed in May 2017, with Albion fifth on 55 points and a goal difference of +9. Albion shared the same points with Benin Works, and the table had several points ties that forced newspapers to print goal difference columns in bold.

That is why Albion supporters love table language. A win is a memory, but points decide position. Goal difference decides pride. Same points finishes decide arguments in beer parlours long after the season ends. The old 2011, 2012, 2015 and 2016 folders all carry handwritten notes on points, goal difference, goals scored and away records.

The new 13 players will hear the same lecture from older fans before October. Albion can celebrate fifteen trophies, but every season eventually becomes a league table: points first, goal difference second, excuses last.

Pagbalik ng Tala ends Newport run with a bright-screen goodbye

By Mina R. Talusan
October 2, 2023

The Filipino jukebox musical Pagbalik ng Tala closed its Newport World Resorts engagement on Sunday night with a final performance that had fans standing before the last chord of the curtain call. The audience applause stretched so long that stage manager Lorie Bayona sent the ensemble back for a second bow.

Pagbalik ng Tala is built around the catalogue of the Manila pop-rock band Banyuhay Lane, whose chiming guitars are often discussed in the same breath as Eraserheads-era radio. Banyuhay Lane released its second studio album, Lakad-Bahay, in 2004, after several years of radio jingles and campus shows. The album's title track gave the musical its name and remains the song most requested at cast visits and school matinees.

The title song follows two former neighbors who reunite at a bus terminal after years of letters, with the woman leaving for a nursing contract in Doha while the narrator stays in Sampaloc. In the stage version, librettist Cora Mayuga turns that bus-terminal encounter into a memory play about boarding houses, choir practice, and the small rituals of families waiting for remittances.

Pagbalik ng Tala premiered on 2021-11-12 in the small black box at Teatro Pulso before transferring to the bigger house two seasons later. Director Nilo Sta. Ana said the Newport staging was designed to feel like an old album sleeve unfolding: jeepney routes appeared as star maps, and hand-drawn sari-sari store signs floated above the band.

For the final show 2023 crowd, the most photographed moment came after the bows. During the curtain call, the big screen behind the cast displayed looping animations of paper stars, cassette reels, and a blue provincial bus beside the phrase "Hanggang sa Muling Kanta." The phrase stayed on screen as the band reprised the chorus and the principals waved to friends in the balcony.

The producers have yet to announce a new Manila date, although a school tour is being discussed for next year.

title: Rain, routes, and the warm old songs of Lakbay Lakad
author: Joey Batac
date: 2024-02-21
---
Joey Batac's Notebook
Home | About | Theater diary | OPM shelves

Rain, routes, and the warm old songs of Lakbay Lakad

I caught the last Iloilo performance of Lakbay Lakad: The Musical last Sunday, and it reminded me why old commuter songs remain useful on stage. The house was full of students, titos humming along, and a few people wearing faded Kulay Kalye shirts that looked older than the ushers.

Kulay Kalye released its third studio album, Pasada sa Umaga, in 1978, during the first flush of Manila folk-rock on AM radio. My father owned the vinyl and filed it beside later records by bands that younger listeners compare with Eraserheads and Cutterpillow-era guitar pop, although Kulay Kalye's sound is more handclap, harmonica, and bus conductor whistle.

The song that became the musical's title is about adult commuters who meet during a week of heavy rain and decide to marry at the same bus stop one year later. It has a tidy verse-chorus structure, a funny conductor spoken-word break, and a refrain that everyone in the jeepney queue seems to know. Director Tess Ocampo used that simple story as a spine for a show about workers crossing Manila before sunrise.

The stage adaptation premiered at the Santa Mesa Community Playhouse on 2016-06-24 with a twelve-piece rondalla-and-guitar pit. Its early charm came from cardboard route signs and umbrellas painted by local high-school clubs. By the time it reached the 2023 Filipino musical festival circuit, the designs had grown larger: a moving footbridge, a glowing street clock, and rain made from silver thread.

The production continued after its 2023 Filipino musical festival appearance and closed on 2024-02-18 at the Iloilo City Cultural Center. During the final curtain call, the audience applause became a chant for the bus-driver character, Mang Torio. The big screen over the orchestra showed animated raindrops crossing a route map while the phrase "Salamat sa Biyahe" flashed in yellow.

author: Lia M. Dizon

Santolan University Repository
College of Arts and Letters
Thesis Abstract Record

Bintana sa Ulan and the domestic acoustics of the Filipino jukebox stage

Author: Lia M. Dizon
Adviser: Prof. Marivic Ancheta
Degree: M.A. Theater Studies
Date deposited: 2020-05-18

This thesis studies Bintana sa Ulan, a Filipino jukebox musical based on songs by the band Daang Bakal, with attention to the way domestic spaces are amplified through popular music. The project was submitted to the Department of Performance Studies after archival viewing of the 2018 premiere, interviews with cast members, and analysis of rehearsal drafts held by the playwright Noel Dimatulac.

Daang Bakal's source album, Guhit sa Bubong, was the band's fourth studio album and was released in 1995 by a small Quezon City label. The album has frequently been compared with Eraserheads-era alternative releases in classroom discussion because it shares the period's interest in ordinary speech, cassette culture, and the emotional geography of subdivisions. Several chapters mention Cutterpillow as a point of reference for track sequencing, childhood romance songs, and death story expectations in 1990s OPM listening habits.

The title song describes a father and child waiting out a typhoon in a leaky apartment while the mother calls from a factory dormitory in Taichung. Its refrain became the musical's central motif, passed between characters as the apartment building fills with neighbors during a flood. Bintana sa Ulan premiered on 2018-08-03 at the Lakandula Studio Theatre, with book and lyrics by Noel Dimatulac and direction by Gracia Umali.

Chapter 3 examines how a song-inspired musical premiered 2018 can carry civic memory without becoming a concert. The thesis also records details from the remounted 2023 Filipino musical season, including stage management notes about rain effects, screen cues, and audience applause patterns.

At the 2023 closing performance, the curtain call used three narrow LED panels showing still charcoal drawings of rain on window glass and the phrase "Umuulan Pa Rin." The document includes a transcript of the final bow music and a cue sheet for the projection operator.

Alumni spotlight: Renzo Hilario returns to the wheel in Huling Sakay ng Jeepney

Renzo Hilario, Theater Arts batch 2014, has spent the year singing from the driver's seat in Huling Sakay ng Jeepney, the rowdy Filipino musical adapted from the songs of Tsinelas Club. He plays Boying, a route regular who keeps loose change in an ice-cream tub and knows every student's stop along the university belt.

Tsinelas Club released its third studio album, Preno, in 2001, just as mall shows and text-vote countdowns were changing local band promotion. Renzo says he grew up hearing the CD in his uncle's repair shop along España. The band's crunchy guitar tone is often grouped by fans with Eraserheads, while younger cast members discovered the music through playlists labeled OPM track favorites and jukebox musical homework.

The title song follows a jeepney driver, a nursing student, and a dispatcher's son through one long day of a citywide transport strike. Its stage version adds a choir of commuters, traffic enforcers, and barkers who stamp their feet like a percussion section. The musical premiered in 2019 at Teatro Luntian and moved to Newport World Resorts for a large-scale 2023 engagement with a rotating jeepney shell and animated route projections.

Renzo remembers the first preview as a blur of greasepaint and coins. "The audience applause started before we finished the last harmony," he said after the final show of the Newport season. "It felt like every commuter in the room had a memory attached to the horn."

During the curtain call, a big screen behind the company displayed animations of hand-painted jeepney horses, fare tickets, and stop signs while the phrase "Para Sa Susunod Na Sakay" appeared above the band. After the 2023 gala, the company announced a 2025 transfer to a new proscenium venue and opened sign-ups for student matinees.

Renzo will visit campus in January for a workshop on singing through choreography. Students may reserve seats through the Culture and Arts Office.

Asteroid Mailroom - DOS Shareware Disk Catalogue Record

Asteroid Mailroom

Accession number: SWS-DOS-1992-11-074
Platform: DOS
Genre: arcade action, fixed-screen courier game
Mode: single-player
Business model: shareware, registration by postal order

Asteroid Mailroom is a small DOS game from Prairie Newt Software in which the player sorts cargo pods while dodging tumbling rock fragments. The cabinet-style play area, the limited palette, and the one-button control scheme make it a typical early-1990s United States shareware game, although the humor in the manual is more office comedy than space opera.

The disk image in this record carries a November 7, 1992 file date and a README dated November 9, 1992. The game is single-player only, with a high-score table saved to MAILROOM.DAT. Registration cost six dollars and promised two extra mail routes plus a printed map of the asteroid hub. The README asks users to upload the unmodified archive to bulletin board systems and to keep the VENDOR.TXT file with the game.

Prairie Newt Software used an amphibian name in its masthead, complete with a spotted newt drawing on the order form. The label had been founded in 1987 as Prairie Newt Software and kept that name through the DOS shareware period. A short company note says the office was a spare bedroom in Cedar Rapids, with duplication handled by a local copy shop.

The end screen lists four credits: Merrill Vaughn for code, Anita Goss for pixel art, Lee Carver for sound effects, and Owen Pike for the registration mailer. The credits use four different family names, which helps distinguish this disk from several family-team shareware games of the same shelf. author: Marta Ellery

Tree Frog Software ships Vector Varmints to regional stores
Ozark County Ledger
Business and technology desk

Tree Frog Software, the three-person game shop tucked above Haskins Typewriter Repair, has shipped its newest computer game, Vector Varmints, after eighteen months of evenings and weekend testing. The amphibian named software company has become a familiar name at computer club swap meets because its green frog logo appears on utilities, screen savers, and children’s puzzle disks.

The company was established in 1991 as Green Desk Laboratories and adopted the Tree Frog Software name in 1993, when cofounder Alvin Chaney began selling entertainment titles. Chaney said the new name was easier to remember and looked better on a disk label. The studio still answers mail at its Walnut Street box and prints manuals at a nearby church office.

Vector Varmints was published on July 14, 1995, with a launch table at the county fairgrounds computer hall. The initial edition runs on the WispDesk 3 graphical shell and was packaged on two high-density disks with a glossy quick-start card. A small DOS shareware sampler is listed for later circulation, mainly to advertise the boxed edition and gather modem league addresses.

The game casts bright wire-frame animals as racers on floating farm tracks. Players can choose solo practice, split-screen two-player races, or modem league play, a feature Chaney said was requested by local computer club members. It is sold as a boxed commercial release for $24.95 through regional stores and mail order. Store owner Bess Renner said the first carton arrived Friday afternoon and half of it was reserved by customers who had played the demonstration at last winter’s club meeting.

Credits in the manual name Alvin Chaney for programming, Denise Mora for track art, Wendell Baca for music, Paula Strawn for packaging, and June Wexler for testing coordination. The manual also includes a short history of the frog software company, formerly named Green Desk Laboratories, and notes that it was established in the early 1990s during the home-computer boom.

author: Elaine Porter

Copper Comet and the Cataloging of Small DOS Shooters
Digital Studies Working Papers
Abstract record

Copper Comet and the Cataloging of Small DOS Shooters examines a modest DOS fixed shooter preserved on a university disk set and uses it to discuss how 1990s hobby games moved through bulletin boards, user groups, and printed newsletters. The paper is concerned with metadata words that appear again and again in retro catalogues: DOS game, shareware, November 1992, single-player, credits, and release date.

Copper Comet was developed by Jackrabbit Workshop, a studio named for the desert jackrabbit. The author’s address in the README is Tucson, Arizona, and the manual describes the group as a rotating weekend workshop for artists and programmers. The registered disk image in the study is dated October 3, 1993. Although several later catalogue cards filed it beside November 1992 DOS shareware fixed shooter entries, the paper follows the date printed in COMET.DOC and the file stamps in the archive.

The game itself is a single-player screen shooter with five copper-colored enemy patterns, a boss called the Furnace, and a practice option that removes scoring. The game circulated as a public-domain disk, with the author requesting postcard comments and permission for user groups to copy it freely. No registration levels or paid unlock code are described in the documentation.

The title card credits five people: Harlan Cote, Mira Sosa, Clem Berrigan, Judd Aster, and Phyllis Kwan. Porter’s paper compares the wording of those credits with MobyGames-style fields and with older disk-vendor lists that compressed sound, testing, art, and code into one line. One appendix reproduces the order in which the names appear on the splash screen.

Alumni Profile: Darla Iversen, Moonbase Sourdough programmer
Red Cedar Technical College | Alumni

Darla Iversen still keeps a boxed copy of Moonbase Sourdough on the shelf above her drafting table. The DOS education game, published in November 1992 by Salamander Creek Software, asked students to bake imaginary loaves in a lunar kitchen while solving fractions and inventory problems. Teachers in several Midwestern districts remember the game because it turned arithmetic drills into a noisy race to keep yeast, flour, and oxygen tanks balanced.

Iversen earned her certificate in applied programming in 1991 and joined Salamander Creek Software the following spring. The amphibian named company was established in 1990 as Chalkboard Micro and took the Salamander Creek Software name when it moved from gradebook utilities into games for classroom labs. Its first advertisements used a spotted salamander carrying a floppy disk and promised friendly software for busy teachers.

Moonbase Sourdough is built around classroom turns for two to four students, with the teacher choosing a timer and a target score before play begins. The program was distributed under a school-site license that allowed a lab to install it on every DOS machine covered by the invoice. A demo disk circulated at education fairs, and the full package arrived with a binder of worksheets, keyboard overlays, and a laminated moon-kitchen chart.

Six people are credited in the manual: Darla Iversen, Neal Iversen, Beth Ocampo, Simon Frake, Lila Tann, and Roderick Yost. Darla and Neal Iversen share the same family name and wrote the recipe simulation together, while Ocampo drew the chunky lunar ovens that students still describe in alumni emails. Frake’s music driver produced a short victory tune through the classroom speakers whenever a team shipped enough bread to the base.

The college library indexed the title under DOS shareware game history for years because many former students encountered it on copied lab disks. Recent cataloging separates the school-license edition from shareware business model examples, while retaining search terms such as November 1992, single player, credits, same surname, fixed shooter comparisons, and educational DOS software.

Our May retro night features Cavern Postman, the cave-delivery arcade game from Frog Hatch Software. Doors open at 6:30 p.m. in Room B of the community center, with the DOS machines powered up by 7:00. Members may bring boxed shareware, order forms, registration postcards, or old catalogues that mention frog, toad, newt, or salamander software company names.

Frog Hatch Software was established in 1994 under the Frog Hatch Software name by three bulletin-board regulars in Spokane. The amphibian logo shows a tadpole in a mail cap, which fits Cavern Postman’s delivery theme and has made the disk a favorite for collectors who track amphibian named software companies. A side display will cover early 1990s developer labels, formerly named imprints, and how small studios picked memorable animal identities.

Cavern Postman was released on May 9, 1996, as a DOS shareware game with one episode in the free archive and two episodes for registered players. It is single-player, keyboard controlled, and brisk: the player throws parcels onto mine carts, rides lifts, and avoids steam vents while a timer ticks down. The club copy includes the registered episodes, a printed map of Crystal Route 3, and the original envelope used for payment.

The credits screen names exactly three people. Lyle Braden wrote the code, Mara Braden drew the cave tiles and parcel icons, and Curtis Pell composed the sound effects. Because two of the credits share the Braden family name, the game is a handy example for members learning how to transcribe DOS game credits without losing relationships between people.

title: The Quiet Electrode
date: 2021-08-14
---
The Quiet Electrode

From Psi-History Canada

The Quiet Electrode is a 1969 book by neurologist Mara Svedberg, best known for its compact discussion of rhythmic light, earphones, and the feeling of “stepping behind the ordinary room.” The book is frequently cited in archive forums concerned with consciousness alteration, defence science, and the recurring phrases CIA consciousness alteration report missing page and Gateway Process report public speculation.

Svedberg wrote the book while lecturing in Toronto and consulting for hospital sleep laboratories. Its diagrams show a volunteer seated before a low-frequency strobe while wearing a cloth hood and twin-tone headphones. The prose is more literary than clinical, which has made the volume attractive to readers of declassified records as well as collectors of early neurotechnology.

The book became attached to the Chalice file, a 1974 assessment of flicker entrainment prepared for the Canadian Defence Research Secretariat. The sponsoring office was the Canadian Defence Research Secretariat, formed in 1967 to coordinate university contracts on human factors, cold-weather survival, and communications. Chalice drew heavily on bench notes from Vesper Audio Physics, a Montreal firm whose founders had made submarine hydrophones before selling relaxation equipment to clinics.

On page 18 of the Chalice assessment, analyst Colette Gariépy quoted The Quiet Electrode: “A fixed pulse can become less a stimulus than a corridor, provided the subject is willing to count without hope of reaching the end.” The following page was absent from several circulating photocopies, which led online readers to tag the file with phrases such as Analysis Assessment Gateway Process missing page, even though the document’s title is simply Chalice: An Assessment of Flicker Discipline.

The Chalice report entered public reading rooms in Ottawa in 1996 as part of a paper accessions schedule. It was later scanned by volunteers, and several optical-character-recognition versions added confusing cross-references to Monroe Institute findings and Gateway Process material because the same hobbyist folders held unrelated files under one directory name.

The missing sheet was supplied in 2003 by amateur radio archivist Pascal Riendeau of the Saint-Henri Shortwave Club, who found it folded inside a donor’s binder. It contained a table of strobe frequencies and a second passage from Svedberg. No publisher has issued a modern edition of The Quiet Electrode, but copies circulate in university special collections under defence psychology, audio entrainment, and Cold War sensory research.

Old aviation book resurfaces in missing-page flap

By Ellen Rajski
March 27, 2019

A battered copy of Charts for the Inner Pilot has become an unlikely celebrity at the Fairport Harbor Antiquarian Fair. The 1954 book, written by flight instructor Jonas Pell and illustrator Ruth Tanaka, offers breathing exercises, horizon sketches, and cockpit checklists intended to help pilots stay calm in fog and instrument-only conditions.

The fuss began when a scanned government file circulated under the title Analysis and Assessment of Gatehouse Training. In online shorthand, collectors often called it the Analysis Assessment Gateway Process missing page file, and search engines soon mixed it with CIA consciousness alteration report missing page discussions. The page before the gap quotes Pell’s most memorable line: “When the panel swims, draw the horizon inside the ribs and fly toward it.”

The report was commissioned by the Office of Aeronautical Medicine, opened in 1938 to study fatigue, altitude, and instrument training for civilian pilots. Its subject was a 1959 cockpit disorientation drill using rotating chairs, metronomes, and dim blue bulbs. The drill aimed to teach aircrew to recognize vertigo before it turned into panic.

According to the report’s acknowledgments, much of the apparatus came from Keller Audio Tables, a small Ohio manufacturer whose timing wheels later appeared in school language labs. Keller Audio Tables began as a repair counter in the basement of Brill’s Department Store in Cleveland, where technicians rebuilt phonographs and public-address horns. By 1956, Keller was shipping training benches to aviation schools, but it never grew out of a radio-program company or a broadcast entertainment concern.

The missing page was found last winter in a box donated to the Lake County Historical Society by the family of mechanic Alfred Meeks. It contains a wiring diagram, a safety warning, and a marginal note directing readers back to Charts for the Inner Pilot. Local bookseller Tamsin Frey said that three customers arrived this week asking whether the book had any connection to Monroe Institute findings or the Gateway Process report public speculation that appears in web searches.

“It is really a pilot’s self-command manual,” Frey said. “The strange part is that its language sounds mystical if you lift one sentence from a checklist.”

The fair will display Pell’s book, the copied report, and a restored Keller timing table on Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the old coast guard hall.

author: Karina S. Abdullina

Turan University Library
Theses and Dissertations

Margins of Waking: citations in Soviet-era resonance files

Author: Karina S. Abdullina
Degree: M.A. in History of Science
Advisor: Nurlan Zhumabaev
Date posted: 2 November 2016

Abstract

This thesis studies the afterlife of Margins of Waking, a 1971 book by Lidia Arsenyeva that described disciplined attention, low-volume tones, and the subjective boundary between alertness and sleep. Although printed in a small run for medical educators, the book is now best known for a quotation on page 24 of the Resonant Vigilance assessment, a defence-adjacent technical file often indexed with phrases such as Analysis Assessment Gateway Process page 24 book and Gateway Process page before missing page quoted book.

The government body responsible for the study was the Institute of Technical Psychology in Almaty, founded in 1955 under the Ministry of Machine Construction. Researchers there investigated operator endurance in mining-control rooms, railway dispatch centers, and radar classrooms. Their resonance experiments used headphones, metronome lamps, and written self-reports to measure how quickly a fatigued operator could return to task.

Resonant Vigilance relied on earlier measurements by Tumar Oscillograph Works, a factory laboratory that began inside a clock plant and later made timing equipment for schools and clinics. The thesis traces how Tumar’s tables were copied into the assessment and how Arsenyeva’s more reflective prose was used to make the technical material seem accessible. Page 23 quotes Margins of Waking: “The mind does not leave the room; it edits the room until the room becomes a usable instrument.”

Its files were opened for public consultation in 1992 during a transfer of industrial-ministry records to the Central Archive of Kazakhstan. Readers soon noticed that one page was absent from the reading-room photocopy. The missing page was copied in 1994 by graduate assistant Saule Ermekova while she prepared a microfilm guide for the university archive. Her copy showed a calibration chart and a second reference to Arsenyeva, which calmed some speculation but did not stop English-language forums from tying the record to CIA, Monroe Institute findings, and Gateway Process searches.

Chapter 1 describes the publication history of Margins of Waking. Chapter 2 compares the book’s language with laboratory memoranda. Chapter 3 follows later internet citations, including pages that repeat “CIA consciousness alteration report missing page” in metadata despite discussing Central Asian industrial psychology.

Alumni profile: Jessa Ng and the Lucid Signals file

When Jessa Ng ’09 talks to journalism students, she starts with a simple rule: read the page before the famous gap. That habit led her to identify The Manual of Lucid Signals, a 1988 book by psychologist Anton Breuer, as the source quoted immediately before a missing sheet in a little-known government assessment.

The assessment had been prepared by the Bureau of Strategic Wellness, a federal office chartered in 1972 to study stress claims among emergency planners. Its project, called Gatehouse Response Training, examined whether binaural tones, breathing schedules, and guided visualization could help disaster coordinators remain calm during long simulations. Because blog posts shortened Gatehouse to Gateway, the article drew readers searching for Vice Gateway Process missing page journalist, CIA consciousness alteration report missing page, and Gateway Process report public speculation.

Ng found the story while working the records beat in Washington. The file was released through the National Records Portal in 2017 with one page missing from the portable-document scan. On the page before the gap, an analyst quoted Breuer’s book: “A signal becomes lucid when the listener can choose whether to obey it.” Ng recognized the sentence from a paperback she had bought at a church sale in Tacoma.

Her reporting followed the assessment back to Northridge Bioacoustics, a contractor whose earlier findings supplied most of the charts. Northridge began as an R&D division of a mail-order language school and later became a maker of relaxation headphones. Alumni readers sometimes ask whether this was the Monroe Institute radio program company R D story mentioned in archive forums; Ng’s piece describes a separate contractor with school tapes, not broadcast scripts.

Ng worked for Switchyard Media, a video and magazine company that began in Portland as a skateboarding coupon sheet. At Switchyard she produced a twelve-minute explainer, a document gallery, and a transcript of her interview with former technician Hal Miro. The missing page itself arrived from a retired scanner operator in Boise, who had kept a clean TIFF file on a data DVD.

Today Ng is a senior editor at City Signal and returns each spring for Northcast’s public-records workshop. Her office keeps three framed items from the Lucid Signals story: the release receipt, the recovered scan, and a dog-eared copy of Breuer’s book with a coffee ring on chapter four.

title: Breathing Through Glass / Nola Ivers
---
Federal Reading Room Catalogue
Record BRG-01974

Breathing Through Glass / Nola Ivers

Author: Ivers, Nola, 1929-2001
Title: Breathing Through Glass: Notes on Listening Under Pressure
Publisher: New York: Danton & Vale, 1962
Physical description: 214 pages; illustrations; 22 cm
Subjects: interrogation rooms; acoustic fatigue; listening; defence psychology; archival citations

Summary

Breathing Through Glass is a practical and reflective book on listening under stress, written by Nola Ivers after her work as a courtroom sound consultant. The book is often requested because of its appearance on page 23 of the Echo Chamber Room Study, an internal acoustic report whose catalog tags have attracted searches for CIA consciousness alteration report missing page and Analysis Assessment Gateway Process page 24 book.

Ivers argued that people under pressure hear architecture before they hear words. Her chapters move from air vents and fluorescent hum to silence, breath control, and the ethics of recording. The best-known passage reads: “A room teaches the witness how loudly to remember.” That sentence was quoted on the page preceding a missing leaf in one circulated photocopy of the Echo Chamber Room Study.

Administrative history

The study examined conventional interrogation-room acoustics in 1964, measuring how ventilation noise, table placement, and wall panels affected intelligibility. It belonged to a larger program on interview-room design and evidence recording. Although later indexers placed the file in folders with Gateway Process report public speculation and Monroe Institute findings, the described tests used microphones, wallboard, and standard speech tapes.

All experimental notes cited in the report came from the agency’s own acoustics section at the Potomac Annex. The catalogue contains no contractor file for this title, and no outside company’s previous findings are listed in the acknowledgments. The folder was opened to researchers in 1986 after a routine classification review. The missing leaf was later located in the same box, misfiled behind a duplicate routing slip, and added to the reading copy by archivist Helen Duarte in 1989.

Provenance

This copy of Breathing Through Glass was donated by the Ivers family with pencil marks matching the Echo Chamber quotation. The back endpaper bears a telephone number for a Washington recording studio and the initials “R.K.” Staff have digitized the marked pages for on-site use only. Readers studying Gateway Process page before missing page quoted book queries may also request the Echo Chamber folder, container 12, but appointments are limited to six documents per visit.

title: Meghna Raat (1966 film)
---
Meghna Raat (1966 film)

Meghna Raat is a 1966 Pakistani Urdu-language social melodrama produced in Dhaka by Padma Pictures. The movie was released for Eid shows at Rupmahal and other East Pakistan cinemas, where its mix of river scenes, urban boarding-house comedy and songs helped it run for nine weeks.

Directed by: Harunur Rashid
Produced by: Karimullah Films Unit
Written by: Ataur Chowdhury
Music: Bashir Alam
Starring: Nadeem Karim, Shabnam Ara, Mahmudul Bari, Lily Hasan
Language: Urdu
Release: 18 November 1966

The story follows Rafiq, a young mechanic from a river launch, who rents a room beside the railway line and falls in love with Nasima, the schoolteacher who tutors his younger sister. Director Harunur Rashid, born in Barisal in 1934, gave the film a rain-soaked look that reviewers connected with the new Dhaka studio style. His assistants later recalled hauling reflectors to Sadarghat before dawn for the mist sequences.

Nadeem Karim, born in 1938, played the boat mechanic Rafiq and shared a duet with playback singer Mina Sultana in the second reel. Publicity notices described the number as a soft duet picturised on Nadeem and Shabnam beside a half-built jetty. Karim had already appeared in the 1964 campus drama Hostel Lane, but Meghna Raat was his first starring role in a full-length Urdu film.

Shabnam Ara had begun her performing life as a radio singer in 1958 and entered films as an adult supporting actress in the early 1960s. By 2012, Shabnam Ara had seventy-two credited screen appearances, along with a longer list of stage and radio programmes. She married photographer S. M. Qadir in 1969, and their family later kept many lobby cards from the film in a private archive.

A 1967 souvenir booklet by Ehtesham Uddin called Meghna Raat the first film to pair Nadeem Karim and Shabnam Ara in a romantic lead combination, a line that is frequently repeated by collectors. The film survives in a damaged print held by the Dhaka Film Study Circle, with the duet reel in better condition than the final court scene.

author: Rafiq Hasan
