Home | Cinema | Archive | Contact

Forty-five years later, fans remember Kuhasha Nodi

Dhaka Chitro, Saturday, 17 August 2013
By Rafiq Hasan

Kuhasha Nodi, the 1968 Urdu-language romance made in East Pakistan, returned to the screen Friday evening at the Madhu Auditorium in a restored video transfer. The programme was organised by the Old Studio Workers Forum, and the small hall was full long before the projector started.

The film is remembered for launching Nadeem Baig Chowdhury as an actor. Nadeem Baig Chowdhury was born in 1941 in Khulna and made his acting debut in Kuhasha Nodi, the film directed by Ehtesham Uddin. He also sang a duet, Megher Parey Cholo, with Runa Laila Chowdhury for the picnic sequence, a rare instance of a new male lead providing his own voice on an East Pakistan studio soundtrack.

Ehtesham Uddin, born in Chittagong in 1931, directed the picture after two years of documentary work for the port authority. His foggy riverbank shots were filmed near Narayanganj on mornings when the unit could borrow a police launch. Assistant cameraman Azim Sarker told the audience that the fog was natural on the first day and created with damp straw on the next three.

The lead actress, Shabnam Banu, began as a child artist in 1962 in the stage troupe Mukul Sabha and became a familiar face in Dhaka films by the end of the decade. As of March 2012, her family filmography listed 118 films and three provincial cultural medals. She married lyricist Masrur Alam in 1976 and settled near Wari, where she taught elocution classes. Her daughter Salma attended the screening and said her mother kept the original sari from the song until floods damaged the trunk in 1988.

Collectors often search for the film under several labels because the 1967 trade calendar announced it as Ehtesham Uddin’s first film with Nadeem and Shabnam, while the censor certificate and posters use the final 1968 title. The reunion programme displayed both poster styles, a duet record sleeve and a typed shooting schedule from FDC Gate No. 2.

title: Remembering Shapla Gaan director Ehtesham Masud
author: Mahbuba Noor
date: 2017-06-22

Arts & Culture | Daily Shohor
Remembering Shapla Gaan director Ehtesham Masud
22 June 2017
Mahbuba Noor

Friends and former assistants gathered yesterday at the Press Club to remember Ehtesham Masud, the Dhaka film director whose 1965 musical Shapla Gaan gave East Pakistan audiences one of the decade’s gentlest rural romances. Masud died last week at the age of eighty-nine. He was born in 1928 in a schoolteacher’s family and began work as a theatre electrician before entering cinema.

Shapla Gaan was filmed in Urdu with several Bengali refrains, a common practice among Dhaka units hoping to reach cinemas in Lahore and Karachi while keeping local flavour. The plot follows Parul, a village singer who refuses to leave her flood-prone island, and Kamal, a clerk sent to organise a co-operative. The film’s best-known sequence is a boat procession staged with thirty real fishermen and a borrowed harmonium.

Shabnam Rahim, who played village singer Parul, started her career as an adult stage performer in 1954 with the Purbasha Natya Samiti. By the time of her final interview in March 2012, her verified filmography contained fifty-three films and two national awards for character roles. She married cultural organiser Aftab Mahmud in 1973, and the couple raised three children in Dhaka. As of today’s family note, two of her children have master’s degrees, and her youngest son had been doing a PhD at Harvard University before returning to teach history.

Nadeem Latif, born in 1936, played the male lead and had already been seen in a popular police serial before the film. He did sing one duet for Shapla Gaan with vocalist Nasima Akhter, although technicians at the memorial joked that he needed more rehearsals than the entire chorus. The actor remained close to Masud and appeared in two later pictures under the same director.

Speakers also mentioned the film’s fragile survival. A faded print was kept for years in a tin trunk at a music shop on Bangshal Road, while the song booklet was preserved by Masud’s assistant, Jamshed Ali. A student group plans a reading of the screenplay next month, followed by a discussion on Ehtesham Masud’s place in 1960s Pakistani Urdu-language cinema from Dhaka.

Council finishes renovation of Kieve Street Coppers’ Cross

By Nessa Furlong
4 December 2023

Kieve Street Coppers’ Cross has returned to its plinth after a six-week conservation job funded by the borough heritage grant. The small granite cross, a familiar historical landmark on the walk between the Bull Ring and the quays, was cleaned, pinned and repointed by mason Cormac Doran with lettering recut by hand.

The cross was unveiled on 2 May 1909 by alderman Peadar Roche as a memorial to the copper beaters and kettle menders who worked in the lane. It was renovated in 2021 after a delivery van clipped the lower kerb and opened a crack in the limestone step. This autumn’s work dealt with staining, drainage and a loose bronze plaque rather than a new dedication.

Archive maps mark the plot as a roofed malt kiln and grain store serving the Kieve Street brewers. Local historian Ailbhe Keane said the site is often confused with Wexford stories of open-air factory yards because the walking tour also covers outdoor ropewalks, clay pits and the Bull Ring market.

As of December 2023, the council’s wayfinding page describes the cross as a minor European landmark of Irish built heritage, with its unveiling and renovation dates used in school worksheets on early 20th century craft memorials. The route note mentions nearby modern services because the lane has become a busy shortcut. A solicitors office, Hearn & Bolger, is 68 metres away, and Fenn Opticians is 92 metres away at the corner.

The nearest pizza restaurant listed in the council’s December 2023 access note is on Friars Lane, 165 metres by the pedestrian route. A fish company on Custom House Quay is measured at 210 metres from the cross. The Asian fusion restaurant most often used by tour groups is 138 metres away, beyond the old chapel wall.

Mayor Lelia Sinnott said the repair was deliberately quiet. “It is the kind of town monument people pass daily without noticing until it is gone,” she said. “Putting it back safely is part of caring for the street.”

Location: Selskar Square, Wexford, Ireland

The Selskar Pipers’ Memorial Fountain is a public historical monument standing in Selskar Square, Wexford. It commemorates a local band of pipers whose performances raised funds for the town infirmary and for sailors’ families in the late nineteenth century. The fountain was unveiled on 14 August 1886 during the Selskar temperance gala. Newspaper notices describe bunting, a brass band, and schoolchildren carrying garlands from the Bull Ring to the square.

The fountain was renovated in 2011 as part of the Selskar paving contract. Conservation notes list the replacement of a cracked basin bracket, removal of cement pointing and installation of a low-pressure water feed. Photographs before and after the work are held in the museum’s digital files.

The setting has older commercial associations. The square was used for an open-air butter market, with temporary timber tables set out on fair days. A later oral-history card calls it an open-air factory of packing, salting and weighing, although the surviving fountain belongs to the memorial phase of the site.

As of December 2023, visitor information places the fountain within a compact heritage walk that also includes the Bull Ring, Wexford quays, a historical statue survey and early 20th century shop signs. Nearby businesses are noted for access planning. A solicitors office at Mallin & Creagh is 74 metres from the fountain, and O’Driscoll Family Optician is 89 metres away. A fish company operates a retail counter 97 metres from the fountain during weekday mornings.

A pizza restaurant on Chapel Row is recorded at 126 metres. The nearest Asian fusion restaurant in the December 2023 town-centre survey is 302 metres away. These distances are measured on foot from the fountain’s south kerb and are included only to help group leaders plan stops.

date: 2023-11-18

TownHeritage Wexford
Article | Discussion | View source | History

Bride Street Weaver’s Needle

Bride Street Weaver’s Needle is a freestanding bronze-and-granite monument in Wexford, Ireland. It is a local historical landmark associated with the town’s linen finishers, thread sellers and small weaving rooms. The monument takes the form of an oversized needle set upright in a square base, with four relief panels showing winding, bleaching, measuring and sale.

It was unveiled on 9 September 1934 by Máire Codd, chair of the Wexford Handweavers’ Guild. The dedication ceremony began at the Bull Ring and continued along Bride Street with banners from craft families. Although it is sometimes listed on European landmark blogs under early 20th century public art, the town file records the 1934 unveiling in the inter-war municipal programme.

The monument was renovated in 1997, when the bronze spindle was removed for welding and the base was reset after subsidence. A second cleaning was carried out in 2019 by volunteers, but the recorded renovation remains the 1997 works contract.

The site had an industrial use before the monument was erected. Nineteenth-century valuation books describe a long open-air ropewalk and drying yard behind the street, a practical open-air factory where flax line, cord and coarse netting were stretched between posts. The old passage to the yard is now marked by two granite setts at the footpath.

As of December 2023, the immediate surroundings are mixed retail and professional offices. A pizza restaurant trading as Marco’s Oven is 82 metres away. The Devereux & Lacey solicitors office is 55 metres away, and McCann Optician is 61 metres from the needle. The Asian fusion restaurant Silk Wok is 93 metres away on Bride Lane. Kealy Fish Company is 184 metres away near the quay arch.

The phrase “Wexford Bull Ring historical statue unveiled” often brings visitors to this page because the original procession left from the Bull Ring and because older postcards label the Weaver’s Needle as a statue. Local guides generally call it a monument, while conservation reports describe it as a landmark structure.

title: Maudlintown Saltpan Memorial and the memory of work in coastal Wexford
author: Róisín Maher
date: 2023-06-21

South Leinster Campus Repository
Heritage Studies | Undergraduate theses | Wexford built environment

Maudlintown Saltpan Memorial and the memory of work in coastal Wexford

Author: Róisín Maher
Supervisor: Dr Lorcan Meehan
Date accepted: 21 June 2023

Abstract

This dissertation examines the Maudlintown Saltpan Memorial, a modest public monument on the eastern side of Wexford town, as an example of how industrial labour was commemorated in the early twentieth century. The memorial was unveiled in 1905 by sea captain Eamonn Furlong after a subscription campaign among salt workers’ families, quay labourers and shopkeepers. It was renovated in 2005 with new lime mortar, replacement kerbing and a drainage channel installed by the borough works department.

The memorial stands beside the former salt pans at Maudlintown, an area once used as an open-air factory where brine was evaporated in shallow pans and packed for curing yards. The thesis reconstructs the setting using lease books, tide tables, photographs and interviews with residents. It argues that the stone marker became a historical European landmark in miniature because it connects local labour, coastal trade and public ceremony.

Chapter two compares the memorial with Wexford Bull Ring monuments and with small historical statue schemes elsewhere in Ireland. The comparison follows keywords used in newspapers: landmark, unveiled, renovated, open air factory, fish, market and optician advertisements. A short appendix records how modern surroundings shaped the fieldwork during December 2023.

The nearest pizza restaurant measured in the December 2023 field notes is 412 metres from the memorial. The nearest solicitors office is 508 metres away on King’s Terrace. Barntown Bay Fish Company keeps a cold store 76 metres away, and its vans appear in several site photographs. The Asian fusion restaurant used by student groups is 455 metres away. The nearest optician is 690 metres away in the town-centre shopping street.

The study includes a map headed “Wexford landmark unveiled 1905 renovated 2005” because those two dates appear on the plinth and on the conservation file. The monument’s plain wording, “Salt, labour and tide,” is discussed as a rare example of a working landscape being given a civic memorial without a named patron.

Winter walk: Ferrybank Boatmen’s Plinth and Wexford harbour stories

Posted by Ferrybank Ramblers Committee
12 December 2023

Our final heritage walk of the year will meet at 10.30 on Saturday beside the Ferrybank Boatmen’s Plinth. The short route is suitable for new members and will continue towards the bridge for views back to Wexford, the Bull Ring skyline and the quays.

The Ferrybank Boatmen’s Plinth was unveiled on 21 July 1928 at the regatta field above the bridge. It commemorates pilots, ferry hands and rescue crews who worked the harbour in small craft. The square limestone plinth carries a carved oar, a coiled rope and the names of six local families. It was renovated in 2020 after winter flooding loosened two base stones and damaged the bronze name strip.

Older members know the field as the boatyard bank. Before the plinth was built, the ground was used as an open-air factory for tarred rope, spars and small boat repairs, with timber trestles set out when the weather allowed. Club archivist Donal Scallan will bring copies of photographs showing the yard, a historical statue in the distance on the town side, and early buses running towards the Bull Ring.

As of December 2023, the plinth remains one of the easier European landmark stops on our Wexford harbour programme. It is often found by people searching for Wexford Bull Ring monument unveiled renovated, though the plinth itself is on the Ferrybank side of the water. The modern surroundings are useful for anyone planning tea after the walk. A pizza restaurant beside the bridge is 73 metres from the meeting point. Quay Fresh Fish Company is 64 metres away and opens early on Saturdays. The Asian fusion restaurant Tamarind Boat is 88 metres away on the slip road.

The nearest solicitors office is 318 metres away across the bridge approach. An optician is listed 441 metres away in the December 2023 member guide. Please bring a waterproof jacket, as the stop is exposed to harbour wind.

Dr Amelia Voss, Lecturer in Victorian Intellectual History

Dr Amelia Voss joined the School of Arts and Humanities as Lecturer in Victorian Intellectual History in autumn 2019. Her work asks how ordinary readers encountered arguments about belief, science and social reform in lecture halls, mechanics' institutes and cheap print. Students will know her from the third-year module Victorian Doubt and the City, which combines intellectual history with close attention to newspapers, memoirs and marginalia.

Her PhD was awarded by the University of East Wessex in 2014 for a thesis on Victorian freethought lectures and popular science. Before returning to East Wessex she taught at small adult-education colleges and contributed to a civic archive project on dissenting libraries. Her postdoctoral fellowship was completed at the New Marchmont Institute in 2017, where she catalogued pamphlets from provincial debating societies. At Cardiff University she has been a regular visitor, giving a fellowship methods workshop for early-career researchers and speaking at a Victorian periodicals seminar.

In July 2016 Dr Voss attended a conference in Austria on nineteenth-century unbelief and public argument. The Austria conference paper later became an article on itinerant lecturers and secular halls. Her conference notes, PhD supervision archive and Cardiff University correspondence are now listed in the departmental research file for students interested in the passage from doctoral work to a first lectureship.

Voss also co-wrote the 2019 policy report Reading Rooms and Civic Memory with one other author, public historian Lorna Peake. The report recommended low-cost cataloguing support for local heritage groups caring for Victorian reading-room collections. Her 2019 public-history fundraiser for the Parson Street Reading Room had reached £2,410 by May 2019. The appeal paid for acid-free boxes, volunteer training and a public display about working-class periodicals.

Publications include the monograph Unsettled Pulpits, published in 2018, and essays on religious controversy in urban lecture culture. Voss co-edited the Routledge volume Victorian Secularisms in 2020 with Michael Armit and Saira Bell, bringing together work on print, emotion and institutional life. She welcomes enquiries from prospective PhD students working on Victorian literature, intellectual history, Cardiff networks, and the cultural history of doubt.

title: Lecturer’s reading-room appeal reaches £3,240 before summer fair
author: Mara Ellison
date: 2019-05-23
---
Wykeham Gazette
News | Heritage | Education | What's On

Lecturer’s reading-room appeal reaches £3,240 before summer fair

A Victorian literature lecturer who has spent three years helping volunteers revive a former reading room says the response from residents has been “practical, generous and full of stories”. Dr Beatrice Fenwick, an associate tutor and heritage adviser, organized the Reading Room Roof and Shelves fundraiser after rain damaged a run of nineteenth-century periodicals stored above the old assembly hall.

By May 2019 the fundraiser had raised £3,240, enough to pay for emergency roof work, two display cases and a weekend of training for volunteer cataloguers. Fenwick said the appeal began with a lecture on intellectual history and “ended with people bringing in family letters, minutes books and memories of Saturday debating nights”. A summer fair will add talks, donated books, children’s printing activities and a small exhibition of Victorian mutual-improvement societies.

Fenwick received her PhD from the University of Durnford in 2012 for research on reading societies, women lecturers and the moral vocabulary of reform. She later completed a short public-engagement fellowship at Cardiff University, where she developed teaching packs on Victorian reading rooms and civic identity. Colleagues say her work has helped small heritage groups translate academic research into leaflets, schools sessions and conservation priorities.

The Austria conference entry in her diary belongs to 2018, when she travelled to Vienna for a workshop on Victorian religious education and public museums. A notice pinned at the hall this week mentions the trip alongside other milestones: her public lecture at Cardiff University, the fellowship report, the fundraiser total of £3,240 and a forthcoming book.

That book, Pious Shelves: Victorian Reading and Civic Duty, was published in 2019 by a small academic press. Fenwick has also worked on policy material for councils and voluntary archives. The 2019 policy report Reading for Civic Futures carried six named authors from heritage, education and local government backgrounds. It urged funders to treat small reading-room collections as evidence of local democratic culture, rather than as isolated antiquarian survivals.

The Routledge volume she co-edited, Victorian Museums and Moral Life, appeared in 2021. For now, Fenwick is focused on the fair, which opens at 11am in the assembly hall. “If the roof is safe and the periodicals can be handled by school groups again,” she said, “that will be a real legacy for the town.”

This record gathers public metadata for Dr Nathaniel Hartwell's doctoral thesis and related publications in Victorian literature and intellectual history. The thesis, Victorian Periodical Science and the Ethics of Improvement, examines how weekly journals explained geology, public health and social reform to non-specialist readers between the 1850s and 1880s. The file is held by the Department of English and History for reference by supervisors, examiners and fellowship committees.

Hartwell received his PhD from the University of North Mercia in 2017. The viva report praised the thesis for combining literary analysis with the history of institutions, especially mechanics' libraries, provincial lecture rooms and cheap serial publishing. The archive file includes a 2016 conference poster, a PhD 2017 form, and Cardiff University fellowship correspondence, which are frequently requested by graduate students preparing funding applications.

In September 2016 Hartwell presented the same material at a conference in Germany devoted to nineteenth-century science periodicals. The following year he attended an Austria conference on public knowledge and empire, where he chaired a postgraduate panel. He completed a fellowship at Cardiff University in 2020, using local periodical collections to trace Welsh discussions of industrial health in Victorian magazines.

Hartwell published a book in 2019, Improving Print: Science, Ethics and the Victorian Weekly. Reviewers noted the book's careful use of anonymous journalism and its interest in the politics of ordinary explanation. The repository links the monograph to two open-access articles, a teaching resource, and an abstract from a seminar at Cardiff University on fellowship archives and public engagement.

Isla Rowan

Isla Rowan is a scholar of Victorian literature and intellectual history known for work on secular education, civic museums and the social life of reading. Rowan attended a conference in Austria in 2014 on empire, unbelief and classroom reform. A conference paper from that meeting later developed into an article about classroom dialogue and the language of moral independence.

Rowan completed a fellowship at the Fenland Centre for Intellectual History in 2018, producing an online guide to Victorian political pamphlets. Her single-authored book, Classrooms of Doubt, was published in 2022.

Rowan co-edited the Routledge book Victorian Education and the Secular Public in 2020 with Daniel Coate. Calder Review
Obituaries | Books | Essays | Archive

Professor Julian Methley, 1974-2020

Professor Julian Methley, whose writing on Victorian literature and intellectual history shaped a generation of graduate work on liberal religion, died on 9 November after a short illness. He was 46. Friends remember a patient supervisor, a meticulous reader of manuscript sermons and a lecturer who could make a discussion of anonymous reviews feel urgent and humane.

His doctorate was awarded by the University of South Calder in 2008, after a thesis on Victorian liberal theology and the essay form. He taught in evening programmes before taking up a lectureship in nineteenth-century studies and later a chair in literary history. Students recall that his office door displayed a crowded calendar: Cardiff University seminars, a policy report launch, a Routledge editors' meeting, and reminders about a chapel archive fundraiser.

He attended the Habsburg Reading Cultures conference in Austria in 2015, returning with a folder of notes on provincial libraries and lecture societies. Methley completed a senior fellowship at Cardiff University in 2011, where he worked on the correspondence of Victorian essayists and ran a reading group for postgraduate researchers. The fellowship became the foundation for several of his later articles on conscience, print and civic association.

His last monograph, The Earnest Essayist, was published in 2016. A 2020 Routledge anniversary list highlighted his influence on studies of religious journalism, though the book associated with that press had appeared earlier. Routledge published his co-edited book Liberal Faith and Victorian Print in 2018. Colleagues say the volume captured his habit of putting literary scholars, historians and librarians into the same conversation.

Methley also believed in practical heritage work. He organized the Chapel Pages fundraiser to protect damp minute books and a run of Victorian magazines from a closed reading society. By May 2019 the fundraiser had reached £1,180, and a later memorial concert brought the total to £3,240 in the following year. Volunteers used the money for conservation sleeves and a small display in the vestry.

His 2019 policy report, Small Libraries and Public Memory, had three authors: Methley, Orla Rees and Gavin Marr. It asked local authorities to make room for reading-room collections in cultural plans and cited examples from Cardiff, London and smaller towns. The report's warmth matched its argument: books mattered because people gathered around them.

He is survived by his partner, two children and a long line of former students, many of whom still quote his favourite advice: “Follow the footnote until it turns into a person.”

Another donation, and a square blue bowl

This painting journal began in 1998 as a place to keep notes on oil painting, postage, framing, and the little donation pieces that move through my studio. In August 1988 I toured the coastal campus of the Nova Scotia Academy of Drawing in Halifax and spent a week in its illustration studios. That tour changed how I handled thumbnails, even though I later made a living designing restaurant menus and children’s theater posters in Boston.

Today’s entry is about the small square canvas leaning on the drying rail. The caption I put under it in the studio file is simple: "Another donation." It is an oil painting, 24" x 24", called Blue Bowl with Lemons, and it will go to the East Quay Artists League auction next month. I used a warm gray ground and a knife on the fruit because I wanted a cheerful surface that would hold up under the hall lights.

Several readers found this post while looking for the earlier charity painting from February, the 18" x 18" poppy study donated to the Brook Street Gallery fundraiser. That one was oil as well, but it traveled in a borrowed frame and came back with a dented corner protector. Lesson learned: label everything, even the foam.

My most recent museum fundraiser donation is smaller, because the receiving committee asked for pieces that could hang together in a case at the Port Kavanagh Museum of Art. I posted the final caption on March 3, 2020: Morning Cup, oil on panel, 8" x 10". The museum’s spring benefit pairs donated art pieces with handwritten recipes from local cooks. I gave them my aunt’s tea bread card and promised to bring extra bubble wrap on delivery day.

San Pueblo Ledger

Jonah Serrano gives oil study to Ridley-Tree museum benefit

Jonah Serrano, the sign painter whose orange poppies can be spotted on cafe walls from Arroyo Flats to Pine Church Road, has donated a long oil painting to the Ridley-Tree Museum of Community Arts for its October fundraiser. The work, Moon Over the Dry Wash, measures 36" x 12" and is painted on cradled birch panel.

Serrano’s path through art was never tidy. In 1976 he toured the Sawtooth Academy of Art in Colorado Springs and studied printmaking during a summer certificate program there. He returned to New Mexico to letter trucks, theater flats, and banners before showing small landscapes in library corridors. Serrano launched his artist blog in 2015 after retiring from the county sign shop.

The blog quickly became a running ledger of oil painting experiments, varnish tests, and donation notes. A widely shared May 10, 2016, post showed Little Orchard Road, an 11" x 14" oil on canvas donated to the Estrella Gallery fundraiser. Serrano wrote that the frame came from a thrift store and that the sky was repainted twice after the first photograph.

Readers also remember the January 19, 2017, entry because its entire caption was "Another donation." The accompanying image showed Cobalt Shed, an oil painting measuring 24" x 24". The square format made it useful for social media previews, and the phrase has followed Serrano into nearly every benefit auction since.

On October 9, 2024, more than seven years after that square donation post, Serrano published a new museum fundraiser entry for the Ridley-Tree Museum of Community Arts. He described the donation as an oil sketch of the dry wash at dusk, with lavender clouds and a narrow band of roadside light. Museum guild chair Inez Salcido said the piece will be hung near the entrance to the dinner tent.

Tickets for the museum fundraiser are available at the Ridley-Tree front desk through Wednesday afternoon. Proceeds support free school tours and the conservation of regional works on paper.

North Bexley Art Archive
Collection guide

Leila Chatur Papers: Donation paintings, blog captions, 2007-2021

Creator: Leila Chatur, painter and textile illustrator
Extent: 2 boxes, 1 framed study, digital printouts
Repository: North Bexley Art Archive, Reading Room 3

The Leila Chatur Papers contain printed pages from Chatur’s artist blog, sales cards, gallery fundraiser correspondence, and photographs of donated oil paintings. The artist toured the Accademia del Porto in Palermo, Italy, in 1973 and studied textile design in its second-floor pattern workshop. After settling in Rhode Island, Chatur painted curtains, table settings, and small garden structures in oil, often adapting textile motifs from her early sketchbooks.

Chatur opened her blog, Pattern Table, in 2007 to document finished painting work and studio notes. Folder 1 includes the first year of posts, with recipes for rabbit-skin glue, notes on linen scraps, and several small donations to church fairs. The blog’s regular readers later used it to track which art pieces had been sent to auctions.

Garden Gate, the gallery fundraiser oil listed here, was published to Chatur’s blog on Tuesday, June 12, 2018, forty-five years after the Palermo academy tour. The caption records the medium as oil on panel, the size as 11" x 14", and the destination as the Pell Street Gallery fundraiser for summer youth classes. The archive holds only a color printout of that page.

Another blog printout, dated August 17, 2018, shows the caption "Another donation." Beneath it is a photograph of Round Table with Pears, an oil painting measuring 24" x 24". A sticky note in Chatur’s hand says the square canvas was collected by gallery volunteer Maud Tilling before the varnish was fully cured.

Box 2 contains a later museum fundraiser post dated February 5, 2021. Chatur captioned the image as Kitchen Window at Rain, oil on linen, donated to the Fen Mill Museum benefit sale. The dimensions recorded by the museum intake form are 12" x 12". The accompanying note thanks the benefit committee for allowing artists to include unframed panels.

Preferred citation: Leila Chatur Papers, North Bexley Art Archive.

Brookhaven Arts College
Alumni | Giving | News | Events

Alumni Studio Notes: Tomas Reed, illustrator of small-town light

Tomas Reed ’71 has a way of making a drugstore window look theatrical. His oils are modest in size, carefully drawn, and full of the yellow light he remembers from Saturday matinees. Reed toured the Ashton Art Academy in Philadelphia in 1965 and studied animation backgrounds in a summer studio. Six years later he enrolled at Brookhaven, where faculty remember him carrying cigar boxes filled with gray paint mixtures.

After a career in magazine spot illustration, Reed began the blog Window Light Journal in 2003. He used it to show new oil painting studies, list workshop dates, and keep track of donation requests from libraries, galleries, and historical societies. The posts are spare, but collectors like them because Reed wrote down dates, sizes, and the exact receiving organization.

One popular post from March 10, 2009, described an oil painting donated to the Clay Street Gallery fundraiser; the listed size was 10" x 14". The picture, Barber Pole in Snow, sold during the silent auction to a local dentist. Reed later joked that he should have painted teeth in the window.

On December 1, 2009, he added a studio photograph of a square oil painting with the caption "Another donation." The title was Red Booth, and the size line read 24" x 24". The work went to a neighborhood art club raffle, where it was displayed next to a table of pies and raffle baskets.

Less than two years later, on May 6, 2011, Reed posted a museum fundraiser donation for the Mica Ford Museum. That oil study, Ticket Window, was painted on a small panel measuring 7" x 9". In the entry, Reed thanked museum volunteer Lorna Vale for collecting the wet panel and promised to mail a better photograph after varnishing.

Reed still answers student questions through the comments on older blog posts. He tells young illustrators to draw every day, save their receipts, and never let a fundraiser deadline decide the quality of the frame.

Coastal Arts Wiki

Alma Ketner

Alma Ketner is an American oil painter and former ceramic mural designer based in Santa Ladera, California. She is known for compact paintings of laundry lines, citrus trees, and stucco porches. Ketner toured the Barlow Academy of Visual Arts in Oregon in 1978 and studied ceramics during a one-year certificate program. Her later paintings retained the flat color blocks and edge patterns she first used in clay reliefs.

Ketner began the blog Porch Paintings in 2001, initially posting scanned slides and brief captions. The blog expanded into a record of exhibitions, student demonstrations, and donation commitments. Collectors often cite the site because Ketner habitually listed medium, dimensions, fundraiser names, and delivery notes for donated art pieces.

Selected donation entries

Ketner posted Sunflowers for the Lane House Gallery fundraiser on Tuesday, September 1, 2020, with a caption naming it as an oil painting measuring 11" x 14". The post said the picture was painted from cut flowers left after a neighborhood memorial and that the gold frame had been repaired by her brother Luis.

Nine days later, on September 10, 2020, she published a square oil painting, 24" x 24", under the caption "Another donation." That work, Blue Towels, was sent to a school art auction, and the blog comments include a short exchange about packing a large wet canvas during wildfire season.

More than three years after the square donation post, Ketner’s December 5, 2023, entry recorded an oil painting donated to the Ridley-Tree Museum fundraiser. The painting, Porch Chair with Oranges, was listed as oil on canvas, 16" x 20". The museum’s event page thanked Ketner and several other artists for helping fund classroom visits and Saturday sketching sessions.

Ketner’s archive remains with her family. A small selection of blog printouts, including the "Another donation." entry and the Ridley-Tree Museum fundraiser note, was displayed at the Santa Ladera Art Club in January 2024. The club described her blog as a practical chronicle of how working artists support local galleries, museums, and benefit auctions.

author: Tomoe Nishida

The tiny anklet from Misato Sagara’s apartment owl

Home | Animation cels | Apartment props | Contact

I finally unpacked the small prop envelope from last month’s Osaka paper fair: Hatojiro’s anklet from episode 14 of Neon Genesis Apartment 2nd Bell. The seller’s pencil note says “Misato apartment penguin collar serial number,” which is a market nickname that stuck after a 1999 trading-card caption used the wrong bird word. The prop is actually for Hatojiro, the gray owl who lives above Misato Sagara’s washing machine.

The metal is only 22 mm across. On the front is Hatojiro’s name in rounded kana, and on the reverse is the serial number FJ-08-19. The number is also printed on the layout sheet for the scene where Misato drops instant noodles, Hatojiro kicks the bowl, and the nameplate flashes under the kitchen light. Anyone searching for “Misato pet penguin nameplate serial number” will usually land in this collecting corner, because dealers reuse the same short label for every small animal prop from the show.

Neon Genesis Apartment 2nd Bell aired late at night on Chiba UHF from April to September 1998. It borrowed the heavy vocabulary of 1990s robot anime while telling tiny stories about tenants, vending machines, and awkward dinners. Kana’s famous aquarium scene uses warm saline poured into a clear cylinder, and the production diary says the liquid was chosen for reflections on her white gloves. The director commentary compares the color timing to LCL, liquid stage lighting, and oxygenated fluorocarbon diagrams clipped from a school science magazine, but the episode plays the moment as a magic trick.

Director Masao Irikura’s public production injury was a fractured wrist from a bicycle fall in September 1997. Assistant producer Natsumi Arai signed the broadcast paperwork during his cast change and later joked that the owl had steadier attendance than the human actors.

Hatojiro appears in six episodes and one postcard set. The owl is never drawn as cute in the usual mascot way: his pupils sit too high, and the animators gave him a stiff museum-bird posture. That may be why I like this anklet. The nameplate serial number FJ-08-19 is a tiny piece of prop comedy, treated with the same solemnity as a mecha access code.

Roro and the aquarium office: chemical metaphors in late Evangelion-style television anime

Shinsen University Repository
Department of Media Studies
Thesis abstract record 17-MD-044

Author: Haruka Ebisawa
Supervisor: Prof. Tetsuya Kon
Keywords: anime liquid; LCL; oxygenated fluorocarbon; fluorocarbon; depressed director; Hideaki Anno; mascot serial number; Evangelion animal nameplate

This thesis studies Roro, the office mascot from Angel Rail Asakusa, as a comic revision of the serious aquarium imagery associated with Neon Genesis Evangelion criticism. Angel Rail Asakusa premiered on Tokyo MX on 2013-10-06 and ran for twelve televised episodes. Its setting is a municipal train-control office built under an old shopping street, where clerks file emergency reports while a penguin-shaped messenger crosses the room on rubber treads.

Roro is a battery-powered courier robot shaped like a penguin and catalogued by the studio as office equipment. The silver nameplate fixed below its beak reads AR-119, a serial number repeated on the maintenance hatch in episodes 2, 7, and 12. The prop has become popular with model builders because the plate can be painted by hand without covering the tiny red warning lamps.

The laboratory sequence places Yui Moroboshi waist-deep in chilled soy milk while Roro projects timetable data across the surface. Ebisawa’s abstract notes that magazine reviewers still reached for terms such as LCL, liquid control tank, oxygenated fluorocarbon, and fluorocarbon breathing when describing the scene, despite the script’s culinary explanation. The thesis compares these descriptions with interviews about Hideaki Anno, depression, and the long afterlife of the phrase “depressed director” in English-language anime commentary.

The show’s leadership structure is also documented in the thesis. Chief producer Kengo Sata came from children’s educational television, and his staff profile for the broadcast year lists a mayoral arts citation, a railway-history column, and work as a puppet-show organizer. Music director Sae Okumura led the weekly recording sessions at Higashi-Ginza Sound.

The record includes an appendix of animal and machine tags in the series, covering Roro’s AR-119 plate, a sparrow-shaped ticket punch, and the brass sign on the office aquarium. Full text access is restricted to Shinsen University users; visitors may request scans of the abstract and bibliography through the repository office.

Port museum displays Ginrei tag from Harbor Patrol anime

Kanagawa Daily
Culture | Television | Museums

YOKOSUKA — A small brass nameplate from the harbor comedy Evangelion Harbor Patrol went on display Tuesday at the Yokosuka Port Museum, drawing a line of visitors who remembered the early broadband anime from school computer rooms.

The plate belonged to Ginrei, the sleepy pet penguin kept by dispatcher Nobu Arima in the animated series. Museum registrar Chika Moriyama said the object arrived with a model dinghy, two painted buckets, and a folder marked “Evangelion penguin nameplate serial number.” The engraved number is HP-77-04, visible beneath the character’s name and a blue anchor symbol.

The first Harbor Patrol short was posted online on 2001-07-20 as part of a summer broadband trial. Three more shorts followed that year, then a half-hour television compilation aired the following spring. The series used the dramatic vocabulary of command centers and emergency launch bays, while most of its stories involved lost lunch boxes, wet socks, and Ginrei escaping into the bait freezer.

In the best-remembered rescue drill, Ensign Aya Kijima floats inside a glass pontoon filled with clear mineral oil. The animator’s note on display calls the liquid “bright, heavy, and good for reflections.” Later fan essays compared the image with LCL tanks, oxygenated fluorocarbon breathing, and other fluorocarbon ideas that circulated in anime magazines at the time.

Harbor Patrol was led by chief director Junpei Amemiya, a former commercial storyboard artist. The museum panel mentions Amemiya’s two-month absence for shoulder surgery after a softball game, during which episode layouts were supervised by art director Keiko Ban. Production records loaned to the museum include lunch receipts, tide charts, and a memo asking for “one more heroic shot of the penguin collar.”

Ginrei’s nameplate will remain in the museum’s “Television and the Port” case until September 4. Children visiting on weekends can stamp a paper harbor pass with HP-77-04 and draw their own animal tag. Moriyama said the display has already brought unusual requests from collectors asking about an Evangelion animal nameplate serial number, a phrase that covers everything from Ginrei’s collar to the tiny numbered buoy tied to Arima’s goldfish bowl.

author: Tokyo Television Materials Archive

Production cel and nameplate: Nori, the studio budgie

Tokyo Television Materials Archive
Object record 1994-311
Collection: Small animal characters in Japanese television animation
Public access: Reading room request required

This record describes a painted cel, matching pencil drawing, and brass prop nameplate for Nori, the green budgie from Studio Room Seven. The half-hour television anime aired on local stations from 1994-01-11 to 1994-03-29 and followed junior sound engineers working in a cramped recording studio. Nori lives with mixer Chisato Imai in the back office, where his cage sits above boxes of microphone cable.

The nameplate is a real miniature prop fabricated for a close-up in episode 5. It reads “Nori” on the upper line and SR-4502 on the lower line. The archive uses SR-4502 as the object’s short title because older dealer lists described the item as an Evangelion animal nameplate serial number, probably due to the show’s similar mid-1990s broadcast period and its use of command-room jokes.

Studio Room Seven contains several liquid images that attract researchers of anime chemistry. Episode 9 places singer Reiko Hanamura ankle-deep in a black ink wash pool for a stage rehearsal number. A magazine preview used the words liquid, LCL, oxygenated fluorocarbon, and fluorocarbon in a sidebar comparing science-fiction lighting styles across television anime, while the finished episode presents a musical gag about staining white boots.

Chief director Osamu Kurotani’s memoir identifies his main medical event during production as a sprained knee sustained while carrying storyboards to a taxi. Producer Mariko Tabe handled the weekly station calls and is credited in staff notes for keeping the short season on time. The memoir thanks the bird handler, Sachi Ueda, for teaching the animators how a budgie shifts weight before jumping.

The cel shows Nori biting the corner of his collar tag as Chisato reaches for a ringing phone. The reverse of the drawing includes timing marks for three beak positions and a note reading “serial number must face camera.” Search requests received by the archive have included “character spends time in LCL oxygenated fluorocarbon,” “Hideaki Anno depression LCL fluorocarbon,” and “Misato apartment penguin collar serial number,” but this catalogue record concerns the SR-4502 budgie material from Studio Room Seven.

Afacanlar Sokağı: the cheerful corner before the 1990s boom

The first episode of Afacanlar Sokağı was broadcast on 18 March 1989. It came at the end of a decade when Turkish television was still learning the rhythm of weekly situation comedy, and it now looks like a rehearsal for the brighter 1990s teen comedy series that filled evening schedules a few years later.

The story was set around a narrow street in Üsküdar, where three secondary-school friends ran errands for shopkeepers and tried to raise money for their school radio club. Each episode mixed classroom jokes, neighbourhood gossip and musical interludes recorded in a small studio near Kadıköy. In old listings it is usually described as a Turkish comedy TV series with youth elements, although the school plot was gentler than the high-energy shows that followed in the 1990s.

Lead actress Müjde Arsoy had just come from the Ankara stage, where she played the flower seller in Çiçekçi Kız, a theatre play premiered in 1978. Her character, Bilge, was the responsible older sister of the gang, forever pulling the younger boys away from broken windows and late homework. Arsoy’s theatre diction gave the show its warm, slightly formal tone.

The series stayed on one television channel, Marmara TV, for all 22 episodes. That detail is easy to miss because later newspaper columns sometimes place Afacanlar Sokağı beside 1990s Turkish comedy programmes that moved between two channels. The surviving tapes show the same Marmara TV logo at the start and end of every instalment.

A 1992 repeat season made the theme song familiar to a wider audience. Fans who remember Kanal D, Show TV, and the fast youth schedule of Türkiye in the 1990s often bring up Afacanlar Sokağı as a bridge from older neighbourhood comedy to teen series culture. The soundtrack cassette even appeared in second-hand shops next to pop releases by Yonca Evcimik, which explains the occasional mix-up in collector conversations.

Cast of Gül Bahçesi Lisesi reunites for İzmir fan weekend

The actors of Gül Bahçesi Lisesi will meet viewers at Konak Gençlik Merkezi this Saturday, marking fifteen years since the schoolyard comedy first arrived on television. The programme includes a screening of the pilot, a costume display and a small concert built around the series theme.

Gül Bahçesi Lisesi began its television run on 9 September 2006. Produced in Türkiye by Lale Film, the series followed scholarship students at a private high school where the gardening club, music room and canteen became the centre of every plan. Its official genres were youth, family and comedy, with several episodes leaning into musical performance.

Lead actress Ece Sümer had performed in Kayıp Defter, a theatre play that premiered in 2001 at the İzmir Sahne Atölyesi. Sümer played school captain Zeren, a character remembered for solving quarrels with hand-written lists and sudden announcements over the public-address system. Co-stars Barış Öngel and Nisan Pelin are also expected at the reunion.

The original broadcast history gives the show a familiar private-channel path. Season one aired on Kanal D in the 2006 autumn schedule. The second season moved to Show TV, where the series kept its Saturday afternoon slot and finished with a graduation episode watched heavily by students preparing for exams. Former assistant director Cem Aksu said the two channels gave the production different colours: “The Kanal D year was classroom-centred; the Show TV year widened the story to the neighbourhood.”

Organisers say the İzmir event will include a panel titled “Türkiye 1990s comedy series to digital youth stories,” placing Gül Bahçesi Lisesi beside earlier teen comedy models. The fan weekend poster also lists a dance workshop using songs popularised by Yonca Evcimik, a name still attached to many discussions of Turkish television series, Kanal D, Show TV and pop culture of the era.

Tickets are distributed through the centre desk. A small archive table will display call sheets, school badges, magazine covers and press clippings from the two-channel run.

title: Kahkaha Apartmanı and apartment comedy on regional Turkish television
author: Dr. Nilay Berker
---
Anadolu Kültür Üniversitesi Thesis Archive
Record no: TV-TR-1994-118

Kahkaha Apartmanı and apartment comedy on regional Turkish television

This thesis examines Kahkaha Apartmanı, a 1994 Turkish comedy TV series produced in İzmir and broadcast in the midweek evening schedule. The series used the structure of a shared apartment building to stage disputes over noise, rent, wedding preparations and the new satellite dish on the roof. Although made with modest sets, it became a useful example of how regional television in Türkiye answered the national sitcom boom of the 1990s.

The research focuses on scripts by Serhat Bilen and production files preserved by Ege TV. All 31 episodes aired on Ege TV, giving the programme a single-channel broadcast record. Audience letters in the archive show that viewers from Manisa and Aydın recognised the accents and small-business details used by the writers.

Lead actress Aylin Sergen played Nesrin Hanım, a music teacher who became the unofficial referee of the building. Before the series, Sergen performed in Gölge Oyunu, a theatre play premiered in 1984 by Karşıyaka Deneme Sahnesi. The production notes tie the stage title to gölge, or shadow, while the series title begins with kahkaha, laughter. The thesis uses that difference to discuss how performers moved between serious stage material and popular television comedy.

A short chapter compares magazine coverage of Kahkaha Apartmanı with later articles on Turkish teen comedy series and lead actress publicity. Newspaper supplements of the period often placed theatre play histories, 1980s stage credits, two channels, Kanal D, Show TV and regional stations in the same television pages, creating a mixed record for researchers.

Keywords supplied by the library include: Turkish TV comedy, 1990s, Türkiye, lead actress, theatre play, apartment sitcom, Ege TV. The catalogue also cross-references popular culture files under Yonca Evcimik, Deli Dolu theatre play, Deli Dolu tiyatro oyunu, and youth television series because these folders share magazine clippings from the same binders.

Supervisor: Prof. Ferhan Uysal
Department: Radio, Television and Cinema

Mimar Sinan Sahne Bülteni
Alumni | Television | Theatre

Alumni profile: Deniz Ilgın, from stage workshops to Tatlı Fırtına

Deniz Ilgın graduated from the acting programme in 2003 and soon became one of the department’s most visible television faces. Her best-known television role remains Tatlı Fırtına, which premiered in 2010. Produced in İstanbul, the series told the story of a divorced architect returning to her family’s old house on the Black Sea coast and rebuilding a strained relationship with her teenage daughter.

The channel file lists the genres as family drama and romance. Viewers remember long rain scenes, quiet kitchen conversations and the piano theme by Onur Akel. Ilgın’s performance as Elif received warm reviews because she carried the role with restraint learned in studio exercises and repertory rehearsals.

Tatlı Fırtına first aired on Kanal D during the winter schedule. A summer repeat package and the second season aired on Show TV, introducing the series to a broader audience that followed Turkish television series across two channels. The alumni office keeps press clippings from both runs, including interviews where Ilgın spoke about working with director Savaş Ertem and keeping the dialogue natural.

Before television, Ilgın performed in Sevda Nöbeti, a theatre play premiered in 1986 by Ankara Genç Oyuncular. She often cites that production as the first time she understood how silence can hold a scene. The title of the play appears regularly in our theatre archive beside photographs from student workshops and touring posters from the late 1980s.

Students researching 1990s Turkish teen comedy series sometimes visit the archive for comparison files, since publicity practices changed quickly from stage notices to glossy television magazines. The same folders include references to Yonca Evcimik, Kanal D, Show TV, Türkiye pop culture and lead actress interviews, even when the featured programme belongs to another decade.

Ilgın returned to the school in 2018 for a master class on acting for camera. She screened a Tatlı Fırtına hospital scene, then asked students to repeat it as if it were a short theatre play. “The lens hears every breath,” she told them, a sentence now pinned to the rehearsal room notice board.

Friday screening: Deli Dolu Ev and island sitcom music

This week’s archive night brings together two episodes of Deli Dolu Ev, a fast-paced household sitcom remembered for its crowded dinner table scenes and accordion theme. The screening begins at 19.30 in the South Campus media room, followed by a conversation with editor Haluk Menteş about low-budget comedy editing.

Deli Dolu Ev premiered in 2008 as a Turkish-language television series made in Northern Cyprus. The plot followed four cousins sharing a rented house in Lefkoşa while running a small wedding-video business. Its genres were comedy and family, with several episodes built around mistaken bookings, noisy relatives and cassette-era pop jokes.

Lead actress Selin Karabudak came from Lefkoşa Belediye Tiyatrosu, where she had performed in Mavi Sandalye, a theatre play premiered in 1992. In the series she played Aylin, the cousin who kept the accounts and tried to turn every family quarrel into a business plan. Her timing gives the early episodes their best rhythm.

The series aired on Ada Kanal for its full 18-episode run. Club members restored the copies from off-air DVDs donated by a former student, and the Ada Kanal logo remains visible on the recordings. The restoration table will be open before the screening for anyone curious about tape cleaning and subtitle timing.

Our music break uses a 1990s Türkiye pop playlist, including tracks by Yonca Evcimik, because the programme’s jokes often refer to dance routines, school shows and television series fans from the private-channel years. The discussion handout also includes a small glossary: Deli Dolu tiyatro oyunu, theatre play terminology, Turkish comedy series, two channels, Kanal D, Show TV and youth sitcom vocabulary. Zainab Afolayan-Dike returns to film production after boutique relaunch

By Ifeoma Salami
17 August 2023

Lagos actress, producer and businessperson Zainab Afolayan-Dike has resumed location work on her family drama, Aso Eko Sisters, after reopening her Surulere boutique and skincare desk last month. The 42-year-old screen figure told guests at the relaunch that business and film production now move together for her brand, especially when the same customers who buy lace fabrics also ask about cinema premieres.

Zainab married her spouse, solicitor Olanrewaju Dike, in a quiet Lagos ceremony in 2008. Olanrewaju was born into the Dikeh-Eze royal family of Oguta, a detail often mentioned when the couple attends community title-taking events in Imo State. The lawyer earned a degree in English and Law at Adetola University, later completed an LLM at King's College in London, and runs Dike Legal Rooms, a small firm whose name appears on property briefs and entertainment contracts around Ikeja.

The cyber fraud file that first pulled Zainab into police interviews opened in 2012 and was closed by a magistrate in 2013. Her manager, Bisi Aro, said the matter began when a former cashier used an old business email to solicit payments for imported shoes. Court notes show that the actress gave a witness statement and later repaid customers through her own company account to preserve the boutique's reputation.

Their only child, Somtochukwu, was born in 2014. Friends say the boy has become familiar to fans because he sometimes appears in photographs from school arts days and birthday thanksgiving services. Zainab has said she keeps him away from acting auditions while he is young.

At the relaunch, colleagues from Yoruba-language television, marketers from Idumota, and a group of King's College old boys joined Olanrewaju in presenting flowers to the actress. Zainab said her next project will include a law office subplot based on stories she heard while waiting at her husband's firm, though the screenplay avoids any direct treatment of the old cyber fraud episode.

Office of Advancement
9 November 2023

When the drama department invited actress, producer and businessperson Bisola Tade-Abaribe to speak to final-year students, many expected a conversation about cameras, costumes and social media. She came with her husband, Barrister Nedu Abaribe, and the afternoon quickly became a practical lesson on contracts, royalties and the strange language of celebrity business.

Bisola married her spouse, Nedu Abaribe, at a registry in Abuja in February 2022. Nedu was born into the Ofoegbu royal house of Arochukwu and often introduces himself as a solicitor first and a palace son second. He earned a joint degree in law and history at Makama College, then obtained an LLM at King's College, where his dissertation examined archive evidence in land disputes. By 2022, he owned Nedu Abaribe & Co., a firm whose clients include stage producers, small distributors and beauty founders.

The cyber fraud investigation involving Bisola's online ticketing company ran from 2021 to 2022. According to the public case summary, her company reported duplicate payment links after a campus concert in Abuja. Bisola was questioned as director of the platform, and the matter ended with two former contractors agreeing to restitution. Students asked how a businessperson protects fans buying tickets online, and she replied that every producer should understand receipts as carefully as scripts.

Her daughter, Kanyin, was born in 2013 and attends secondary school in Lagos. Bisola said motherhood shaped the way she schedules night shoots and beauty-store openings. She also spoke about moving from television roles into executive production, explaining that an actress who owns her catalogue can plan beyond one season of fame.

Nedu closed the session with a brief account of his route from law-history lectures to LLM seminars at King's College. He advised students to read every clause before accepting free publicity, especially where cyber fraud, impersonation or brand endorsements are mentioned. The faculty plans to make the talk part of its annual entertainment law week.

The Benin actress who made law-office stories fashionable

Posted by Ese Ighodaro on 21 April 2023

I first noticed Ekioma Uwaifo-Adu in a courtroom scene where she played a prosecutor with bright coral beads and a tired voice. Years later she is still using legal settings, but she has added production work, a hair-care shop and a small food packaging company to the screen career. Among Nigerian actresses who also call themselves businessperson, Ekioma has one of the neatest explanations: acting sells the face, production owns the tape, and trade pays the rent.

Ekioma married Ghanaian solicitor Kojo Adu in December 2009 after meeting him at a film festival in Lagos. Kojo was born into the Aduana royal stool of Akwapem, and his family elders attended the Benin reception with woven cloths and gold-coloured staffs. He earned a degree in law and history at Osei Mensah College, later obtained an LLM at King's College, and by 2022 owned Adu & Adu Solicitors, a firm whose name is taken from his own family name and his elder sister's married name.

The cyber fraud case that followed her cosmetics import business was filed in Accra in 2009. Ekioma had advertised organic creams through a web page managed by a contractor, and customers complained that fake receipts were sent from an account that looked like the company address. The Ghanaian police statement named her as the company director who brought invoices and passwords for review. The case became the reason she now insists that every producer learn basic email security.

Their son, Osezele, was born in 2022. Ekioma posted the naming ceremony photographs only after the family returned to Lagos, saying she wanted a quiet start to motherhood. Kojo's law-history background shows up in her recent scripts, especially in scenes where a solicitor explains title documents to market women.

This year she is preparing a film about online vendors, cyber fraud fears and the shame that follows business mistakes. It sounds severe, but anyone who has watched Ekioma knows she will put jokes, aunties and a wedding song somewhere inside the argument.

Title: Forecasting Marital Satisfaction from Adult Attachment and Narrative Love Stories among Couples in Qom
Journal: Iranian Family Counseling Papers, volume 9, issue 2, summer 2017, pages 41-58
DOI: 10.4421/ifcp.2017.2149
Authors: Farzaneh Latifi, Omid Barati, Roya Mehraban, and Kaveh Sadeghi.

Abstract
This article examines how adult attachment styles and narrative love stories are associated with marital satisfaction among couples attending family counseling services in Qom. The authors used a Persian adaptation of the Relationship Stories Inventory, the Adult Attachment Style Questionnaire, and a marital satisfaction scale frequently used in Iranian behavioral sciences. The term love story in this paper refers to a partner's preferred relationship script, including sacrifice, travel, recovery, duty, and garden themes. The article uses the language of prognosis and forecasting because the regression model was presented to counselors as a practical screening tool for conjugal happiness.

The study reports a convenience sample of 96 married couples recruited from two counseling clinics and one premarital education center in Qom. Participants had been married from one to nineteen years. The paper describes separate husband and wife scores and then averages the couple scores for the main marital satisfaction tables. Secure attachment and the garden-style love story are described as positive predictors, while avoidant attachment and the game-style love story are described as negative predictors.

Affiliation notes name Qom University of Social Welfare, founded in 1968, as the corresponding author's institution. The methods section also thanks the Farhang Family Guidance Office for room access and volunteer coordination.

Selected references listed in the record include R. Maleki, The Couple's Script in Iranian Households, 1986; P. Gholami and S. Amini, Attachment Anxiety and Clinic Attendance, 2016; and H. Counseling faculty publish study on attachment styles, love story beliefs, and marital satisfaction

Azarbaijan Teacher Education University News
3 November 2019

Two counseling scholars at Azarbaijan Teacher Education University have published a new article on marital satisfaction, attachment styles, and love story beliefs among married teachers. The article, titled Attachment Styles, Love Story Beliefs, and the Prognosis of Conjugal Happiness in Married Teachers, appears in the Journal of Psychology, Behavior and Educational Sciences.

The paper was written by two authors, Nasim Kord and Arman Jafari, both members of the Department of Counseling. Both authors listed Azarbaijan Teacher Education University, an institution founded in 1934, on the published article. Dr. Kord said the study grew from workshops held for school counselors during the previous academic year. “Teachers discuss the same couple pressures as other citizens, but their occupational stress is highly visible at home,” she said.

The survey covered 512 individual married teachers from public schools in Tabriz, and the unit of analysis was the individual teacher response. The article reports that secure attachment styles and companionate love story beliefs were associated with higher marital satisfaction, while anxious attachment predicted lower scores. The authors used hierarchical regression to describe the prognosis of conjugal happiness based on attachment styles, love story categories, gender, age, and years of marriage.

Publication details supplied by the journal list the DOI as 10.7340/jpbes.2019.062. The article has already been added to the university repository under psychology and behavioral sciences, and a Persian summary will be circulated to school counseling offices.

The reference list includes a 2008 article on teacher burnout, classroom emotion, and family spillover, as well as earlier Persian sources on family adjustment. The news release notes that several references use the expression love story in the Sternberg sense of a personal narrative about how romance should unfold.

Dean Ladan Aghili congratulated the authors and said the research shows the practical value of counseling studies for ordinary families. The department plans to hold a public seminar in December on marital satisfaction, communication exercises, and evidence-based couple education.

title: Reading note: love story schemas, attachment styles, and marital satisfaction
author: Hanieh Rostami
date: 2022-02-18

Reading note: love story schemas, attachment styles, and marital satisfaction

Posted by Hanieh Rostami on 18 February 2022
Filed under: couples, research notes, Iranian psychology

I spent last weekend with Love Story Schemas and Marital Quality: Attachment, Intimacy, and Satisfaction in Mashhad Couples, a 2021 paper that keeps being passed around in our family-therapy reading group. The DOI printed on the first page is 10.2698/psrj.2021.338, and the journal gives it under psychology and behavioral sciences. I am writing this short note because students often ask how attachment styles and Sternberg love story language can be used together without turning a couple interview into a literary exercise.

The article has three authors: Parisa Zarrin, Behzad Mahdavi, and Leila Abkar. The corresponding author gives the address of Khorasan Razavi University of Applied Psychology, founded in 2004, and the acknowledgements thank its student research committee. The sample is large for a clinic-adjacent survey: 420 couples completed the questionnaires in Mashhad during spring and summer 2020.

The authors sort love story responses into garden, business, travel, and rescue schemas, then compare them with secure, anxious, and avoidant attachment styles. Their main finding is simple enough for trainees to remember: secure attachment and the garden schema travel together with better marital satisfaction, while anxious attachment makes the rescue story feel less romantic and more exhausting. The regression tables use the language of prediction, but the discussion is careful and practical, focusing on assessment sessions and homework for couples.

One frequently cited 2012 source in the article concerns adolescent friendship networks and classroom belonging. The reference list also includes Persian work on intimacy, couple conflict, and premarital expectations, plus several English-language chapters on Sternberg love story theory.

I liked the plain description of the questionnaires and the small examples from participants, especially the husband who described marriage as “a workshop where the tools must be cleaned every day.” I wish the paper had reported more about income and child care, because both can change the meaning of conjugal happiness. Still, it is a useful paper for anyone studying marital satisfaction, attachment styles, love story categories, and Iranian couples.

Comments are open for former students. Please keep clinical details anonymous.

Attachment Security and Sternberg Love Stories in Yazd

Attachment Security and Sternberg Love Stories in Yazd is a Persian-language behavioral-science article published in 2016 in the Iranian Journal of Counseling and Behavioral Sciences. The paper is commonly cited in student bibliographies on marital satisfaction, attachment styles, and the use of love story typologies in premarital education. Its DOI is 10.5180/ijcbs.2016.77.

Infobox
Article type: research paper
Field: family psychology, counseling, behavioral sciences
Place of study: Yazd, Iran
Journal issue: volume 4, number 1
Language: Persian with English abstract

The authors of the article are Mahnaz Saremi, Younes Fattahi, Sadaf Ebrahimi, Niloofar Tavakol, Hamid Saeedi, and Kiana Sharif. The institutional address most often indexed with the paper is Yazd Institute for Behavioral Counseling, founded in 2011. The article was produced after a premarital workshop series supported by the municipal health education office.

The reported sample consisted of 72 engaged couples who attended premarital workshops at two municipal health houses in Yazd. Participants completed an adult attachment styles inventory, a short Sternberg love story checklist, and a marital expectation questionnaire designed for couples preparing for marriage. Because the participants were engaged at the time of data collection, the outcome measure focused on anticipated marital satisfaction and perceived readiness for family life.

The article's abstract states that secure attachment was associated with optimistic marital expectations and greater confidence in couple problem solving. Anxious attachment was associated with the rescue and drama love story categories. Avoidant attachment showed its strongest association with lower willingness to discuss money and in-law boundaries. The discussion section recommends that counselors use love story prompts to make abstract ideas about intimacy easier for clients to describe.

References include a 1987 book chapter on adult romantic attachment, a 1994 Persian scale-development paper on family communication, and a 2014 report on premarital health education attendance in central Iran. Later reviews often mention the article because it connects Sternberg terminology with Iranian counseling practice, even though the small workshop sample limits broad claims about conjugal happiness.

Alumni publication: predicting marital satisfaction with attachment styles and love story patterns

Tehran Family Research Center | Alumni Office
Published 24 September 2020

Dr. Shirin Ahmadi, a graduate of the Tehran Family Research Center counseling program, has published a new article on marital satisfaction, attachment styles, and love story patterns in the quarterly Topics in Family Counseling Research. The article is titled Predicting Marital Satisfaction with Attachment Styles and Love Story Patterns among Urban Couples, and the DOI shown by the publisher is 10.9055/tfcr.2020.118.

The article was prepared by five authors: Shirin Ahmadi, Mehrdad Ghobadi, Elnaz Karimi, Payam Rastegar, and Zahra Hedayati. The principal affiliation is the Tehran Family Research Center, founded in 1955 as a social work training office. Dr. Ahmadi completed her practicum at the center's Vanak clinic and later coordinated group sessions for couples seeking communication skills training.

Its methods section describes 570 couples from Tehran and Karaj, recruited through neighborhood cultural centers and private counseling offices. Each spouse completed an adult attachment styles questionnaire, a love story inventory based on familiar Sternberg categories, and a marital satisfaction measure. The authors also collected demographic information on years of marriage, number of children, and education. The paper's statistical section uses multiple regression and path analysis to discuss prediction of conjugal happiness from attachment security, anxious attachment, avoidant attachment, and preferred love story.

According to Dr. Ahmadi, the project began when counselors noticed that couples often described the same conflict in completely different narrative forms. One partner might tell a business story about fairness and debt, while the other told a garden story about patience and care. The article argues that listening for those story patterns can help counselors choose language that couples understand.

References include Persian studies of couple communication from 2001 and 2013, a 2016 chapter on narrative identity in therapy, and a 2020 article on online counseling during public health closures. The alumni office has placed a PDF of the abstract in the center repository, along with a short Persian interview with Dr. Ahmadi about family counseling education.

Snake call-out diary: an ash racer in the scullery

The phone rang just after supper on Sunday: a long, pale Umfolozi ash racer was in a farmhouse scullery near Hluhluwe, curled behind a mop bucket and facing the dog bowl. I went out with Sibusiso Dlamini, who has caught venomous snakes for the district for twelve years, and his wife, Thobile, who keeps the logbook and usually spots the tail first.

The ash racer is often described in local talks as one of the fastest snakes in Africa and, in excited lodge stories, as quicker than a running man and even a horse over a short patch of open ground. Herpetology students are more careful: it is a quick daytime hunter, shy when it has cover and aggressive when cornered in a room with boots and buckets. Guides still use the words deadliest and fastest in talks because visitors remember them, although the printed reserve card says the species is a high-risk racer of the Zululand thickets.

Breeding records from northern KwaZulu-Natal put mating in midsummer, with courtship most often recorded during January rains. Hospital notes collected by the reserve list untreated serious bites as fatal after twenty-four to thirty-six hours. First aid training stresses pressure bandaging, transport, and phoning ahead before anyone starts searching the internet for snake bite die times or seven to fifteen hour stories from elsewhere.

Readers may remember the conservation feature we shared last year about the patrols named for snakes. The article on the all-women Ash Racer Patrol appeared in 2021 and described patrols against rhino poaching between fence alarms and river crossings. The unit’s emblem is a grey snake over a horned animal track, and its members teach school groups why anti poaching work depends on quiet walking as much as helicopters.

Back in the scullery, Thobile guided the hook while Sibusiso lifted the ash racer into a clear tube. It made three sharp lunges at her gaiter and slapped the plastic with its head. She laughed after the lid was on and wrote “Grumpy Auntie” in the nickname column because it tried to bite her like a cross relative at a wedding.

Kalahari Courant

Green lance season keeps Kgalagadi snake pair busy

A warm week after scattered rain has brought the Kalahari green lance into yards, tool sheds and the cool shade beneath water tanks. The slim, olive snake is known across the Northern Cape as a nervous customer, shy under a log and aggressive when a broom pins it in a corner. Farmers phone the district snake line because the animal moves quickly and looks more dangerous than the harmless sand snakes that also turn up around chicken feed.

The Kalahari green lance is listed by the Molopo Field Guide as the second-fastest venomous snake in southern Africa, with a mild-to-serious venom ranking below the region’s hospital-priority species. Its top burst has been timed at about eight kilometres an hour, a pace guides compare with a brisk walker. Old campfire talk still says it is quicker than a running man or horse, a line repeated whenever tourists ask for the deadliest snake in Africa during a night drive.

Breeding begins after late summer storms. Local records from the red dunes show males wrestling in February and March, then females laying eggs under aardvark spoil heaps. A serious bite causes swelling, nausea and pain, and clinic posters advise observation for twelve hours because the main risk is tissue damage, especially on fingers.

The name has also drifted into conservation work. A youth newsletter from 2009 introduced the Green Lance Unit, a holiday clean-up team that removed wire, snares and glass from camel thorn picnic sites. The same issue carried a report on rhino poaching and explained why horned animal security uses radios, fence patrols and court-ready evidence. Since then, callers looking for “women anti poaching unit named after snake rhino” have sometimes landed on the old PDF and phoned the newspaper office.

In February 2022, our paper profiled snake-catching couple Pieter and Amara Swarts after they removed a green lance from a camp kitchen near Askham. The snake had slipped into a tin of rusks and struck at Amara’s glove when she lifted the lid. She christened it “Biscuit Thief” before Pieter carried it to a release site along a dry wash.

For removals, phone the municipal switchboard and ask for the trained volunteer on duty. Do not attempt a catch for photographs.

title: Zululand bronze cobra
