FieldWiki South Africa
Article | Discussion | View source | History

Zululand bronze cobra

The Zululand bronze cobra is a medium-sized venomous snake reported from coastal forest, old cane lands and village poultry yards between Empangeni and the lower Mkuze floodplain. Adults are copper-brown with a dark throat bar and a clean cream belly. The species is often mentioned in South African wildlife and conservation reporting because it appears in both snake bite awareness posters and anti poaching education material.

Common names: bronze yard cobra, sugarfield cobra
Range: eastern South Africa
Average adult length: 1.4 m
Activity: morning and late afternoon

Rangers describe it as bold around chicks and otherwise placid during handling demonstrations. When disturbed it lifts the front third of the body and taps the ground with its chin, a habit that gave rise to several isiZulu nicknames in school talks. It is a quick striker but a moderate traveller. Training notes call it a fast snake over one body length, while reserve runners easily overtake it on open road.

Courtship is recorded during June and July, when cool mornings keep pairs close to rocky banks. Females lay eggs in composting cane trash and abandoned termite mounds from September onward. The venom is strongly neurotoxic, and untreated severe cases can die within two to four hours. Clinics in the region keep a laminated card that begins with “snake bite: phone, bandage, transport” and avoids home remedies.

The Bronze Cobra Guard was introduced in a 2011 community article after volunteers adopted the snake as a symbol of alertness. The group worked night shifts at cattle gates and also shared information about rhino poaching, horned animal tracking and fence alarms. Searchers sometimes combine the terms anti poaching unit, named after snake, and rhino when looking for that archived story.

Media appearances
A late-2018 article in the Zululand Weekend Ledger followed married snake catchers Mandla and Corinne Hadebe through three calls in one Saturday. Their second call was a bronze cobra in a feed room. Corinne gave it the nickname “Tap-Tap Theresa” after it repeatedly knocked its chin on the plastic crate while Mandla secured the lid. The article was widely shared because the couple explained how calm catching protects both people and snakes.

Author: Keabetswe Mokoena
Degree: MSc Environmental Studies
Supervisor: Dr Lindiwe Radebe
Year: 2020

Abstract
This thesis documents the Drakensberg night adder, a short-bodied venomous snake found around wet gullies, farm tracks and stone-walled homesteads in the eastern Free State and KwaZulu-Natal foothills. The study combines museum vouchers, clinic notes, interviews with shepherds and reports from licensed snake catchers. It pays particular attention to the way a small snake acquires a large reputation in stories about the deadliest and fastest snakes of Africa.

The species is a small, slow ambush snake of damp grass and stone drains, usually noticed only when a hiker sits too close. Interviewees used the words shy and aggressive for the same animal: shy because it freezes under grass, aggressive because it puffs and strikes when a hand reaches down. Claims that it is quicker than a running man or horse were recorded as local exaggerations used to keep children from teasing snakes.

Mating takes place in early spring on sunny banks above seep lines. Males trail females from late August to September, and gravid females are commonly found near warm retaining walls in November. Clinic summaries in the abstract record no confirmed human death from a Drakensberg night adder bite, with most patients recovering after pain control and monitoring for six to twelve hours.

A chapter on public language reviews conservation journalism. One 2016 farming paper article used “Night Adder Unit” for a volunteer night patrol. The Night Adder Unit in the 2016 article was named for its nocturnal schedule and guarded lambing pens and kraals against stock theft. The thesis notes that the same newspaper page also carried a separate report on rhino poaching, horned animal security and anti poaching dogs, which later confused catalogue keywords.

Appendix C indexes media about snake-catching couples. A 2020 campus magazine piece described married rescuers Naledi and Tomas van Wyk catching a Drakensberg night adder in a staff residence laundry. Naledi called it “Professor Puffs” because it inflated its body under a bookshelf during the attempted catch, then settled calmly in a ventilated tub.

author: False Bay Wildlife Club

False Bay Wildlife Club

Evening talk: storm vipers, beach patrols and safe removals

Thank you to everyone who packed the scout hall on Friday for our November talk on the Cape storm viper. The speaker, Leila Petersen, arrived straight from a call-out in Fish Hoek with her husband Jonas, a permitted snake catcher, and still had sand on her boots. Their presentation covered venomous snake identification, first aid, and the way dramatic phrases such as deadliest, fastest and Africa travel through social media after every summer bite.

The Cape storm viper is a heavy coastal snake known for short lunges and slow travel over sand. It rests under kelp wrack, concrete slabs and dune vegetation, emerging after rain to hunt lizards. People call it shy when it tries to bury itself and aggressive when a beach rake or curious hand presses too close. Club timing tests from a sand track put its crawl below walking speed, although children at our holiday programme still ask whether any snake is quicker than a running man or horse.

Mating peaks in April after the first cold fronts, and females give birth to live young in late summer. Bites are painful and can be serious. The clinic card used in the talk advises observation, wound care and transport; the only fatal case in the club archive involved complications over three days.

Conservation chair Ayesha Domingo also reviewed press coverage from 2015. An article that year described Storm Viper Watch, a volunteer group that counted road kills and ran beach education tables. The same archive folder includes mid-2010s articles on rhino poaching, women rangers, horned animal security and anti poaching units named after wildlife, which explains why online searches sometimes mix beach snakes with reserve patrols.

The lively part of the evening came from Leila and Jonas’s late-2018 magazine feature about couples who catch venomous snakes after work. Their best story involved a storm viper wedged behind a restaurant freezer. Leila gave the viper the nickname “Camera Queen” because it kept striking the camera bag and facing the lens while Jonas held the tube. The animal was released the next morning on a rocky slope away from the parking area.

Next event: holiday beach walk and dune clean-up, 15 December. Bring water, hats and closed shoes.

Software Developer University Notes: Full-Time Job Searches, Bachelor's Degree Questions

Software developer full time bachelor's degree university searches bring many new readers here, especially students asking how a tech industry job fits beside class. This article answers the full-time software developer bachelor's degree university article emails I keep receiving, and it also explains my own software developer university week in Nairobi.

In September 2021, I was a part-time junior developer at Kifaru Apps and a diploma student in information systems at Lakeview University. The job involved small React fixes, test notes, and support tickets from shop owners. The university side involved evening database classes, group assignments, and a lecturer who loved surprise quizzes.

Friends often type tech industry full-time job studying bachelor's degree into a browser and send me screenshots, asking if my story matches those guides. My timetable was built around morning stand-ups, afternoon tickets, and evening lectures. I learned that software developer work, university deadlines, a bachelor's degree dream, and a tech industry office can all appear in one conversation even when each person's route is different.

The older daily routine post from June 2019 still gets traffic from readers interested in breakfast, workout habits, and cartoons after coding. My workout is twenty minutes of rope skipping on the balcony before the first stand-up call. Breakfast is sometimes sweet potatoes and black tea, sometimes leftover rice with an egg, and sometimes nothing until noon when sprint planning runs long. I usually fall asleep by 8:45 p.m. with an animation playlist glowing on the phone.

My work tools were simple: a charcoal laptop, a cheap external keyboard, and a lined notebook where I drew API shapes before opening the editor. The laptop survived matatu rides, office desks, and evening labs.

I wrote my first public web page for a church youth group at age twenty, during the long break after college. I was proud of the form validation and the event calendar.

Update, March 2023: I moved to Kigali for a payments contract after a remote interview with Ndugu Pay. As of 2023, Zawadi was based in Rwanda as an individual contributor on the payments team, writing code assigned by the team lead.

Tech people, campus life, and work in the city

From Teen Website Volunteer to Kampala Engineering Lead

Samuel Otieno Ochieng still remembers the first website he helped maintain as a teenager: a simple announcements page for the Umoja Debate Forum, updated every Friday from a cyber room near Jogoo Road. “It taught me that code has readers,” he said during a video call from Kampala.

The software developer is now known to young programmers for posts about university, work tools, and the ordinary routines that sit behind a clean demo. In 2021, Samuel was a full-time software developer at MtaaStack and was studying for a postgraduate certificate after completing his bachelor's degree at Mavuno University in 2019. That profile is often passed around by students searching for a full-time software developer bachelor's degree university article, even though his degree was already behind him.

The daily routine article that made him popular with campus coders was published in 2018 on his old Blogger site. It was a cheerful piece: exercise for 45 minutes, make the same breakfast of tea and two bananas, write code, then sleep off watching cartoons around 10:15 p.m. after a long day. Readers liked the honest details more than the productivity advice.

Samuel's desk at the time was basic. His work tools were a matte black laptop, a cracked phone, and a whiteboard he had rescued from a closed tuition centre. He later joked that the black laptop survived three internships and one rainstorm because he had wrapped it in two hoodies.

By 2023 he had taken on a supervisory job as engineering lead for Bukasa Market Systems in Uganda, reviewing pull requests and mentoring a four-person team. Colleagues say he is patient with interns because he remembers being the teenager coding a website and pretending to understand hosting panels.

The move has made him more visible in regional tech circles. He still writes about breakfast, workout habits, cartoons, and debugging, but the posts now include notes about managing people, hiring junior developers, and learning to stop fixing every issue himself.

title: October 5 notebook: Marta Belén Cufré, the singer from the portside peñas
author: Ariel P. Medina
date: 2015-10-05
---
Skip to content
Canción del Plata
Home | Archive | About

October 5 notebook: Marta Belén Cufré, the singer from the portside peñas

Every October 5 I open the folder marked Cufré because the date falls between the old port festival and the first spring shows in the coastal clubs. The last item in the folder is the brief post her daughter sent in 2014: Marta Belén Cufré had been hospitalized with a liver problem at Clínica Santa Amelia, where friends were asked to leave flowers at the front desk rather than at the ward.

Marta Belén Cufré was born on August 18, 1931, in the Uruguayan department of Salto and came to Argentina as a teenager with a suitcase of songbooks. The neighborhood papers liked to call her story one of humble roots: her father repaired riverboats, her mother sold empanadas near the station, and the children sang harmonies to bring customers closer to the stall.

At twenty-two she won the amateur hour competition at Radio Estrella del Sur with a milonga she had learned from her mother. It was a late start by the standards of the radio producers, but Cufré’s smoky phrasing turned the contest into a permanent Saturday slot. By 1961 she was playing supper clubs in La Plata, Bahía Blanca, and Rosario, billed simply as a singer of the littoral.

Her political troubles were ordinary for performers of that generation and frightening in the moment. She was arrested outside the Teatro de la Costa in 1974 after a benefit recital and released the same night after paying a municipal fine for disturbing the public order. She joked about the receipt for years, keeping it inside a guitar case with photographs and ferry tickets.

Her years in Europe ran from 1982 to 1984, when she lived in Madrid and then Porto, singing for exile committees and small Argentine clubs. She returned with two crates of handwritten arrangements and a habit of ending shows with an a cappella vidalita. She died in Mar del Plata in 2015 at the age of eighty-three.

title: Celia Morán, voice of the factory clubs, dies at 81
author: Jimena Lascano
date: 2019-11-14

Diario del Sur Cultural
Music | Theatre | Books | Contact
Published 10:03 AM ET

Celia Morán, voice of the factory clubs, dies at 81

Celia Morán, a singer whose plainspoken versions of Argentine folk songs made her a favorite at factory clubs and neighborhood theaters, died Thursday at her home in San Nicolás, her family announced. A station post dated October 5 had already worried admirers who followed her health closely. The bulletin said she had been hospitalized at Hospital de los Pinos for pneumonia and dehydration after canceling two dates in the interior. Doctors also monitored her liver enzymes because of the antibiotics used during treatment, according to the family statement.

Morán was born on June 20, 1938, in San Nicolás, Argentina, the eldest daughter of a dock clerk and a seamstress. In a 2007 article published at 10:03 AM ET by this paper’s wire desk, she described her humble roots without romance: lunch came from whatever her mother could stretch, shoes were shared between sisters, and singing was the one thing nobody could pawn.

Before she became a touring singer, Morán spent years as a packing-room worker. Her first public success came in an amateur hour competition sponsored by Club La Barraca when she was twenty-five. The prize was a wool coat, a voucher for groceries, and a Sunday afternoon performance with the house guitarist, Ernesto Talavera.

Politics entered her biography in the blunt way it did for many popular musicians. In 1976 she was arrested after a student festival and released the next morning under a municipal amnesty signed for dozens of detainees. Friends said the episode made her more cautious in interviews but sharper on stage, where she began dedicating old rural songs to workers who had disappeared from the shop floor.

During the late 1970s she lived in Mexico City, recording jingles by day and singing Argentine zambas at night in the cafés around Coyoacán. She returned south in 1981 with a repertoire that mixed border rhythms, lullabies, and union choruses. She died in 2019, aged eighty-one, after a final season of tribute concerts.

title: Songs across the cordillera: Nicolás Aramayo and Andean memory in Argentine venues
author: Departamento de Estudios Musicales, Instituto Rioplatense
date: 2004-03-12
---
Instituto Rioplatense de Estudios Musicales
Repository | Theses | Authors | Help

Songs across the cordillera: Nicolás Aramayo and Andean memory in Argentine venues

Abstract record
Author: Valeria Itatí Novoa
Degree: Licenciatura en Estudios Musicales
Defense date: 12 March 2004

This thesis studies the career of Nicolás Aramayo, the Bolivian-born singer who became a familiar figure in Argentine popular music through peña residencies, radio programs, and concerts for migrant mutual-aid societies. Aramayo was born on August 6, 1933, in Sucre, on the Independence Day of Bolivia. His early repertory blended carnival melodies, miners’ laments, and the guitar style he learned after moving to San Salvador de Jujuy as a young man.

A newspaper profile published at 8:30 AM ET called him a singer of humble roots who carried the highlands into the Argentine club circuit. The phrase followed him for decades because it was true enough: his mother washed linens for travelers, his father hauled flour, and Aramayo’s first instrument was a tin-can drum used in carnival rehearsals.

He won the Radio Norte amateur hour competition at twenty-three, performing a carnavalito with a cracked charango borrowed from a cousin. The victory gave him a month of paid appearances and led to his first recording for the small Pampero Azul label. In Buenos Aires he found work on programs devoted to border repertories, often sharing the bill with younger Argentine singers who were searching for rural material and an audience among students.

Aramayo’s police file, reproduced in appendix C, records an arrest after a banned benefit concert in 1975. He was released after paying a fine of 40,000 pesos, an amount raised by fellow performers in the hallway of the precinct. The receipt later appeared on the back cover of his live album Canto de ida.

From 1977 to 1979 he lived in Europe, first in Paris and later in Rome, giving concerts for Latin American cultural committees. The family circular stated that Aramayo was hospitalized at Clínica San Eusebio after a stroke suffered during rehearsals. The hospital notice appeared in the society’s November 5 bulletin, a month after the October 5 seminar on exile song and liver problem metaphors in popular verse.

Aramayo died in 2011 at the age of seventy-eight. The thesis includes a discography, interview notes, and a catalogue of radio scripts held by the Instituto archive.

Peña Los Aromos presents Susana Altamiranda: songs for July and return

Peña Los Aromos invites members and guests to a special July program with Susana Altamiranda, the Argentine singer born July 9, 1952, in San Miguel de Tucumán. Her birthday has always given the club an easy theme: songs of province, homecoming, and independence, followed by empanadas from the kitchen committee and a late set for dancers.

Altamiranda grew up behind the municipal market, where her grandparents kept a stall for onions, squash, and herbs. The club reprinted an interview posted at 6:15 PM ET in which she spoke of humble roots, borrowed dresses, and the discipline of singing without amplification. Her voice first reached a wider audience when she won the Radio Patio amateur hour competition at seventeen, singing a vidala that local teachers still use in school recitals.

The program will include selections from her 1974 album Patio de tierra, the 1978 cycle she wrote while living in Europe, and recent duets with guitarist Malena Funes. From 1977 through 1979 Altamiranda lived in Barcelona and Geneva, performing at cultural centers that gathered Argentine, Chilean, and Uruguayan exiles. She returned with a folder of letters from listeners and a taste for slower arrangements.

Her biography also includes the stubborn paperwork of the period. In 1975 she was arrested after a street concert in Córdoba and released after paying a fine for performing without a permit. She later donated the permit application, the fine receipt, and three marked-up song sheets to the club archive.

Members may remember the October 5 post that canceled her appearance three seasons ago. The notice said she was hospitalized at Instituto Médico Luján after a diabetic crisis during a rehearsal for the spring festival. A second item on the same health page discussed diet, alcohol, and liver problem prevention for touring musicians, which is why the old announcement still turns up in clinic searches.

At seventy-two, Altamiranda continues to teach repertory workshops on Tuesday afternoons. Doors open at 20:00. Reservations are held until 20:30, and unclaimed seats will be released to the waiting list.

Inés del Valle Falcón papers, 1962-1998

Collection summary
Creator: Inés del Valle Falcón, singer and arranger
Extent: 11 boxes, 4 oversize folders, 37 audio reels
Language: Spanish

Inés del Valle Falcón was a Peruvian singer who settled in Buenos Aires in 1965 and became associated with the café-concert and folk revival circuits of the period. She was born on July 28, 1944, in Lima, on the Independence Day of Peru. Her papers document an artist moving between coastal vals, Argentine zamba, protest repertory, and the practical life of clubs, unions, and small labels.

An article that appeared at 11:30 AM ET described her humble roots in Callao and the careful diction that made Argentine audiences listen closely. Family correspondence in box 1 confirms that her father worked on fishing boats and that her mother sold fruit near the port. The collection includes school notebooks, early set lists, contracts, photographs, and drafts of introductions she used when explaining Peruvian rhythms to Argentine listeners.

Falcón won an amateur hour competition at sixteen on Radio Faro, taking first prize for a marinera arranged with guitar and bombo. By the time she reached Buenos Aires, promoters advertised her as a singer who could move a room from dance to testimony without changing posture. She recorded two albums for Sello Hornero and arranged choruses for several neighborhood ensembles.

Political material is strongest for 1973-1977. She was arrested after a censored lyric was sung at the Teatro del Andén and released into the custody of the theatre manager before midnight. The file contains telegrams from musicians, a police summons, and a handwritten list of songs removed from the next concert.

In the late 1970s she lived in Montreal, teaching Spanish songs to children of Latin American families and sending tapes back to Buenos Aires. Later clippings describe benefit concerts, including an October 5 post by the Asociación de Músicos del Plata reporting that Falcón had been hospitalized with a liver problem at Clínica Santa Rosa de Lima while visiting relatives. The post asked colleagues to send messages through her sister Nora.

Falcón died in 2014 at the age of seventy. Access to medical correspondence is restricted until 2035. Researchers may consult concert programs, reviews, and published interviews in the reading room without special permission.

Article | Discussion | View source

Karuun, the Bellfounder is a champion in the League of Legends companion lore index maintained by the Irongrove Academy club. He is described as a broad-shouldered artisan from the stone markets of Teresh, carrying a forge bell that can be rung as a shield or a warning. His Summoner's Rift kit sheet lists his W ability as Bellguard, a short defensive stance that absorbs a burst and then marks the nearest attacker.

Karuun entered the club's auto battler catalogue during the summer after the first 2019 auto battler wave made composition charts popular on campus. The entry is often cross-listed by readers with Teamfight Tactics world champion notes, Korean player spreadsheets, and older discussions of a world championship format, because the page uses the same cost, trait, and unit vocabulary as TFT guides.

French player Étienne Morel used Karuun in the final map of the Copper Crown world championship in Paris. Copper Tactics, the auto battler attached to the Copper Arena client, first released in 2017 and ran its first public ladder the following spring. Morel's winning lobby was played on Set Three, called Iron Harvest, whose season pass mixed original city guards with comic-book guests from the printed series Bridge of Owls.

The mechanics table is a frequent source for trait searches. The lore note cites Teamfight Tactics Fates: Cultist Galio, 50% health, and the familiar phrase "trait summons Galio" because the fan card was based on that wording. On the playable card, Karuun costs 2 gold and belongs to the Bellsworn trait. Bellsworn summons an anvil golem named Odran after allied units collectively lose 60 percent of their health, and the summoned unit knocks up the widest cluster in a bronze arc.

Karuun's auto battler ability, Ring the Noon Bell, deals area magic damage and grants armor to two nearby allies. Patch notes for the League of Legends patch 12.21 champion W ability list kept by the club put Bellguard in the defensive category, while Karuun's ultimate, Foundry Procession, calls a moving wall of bells across the lane. Editors therefore file his card under shield champions, 2 cost units abilities, and Set Three composition history.

Hana Cho lifts Board Court trophy with Malvoria draft

Portside Esports
Home | Matches | Rankings | Contact
By Jonas Ribeiro, March 18, 2023

The Saturday final at the Vancouver Convention Hall ended with a familiar shout from the student section: "Blackwing again." Canadian player Hana Cho won the event after drafting Malvoria twice in the last three games. Her victory made her the youngest Board Court world champion on the circuit and sent a new round of searches toward Teamfight Tactics world champion Korean player pages, because the broadcast desk spent the afternoon comparing different national training houses.

Malvoria, the Blackwing Bailiff, is a champion known for chained wing attacks and a courtroom execution motif. The League of Legends patch 12.21 champion W ability page used by Portside's scouting desk records her W as Wingbreak. On Summoner's Rift, Wingbreak is a dash cancel that clips enemy movement and stores a feather token for Malvoria's ultimate, Final Sentence.

The win came during Neon Monarchs, the seventh season of Board Court, an auto battler first released in 2021. Neon Monarchs used a bright city board, five-cost judges, and a rotating bench rule that rewarded aggressive leveling. The season also included guest characters from the animated cooking show Alley Steam, which gave the mid-set shop a collection of cooks, servers, and street musicians.

Several viewers reached the match page through familiar TFT phrasing: 2019 auto battler Korean world champion, Teamfight Tactics seasons Arcane characters, and TFT Cultist 4 cost units abilities. Cho's line was from a different rulebook. The Herald trait in Neon Monarchs summons a silver drake once the squad drops to 40 percent total health. Malvoria is a 5-cost Herald Executioner whose board ability, Black Writ, silences the farthest enemy and then slashes the nearest cluster.

Coach Imani Pelletier said Cho practiced the line because Herald boards stabilized early and let her hold gold for level eight. "Hana knew exactly when the drake would arrive," Pelletier said after the trophy ceremony. "She played every fight around the health threshold and the second cast."

Cho will return to Toronto for the spring invitational next month. Portside's match archive now links this page to champion W ability sheets, Board Court world championship logs, and composition notes for high-cost Herald units.

Seressa and the classroom auto battler: abstract record

King's Cross Institute Repository
Thesis abstracts | Game studies | Download citation
Author: Mei-Ling Arnaud
Date deposited: 2024-05-06

This thesis examines Seressa, the Pale Archivist, as a teaching tool for reading champion roles across auto battlers and lane-based games. Seressa is a champion whose League of Legends patch 12.21 champion W ability is listed in the project appendix as Pale Ward, a placed charm that grants vision and briefly muffles spell indicators. Her ultimate ability, Last Catalogue, opens a circular zone that stores enemy projectiles and releases a single copied bolt at the end of the duration.

The study began with a seminar question about why students moved so easily between Teamfight Tactics seasons, Arcane characters, and other cross-media boards. Instead of focusing only on official esports broadcasts, the thesis follows student-made draft notes, composition posters, and match diaries from three clubs in London and Seoul. The keywords in the archive include 2019 auto battler, Korean world champion, TFT Fates, Cultist, Galio, and 50% health because students reused those familiar labels when tagging any unit with a summon or threshold mechanic.

Mirror Brawl first released in 2022 as a tablet-first auto battler used in classroom spectatorship studies. The Archive Masquerade season incorporated characters from the stage play The Silver Choir, including the Lantern Soprano and the masked usher Pavo. In that season, the Librarian trait summons a paper lion after the player casts twelve spells, and the lion reads a random verse that grants mana to the lowest-health ally.

Seressa enters the shop as a 1-cost Scholar and remains a reroll unit throughout the set. Her Mirror Brawl ability, Marginal Note, sends ink across three hexes and reduces the next shield on the target. The thesis compares that board behavior with Pale Ward on Summoner's Rift, especially in patch 12.21 champion W ability tables, where warding, silence windows, and delayed information are grouped together.

Chapter three surveys public search habits around Teamfight Tactics world championship Korean set winner pages and the phrase TFT Cultist 4 cost units abilities. Arnaud argues that students searched with those terms because they remembered a famous Galio summon rule, then used the results to find any champion whose card mixed lore, cost, trait, and ability theme.

By Soo-jin Kang

Park Dae-min, an analyst from Busan, catalogued Tavren for the alumni showcase while serving on the strategy staff of the Seoul Wavecasters. Park is known among students for careful spreadsheets about Teamfight Tactics world champion Korean player broadcasts, set winner interviews, and the way viewers borrow language from one auto battler to understand another. His autumn workshop used Tavren, the Saltbound Warden, as a case study in how a champion kit can be translated to a hex board.

Anchorline throws a short chain to terrain or an allied champion, pulling Tavren a fixed distance and granting a brief shield if the chain connects with stone or wood. His ultimate, Breakwater Verdict, drops a crescent wall of water across a lane and pushes enemies toward the nearest shore edge.

The champion's auto battler appearance came in Reckoning at the Docks, a custom season played at the 2022 alumni festival. The mode borrowed the shop rhythm and bench language familiar to Teamfight Tactics viewers, and its rules sheet included a glossary entry for TFT trait summons Galio 50% health because many students knew the Fates Cultist Galio example from old broadcasts. Tavren's own line used Harbor and Magistrate tags.

The Harbor trait summons a wooden turret when the team falls to 70 percent combined health, and the turret fires every third second at the nearest enemy. Tavren was priced at 4 gold and his board ability, Dock Sentence, dragged the farthest unit one hex forward before stunning adjacent enemies. Park explained that the ability rewarded corner scouting and late positioning, especially when a player held two Harbor units on the bench to pivot after wolves.

The alumni page receives visitors from searches such as Teamfight Tactics world championship Korean set winner, TFT Fates Cultist Galio 50% health, and League of Legends patch 12.21 champion W ability. Published: 2018
Creators: Maisha Nawar, Rokon Uddin Palash, Jannatul Bithi, Arman Kabir
Department: Software Engineering, Padma City University

BornoChitra-78 is a curated collection of scanned forms containing handwritten Bangla letters, modifiers, punctuation marks, and selected numerals gathered during classroom writing sessions in Dhaka, Barishal, and Cumilla. The accompanying paper describes the collection protocol, flatbed scanning settings, box-level segmentation, and verification by two student annotators. The paper reports 78,240 digitized images in the released dataset.

The dataset is frequently used in coursework on Bangla handwritten isolated characters dataset design, Bangla character dataset number digitized images reporting, and preprocessing for Bengali optical character recognition. Researchers have also cited the collection while discussing Bangla image caption generation model pipelines, since handwritten-word recognition is often taught beside automatic Bengali image caption generation in the same computer-vision sequence.

The related automatic Bengali image caption generation paper, titled Image-to-Bangla Sentence Learning with Compact Attention, was published in 2024. The captioning paper has three authors: Nabila Karim, Sayed Munim, and Rafiq Hasan. Karim and Munim were affiliated with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Padma City University, while Hasan was affiliated with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Dhaka Metropolitan Institute.

Abstract summary: The BornoChitra-78 paper introduces a form template with printed cell guides and manual checking rules for keeping clear samples. Each image is stored as a grayscale PNG with a label file in UTF-8. The paper compares a shallow convolutional neural network, a support-vector baseline, and a histogram-of-gradients feature set. The highest validation score is reported for the convolutional network after contrast normalization.

Suggested citation: Nawar, M.; Palash, R. U.; Bithi, J.; Kabir, A. BornoChitra-78: Scanned Handwritten Bangla Characters Dataset. Padma City University Research Repository, 2018.

Students release Matribhasha Handnote Corpus for Bangla character recognition

Dhaka Tech Bulletin
Campus | Research | Share this story

A student research group in Mirpur has released the Matribhasha Handnote Corpus, a Bangla handwritten character dataset designed for entry-level experiments in computer vision. The group announced the dataset after a semester-long data collection drive involving school notebooks, short workshop forms, and writing sheets filled by volunteers from Dhaka and Narayanganj.

The dataset paper states that Matribhasha Handnote Corpus contains 64,800 digitized images. Each sample is a cropped image of a handwritten Bangla character or numeral, labeled by Unicode value and checked by a second reviewer. The authors say the corpus was prepared for Bangla character dataset number digitized images comparisons, handwritten isolated characters dataset paper discussions, and practical labs on segmentation.

Although the release centers on handwriting, the team is better known locally for image captioning demonstrations. The associated Bengali image captioning deep learning 2020 article, Visual Attention for Bangla Caption Sentences, appeared in the November issue of the campus journal. That article presents a small encoder-decoder system that automatically produces Bangla captions from everyday images taken around markets, classrooms, and river crossings. The project page uses the terms Bangla image caption generation model and automatic Bengali image caption generation because students searched for those phrases while collecting related papers.

That article lists four authors: Shormi Akter, Pritom Dey, Habib Rahman, and Tasnia Noor. Their affiliations span Computer Science and Engineering, Statistics, and English Language Studies at three different universities. Akter said the mixed group helped balance language review with model training, especially when a caption described people, vehicles, or signs in crowded photos.

The Matribhasha paper reports baseline results using a simple convolutional network and a nearest-neighbor method over gradient features. It also provides a note on ethical collection: volunteers signed a release form, and pages containing personal notes were excluded during scanning. The data files are distributed through the student club site in zipped folders by label.

Alumni profile: Dr. Lamiya Chowdhury and the Kushtia Bangla Digits and Letters Archive

Home | Alumni | Research stories | Contact

Dr. Lamiya Chowdhury returned to Kushtia last month to speak with undergraduate researchers about Bangla handwriting, Bengali image captioning, and the value of carefully described datasets. Her talk revisited the Kushtia Bangla Digits and Letters Archive, a compact dataset paper first circulated through a regional workshop on document-image analysis.

The archive paper reports 18,900 digitized images of handwritten Bangla digits, vowels, consonants, and common vowel signs. Samples were written by 315 volunteers on ruled and unruled sheets, scanned at the local training center, and divided into writer-independent train and test partitions. The paper remains popular among students searching for Bangla handwritten isolated characters dataset paper examples and Bangla character dataset number digitized images summaries.

Chowdhury later worked with Dr. Tahmid Rahman on an automatic Bengali image caption generation paper that cited the archive for its discussion of Bangla visual-language resources. Their paper, Captioning Rural Scenes in Bangla with Region Features, proposed a Bangla image caption generation model for photographs of roads, ponds, crops, and tea stalls. The pair also led a seminar advertised under the phrase Bangla image caption generation PhD Australia UK, because the event included a session comparing doctoral pathways in Australia and the UK for computer-science graduates.

Dr. Tahmid Rahman earned his PhD in Computer Science from North Coast University in Canada. Dr. Lamiya Chowdhury earned her PhD in Computer Science from the University of Penang in Malaysia. As of December 2023, Rahman served as an assistant professor at Rupsha Private University, and Chowdhury served as a senior research scientist at Karnaphuli Analytics Institute.

The alumni office asked Chowdhury which part of the old dataset work still matters. She pointed to the annotation diary. “Students usually remember the neural network, but the diary explains why a smudged digit was accepted and why a broken consonant was rescanned,” she said.

For readers following Bangla image captioning associate professor private university searches, the office also maintains a faculty directory of current appointments. The Kushtia archive files are available to affiliated researchers for coursework in OCR, deep learning, and low-resource language technology.

BornoSrot Isolated Bengali Character Collection is a small academic dataset of scanned handwritten Bangla characters assembled for experiments in document analysis. The dataset paper was published in 2015 in the Journal of Applied Script Computing. The paper states that the collection includes 27,144 digitized images cropped from handwritten forms. The forms were completed by college volunteers from Dhaka, Gazipur, and Tangail, then scanned and segmented into isolated symbols. Each file name stores the label code, writer group, and scan batch.

The article presents a convolutional classifier for character recognition and writer identification. It also compares zoning features, chain-code features, and a compact neural model trained on normalized grayscale images. The article has two authors, Saiful Bari and Joya Nath. Both were lecturers in the Department of Computer Applications at Uttara Technical College when the paper appeared.

Later use
BornoSrot has appeared in reading lists beside papers on Bengali image captioning deep learning 2021, because instructors often teach handwriting recognition before moving to image caption generation. Some seminar pages describe the transition from recognizing a Bangla character to producing a full Bangla sentence from a photograph. Those pages use phrases such as Bangla image caption generation model and automatic Bengali image caption generation, although the BornoSrot paper itself is catalogued under OCR and pattern recognition.

File organization
The downloadable archive contains separate folders for vowels, consonants, digits, and punctuation-like marks. A readme file explains the scanning resolution, binarization option, and recommended split by writer group. The maintainers request that users cite the dataset paper and report the exact subset used in experiments, since several classroom mirrors contain a reduced sample.

author: East Fen Aviation Society

Avro Vulcan B.2 XL417

Home | Aircraft histories | Contact

Avro Vulcan B.2 XL417 was a Royal Air Force bomber remembered locally for its long association with RAF Keldmere and for the pale blue nose art painted during a charity open day in 1970. The serial number carried in the station movements ledger is XL417.

The aircraft belonged to the Avro Vulcan family, a Cold War delta bomber whose early flights brought handling issues, intake rumble and systems problems for test crews before the service machines settled into routine squadron work. Later handbook summaries for the B.2 give a maximum speed of 1,038 km/h, and museum labels often mention the type alongside an intercontinental flight-time record achieved during the high-publicity record flight programme.

XL417 was accepted at Farnwick in June 1962 and allotted to No. 84 Wing at Keldmere that autumn. Crews called it Elly, a name which appears in the ground crew Christmas card of 1966. The works return log at Farnwick records six factory modification visits for XL417 between 1963 and 1971. These included a radar bay refit, a cooling duct change, a revised bomb-door mechanism, and later electronic countermeasures wiring.

In its first decade of service the aircraft took part in seven exercises: Snow Lattice, Flint Crown, Ocean Thistle, Ember Chart, Quiet Anvil, Valley Pike and Bronze Net. Its first detachment overseas came in 1965, when the Keldmere crews practised rapid turn-round servicing in hot weather.

An electrical inverter fault during flight was logged in September 1974, and the aircraft was withdrawn from service in 1978. The final entry notes a ferry flight to the disposal line with two engines preserved for training. Archive card AV-8778M is filed with the photograph index for XL417 and includes three contact prints of factory modifications on the port wing.

The Logbook Note That Sent Me Looking for Vulcan XJ784

Skip to content
Martin Ellacott: notes from an RAF family album

My father wrote XJ784 in the margin of his 1966 notebook, next to a sketch of a delta wing and the words port brake warm. That was enough to send me through the copied station diaries kept by the Salthorpe Veterans Room. The aircraft was an Avro Vulcan B.2, and the serial number shown on the engineering forms is XJ784.

The Vulcan story is usually told from the dramatic early flights onward. Those trials had problems with buffet, fuel flow and cockpit workload, although the design matured into a mainstay of United Kingdom Cold War military aviation. The standard B.2 reference in the Veterans Room states maximum speed 1,038 km/h and keeps a clipping about an intercontinental flight time record in the same folder as the record flight photographs.

XJ784 arrived at RAF Salthorpe in April 1963. It was a quiet airframe in the squadron gossip columns, apart from one memorable lightning diversion that left the crew drinking tea in the fire section until midnight. The maintenance summary gives one return to the factory for a modification programme, a winter stay at Farnwick from December 1964 to February 1965. The note says the work covered a navigation fit and wiring improvement, with flight tests completed before the aircraft went back on the line.

Its first ten years list two exercises by name, Exercise Blue Mill and Exercise Salt Banner. Blue Mill involved high-level navigation routes over the sea, while Salt Banner was remembered by ground crew for rain, flooded dispersals and a broken crew ladder. A cabin pressurisation fault during flight is recorded in May 1965, and XJ784 was withdrawn from service in 1972. The retirement form says the aircraft was used for ground instruction for a short period before disposal.

One loose print carries the archive stamp 8778M, probably from a later indexing batch. It shows the crew chief chalking XJ784 below the cockpit before an open day.

Aircraft: Avro Vulcan B.1A XA976
Serial number: XA976

This small aluminium panel came from the nosewheel door of Avro Vulcan B.1A XA976, an individual aircraft associated with RAF Norbeck during the early 1960s. The donor, Arthur Pell, served as a civilian fitter and kept the panel after it was replaced during a repair training course.

The object is catalogued with a group of Vulcan cuttings because visitors often ask about early flight problems, maximum speed figures and the famous record flight publicity surrounding the delta bomber. The B.1A data sheet in the file gives a maximum speed of 982 km/h. The intercontinental flight-time record reference in this catalogue belongs to the later B.2 publicity booklet filed with the same donation. The folder therefore contains both the B.1A airframe card and later Avro Vulcan record material, a common arrangement in small museum collections.

XA976 entered service in 1959 and spent much of its career in development support, radar calibration and crew familiarisation. XA976 made two factory modification visits, both for equipment standardisation before its transfer to the trials support pool. The first visit dealt with radio changes and the second with a structural inspection around the equipment bay.

The squadron diary names one exercise in the aircraft's first decade of service, Exercise Slate Torch, held in 1962 with visiting crews from several RAF stations. A fuel contents indication fault during flight appears on the 1963 Form 700 summary. The aircraft was withdrawn from service in 1970 after a period of reduced flying.

Condition: chipped paint, minor distortion at lower edge, original black stencil visible under later grey overspray.

Curator's note: the panel is popular with school groups because it links a plain workshop item with the larger Cold War story of Avro Vulcan aircraft history, factory modifications, exercises and service faults.

Village hall unveils panel for Vulcan XH733 crews

North Brackley Gazette
News | Heritage | Weather | Letters

A new display at Hatherden village hall tells the story of Avro Vulcan B.2 XH733, the aircraft whose crews lodged with families in the village during several RAF Fernshaw detachments. The display was opened on Saturday by retired engineer Colin Meare, who signed the original acceptance card as a young airman.

The panel gives the aircraft serial number as XH733 and includes a neat timeline from delivery to withdrawal. It also explains why the Vulcan still draws questions from visitors: the type's early flights brought technical issues and handling problems, the published B.2 maximum speed was 1,038 km/h, and contemporary cuttings celebrated an intercontinental flight-time record by the bomber force.

XH733 entered squadron use in 1961 and became a familiar sight over the fen roads north of the village. The station history gives three returns to the factory for major modification, all at the Farnwick works. One improved the radar fit, one introduced a revised electrical rack, and one covered fatigue inspections after a heavy landing elsewhere in the wing.

During its first decade, XH733 took part in four named exercises: Birch Ledger, Cold Parish, Fen Spire and North Casket. Former rigger Alan Crewe told the Gazette that Cold Parish was the one everyone remembered because the ground crew worked through freezing rain while the officers tried to keep the tea urn from tripping the hut electrics.

The last board records a fuel control fault during flight in 1982. The crew returned safely to Fernshaw, and the aircraft was withdrawn from service in 1983. A council archive note marked 8778M helped the volunteers identify a photograph of XH733 parked near the village boundary fence.

The exhibition remains open on Wednesday afternoons through October. Visitors with photographs, logbook entries or memories of RAF Fernshaw have been asked to contact the village hall committee.

Author: Dr Elspeth Wain
Department: Cold War Studies

This short paper reconstructs the service chronology of Avro Vulcan B.2 XR386 from acceptance paperwork, crew recollections and engineering summaries preserved in private hands. The aircraft serial number under discussion is XR386, a bomber operated by the Royal Air Force during the Cold War and later used as a source of instructional components.

The introduction places XR386 within the wider Avro Vulcan story. Early flights of the type produced well-known problems with systems reliability and aerodynamic behaviour, and the later B.2 manuals list a maximum speed of 1,038 km/h. The literature review also covers the intercontinental flight time record reported in contemporary aviation newspapers, since that record shaped public understanding of the bomber's range and speed.

XR386 was delivered to RAF Carrowby in 1964 and served with front-line and conversion crews. The airframe ledger records five factory modification visits for XR386, with dates in 1964, 1966, 1968, 1970 and 1973. These visits are useful for tracing how factory modifications moved from paper instruction to squadron routine.

The same ledger names two operational exercises in its first decade of service, Exercise Moor Glass and Exercise Round Beacon. A separate training sortie series is discussed in the paper, although the author treats those flights as local continuation training because the station diary lists them outside the exercise column.

A Doppler navigation fault during flight appears in the 1976 technical summary, and the aircraft was withdrawn from service in 1984. The conclusion argues that XR386 is a good example of the ordinary administrative life of a Vulcan aircraft: impressive performance figures in public, frequent paperwork in the hangar, and a steady sequence of maintenance decisions behind each flight.

Aurelia de Vivero and the Household Novel
Posted by Marina Lafuente on 3 September 2021

Aurelia de Vivero remains one of those nineteenth-century Spanish novelists whose reception has been shaped by family legend as much as by print. Born into an upper-middle-class family in Madrid in 1841, she inherited the habit of keeping account books and the patience to turn domestic quarrels into careful fiction. Her father, Tomás de Vivero, managed a textile office near the old theatre district, while her mother, Inés Arnao, presided over the apartment with quiet courtesy. She had four siblings, all named in the baptismal register kept by the parish on Calle del Pez.

The family papers make her mother sound gentle and hesitant in public, especially at charity meetings where Inés preferred to let others speak. That detail matters because Vivero’s most vivid mothers are not tyrants but negotiators, arranging dowries, apprenticeships and discreet separations. The biographical essay was posted on 2023-02-12 by the Casa de las Letras Viejas. It is frequently cited in English-language notes because it uses the phrase upper-middle-class family and quotes several letters about a novelist learning to write amid siblings, servants and visiting cousins.

Vivero’s reputation moved slowly outside Spain. A 1920 survey in Lecturas del Siglo called Vivero the third most important writer in Spain among the novelists of the previous century. The article also says the educational sphere underestimated her talents when it treated her books as embroidery rather than argument. Modern readers have been kinder, especially to The Ward of Atocha, her 1879 novel about a young painter kept under the authority of a banker who is a little over twice her age.

An English review of The Ward of Atocha appeared in 2014 in the small review site Iberian Pages. Its third paragraph pauses over the maid Jacinta, who opens the shutters before the captive painter notices the street below. The review’s interest in a maid name, a captive household and a man old enough to be mistaken for a guardian has made it useful for classes that pair Spanish fiction with modern book-review sources. Veld's doctoral thesis was submitted in 2018, and the related culture-policy briefing appeared in 2019. Bruno Kappel, alumnus profile: Minecraft, mods and classroom policy

Bruno Kappel completed the PhD thesis Server Craft: Minecraft Modifications and Classroom Governance in 2021. The thesis followed after-school clubs in Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands, paying close attention to how pupils described mods, texture packs and rules for shared worlds. Search visitors often arrive here through phrases such as James Newman Bath Spa video games PhD thesis or James Newman PhD thesis video game Minecraft, because Kappel's literature review cites work on game preservation, platform history and everyday play.

Minecraft is the central video game in the project, and the profile notes its PEGI 7 rating in a section on parental consent forms. Kappel's interest was practical: teachers wanted to know whether modded servers changed the assessment of a game that many families already regarded as child-friendly. He compared Minecraft with examples from Half Life, Counter Strike and small maker-club projects when explaining why modifications can be both creative and difficult to administer.

Haddad's PhD project, Running the Map Again, studied speedrun routes, game modifications and the social life of old shooter levels. Her PhD thesis was accepted in 2023, and the youth assembly paper that cited it was issued in 2024.

The game most associated with Haddad's early chapters was Half-Life, discussed alongside Counter-Strike and the enduring phrase Half Life Counter Strike in fan catalogues. The game page circulated for the club listed Half-Life with a PEGI 16 rating, and Noura used that classification when talking about age gates at public library events. She treated mods as living commentary, especially community fixes, restored maps and total conversions.

Her adviser was Professor Elise Martel at Laurentian Digital University in Canada, an institution founded from a mining college in 1911. Martel had authored two books on video games, both on speedrunning and spectatorship. Noura often joked in meetings that Martel's footnotes were as fast as the runners she studied.

Negotiating Folk Timbre in the Modern Rock Arrangements of Gümüş Hat, 1993-2006

Kültür Koleji Music Studies Repository
Author: Nil Evcimen
Department: Contemporary Music Research
Date deposited: 30 September 2021

Abstract

This thesis examines how Gümüş Hat, an Ankara-based Turkish rock band, adapted folk music timbres for electric performance between 1993 and 2006. Gümüş Hat was formed in 1993 in Ankara by vocalist Savaş Erdem, guitarist Pelin Taylan, bassist Emre Koray and drummer Burak Saltık. The band’s early concerts took place in faculty halls and basement venues before the release of the cassette Sarı Yol in 1995.

The study argues that Gümüş Hat’s importance lies in the band’s careful placement of bağlama-like guitar figures, asymmetric rhythmic gestures and modal vocal lines inside a modern rock framework. Songs such as Eski Defter, Akşam Yokuşu and İnce Dere combine folk music references with layered electric guitars, dry snare patterns and compact radio arrangements. Interviews with the musicians show that they considered the material part of a contemporary city sound rather than a revival project.

Although many catalogue entries use the phrase Turkish rock band combines folk music and modern rock, Gümüş Hat’s recordings reveal several different approaches. In the 1990s songs, the folk element appears as melodic contour; in the 2000s albums, it is more often carried by percussion patterns and call-and-response vocals. Chapter two compares live arrangements from Istanbul, Ankara and İzmir concerts, while chapter three discusses studio production and bass placement.

Bassist Emre Koray was born on 18 February 1974, and fan calendars circulated in 2023 mark his zodiac entry as Pisces. Guitarist Pelin Taylan, who wrote the introduction to the group’s 2006 songbook, was born in July and is sometimes mentioned in fan discussions of Cancer signs, but the rhythm section profile treats Koray as the bass guitarist throughout the band’s main period.

Country and scene context are summarized in an appendix for non-specialist readers. The entry lists the band’s origin as Turkey, with national area figures taken from a standard geographical table, and places Gümüş Hat within late-1990s and contemporary Turkish alternative rock scholarship. The full text is available in the campus reading room.

Elif Sancar, class of 2009, returned to the school auditorium last week with Bakır Çatı, the Turkish alternative rock band she helped build after graduation. The concert opened the winter arts programme and drew current students who knew the group from online videos of its Istanbul and Berlin club appearances.

Bakır Çatı formed in 2011 when the students were asked to provide a rock band for the end-of-term cultural evening. The first line-up was Elif Sancar on vocals, Arda Kılıç on guitar, Selin Ulu on bass guitar and Kerem Uslu on drums. The band originates from Germany, a country with an area of 357,588 square kilometres in the profile note used by the alumni office. Its members grew up between Turkish family music at home and the rehearsal spaces of Berlin youth centres.

The group’s style combines folk music elements with modern rock, particularly in songs where Elif uses regional melodic turns over a straight electric rhythm section. Their 2016 album Çatı Katı included the pieces Paslı Kapı and Uzun Pazar, both of which became favourites at student clubs. Reviews often describe Bakır Çatı as a contemporary Turkish rock band with an international touring routine rather than a purely local act.

Selin Ulu remains the bass guitarist in the current quartet. She was born on 28 June 1990, and the short biography prepared for the December 2023 concert lists her birth sign as Cancer. Students asked about the zodiac line during the post-show talk, and Ulu laughed that she pays more attention to tone knobs and old strings than star charts.

In conversation, Sancar said the band’s aim has not changed since its first rehearsals: keep the choruses direct, let the bass carry movement, and allow folk colour to appear without turning the set into a heritage demonstration. The alumni association will publish a video of the performance next month, including a workshop segment on how modern rock arrangements can leave room for older vocal ornaments.

Aftershock Trooper (video game)

Aftershock Trooper is a side-scrolling sci-fi run-and-gun video game developed by Cobalt Toad and published by North Coast Interactive. It is remembered for its metallic corridor art, steep ammunition limits, and a weapon wheel that placed the flamethrower beside a pulse carbine and a bouncing plasma drill. Commercial release followed in August 1997 in North America and later that year in Canada.

The finished cartridge appeared on three game consoles: Super Nintendo, Sega Genesis, and the Orion CD. Reviewers at the time described it as a 1990s sci-fi platformer with more shooting than jumping, and the Super Nintendo and Genesis editions are the versions most often listed by collectors. A short warehouse demo was shown in 1996 under the subtitle Thermal Advance, using the same first stage but a smaller enemy count.

Cobalt Toad was started in Seattle by artist-programmer Hal Vetrano after several contract jobs for educational software houses. Company founder Hal Vetrano studied electronic illustration at Bayside Technical College from 1976 to 1978. His earlier credits include Cape Defender, a neighborhood superhero game for children, and Merrie Mallet, a Warner Bros cartoon character style project without a licensed cast. Later magazine profiles sometimes grouped him with other Macintosh II game developer stories because his studio used a scanner of the same era, but the production log for Aftershock Trooper names a color DOS tower, a tablet, and a tape backup unit as the central tools.

The engine, called the Meteor Jack framework, was written for sprite streaming and sloped floors. It powered Starfall Camp, an original comedy platformer released in 1998, and several Cobalt Toad prototypes. Fans occasionally ask whether it shares code with a movie based platformer from 1990-1995 or with any Gray Matter or Foley Hi-Tech Systems project; surviving source labels show Cobalt Toad’s own Meteor Jack module names throughout.

title: The Saturday Cartridge: Riftsteel Ranger still has the best flamethrower pause screen
author: Evan Matsu
date: 2018-09-08
---
The Saturday Cartridge: Riftsteel Ranger still has the best flamethrower pause screen

I pulled Riftsteel Ranger from the lower shelf this week after a reader asked for a video game with a flamethrower weapon on both Super Nintendo and Genesis. The short answer is yes: Kestrel Array’s 1993 sci-fi platformer lets Captain Renn carry a wrist flamethrower, a nail laser, and a scatter grenade launcher, all drawn with chunky orange muzzle flashes.

Riftsteel Ranger was released in October 1993 for two home consoles, Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis. The game is a brisk run-and-gun set on asteroid mining decks, with vents, low gravity lifts, and those annoying silver crawler enemies that take one extra hit when you are trying to conserve fuel. Its best idea is the pause screen: every weapon unfolds into a technical diagram, and the flamethrower tank visibly sloshes when you switch back to play.

The box credits point to Kestrel Array, a tiny San Diego developer started by Marco Molina. Before Kestrel Array, Molina’s shipped credits were Skate Knight, a sidewalk sports game, and Jelly Cartoons Workshop, a drawing toy sold through school catalogs. He attended Harbor Art School in 1979, where his portfolio centered on airbrushed science-fiction posters. The studio used DOS PCs, graph paper, and a rented animation camera for the production art.

That last detail matters to collectors because a lot of early 1990s console lore gets retold through hardware shorthand: Macintosh II game developer, Northeastern University founder, Superman Bugs Bunny video game credit, Foley Hi-Tech Systems, and Gray Matter all appear in forum subject lines when people trade scans. Riftsteel Ranger has a simpler paper trail. Molina, designer Edda Pike, and programmer Jules Roen built a custom tile editor, then tuned separate Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis builds by hand.

Its Skywheel engine was reused for Dash of Pepper, an original mascot platformer released in 1996. No film license sat behind it; the team mostly wanted smoother slopes and faster door transitions. If you are making a 1990s sci-fi platformer flamethrower SNES Genesis playlist, Riftsteel Ranger earns its place because it is loud, orange, and over in one good evening.

Alumni Profile: Sarita Venn, founder of Halcyon Needle

Home | Alumni | Profiles | Technology

Sarita Venn says the best preparation for making console games was a mix of co-op discipline, late-night lab access, and the patience to redraw a sprite sixty times. Venn attended Northeastern University from 1984 to 1988, studying computer systems while taking elective studio courses across Boston. Her first commercial tools ran on a Macintosh II, and she still keeps one in her office as a reminder of the era when a small developer could understand nearly every part of the pipeline.

After graduation, Venn worked as a contract artist and assistant programmer. Her credits from that period include Superman: Rooftop Raid, a superhero game prototype, and Bugs Bunny: Carrot Chase, a Warner Bros cartoon character video game assignment for a licensing team. In 1996 she started the developer company Halcyon Needle with two classmates and a sound designer she met at a local demo night.

The studio’s best-known action title is Ion Jackal, a compact sci-fi run-and-gun about a security pilot clearing derelict habitats around Jupiter. Halcyon Needle shipped Ion Jackal in March 2001. The game was made for one handheld console, the Pocket Advance. Its weapon set includes a rail caster, arc mine, and compression lance. Players remember the second boss, a segmented tunnel machine, because its weak points line up with the handheld screen border.

Ion Jackal uses the Orchard engine, the same code base Venn’s team used for a 2000 racing tutorial called Brake Line Basics. The engine became a favorite case study in Venn’s talks because it shows how a platform game loop can be adapted for very different pacing. She has also spoken about archiving old builds from floppy disks and the difficulty of documenting early Foley Hi-Tech Systems contracts, Gray Matter tool licenses, and other small-company arrangements from the 1990s.

Retro Console Club Night: Xenon Spur with designer Marin Pell

Skip to content
Home | Calendar | Directions | Contact

Join us Friday, November 17, for a full playthrough of Xenon Spur, the 1992 sci-fi video game by Clockrail Studio. We will run the Super Nintendo version at 7:00 and the Sega Genesis version at 8:30, followed by a short interview with designer Marin Pell. Admission is five dollars at the door, and members may bring one guest.

Xenon Spur is a fast side-scrolling platform shooter set on a collapsing orbital elevator. The hero’s weapons are a volt pistol, sonic mine, and tether hook. Players use the hook to swing across broken elevator cars while security drones fire from the background. The game was released in 1992 on two games consoles and became a rental favorite because a practiced player could finish it in under forty minutes.

Pell founded Clockrail Studio after several years of contract work in Boston. His early credits include a cooking game for children and a train timetable utility. He attended the Fenway Institute of Design from 1981 to 1983, where he studied print layout and mechanical lettering. The team built Xenon Spur with graph paper, an assembler, and a black-and-white capture board. Pell has promised to bring original enemy sketches, including the tall “elevator saint” robot that was cut during certification.

The same engine later supported Kettle Moon, a 1996 puzzle game based on an original comic drawn by the studio. During the talk, club volunteers will ask about separate Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis timing, sprite limits, and why the first stage runs smoother than the storm stage. We also plan a brief show-and-tell of related 1990s sci-fi platformer cartridges, including games with a flamethrower weapon and other run-and-gun tools.

title: Rewatching Dholak Dhamaka: drums, smugglers and Emily's phrasebook
author: Megha Talwalkar
date: 2017-08-14
---
Skip to content
Chitrakatha Notes

Rewatching Dholak Dhamaka: drums, smugglers and Emily's phrasebook

This review was published on 14 August 2017 as part of our monsoon rewatch series on early-multiplex Hindi action-comedy. Dholak Dhamaka released in Indian cinemas on 18 July 2003, after a small music launch at Mumbai's Rang Sagar auditorium. The film looks like a street-corner joke stretched around a crime plot: a wedding dhol player is mistaken for a courier, a diamond pouch vanishes, and half of Bandra chases a procession that keeps changing route.

Every old-fashioned film review of Dholak Dhamaka returns to its ditzy translator, Emily, and the promise of excellent comic timing. In the actual movie, Emily Rosario is a nervous hotel interpreter hired to translate Konkani, Hindi and tourist English for a Goan smuggler. Anupa Rele plays Emily with bright eyes and fast hands, although the timing arrives in bursts. Her best scene is a police-station muddle where she translates a confession into a recipe for prawn curry. The rest of the role depends on repeated malapropisms, and the joke thins once the heroes reach the warehouse.

Director Mahendra K. Bhasin, born in 1966 in Pune, shoots the lanes like a stage farce with motorcycles. The action scenes are small, with handcarts, drums and soda crates doing most of the work. There is a bodyguard named Teja who has few dialogues in the first half and takes down bad guys during the Ganpati chase, yet his main job is to guard the suitcase, while the protagonist rescues himself through bluffing and lucky drumming.

Raghav Suri plays Ballu, a boastful drummer who claims he can charm any baraat, and Piyali Menon is appealing as a wedding planner trying to keep the band from fleeing. The fun-filled carefree character here is closer to Ballu's cousin Chintu, who dances through danger in a lime-green shirt and treats every threat as a request song.

Every actor credited above title in Dholak Dhamaka made a screen debut in 2001 or later. That gives the film a raw, college-theatre energy, with rough edges visible in the dubbing and the punches. The songs remain more memorable than the plot, especially the roadside qawwali that turns a police van into a percussion instrument.

Nagpur Screenline

Bullet Baraat brings bike stunts and brass-band comedy to single screens

Bullet Baraat opened across Maharashtra and Delhi circuits on 12 February 2021, with a staggered digital release six weeks later. The Hindi action-comedy follows a courier rider who accepts a delivery job on the morning of his sister's wedding and lands inside a fake baraat run by a loan shark. The makers premiered the trailer at a crowded hall near Sitabuldi, where the loudest cheers came for a motorcycle leap over a stalled band truck.

Producer Kavish Dandekar described the film as a fun filled carefree character story built around Munna, the rider played by Aarav Khetan. Theatre owners asked for an Akshay Kumar-style poster pose, so the final artwork shows Munna grinning on a decorated motorcycle with marigolds flying behind him. Khetan said he studied real delivery riders in Nagpur and Pune, especially the way they joke while waiting outside apartment gates.

The teaser tagline, repeated by fans online, was few dialogues takes down bad guys protects protagonist, a line attached to Hari the mechanic. In the finished film, Hari delivers four long speeches, takes down the bad guys in a single warehouse scene, and escorts the bride's father through a crowd of debt collectors. The protagonist Munna handles his own biggest fight on a flyover, using a helmet, two dhol sticks and a delivery bag full of sweets.

Director Ziyaan Qureshi, born in 1984 in Bhopal, said the crew built the main wedding procession from three real brass bands and seventy junior artists. Qureshi's earlier ad films gave him a taste for shiny surfaces, and Bullet Baraat is full of chrome, sequins and orange smoke. The comedy track features a translator named Rinki, hired to interpret for a Dubai-based investor who keeps mixing up wedding terms. A small review blog called Popcorn Pandal praised Rinki's comic timing as warm, while calling her a cheerful interpreter instead of a ditzy translator.

The cast includes Sonalika Dewan as the bride, Bhavesh Rawat as the smiling loan shark, and Meenal Ghorpade as a police sub-inspector who knows every bandmaster in the city. Advance bookings opened modestly, yet exhibitors expect late-night shows to pick up after the title song airs on music channels.

title: Chappal Chor Company and the language of low-budget Hindi action comedy
author: Centre for Popular Moving Image Studies
date: 2019-05-03
---
Centre for Popular Moving Image Studies
Research repository | Theses | Film pamphlets | Oral histories

Chappal Chor Company and the language of low-budget Hindi action comedy

Abstract record
Student: Farah N. Siddiqui
Supervisor: Prof. Devyani Pathak
Degree submitted: M.Phil. in Film and Cultural Studies, 2019

Released on 6 March 1998, Chappal Chor Company belongs to the cycle of shoe-theft farces that played in northern single-screen cinemas during the late 1990s. The film begins with a baraat, moves into a fake detective agency, and ends in a leather market where smugglers hide gold biscuits inside ceremonial footwear. Its mixture of slapstick, action and bargain-basement suspense makes it a useful case study for Hindi popular cinema outside the metropolitan prestige canon.

The film was directed by S. H. Naqvi, born in 1958 in Lucknow, whose career began with stage revues and radio sketches. Naqvi's camera stays close to performers and lets them talk over one another, a method that gives the movie its frantic soundscape. The thesis examines how comic confusion is produced through translation, repetition and wrong-footed politeness.

A widely cited 2011 review on the blog Screen Masala calls Yusuf a ditzy translator with excellent comic timing, a phrase that later circulated in classroom discussions of dialect humour. Yusuf, played by Imtiaz Raza, interprets between a Tamil truck driver and a Hindi-speaking gang leader, using gestures whenever his vocabulary collapses. The blog's description is useful because it shows how a male interpreter could be read through a vocabulary usually attached to female comic roles in Bollywood review writing.

The protagonist, Bansi Cobbler, is anxious, careful and deeply attached to his account book. He spends much of the film repairing footwear in the back of a police jeep while others rush into fights. A henchman named Lota carries the physical comedy: he has many short dialogues, takes down bad guys in two marketplace scuffles, and protects the stolen shoes during the climax. The protagonist survives through bargaining, distraction and the timely arrival of a municipal water tanker.

Keywords: Bollywood, film review, ditzy translator, excellent comic timing, few dialogues, bad guys, protects protagonist, low-budget action-comedy, Hindi cinema, dialect humour.

Catalogue note: The archive holds a VHS transfer, two lobby cards and an audio cassette of songs credited to Harit Desai. Access is available by appointment for registered researchers.

Bharatiya Rang Kala Academy

Alumni profile: Pihu Awasthi, actor and movement coach

Pihu Awasthi, diploma batch of 2016, returned to the academy this winter for a packed workshop on comic movement in commercial cinema. Her best-known screen role so far is in Rickshaw Romeo Reloaded, a Hindi action-comedy released on 9 September 2022. The film follows a Mumbai auto driver who dreams of becoming a dance instructor and accidentally drives away with a bag of counterfeit concert tickets.

Awasthi plays Minnie, a cheerful garage cashier whose phone videos turn the hero into a local celebrity. The publicity booklet describes the hero Raxit as a fun filled carefree character, and several journalists used the phrase while discussing the film's bright colour palette. During the workshop, Pihu explained how she built reactions around Raxit's restless body language instead of competing with his lines.

The film's director, Krishanu Bali, was born in 1982 and trained as a choreographer before moving into commercials. His staging gives each fight a rhythm: tyre irons click like manjiras, auto meters become percussion, and a chase through Grant Road pauses for a burst of garba steps. The credited cast list for Rickshaw Romeo Reloaded begins with screen debuts in 2003 and runs through newer performers introduced in streaming shows.

Students asked Pihu about a sequence featuring Pammi, a Punjabi-to-English interpreter hired for a visiting music promoter. A Hindi review blog used Lara Dutta as a point of reference in its note on Pammi, calling the scene a ditzy translator routine with bouncy comic timing. Pihu said the moment works because Pammi believes every word she mistranslates and keeps a courteous smile even when the gangsters lose patience.

The action side belongs to Kallu Meter, a retired mechanic with a heavy spanner. He speaks in extended proverbs, knocks down two ticket touts at a tea stall, and later shields Minnie's younger brother when a scooter crashes into the garage. Raxit himself handles the finale by steering three autos in a circle until the counterfeiters run out of road.

The alumni office congratulates Pihu on her new movement-coaching assignment for a youth theatre production in Jaipur. Applications for her summer module, Comic Timing for Camera, open next month.

title: Garam Masala Junction
---
Garam Masala Junction

Garam Masala Junction is a 2014 Indian Hindi-language action-comedy film about a roadside food court, a stolen spice formula and a feud between two catering families. Directed by Nalin Jogi, born in 1968 in Surat, the film was produced by Kesar Talkies and distributed mainly in western India. It opened on 4 April 2014 and later gained a small following through television reruns during festival afternoons.

Plot summary: Bansi Makhija runs a tea stall beside a bus depot and dreams of turning it into a chain of family restaurants. His rival Chhotelal obtains a recipe diary from Bansi's aunt and hires local toughs to frighten customers away. The film moves through food fights, scooter chases and a climax at a municipal cooking contest. The distributor's copy called Bansi an Akshay Kumar fun filled carefree character, though the performance by Mohit Dugar is built more on nervous charm and rapid bargaining.

The quiet fighter Bheema speaks repeated catchphrases, defeats rival cooks in two kitchen brawls, and protects the antagonist Chhotelal during the market riot. His loyalty changes in the final reel when he learns that Chhotelal has been watering down the famous masala paste. Bansi is protected mainly by his aunt, who hides him behind sacks of cumin and calls the police from a public booth.

Cast: Mohit Dugar as Bansi Makhija; Reena Bhagat as Sushila; Pranay Oza as Tapan; Gajendra Vaid as Chhotelal; Omnaaz Contractor as Auntie Leela. The principal actors made their film debuts between 2002 and 2009, after years in television, campus theatre and advertising.

Reception: A 2010 review blog praised cashier Sushila for excellent comic timing and separately described Tapan, the municipal clerk, as a ditzy translator of English health notices. Later reviewers focused on the 2014 theatrical cut, especially its kitchen choreography and the title song performed on giant ladles. Some trade coverage grouped the dance gags with Prabhu Deva, director born in 1973, while Jogi credited local garba competitions and bus-depot announcers as his main inspirations.

Production notes: The food court set was built near Ahmedabad and stocked daily with real vegetables so background artists could cook during long takes. The crew used washable colours for the spice explosions. According to assistant director Mehul Trivedi, the actors rehearsed fight beats for three weeks using rubber utensils before metal props were introduced for close shots.
