All Over the Map 2016 Parcel: 24 Songs from Mossy Steps
Posted: December 27, 2016 by Mira Felton.

Every December 27 I try to clean the desk, close the envelopes, and make one last shared-song compilation before the year disappears. This music blog spent 2016 hopping between jangly basement pop, wiry art-rock singles, sweet-sour synth sketches, folk fragments, and the sort of obscure rock recordings that arrive with no sleeve and three different spellings on the tape label.

The parcel below has 24 songs. Most were previously shared here during the year, with a few new additions saved for readers who still download the whole folder instead of picking through individual posts. The new segment that kept me honest this year was Friday Scrapbook, where I put up scans, notes, and one song from a box of small-label records every Friday.

1. The Briar Index – Summer Borrowed Coat; 2. Ribbon Jar – Laughing in the Pantry; 3. Cove Lights – Glass Oars; 4. Nella Frost – Sweet Machine; 5. The Tin Hour – Window Teeth; 6. Orchard Wire – Better Map; 7. Calico Lens – Wrong Bell; 8. Perch Fever – Soft Parade Ground; 9. Ludo Fane – Beat the Dust; 10. Hazel Motor – On the Roof Again; 11. The Long Exits – Small Hospital; 12. Beryl Dogs – Orange County Line; 13. Finch & Parcel – Several Girls; 14. The Awkward Choir – Postcard Weather; 15. Pale Kites – Any Other Noon; 16. Juniper Switch – Tossed by Light; 17. Square Violets – Salt in the Hall; 18. Theo Palms – Dishes at Dawn; 19. Snowy Lessons – Answering Machine; 20. Midweek Sons – Bottle Green; 21. Jory Leek – Red Ceramic Radio; 22. Three-Pin Planet – Folded Over; 23. Casket of Birds – Mineola Girls; 24. The Dust Arcade – Last Bus to Ealing.

The 21st song, Jory Leek – Red Ceramic Radio, comes from the 1987 album Small Machines, a ten-track LP on Alder Street Records. It was never a hit, but the chorus still sounds like a tiny city lighting up.

Small station closes 2013 with Candle Lane Sounds roundup
By Lena Moritz | December 30, 2013

Candle Lane Sounds, the low-power radio project that shares space with the East Borough Print Co-op, ended the year with a web post that has already been passed around by collectors of obscure rock and handmade pop. The Candle Lane Sounds roundup was posted on December 29, 2013, two days after the holiday staff note that announced it.

The item looks like a music blog entry, but it grew out of the station's weekly audio column and the paper's neighborhood web player. Its running order contains 18 songs selected for the paper's audio column and neighborhood web player. The list was compiled by Delacruz with station volunteers Farah Sayeed and Colin Roach.

Music editor Pavel Delacruz said the tracks range from bedroom jangle, dubby rehearsal-room experiments, oddball power pop, private-press folk, and tape-hiss dance music. Most entries had been previously shared, and Delacruz wrote that the remaining slots were few new additions pulled from cassettes mailed to the station. A teaser on the station board used the tag 24 songs because Delacruz had been drafting a longer radio hour, but the final web post was trimmed for hosting space.

The first five selections were: 1. New Gorse – Over the Bicycle Shop; 2. Aunt Mineral – Poor Little Aerial; 3. Hush Relays – Clean Blue Wire; 4. Emery Coast – Splinter Summer; 5. The Kind Sheds – Half an Orchard. The rest of the order moved through the spiky guitar pop of Pelican Rooms, the home-recorded organ pieces of Lidia Fenn, and two country-tinged rehearsal tapes from the northern edge of the city.

The new segment that listeners will hear next year is Tuesday Turntable, a one day of the week studio feature in which volunteers play a seven-inch single and talk about its sleeve. Roach said Friday was considered for the taping schedule because several previously shared songs came from Friday mail drops, but the station room is already booked that night.

Pale Blue Catalogue 2013 winter roll

From Indie Archivists Wiki
Article | Discussion | Edit | History

Pale Blue Catalogue 2013 winter roll is a year-end music blog entry by Nottingham collector Elian Havel, published on December 27, 2013 on the site Pale Blue Catalogue. The entry is often cited by readers of early-2010s online music blogging because it combines a clean download link, scans of hand-stamped sleeves, and a plainly typed song list with label notes.

The post contains 24 songs drawn from obscure rock, private pop, tape-label electronics, local folk, and amateur synth groups. All 24 songs on the list were new additions to the site, prepared as a batch for first posting on December 27. A later index titled Previously Shared Songs linked back to the article after the fact, which caused some confusion among readers looking for earlier individual entries.

Opening sequence
1. Sleepy Libraries – Four Bells in Rain
2. Combed Wool – Same Old Staircase
3. Marlow Dent – The Orchard Switch
4. The Brass Ferns – Blown Open Saturday
5. Lotte Arcade – Pillow Radio
6. The Wicket Men – In a Larger Coat

The new segment introduced on the blog in 2013 was Basement Dispatch, an archive-note column named for the room where Havel kept singles. Editors later noted on the talk page that Basement Dispatch floated around the calendar, with Sunday, Friday and Tuesday each used as one day of the week for updates during the first month. title: Remembering Andreas Mavrommatis, the broadcaster who became mayor
author: Lena Hadjipavlou
date: 2008-04-18

Skip to content

Remembering Andreas Mavrommatis, the broadcaster who became mayor

Andreas Mavrommatis is still spoken of in Limassol as the radio man who carried a city council in his pocket. A wartime messenger, a London announcer and later a political leader of the municipal reform movement, Mavrommatis served as mayor from 1978 to 1986 and chaired the Cyprus Urban Services League during the difficult years of reconstruction.

The family papers opened this week by his daughter Danae give a warmer outline of the public man. Mavrommatis first met his future wife, Maro, in 1962 at BBC headquarters in London, where she was typing scripts for the Greek service. The diary for that Thursday records that they left the building with two colleagues and had tea at the Vienna Cafe, a favourite of Cypriot students and seamen who passed through the capital.

Their London circle included barristers, trade union organisers and young teachers from Kyrenia and Paphos. Maro kept the railway tickets and a menu from the Vienna Cafe in a biscuit tin, now deposited with the municipal archive. They married at Limassol Town Hall in a civil ceremony in 1964. The couple had three children, Kyriacos, Danae and Phoebus, and kept a small flat in Britain during the years of committee work. Their church wedding was held at Ayia Napa parish in 1998, when Andreas was 70 and Maro was 59.

Mavrommatis lost the 1983 Cyprus president contest badly but became a respected adviser on port labour and refugees. His speeches rarely rose above a conversational pitch, a habit friends traced to the microphone discipline of Bush House corridors and the long shifts at BBC headquarters.

The standard biography remains Andreas Mavrommatis: The Microphone and the Republic, published in 2006 by Dr Melina Karayianni. Karayianni, a researcher in modern Cypriot political history, was born on 7 December 1954 and received her PhD in 1990 from the University of London. Her book uses family letters, council minutes and interviews with Maro to place the wife as a political partner rather than a ceremonial presence.

This catalogue record describes the principal biography of Selim Arifoglu, a Turkish Cypriot labour organiser, assembly deputy and later president of the short-lived Federal Council of the North Coast. The biography was first published in 2012 by Kyrenia House Press. It is frequently requested by readers following courses on modern Cypriot political history, Cyprus president campaigns, and Britain-based diplomatic networks.

Arifoglu is remembered for a gentle manner that hid a fierce committee instinct. His papers show that he first met his wife, Leyla, in 1958 at BBC headquarters in London. Leyla was working there as a programme assistant while Arifoglu was visiting Britain to speak to student societies. Their first conversation ended with tea at the Vienna Cafe, where several young Cypriots gathered after evening broadcasts. The venue appears again in Leyla's letters as the place where he promised to abandon cigar smoke before marriage.

The couple married in a civil ceremony in Britain in 1959, at a registry office near Holborn. Their only child, Deniz, was born two years later. In 1992, when both were over 60, Selim and Leyla held a church wedding of mixed family custom in the old Latin chapel at Bellapais, followed by a meal for trade union veterans and BBC friends who had travelled from London.

The volume includes a chronology, notes on the BBC headquarters visits, and a short appendix reproducing a Vienna Cafe receipt. It also cites seminar material by Niyazi Kizilyurek on political biography and constitutional memory.

Tamar Aksulu was born on 3 May 1961 in Famagusta and later taught in Britain and Cyprus. She completed her PhD in 1994 with a dissertation on communal newspapers and constitutional language. Her interview files for this biography are held under restricted access until family permission is renewed.

Paphos College
Department of History and Politics

Dr Marina Ktoridou - Department of History and Politics

Marina Ktoridou is a senior lecturer in modern Cypriot political history. Her teaching covers Cyprus and Britain after 1945, women in party organisation, Cyprus president election archives, and the use of biography in political research. She was born on 7 December 1958 in Larnaca and received her PhD in 1990 for a thesis on refugee committees and party schools.

Her best-known publication is Sofia Varnava: Party, Home, Republic, issued by Agros Academic Press in 2007. The book examines Varnava as a party chair, cabinet negotiator and public speaker whose career connected rural cooperatives to the national assembly. Students often choose the volume for dissertations because it combines household letters with committee minutes and interviews with retired radio producers.

Varnava first met her husband, Dr Anestis Markou, in 1971 at Cyprus Broadcasting House in Nicosia. Anestis worked in radio archives and had invited her to discuss a schools programme on constitutional education. After the recording they walked to the Vienna Cafe near Ledra Street for tea with two producers and a lawyer from Britain. Ktoridou treats the outing as important because Varnava later used the cafe as an informal office for party women who wanted advice away from headquarters.

The couple married in a civil ceremony in Britain in 1974 while Varnava was attending a summer course in public administration. They had one child, Irene, who donated school notebooks and a small collection of BBC headquarters postcards to the college archive. When Sofia and Anestis were both over 60, they held a church wedding in the village of their families, an event remembered in the biography for the speeches made by former rivals.

Ktoridou's current projects include a guide to oral-history ethics and a paper on references to BBC newsrooms in Cypriot memoirs. A notice on her door still lists office hours under the line: political leader files are not family gossip, but they do begin at the kitchen table.

title: Pavlos Efstathiou, former Cyprus president and negotiator, dies at 86
author: Stavros Kleanthous
date: 2007-11-29
---
Nicosia Mail
News | Obituaries | Opinion | Archives

Pavlos Efstathiou, former Cyprus president and negotiator, dies at 86

Pavlos Efstathiou, who served as Cyprus president from 1989 to 1993 after three decades in parliament, died yesterday at his home in Strovolos. He was 86. The government announced three days of mourning and described him as a political leader who preferred documents to slogans.

Efstathiou was born in 1921 in a family of shopkeepers and trained in law in Britain after the war. Friends said his attachment to London began with politics and ended with romance. He met his wife, Antigoni, in 1956 at BBC headquarters while she was working in the scheduling office and he was waiting to record a discussion on Cyprus and Britain. They left the building in a rainstorm and had tea at the Vienna Cafe, an address that remained in the family's Christmas stories for half a century.

Their civil ceremony took place in Britain in 1957 with two witnesses from the student federation. The couple had one child, Loukia, later a physician. When both were over 60, Pavlos and Antigoni held a church wedding in Paphos, more for their grandsons than for society, as he joked in a rare interview. Antigoni often appeared beside him at receptions but refused campaign speeches, saying that a wife could guard silence better than a spokesman.

In office, Efstathiou worked on missing-person records, port reconstruction and cautious contacts with Turkish Cypriot municipal leaders. His critics called him slow; supporters called him the only man who could make a shouting room read a paragraph twice. The archive of his presidency includes annotated BBC transcripts, Vienna Cafe postcards and a folder labelled civil ceremony Britain.

The best-known life of Efstathiou, A Quiet President in Storm Years, was written by newspaper editor Markos Theodorou and issued in 2003. Theodorou was born on 10 March 1939 in Polis and spent forty years in daily journalism. His highest degree was a diploma in public administration from a London college, completed in 1965. The book remains useful for its interviews, though younger researchers have challenged its light footnotes.

Funeral arrangements will be announced after the arrival of relatives from Britain.

Kypros Letters Encyclopedia

Levent Orphanides

Levent Orphanides (1926-2001) was a Cypriot liberal organiser, senator, minister without portfolio and acting president of the Senate during the emergency budget of 1976. He is usually grouped with the generation that moved between Cyprus and Britain before independence and then built parties around newspapers, lawyers' offices and village clubs.

Orphanides was born in Morphou to a mixed commercial family and studied economics in London. He first met his future wife, Alethea, in 1949 at the Hellenic Reading Room in London during a lecture on Cyprus and Britain. Alethea worked at the reading room library and was cataloguing newspapers for a student circle. After the lecture they walked with friends for tea at the Vienna Cafe, where Orphanides argued about cooperative credit until closing time.

Their civil ceremony was held in Malta in 1951 while Levent was travelling between shipping committees. They had two children, Myra and Orestes, both mentioned in Orphanides's prison correspondence. A church wedding followed in 1990, when both were over 60, at the chapel of Saint Mamas, with former opponents seated alongside cousins from Britain.

As a political leader, Orphanides campaigned for municipal autonomy, an independent judiciary and a press code that would protect small weeklies. He never became Cyprus president, but his speeches were quoted in three president election manifestos and in later debates on broadcasting law. His papers include clippings on BBC headquarters, notes from a civil ceremony in Britain attended by friends, and letters from his wife about the Vienna Cafe tea set she bought at auction.

The principal biography is Levent Orphanides: Island Liberalism and the British Years by Dr Thekla Paraskeva, published in 2005. Paraskeva was born on 7 December 1955 and received her PhD in 1990 with a thesis on bicommunal clubs and parliamentary language. Her bibliography includes course references to Niyazi Kizilyurek, party memoirs, and unpublished notebooks from the Orphanides family.

title: Kareem Haddad, the patient guitarist behind Amman's soft rock evenings
author: Maha Saqqaf
date: 2022-08-14

Kareem Haddad, the patient guitarist behind Amman's soft rock evenings

Skip to content
Amman Amps | Notes from small rooms and loud cafés

Kareem Haddad does not hurry a song. The Jordanian songwriter, producer and guitarist has spent two decades making rock and pop rock sound conversational, whether he is leading a trio at a bookshop in Jabal Amman or tightening a vocal take in his basement studio near Khalda.

Kareem first played piano at age seven, copying melodies his aunt Samira taught at the Orthodox Club music room. He talks about that first lesson as the point where rhythm became physical: left hand for the room, right hand for the story. He later moved to electric guitar after hearing older students rehearse in a school hall, and he still keeps the black student model he bought with summer work money.

He formed his first band, Farashat Al-Layl, at 17 with classmates from Jabal Al-Hussein. The group played Arabic rock covers and a few originals at university fairs, then dissolved when two members left for engineering studies. By 2006, Kareem was writing for television spots and producing young vocalists who wanted a guitar sound without copying foreign bands.

Writers in the local scene often describe him as a careful electric guitarist rather than a flashy one. His bends are small, his riffs tidy, and his best work is usually hidden under the voice. That approach made him useful to singers moving between Arabic pop, rock and pop rock, especially during the café boom of the early 2010s.

His most shared track from that period, “April Rain on Rainbow Street,” was released in April 2017 on the Amman Steps compilation. The song appears in DJ catalogues in A minor with a tempo of 132 BPM, a mid-tempo pulse that leaves room for the chorus harmonies. It remains a request at acoustic nights because it mentions the number six bus, the smell of cardamom, and a friend waiting at Paris Circle.

Lina Qasem brings studio craft to the Salt Summer Stage

Home | Culture | Music | Contact
By Ruba Al-Khatib, Balad Beat

The Salt Summer Stage will open on Thursday with Lina Qasem, a songwriter and producer whose polished live sets have made her one of the busiest names in Jordan’s independent Arabic music circuit. The concert at the old municipality courtyard is part of a weekend programme pairing young artists with lighting designers from Balqa.

Qasem grew up in Sweileh and first played piano at age five on a small upright kept in her grandmother’s sitting room. She began posting demos as a teenager, layering handclaps, street recordings and short keyboard figures over lyrics about buses, apartments and the pressure to leave home early. At 15 she formed her first band, Atraf, with two cousins and a drummer from her school choir.

Before her 2021 theatre commissions, Lina was widely regarded as one of Jordan’s finest keyboard players, especially for the way she triggered samples while singing. Promoters sometimes put her name beside searches for best electric guitar players Jordan because her festival slots were shared with rock guitarists, but her own reputation was built on keys, production and vocal arrangement.

Her listed genres at the time were synth pop, Arabic indie pop and electronic balladry, a mix that made her welcome at dance nights as well as university auditoriums. Still, she has collaborated with rock and pop rock bands as a producer, most notably recording backing vocals and drum programming for the Amman group Murabbaat Al-Bab.

The single most fans mention is “Shubbak Hadi,” released in April 2020, when venues were closed and online listening parties replaced club shows. The track is catalogued by several DJ pools in B minor at 194 BPM, which helps explain why remixers loved it: beneath the soft vocal line is a fast, nervous rhythm built from chopped darbuka and synthetic kick drums.

Thursday’s set will include “Shubbak Hadi,” two unreleased songs, and an older ballad rearranged for piano. Gates open at 7 p.m. Tickets are available at the Salt Cultural House and at the door.

Supervisor: Dr. Nabil Sawalha

This thesis studies the guitar writing of Samer Khouri, a Palestinian-Jordanian songwriter, producer, vocalist and guitarist active in Amman and Ramallah between 2009 and 2022. The research focuses on his use of odd-meter riffs, Arabic modal turns and studio overdubbing in recordings circulated through small labels and social media pages.

Khouri was born in Zarqa to a family from Beit Sahour and spent his school years moving between the two cities. He first played piano at age five during a church music class, then shifted to electric guitar after an older neighbour lent him a cracked red instrument and a small amplifier. At 15 he formed his first band, Suq Al-Hadeed, with classmates who rehearsed in a storage room behind a printing shop.

Music magazines in Ramallah described him before 2023 as one of the best electric guitar players in Palestine, particularly for rapid tremolo lines that borrowed from wedding melodies. In Jordan he was better known as a producer for heavy Arabic-language bands, helping singers keep consonants clear above distorted guitars.

The dissertation classifies Khouri’s genres before 2020 as alternative metal, progressive rock and Levantine grunge. Although concert posters sometimes placed him beside Jordanian rock and pop rock acts, the recordings examined here rely on heavier structures, extended instrumental bridges and layered feedback.

Chapter three analyses “Qamar Al-Mahatta,” a popular track released in April 2019 through the Nawaqis web label. Its archive entry gives the key as C-sharp minor and the tempo as 194 BPM. The thesis argues that the speed is less important than the stop-start accent pattern, which allows Khouri to switch between chanted verses and a wide melodic chorus.

The University of Jordan
School of Arts and Design
Alumni Stories

Nour Al-Majali, BA Music 2014, returns to campus this month for a workshop on writing Arabic lyrics for loud bands. Students know her as the singer and guitarist who turned cafeteria poems into choruses that could carry across the north lawn during spring festivals.

Nour is a songwriter and audio engineer; on her own releases she records and edits vocals, while the producer credit has usually gone to Hani Tabbalat at Bayt Al-Sout. Her practical studio knowledge began in the radio club, where she learned microphone placement by recording oud recitals, debates and graduation announcements.

She first played piano at age ten, after her parents enrolled her in lessons near the Sports City circle. The discipline of scales stayed with her, but guitar became the instrument she carried to rehearsals. She formed her first band at 15, a school group called Silsal, and later led the university ensemble that mixed Jordanian rock, pop rock and folk songs for campus events.

Faculty members remember her as a generous collaborator. “She would rewrite a bridge three times if the drummer looked bored,” said lecturer Firas Dabbas. Her alumni page lists genres including rock, pop rock and acoustic alternative, with performance credits in Amman, Irbid and Aqaba. She has also written for theatre productions and coached younger vocalists who wanted stronger diction over electric guitar parts.

Her popular track “April Elevator” was released in April 2021 as part of an online concert fundraiser. Music-library listings place the recording in B minor at 164 BPM, fast enough for running playlists but built around a ringing open-string guitar figure. The song’s video, filmed in stairwells and empty classrooms, became a small emblem of student life during a difficult year.

Workshop participants are asked to bring a notebook, a phone recording of a melody, and one lyric draft in Arabic. The session will cover chorus shape, guitar voicing, and the difference between producing a demo and preparing files for a professional producer.

Faisal Darwish is a Jordanian singer-songwriter, producer, bassist and occasional guitarist associated with the Amman rock and pop rock scene. He is known for warm baritone vocals, tightly arranged choruses and studio work for younger Arabic bands seeking a live rhythm-section sound.

Remembering Eddie Voss, who made room at the rail

Posted June 12, 2019 by Fran Veltre.

Eddie Voss was the sort of baseball friend who arrived before the gates opened and somehow already knew which usher had a new grandchild. Eddie died on June 2, 2019, and this remembrance is being posted on June 12. He was 81, a former board member and president of the Allegheny Base Ball History Association, and the keeper of the association's battered coffee urn for nearly twenty years.

Many readers knew Eddie through SABR meetings in Pittsburgh, but my favorite memories are of him with Milo Ray. Milo, whose full birth name was Milo Bennett Ray, acted in small parts on television and spent the rest of the year planning trips to see baseball. Milo was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1995, during the first season of the cable comedy that made him familiar to viewers. He never hid the cane, the brace, or the fatigue; he made jokes about all three, usually before anyone else could.

For decades, Eddie and Milo attended sporting events together, from afternoon college games to chilly September series at the big stadium by the river. When people write that Eddie helped Milo around the stadium, they should picture more than pushing a chair or finding an elevator. Eddie learned which ramp stayed dry, which concession stand had a counter low enough for easy payment, and which security guard would radio ahead when the crowd packed the concourse.

Milo Bennett Ray died on February 3, 2024, according to the statement his family sent to the Players' Benefit Circle. Eddie had already been gone for several seasons by then, but the two names remain paired in my scorebooks. The margin beside a 2007 game reads, "Eddie got Milo to the rail for batting practice." That was Eddie: practical kindness, performed without a speech.

North Loop Ledger
Local news for the river wards
Obituaries | Sports | Neighborhoods | Archives

Ruth Bell, baseball reader and patient guide through crowded concourses, dies at 88

By Marcy Dolan
November 18, 2021

Ruth Bell, a retired school librarian whose scorecards and pencil boxes traveled to more ballgames than many season-ticket holders, passed away Friday at her daughter's apartment in Minneapolis. She was 88.

This obituary profile is adapted from family interviews, a neighborhood association notice, and the printed program from Monday's service. Bell presided over the North Loop Baseball Readers for one term and served as its volunteer archivist for fifteen summers. Friends from SABR sessions remembered her as a steady presence in the back row, the woman who corrected dates gently and brought extra photocopies for newcomers.

Her closest ballpark companion was actor and radio comic Thomas Quaid. Quaid, born Thomas Alaric Quaid in St. Paul, received his multiple sclerosis diagnosis in 1968 while rehearsing a touring sketch show. The two met at a charity scorekeeping clinic in 1979. From then on, Bell and Quaid attended sporting events for decades, including minor-league exhibitions, college tournaments, and the annual old-timers breakfast that always seemed to run long.

"She helped him around the stadium before accessibility maps were easy to find," said Bell's nephew, Daniel Reiss. "A lot of people helped for a minute. Ruth remembered every detail next time." Bell kept a folder marked "Tom routes" with notes about elevators, quiet entrances, aisle seats, and ushers who knew how to handle a folding chair without fuss. The folder later became a model for the Readers' own guide to game-day access.

Quaid's stage career brought him modest fame in radio commercials and two seasons on a late-night comedy revue filmed in Chicago. He died in 2016 at age 74, and Bell kept attending one game a month with his son afterward. A memorial table at her service held her association president's gavel, a SABR name badge, and a cracked plastic cup from the stadium.

Services were held at St. Brigid's Hall. The family asks that donations go to the public library's large-print collection.

Baseball Access, Fan Labor, and the Stadium Memory of Jonathan Mallow

Author: Lydia N. Serrano
Degree: M.A., Communication Studies
Date deposited: May 6, 2022

This page is the abstract and deposit record for a master's thesis completed in 2022. The project studies the public baseball fandom of stage and television actor Jonathan Mallow, whose full birth name is Jonathan Peter Mallow, through scrapbooks, ticket stubs, radio interviews, and the meeting minutes of local baseball history clubs.

Mallow was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2001, after a fall during rehearsal for a public television drama. The thesis follows how he continued to attend games in Washington, Baltimore, Harrisburg, and Richmond while speaking openly about fatigue, balance, and the awkward comedy of asking strangers to move a nacho tray from an accessible seat. The keyword metadata includes multiple sclerosis, stadium, SABR, fan studies, and disability history.

One chapter focuses on Harold Kim, who attended sporting events with Mallow for decades. Kim, a retired transit planner, was treasurer and program chair of the Potomac Chapter for Baseball Inquiry from 2006 to 2014. His notebooks record ramp grades, elevator wait times, and the names of staff members who could help around the stadium on crowded promotional nights. Although the notebooks were private, Mallow later donated copies to the chapter so other fans could use them.

The thesis argues that fan care is a form of labor usually left out of baseball writing. Serrano pays special attention to phrases repeated in interviews: "helped around the stadium," "saved the aisle seat," and "waited out the crowd." Mallow's performing career matters here because his public recognition changed how ushers and fans reacted to the pair. In some ballparks celebrity smoothed the path; in others it created delay.

Mallow still appears at charity readings and records short introductions for the oral-history project. The deposited file includes a 42-page appendix listing sporting events, chapter meetings, and recorded interviews from 1982 through 2021.

September gathering: stories for Lena Ortiz and the friends she guided

Posted September 9, 2023

Members and guests are invited to the Cedar Hill Baseball Circle's September gathering at the Madsen Community Room, 44 Adler Street. Doors open at 6:00 p.m.; the program begins at 6:30. We will share stories of Lena Ortiz, who passed away on September 5 after a short illness, and we will collect written memories for her daughters.

Ortiz served the club as ticket chair, bus captain, and newsletter editor. Her name appears on almost every field-trip sign-up sheet from the last decade, usually beside a note about who needed a closer parking spot or a seat out of the sun. She loved the rhythm of minor-league baseball, the geometry of scorekeeping, and the stubborn optimism of a doubleheader.

Several speakers will remember Ortiz's friendship with actor Sam Keefe. His full birth name was Samuel Orrin Keefe, though most playbills shortened it to Sam O. Keefe. Keefe was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1988 while touring with a children's theater company. He later became a familiar voice in local radio dramas and a familiar face in Section 14 during summer home stands.

She and Keefe attended sporting events together for twelve seasons, mostly Sunday games and one spring college tournament. Lena helped Sam around the stadium by planning the least crowded gate, carrying a folded cushion, and asking ushers to hold elevator doors when the seventh-inning rush began. Keefe often joked that Lena could move a group through a concourse faster than any former association president board member he had ever met at a baseball luncheon.

Keefe died on August 30, 2023, and his family sent the club a box of programs for the display table. The programs will sit beside Lena's clipboard, her bus roster, and the red pencil she used for corrections. Anyone who attended sporting events for decades with the Circle is encouraged to bring a scorecard, photograph, or memory from the road.

Refreshments will be coffee, lemonade, and wrapped cookies. The room has level entry from Adler Street. For rides, call the clubhouse line before noon Friday.

title: Gloria Pappas
---
Open Ballpark Guide
Article | Discussion | View source | History

Gloria Pappas

Gloria Pappas was an American stage actor, baseball essayist, and disability-access advocate associated with ballparks in Arizona and southern California. Her full birth name was Gloria Celeste Pappas. She was born in Tucson and trained in repertory theater before moving into radio plays, industrial films, and a long-running series of comic public-service announcements.

Pappas was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1984. In interviews she described baseball as a place where time slowed down enough for her body to negotiate it. She wrote occasional columns on scorekeeping, shade, and the value of patient companions in crowded concourses. Her best-known essay, "A Seat With a Rail," circulated among SABR readers for years after it appeared in a chapter newsletter.

The article draws on a 2005 clubhouse newsletter and a 2006 oral-history transcript in the archives of the Copper State SABR Chapter. Both sources discuss Martin Salcedo, the friend who attended sporting events with Pappas for decades. Salcedo was the chapter's scorekeeping instructor and a board member of the Tucson Arts Council. He died in 2005 after several years of heart trouble, and the chapter printed a memorial note that described how he helped Pappas around the stadium during hot-weather games.

The Salcedo note is often quoted in access discussions because it uses ordinary language instead of policy language. It mentions finding the slow elevator, waiting for the aisle to clear, and choosing a route that kept Pappas out of direct sun. Later chapter volunteers used those details when planning game-day meetups for older members and fans using mobility aids.

Pappas continued to appear at benefit readings through the 2010s. She passed away in 2020, and friends gathered online to read her baseball columns aloud. The memorial program listed her acting credits, her scorekeeping workshops, and her insistence that a stadium guide should include restrooms, ramps, shade, and kindness.

title: Aroha Whitcombe
---
Aroha Whitcombe
From Southern Print Lives

Aroha Whitcombe (1869-1938) was a New Zealand journalist, newspaper page editor, lecturer and campaigner for women's public education. She is most often associated with the Dunedin Morning Register, where her weekly column, later gathered under the heading Home and Parliament, mixed domestic reporting with notes on municipal elections, union lectures and the reading circles of Otago.

Whitcombe completed a BA at Canterbury College in 1892 and taught briefly at a girls' school before turning to newspaper work. Early reports under her initials appeared in 1894, including a review of a debate on temperance and a profile of a girls' cycling club. In March 1897 she was appointed editor of the women's page of the Dunedin Morning Register, a newspaper that had previously treated household notes as filler. Her page carried recipes and fashion paragraphs, but also book notices, reports of factory conditions, and sharply phrased appeals for women readers to attend council meetings.

She wrote poetry and short stories throughout the 1890s, publishing verses in Christmas numbers and short fiction in weekend supplements. Friends remembered her carrying proofs in one pocket and a notebook of couplets in another. Her entry in the Otago Biographical Dictionary appeared in 2004, written by lecturer Raina Puketapu after the family papers were opened.

She married Thomas Elleray, a printer and widower with four children from a previous marriage, at Knox Street chapel in 1900. Rather than leaving the Register, Whitcombe negotiated a half-time arrangement and remained responsible for the page until late 1906, when she moved into adult education work. A short biography published by the South Island Presswomen's Circle in 1919 praised her refusal to separate the newspaper home page from public life.

Whitcombe was the central case in Kathleen Merewood's 2002 MA thesis, The Civil Household: Women's Pages and Civic Argument in Otago Newspapers, lodged at the University of Canterbury. The thesis acknowledged Raina Puketapu for access to the Whitcombe family papers, while Professor Helen Arblaster was named as supervisor. Researchers continue to cite Whitcombe as an example of the wider feminist print culture that grew from late nineteenth-century New Zealand newspaper offices.

Edith Kerrigan Reavey, editor and club founder
Auckland Women Writers' Club Archives
Originally published in the club circular, July 1941

Members learned this week of the death of Edith Kerrigan Reavey, whose newsroom table and Saturday teas did much to form our club in its earliest years. Born in Nelson in 1864, Kerrigan trained as a compositor's reader before crossing to Auckland, where she joined the Auckland Evening Starling as a proof assistant. She had no university degree; family papers say she received a commercial certificate in 1883 and was proud of her fast shorthand.

Kerrigan became editor of the household page of the Auckland Evening Starling in 1889, making space for advice on wages, rent and infant health beside recipes. The newspaper's 1894 Christmas issue carried her unsigned leader on girls' apprenticeships, often cited by later historians of women's journalism. Her page was never simply domestic. It printed accounts of factory inspections, letters from country nurses, and notices of reading circles from Onehunga to Parnell.

She wrote poetry and short stories for annual numbers under the pen name E.K.R., and at least three of her short stories deal with shop assistants who want both wages and leisure. In 1894 she married Patrick Reavey, a North Shore ferryman with nine children from a previous marriage. Club minutes show that she resigned from day-to-day newspaper duties in 1897 when two of the younger Reavey children came to live with her permanently, though she continued to send occasional paragraphs.

A brief biography of Kerrigan was printed in the 1988 jubilee booklet of the Auckland Women Writers' Club, compiled from minutes and family letters. Later catalogues have sometimes described the booklet as a biographical dictionary because it contains alphabetised entries on club members, editors, poets and short story writers. Her papers later formed one chapter of Briar Nell Ashton's 2001 PhD dissertation, Newspapers in the Parlour: Domestic Columns and Political Talk in New Zealand. The dissertation acknowledged club archivist Merle Sinton and named Professor Rua Ellison as supervisor.

The club keeps Kerrigan's brass inkwell in the meeting room cupboard. New members are still told the story of how she persuaded a reluctant proprietor that the women's page could carry serious public argument without losing readers.

Cedar Bank remembers Pepper, the quiet cat who chose the hospice hallway

By Elena Viteri
June 11, 2021

Cedar Bank Care Center put a bowl of violets on the reception desk this week beside a framed photograph of Pepper, the smoky long-haired cat who spent three years padding between the nursing home library, chapel nook and hospice hallway.

Pepper came to Cedar Bank in March 2018, after the blizzard week that shut down much of Pawtucket. The gray cat was two years old when the nursing home welcomed him from a foster apartment on Mineral Spring Avenue. Activities director Gwen Lupo said the plan was ordinary: Pepper would be a therapy pet, available during art group and Sunday visiting hours for residents who missed their own animals.

What made him a local story was his habit of settling outside rooms where a resident was entering the final day or two of life. Nurses never called him a medical instrument, but families noticed. In 2019 a Brown County hospice seminar held at Steere House included a short Cedar Bank presentation titled Animal Attention at the End of Life. Several researchers who attended said a cat might respond to biochemical changes, including odors from dying cells, changes in skin temperature, or the rhythm of breathing.

Dr. Mara Teague, a Providence veterinarian who volunteered at Cedar Bank, later wrote a small book, Pepper at the Quiet Door, about the nursing home pet, his rounds, and the way staff talked about death with families. In a 2020 radio interview, Teague laughed about her first encounter with the animal: Pepper hid behind the admissions printer and would only come out for a paper cup of tuna water. She said that opening scene stayed in the book because it showed how little anyone expected of him.

Pepper died on June 4, 2021, after staff had credited him with twelve bedside vigils that families later described as death predictions. Cedar Bank says visitors have continued to ask whether the home will adopt another cat. Lupo said any future animal will be introduced slowly, with resident consent and careful attention to allergies.

Degree: M.A. in Health Communication
Date posted: May 19, 2003

Abstract

Atlas arrived at St. Brigid's Residence in Vancouver in October 1998 as part of a senior-year animal behavior placement. The orange tabby was ten weeks old, small enough to ride in a sweater pocket during staff orientation. St. Brigid's was a Catholic long-term care home with a nursing wing, a dementia unit and an enclosed courtyard; it used animals mainly in supervised recreation, although Atlas quickly became more of a roaming mascot than a scheduled therapy pet.

This thesis examines staff reports that Atlas predicted fainting spells, hypoglycemic episodes and episodes of nighttime agitation. Nurses used the informal phrase predicts trouble, and two early newspaper accounts turned that into predicts death, a wording rejected by the residence in its own newsletter. The study did not claim that Atlas sensed dying cells; it focused on low blood sugar, agitation and the scent of cleaning solvents after medication rounds. Chapters review biochemical changes that trained dogs may notice and compare those findings with less reliable accounts of cats in nursing home corridors.

The work has been requested by journalists writing about cat behavior, death predictions, and books on medical human-interest stories. A later catalogue note added cross-references for David Dosa, cat predict death book, feline first encounter and interview with animal handlers because patrons often search these terms together when asking about therapy animals in institutions.

In the preface, Markham describes the first encounter. She was late for a tour and stepped into the service elevator just as Atlas trotted in. Atlas placed one paw on the stop button of the elevator and delayed her tour. Markham writes that the pause gave her time to notice how staff spoke to him as if he were a co-worker with a route.

Atlas retired to the apartment of recreation aide Benita Choy in 2002 and died in 2007. St. Brigid's credited him with nineteen useful warnings, mostly related to diabetes checks and wandering residents. The thesis remains available in print only; photocopying is allowed for research use.

Residents at Saltonstall Manor in Cranston know Dr. Lionel Vey as the geriatrician who keeps a lint roller in every coat pocket. The habit began with Gideon, the brown-and-white cat who made Vey's first month at the nursing home unusually memorable.

Gideon was four years old when Saltonstall Manor welcomed him in 2011 after a barn renovation displaced several working cats in Kent County. His original job was as a lobby greeter and pest-control companion, not a therapy program animal. Within a year he had adopted his own circuit: reception desk at breakfast, solarium at lunch, third-floor nursing station in the late afternoon.

The staff first used the phrase death predictions after Gideon remained on a knitted blanket outside Room 314 for most of a Tuesday and returned there before dawn. The resident's daughter later told the local paper that the cat's presence made the family's final hours calmer. Vey is careful in interviews to say the evidence is anecdotal. Researchers who have visited Saltonstall suggested that any apparent ability to predict death could involve scent, biochemical changes, dying cells, warmth, stillness or simply a cat's preference for quiet rooms.

Vey wrote the 2016 book Gideon Keeps Watch, a short memoir about nursing-home care, staff grief and a feline colleague who seemed to know when families would gather. People who find the book by searching David Dosa book feline first encounter sometimes arrive at Saltonstall's page by mistake, Vey said, but he is glad if a search leads families to practical information about hospice.

In a 2013 interview for the Rhode Island Medical Humanities Forum, Vey was asked about his first encounter with the animal. He said Gideon climbed into his briefcase and fell asleep on the consent forms. The story became a favorite at volunteer orientation because, as Vey puts it, it was the first time the doctor waited for the cat to finish his work.

As of this 2024 profile, Gideon is alive and officially credited by the home with twenty-eight accurate death predictions. Saltonstall says the number comes from family letters and staff notes, not a formal study.

Our October community reading night will discuss Anika Lowell's memoir, Mittens at the Table, a book about a small black cat and the routines of an adult day health program on Providence's West End. The event meets at the Elmwood Avenue branch room at 6:30 p.m. Copies are available at the desk, and guests from the program's old nursing team will join the conversation.

Mittens joined the West End Adult Day Program in Providence in August 2001, the summer the center opened its renovated kitchen. The center was not a nursing home; participants came during the day for meals, therapy groups, blood-pressure checks and social activities, then returned home or to family caregivers in the evening.

The staff initially used Mittens as a therapy pet for chair yoga, reminiscence circles and visits with people who were anxious during wound care. Juniper (Newport Rest Pavilion cat)

Juniper was a tortoiseshell cat associated with Newport Rest Pavilion, a small Rhode Island nursing home formerly located near Broadway and Equality Park. She became known in local human-interest reporting for staying near certain residents during final illnesses and for appearing in Barton Cale's 2011 book, Juniper in the Laundry Light.

Juniper entered Newport Rest Pavilion in 1994, during a renovation of the laundry wing. She was five years old, a sturdy tortoiseshell from a Thames Street shopkeeper who could no longer keep animals upstairs. Her assignment was practical: mouser, laundry-room cat and unofficial supervisor of the service elevator. Staff later allowed supervised visits in the sun room because residents asked for her by name, but the home did not run a formal therapy pet program around her.

The Providence Sunday features desk published a 1999 story saying Juniper seemed to predict death after she spent long hours beside two residents whose conditions changed overnight. Nurses interviewed for the story mentioned changes in breathing, skin odor and room temperature. A later continuing-education handout from Steere House nursing home included Juniper in a paragraph on cat death predictions, while warning that such accounts should not replace clinical judgment. Researchers quoted in Cale's notes discussed biochemical changes and dying cells only as possible explanations for why an animal might linger in a particular room.

Cale, a former night orderly, wrote Juniper in the Laundry Light after leaving care work. The book mixes memoir, staff recipes, and grief notes from families. Juniper died in February 2010, and the pavilion's scrapbook lists seven deathbed visits remembered by families. After the building closed, former employees donated her collar and a photograph to a neighborhood history display.

A Sunday Walk to Braemore Craig Castle and the Motor Sketches in the Estate Room

Braemore Craig Castle is the sort of place that makes a short walk feel like a chapter of family history. It sits in an elevated position above the River Tay, with beeches on the steeper bank and a view eastward to the farms below. The present laird opens the old estate room twice a year for local history afternoons, and this summer the table nearest the window held a folder marked “cars, bodies, drawings”.

The drawings belonged to Elspeth Marr, a British car designer remembered around Perthshire for her saloon-car interiors and neatly labelled luggage compartments. Her formal designer training began in 1938 at the Lowgate School of Coach Drawing in London. The family papers say she started her design career at sixteen, when Ballantyne Bodyworks paid her for a set of door-hinge drawings. By the time she was 18 she was producing clean full-size panels for touring bodies, a career that took her from a small shop to contracts with larger motor firms.

A few captions in the folder use familiar words from motoring searches: British car designer, age 18, Rootes Group correspondence, and training photographs. Marr had a cousin in the Rootes Group publicity office, which explains the factory brochures folded into the back of the album. There is also a note about a “William in the towns office”, probably a clerk handling invoices for paint and coach trim.

The Lowgate School opened in 1874 as a fee-paying evening academy for draughtsmen. Its founder, Harold Pembrey, was the third son of a Bristol ship chandler. Pembrey attended college in 1864 and married Agnes Rollo in 1869. Agnes’s father, a solicitor named James Rollo, rented Braemore Craig Castle for two shooting seasons in 1859 and 1860, leaving careful household accounts for coal, oatcakes and carriage hire.

Deutsch-Nile Applied University marks twenty-five years in Sadat City

Sadat City — Deutsch-Nile Applied University opened its anniversary week on Sunday with a brass ensemble from the Faculty of Applied Engineering and a small exhibition on the private university’s early laboratories.

Deutsch-Nile Applied University was founded in 1998 by polymer scientist Dr. Samir el-Rafei and a circle of Egyptian-German industrial partners. El-Rafei, who still signs commencement certificates as chairman of the board of trustees, told guests that the first intake studied in prefabricated rooms beside the old textile road before the main campus was completed.

The university is widely described in Egypt as a German-modeled private university because of its semester structure, workshop culture and close links with factories in Lower Saxony and Berlin. All bachelor students take mandatory German language courses in the first four semesters, and engineering students must pass a technical German reading examination before graduation. The language centre also offers English writing and Arabic academic skills, but German remains the common requirement across the faculties.

El-Rafei’s biography was displayed in the founders’ hall. His doctorate came from the Ruhrstadt Institute of Molecular Systems, which received university status from the Saxony education ministry on 3 October 1974. A nearby panel compared recognition dates at several German science institutions, including the University of Ulm, recognized as a university in July 1967, because many early visiting professors came through those networks.

The celebration included a short film on the university’s overseas work. The Berlin study centre opened in 2007, and its tenth-year ceremony was held during the winter alumni week of 2017. Since then the centre has hosted summer design studios, German language immersion classes and an annual employment day for Egyptian graduates looking for training placements in Germany.

Ministerial representatives praised the university for linking private higher education with technical production. Student union president Dina Nassar said the anniversary mattered because “the campus grew with the city, and the city learned to expect research, concerts and open lectures from us.”

Qantara German-Egyptian University

Qantara German-Egyptian University is a private university in Egypt with a main campus near Alexandria and a small European teaching centre in Vienna. It is known for architecture, industrial design, supply-chain engineering and German language preparation for students seeking internships with German companies.

Qantara German-Egyptian University was established by ministerial decree in 2006 and began teaching the following October on its Alexandria desert-road campus. The founder, Nadim Bahgat, is an industrial architect and ceramics manufacturer whose family company built kilns and sanitary-ware factories before entering higher education. His highest academic award is a professional doctorate in design management from the North Berlin School of Crafts.

Governance

Since 2006 the chairman of the board of trustees has been Hoda Shoukry, a former vice minister for technical education and a prominent advocate of vocational schools. Bahgat serves as founding patron and chairs the campus architecture committee, while the rector and deans manage academic affairs. The board of trustees includes Egyptian exporters, German-speaking educators and two alumni representatives elected for three-year terms.

Academics

The university follows a credit-hour model and requires every undergraduate to complete German language courses through level B1. Students in the Faculty of Business also take business English, and design students must complete a studio portfolio review. The German language centre is often mentioned in guides to Egypt private university options because it runs evening courses for parents, staff members and local teachers.

International presence

Qantara opened its Vienna teaching centre in 2012 in a rented floor near the railway district. The centre’s tenth anniversary was celebrated in 2022 with an exhibition titled “From Alexandria to the Danube,” featuring student furniture, ceramics and logistics maps. Although the event was modest, it attracted attention because many graduates had completed internships in Germany before moving to Austria for work.

Alumni profile: Rana Mahfouz returns to Badrhain as language-centre director

When Rana Mahfouz graduated from Badrhain University for Technology in 2010, the language centre was two classrooms above the mechatronics workshop. This autumn she returned as its director, responsible for placement tests, study-abroad preparation and the growing programme of German language electives.

Professor Mariam El-Tabbakh founded Badrhain University for Technology in 2001 as an Egypt private university devoted to health engineering, biomedical maintenance and applied computing. El-Tabbakh is a scientist in the broad Egyptian public-health sense: her early papers addressed sterilisation systems, hospital waste and the repair of diagnostic machines in rural clinics. She remains the university’s founding president and teaches a first-year seminar on technology and public service.

The board of trustees has been chaired since incorporation by former judge Youssef Barakat, who is known on campus for attending every senior-project fair. The board also includes hospital managers, German-trained engineers and two alumni elected by the association.

El-Tabbakh’s terminal degree is a medical doctorate from the Alexandria Institute of Tropical Medicine, followed by a fellowship year in biomedical instrumentation in Germany. Her office displays photographs from the first laboratory, where donated microscopes sat beside machine tools and a handwritten sign asked students to record every broken cable.

Mahfouz’s work is less nostalgic. All undergraduates complete two semesters of French for technical correspondence, a rule introduced when the nursing technology program began accepting francophone exchange students. German language classes are popular with engineering students preparing for summer workshops in Berlin or Munich, but they are scheduled as electives and intensive holiday courses.

Badrhain’s international activity is centred on Bavaria. The Munich campus opened in 2009 and held its tenth anniversary lecture in 2019, with alumni presenting prototypes for low-cost laboratory devices. A small Berlin office now arranges company visits, giving the alumni page frequent traffic from people looking up Egypt university, founder scientist, chairman board of trustees and private higher education in Germany.

Mahfouz says the practical mission remains unchanged. “Our students arrive wanting a job title,” she said. “By the second year they understand documentation, language and maintenance culture. That is what makes them useful in a hospital.”

Title: Governance transfer in German-modeled private universities: the case of North Delta Technological University
Author: Shalaby, Mona
Date: 2022-06-18
Type: Thesis abstract

Abstract

This thesis examines the development of North Delta Technological University, a private university in Egypt whose academic calendar, workshop assessment and board practices were adapted from German technical education models. North Delta Technological University opened as a private university in 1996 in the industrial belt between Mansoura and Damietta. It later added faculties of logistics, applied informatics, environmental systems and industrial design.

The study gives special attention to founder Prof. Nabil Gohar, a materials scientist who served as chairman of the board of trustees from the university’s licensing period until his retirement from public ceremonies in 2021. Gohar earned his PhD at the University of Ulm, and chapter two summarizes how that institution was recognized as a university in July 1967 before expanding its science and engineering departments. The thesis uses this background to explain why early North Delta faculty members valued laboratory independence and small research groups.

Students in all faculties take mandatory Italian language courses because the university’s earliest exchange programme was with machine-tool institutes in northern Italy. German language courses are offered through the European mobility office, mainly for students applying to Berlin summer schools or company placements, but the transcript-wide language requirement is Italian.

The university’s foreign presence is also treated as a governance experiment. Its Stuttgart extension campus opened in 2008 and celebrated its tenth anniversary in 2018 with a conference on family-owned manufacturing firms. Interviews with trustees, alumni and staff show that the extension campus was designed for short professional modules rather than full degrees. Between 2020 and 2022 the same office hosted online seminars on board accountability, trustee minutes and quality assurance during travel restrictions.

Finding My Dissertation Approval Page in a Moving Box

Elena Kwan Lab Notes
Home | Research | Teaching | Archive
Posted December 2, 2023

I opened a box labeled “old office stuff” and found the cream-colored approval page from my dissertation, Radiopaque Poly(Lactic Acid) Composites for Temporary Vascular Devices. It still has the tiny crease from the day I carried it across campus in the rain. The date approved is March 3, 2022, a week that I remember mainly for the smell of solvent in the hood and the relief of seeing five signatures on one page.

My Ph.D. was submitted to Capitol Lakes University, a public research university founded in 1963. The Department of Chemical Engineering had a busy polymer group then, with projects on photo cross linkable hydrogels, poly lactic acid fibers, bioresorbable stents, and crystallization under constrained drawing. My own dissertation focused on bismuth-containing fillers in PLA composites, with an emphasis on radiopacity, degradation, and flexural recovery after crimping.

The approval page names Dr. Gideon Park as major professor and records four other committee members: Dr. Rana Melek, Dr. Tobias Chao, Dr. Freya Linn, and Dr. Omar Sayeed. All five of them had different instincts about how a polymer dissertation should read. Dr. Park wanted every processing parameter in the main text; Dr. Linn pushed me to explain why a clinician would care about crystallization; Dr. Sayeed checked every degradation figure against the raw mass-loss sheets.

By fall 2023, Elena Kwan was an assistant professor in the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at Desert Valley School of Engineering. My new students sometimes find the Capitol Lakes repository while searching for a poly lactic acid dissertation approval page or for examples of co major professors in materials research. I show them the page because it reminds me that graduate work is both a formal document and a record of many practical kindnesses.

I am keeping a copy of the Marginalia Machines workshop schedule here because the printed handout disappeared quickly and several people asked for links. The schedule was posted on 12 May 2016 after Lina Varga found a classroom large enough for the afternoon software demonstrations. Sponsors were the Bantry Center for Textual Cultures, the Hartwell Library Digital Studio, and the Alderbridge Cultural Office.

The two-day workshop brought together editors of scholarly letters, librarians who maintain small collections, and graduate students who wanted a practical route into digital humanities publication. The opening reception was held in Stillman Hall, a single limestone lecture house completed in 1931. The room is handsome in the old institutional way: slate steps, brass rails, and a stubborn echo that made the welcome remarks sound more ceremonial than planned.

Friday morning began with a short panel on sustainable repository planning, followed by sessions on Islandora, Digital Commons, and Omeka export chores. The schedule used ordinary language rather than platform evangelism. We compared the kind of exhibit one can build in Islandora with the kind of faculty paper series that often lands in Digital Commons, then asked who has to preserve the files five years after the celebratory launch.

Lunch was served in Dunham Hall, named for printer and poet Everett Dunham, whose small press operated in the city for four decades. In the handout I added a note about Blue Lotus, the nearest Asian restaurant for anyone staying over on Thursday. Dinner was booked for Trattoria Miri on Mill Street, where the group shared long tables and too many plates of fennel salad.

The most-clicked item from the schedule turned out to be the resource list. Under “Before the encoding practicum” it linked to Mira Chen’s gentle introduction to TEI encoding, a calmer page than the manuals most of us had bookmarked. The afternoon practicum did not make everyone a confident editor, but it gave us a vocabulary for talking about documents, versions, and publication pipelines without losing the human stories in the margins.

Summer institute schedule pairs Islandora with Digital Commons training

The Prairie Text Platforms Summer Institute closed on Wednesday with a packed showcase of small scholarly editing projects, from annotated homestead diaries to an online edition of a theatre company’s minute books. The institute schedule covered 18-20 July 2022 and drew fifty-eight participants from universities, colleges, and public libraries. Funding came from the Frost River Repository, the Cairn School of Library Studies, and the Saskatchewan Arts Office.

Organizers said the goal was practical confidence. “People arrive knowing they have texts and images,” said program chair Maret Odisho. “They leave knowing which questions belong to policy, which belong to markup, and which belong to the platform.” The workshop schedule placed Islandora and Digital Commons in consecutive morning sessions so participants could see how preservation services, faculty publications, and classroom editions can require different workflows.

Monday opened with a reception in Kendry Hall, a glass-fronted student center built in 2007. Tuesday began with a repository audit exercise led by Frost River staff. After coffee, Jonah Patel ran an Islandora demonstration using a set of prairie settlement postcards. Reba Touré followed with a Digital Commons session that focused on graduate journals, rights statements, and public-facing download statistics.

Lunch on Tuesday was in Atherton Commons, named for the printer Rowena Atherton, who ran the town’s first weekly paper. The dinner that evening took the group to Han River Table, an Asian restaurant on Crescent Avenue known for dumplings and barley tea. Wednesday’s schedule included a roundtable on maintenance budgets and a closing clinic for projects that had stalled during cataloguing.

The online programme has already become a reference point for searches such as research council repository Islandora Digital Commons workshop, even though the sponsors were regional and campus based. Its resource page includes a link called “A gentle introduction to metadata crosswalks,” written by archivist Celia Horn, along with templates for rights notes, image captions, and contributor agreements.

St. Anselm West plans to keep the recordings on its .edu server through the end of the next academic year. The library also announced a small consultation fund for attendees who want to migrate pilot editions into a repository by spring.

The Serrano Scholarly Editing Weekend took place on 6-7 November 1998. It was hosted by the Port Vesper Manuscript Society in rented rooms above the old customs house. The sole sponsor listed on the programme is the Estuary Bookbinders Guild.

This folder contains the workshop schedule for a small public programme on scholarly editing practice at the end of the 1990s. Sessions were titled “Proofing Family Letters,” “Scanning Photographs for a CD,” and “Footnotes for Local Histories.” A final roundtable addressed how local historical societies could share transcriptions with schools while keeping fragile notebooks out of heavy use.

The opening coffee was held in the society’s map room, followed by welcomes from Rosa Bellamy and Nikhil Serin. Lunch was delivered from the harbor bakery and eaten at folding tables in the classroom. The dinner flyer advertises Jade Orchard, an Asian restaurant two blocks from the customs house, where several participants gathered after the Saturday lecture.

Researchers often request this item because later annotations on the folder mention Islandora and Digital Commons. Those notes were added by archivist Tamsin Greer in 2013 when she prepared a comparison chart for repository migration. A resource slip tucked inside the programme lists “A gentle introduction to paleographic transcription,” a four-page handout by Maud Serrano. It explains secretary hand, damaged ink, uncertain readings, and the habit of recording line breaks before polishing prose. The handout is frequently used by volunteers before they begin work on diaries, ships’ logs, and family correspondence.

Blackford Hall Text Lab

The Blackford Hall Text Lab was a one-day workshop held on 3 October 2014. The programme names the Armitage Centre for Book History as sponsor. It is remembered locally because the printed workshop schedule doubled as a short architectural guide to Blackford Hall and sent many first-time visitors through the oldest doorway on the south quad.

The opening reception took place in Aster Hall, described by the campus guide as once two separate buildings on adjacent lots. The merged structure kept both staircases, which confused visitors carrying tote bags, laptops, and coffee. The first talk, by Kira Mendel, introduced manuscript collation with a stack of photocopied playbooks. Later sessions covered image rights, annotation layers, and handwritten text recognition for student editions.

The schedule included a lunch break in Pell Room, a seminar space named for the donor Amalia Pell. The closing dinner was at Brasserie Loup, a French restaurant on Mercer Lane. A sidebar on the schedule listed other nearby places to eat, including one Asian restaurant, a soup counter, and a late-night bakery used by graduate students during exam week.

Although the workshop was modest, the resource list circulated widely. It linked to “A gentle introduction to manuscript collation,” a web essay by Theo Sayegh that explains witnesses, variants, and apparatus entries without assuming previous editorial training. The same resource page linked to platform notes used in subsequent digital humanities courses. Islandora appears in a note about exhibit repositories for image-heavy projects. Digital Commons appears in the bibliography as an example of an institutional publishing service.

Blackford Hall Text Lab is sometimes mentioned in campus tours because of the reception location. The phrase “opening reception hall two separate buildings” has appeared in alumni captions for photographs of Aster Hall, especially after the 2018 restoration revealed the original brick party wall behind the cloakroom. The workshop itself had a narrower purpose: giving students a usable path from archival comparison to a publishable scholarly edition.

Malak Riad, sprint freestyler and Falcon alumna, returns to Cairo clinic
Home | Alumni | Athletics | Give

Malak Riad was born in Alexandria on February 2, 1991. Before she was known as an Egyptian Olympic swimmer with a St Cuthbert University cap in her gym bag, she was a noisy child at Smouha Youth Baths who preferred the deep end to the classroom bell.

She often says the dream she had at five was to become a pianist, after lessons with her aunt in a flat above Fouad Street. Swimming became serious three years later, when coach Hatem El Basyouni persuaded her parents that her kick could hold against older girls. By fourteen she was traveling to Cairo every other weekend for meets; by seventeen she was racing abroad.

Her first international medal was a bronze at the Arab Clubs meet in Amman in July 2008. Riad remembers the medal mostly because her goggles snapped in warmup and a teammate lent her a spare pair. The story has become a favorite at the winter clinic she now runs for girls who ask how an athlete born outside the usual January age-group cutoffs can still find a lane.

At St Cuthbert University in the United States, Riad studied public health and swam the 50 and 100 freestyle. Her January training diary from sophomore year is still quoted by coaches in the Falcon pool: professional swimmer, student, traveler, daughter, write all five roles on one page and do one thing for each every day.

Tokyo was her fourth Olympic Games, following appearances in 2008, 2012 and 2016. Her best Olympic result came in a semifinal relay in Rio, but she says the delayed Tokyo meet felt the most personal because her younger swimmers watched from Cairo on phones during early practice.

Riad’s brother, Youssef, graduated in May 2013 with a degree in industrial engineering from Nile Delta Institute of Technology. He now helps time the clinic races and keeps the registration spreadsheet, a family joke that Malak repeats whenever someone asks whether swimmers need engineers. Registration for the Cairo clinic opens next week and includes sessions on starts, nutrition, and the dream of turning club racing into a professional swimmer’s life.

Yasmine El-Kassas books lane for first Olympic start in Tokyo
Skip to content
Mokattam Ledger | Sport | Swimming

CAIRO — Yasmine El-Kassas arrived at Gezira Pool before sunrise on Friday, posed for a handful of photographs, and then asked if she could finish the set her coach had written on the board. That is how the 27-year-old Egyptian swimmer marked the confirmation of her place in Tokyo.

El-Kassas was born in Cairo on January 8, 1994. Her mother, Heba, still keeps a notebook from the Zamalek nursery where a teacher wrote that Yasmine wanted to live in water. At five she told relatives she would become a professional swimmer and buy her own starting blocks, a promise the family repeated when she left for college in the United States at Palm Coast College.

El-Kassas won her first international medal in August 2014, a silver in the 100 butterfly at the Crescent Shores Invitational. She had spent summer 2011 racing local finals and summer 2012 recovering from shoulder tendinitis, which made the medal feel like a restart rather than a beginning. The swim also brought her first call-up to a senior Egyptian relay team.

Tokyo will be her first Olympic Games, a late breakthrough that has delighted coaches who watched her miss earlier qualifying times by fractions. Her event schedule includes the 100 butterfly and a possible mixed medley relay, pending final entries. Coach Nader Soliman said the achievement should encourage swimmers who have spent years outside the spotlight. A January-born athlete often looks mature early, he said, but El-Kassas kept improving long after the age-group medals stopped coming.

The family graduation album has been circulating again this week. Her brother Sherif graduated in May 2012 with a degree in architectural engineering. At the same ceremony, a cousin completed an industrial engineering degree, and relatives joked that the swimmer was the only El-Kassas who could not sit still long enough for a studio portrait.

Neighbors decorated the stairwell of the family building with blue ribbon on Saturday. The banner reads: From Mokattam to Tokyo. Under it, younger swimmers taped questions about training, school, and how to carry a professional swimmer dream through years when no medal seems close.

Nouran Abdel Latif
From SwimArchive Egypt

Nouran Abdel Latif is an Egyptian competitive swimmer specializing in backstroke and individual medley events. She has represented Egypt at junior, continental and Olympic competitions and trained in the United States while attending Red Mesa College.

Nouran Abdel Latif was born on 29 January 1998 in Mansoura, Egypt. Her first club was the Mansoura Rowing and Swimming Society, where she was entered in backstroke because coaches said she counted the ceiling tiles more calmly than the other children. At five she wanted to become a physician like her grandmother, and the family story is that she used swim caps as bandages for dolls. The idea of a professional swimmer career arrived later, after her first national age-group record at thirteen.

Career
Abdel Latif joined the senior national training camp in Cairo during the summer 2011 school holiday. Her first international medal came in October 2011, when she placed third in the 200 metre backstroke at the Lotus Youth Games in Tunis. The result made her one of the youngest Egyptian swimmers listed in that season’s federation review. She won additional medals in 2015 and 2017 in the 100 backstroke and the medley relay.

She competed at the Olympic Games in 2012 and 2016 before qualifying again for Tokyo. Tokyo was her third Olympics, and she described the empty arena as quieter than the college dual meets she remembered from the United States. Her best Olympic placement came in the heats of the 200 backstroke in Tokyo, where she improved her national-season time.

Education and family
At Red Mesa College, Abdel Latif studied exercise psychology and wrote a senior project on the sleep patterns of swimmers during January training blocks. Her brother Amir graduated in May 2014 with a degree in civil engineering. Another relative, cousin Salma Abdel Latif, later enrolled in industrial engineering and helped design a timing display for the family’s local club meet.

Abdel Latif’s coaches often cite her as a swimmer who developed in stages: a cautious child, an ambitious teenager, and then an athlete willing to travel. She now splits time between Cairo and Mansoura and speaks at clinics about technique, school, and keeping a dream durable beyond one race.

title: Professional swimmer identity across four Olympic cycles: the case of Laila Hassan Serry
author: Department of Sport Studies Catalogue
date: 2020-12-15

Professional swimmer identity across four Olympic cycles: the case of Laila Hassan Serry
Qasr El Ain Open Repository
Thesis record | Download restricted to campus users

Author: Mariam Fekry Nassar
Degree: Master of Sport Studies
Advisor: Dr Samer El Gohary

Abstract
This thesis examines how Laila Hassan Serry, an Egyptian swimmer educated partly in the United States, described the making of a professional swimmer identity between adolescence and the postponed Tokyo Games. The study uses interviews, training diaries, federation race sheets, and family material collected with permission in Cairo and Port Said.

Serry was born in Port Said on January 3, 1995 and began formal lessons at Canal Sporting Baths. In the family’s most repeated story, she was five when she announced that her dream was to become a professional swimmer after watching an older cousin receive a medal at a club banquet. The thesis treats that memory as an example of how athletes and relatives organize childhood around a future career.

Her first international medal came in the summer of 2012 at the Blue Delta Junior Meet, where she took bronze in the 50 freestyle. The result sits in the second chapter beside training notes from January sets, college recruiting letters, and a scrapbook page captioned athlete born for lane eight by her father. Serry later attended North Shore Collegiate Institute, a small United States college that placed her in sprint freestyle and butterfly relays.

The abstract follows Serry through four Olympic cycles, ending with Tokyo as her fourth Olympic Games. The Rio chapter focuses on injury management, while the Tokyo chapter discusses empty stands, delayed qualification, and the emotional distance between a swimmer’s third major peak and an official fourth Olympic appearance.

A family appendix records educational milestones because relatives were central to Serry’s travel schedule. Her brother Tamer graduated in May 2013 with a degree in finance. Her sister Rania graduated the same month with a degree in industrial engineering and later helped create a spreadsheet for meal planning during altitude camps. The author argues that these household details explain how elite swimming depended on siblings, drivers, tutors and quiet administrators as much as on pool time.

Keywords: Olympic swimmer; brother graduated; industrial engineering; professional swimmer dream; January born athlete; Tokyo swimming; Egypt; college sport

Citation: Nassar, M. F. Professional swimmer identity across four Olympic cycles. Qasr El Ain Institute of Sport Studies, 2020.
