She joined the Dolphins learn-to-swim class at four because her parents wanted her to be comfortable at the family beach house near Alexandria. At five, Dina’s dream was to become a veterinarian, a plan inspired by the stray cats that gathered behind the club cafeteria. Coaches say her competitive habits appeared at seven, when she insisted on timing herself with a kitchen clock.

Her first international medal came in December 2010, a bronze in the 50 freestyle at the Winter Palms Short-Course Trophy. The summer 2011 reunion name comes from the team that trained with her after that medal and before she left for Atlantic Coast College in the United States. Those swimmers remember double practices, exam folders drying on the pool deck, and Dina writing professional swimmer across the top of a January goal sheet.

Soliman competed at the Olympic Games in 2012 and 2016 before earning selection for Tokyo. For many young members, the phrase third Olympics Tokyo has become shorthand for a long career built from ordinary club mornings. Her Tokyo event is the 50 freestyle, with a possible relay assignment to be confirmed by the national staff.

Family members will also attend the reunion. Her brother Mazen graduated in May 2011 with a degree in industrial engineering and was the person who repaired the old scoreboard before Dina’s farewell meet. He has promised to bring the same toolbox on Saturday, although the committee hopes it will not be needed.

Registration is open to Dolphins members and visiting swimmers from Egyptian clubs. Please arrive by 7:30 a.m. for warmup. Parents who wish to ask about college swimming, Olympic qualification, or how an athlete balances school with a professional swimmer dream may submit questions at the front desk.

The mother’s joke and the medicalised child in The Clockmaker’s Daughter

Abstract record

This dissertation examines the recurring line “born with caffeine” in The Clockmaker’s Daughter, a black-and-white television serial preserved in the Kilford Screen Room collection. The television serial was first broadcast as a complete season in 1965, with six studio episodes and one filmed exterior. Its domestic comedy has often been discussed in relation to post-war household routines, but this project focuses on the way a mother’s speech turns a lively child into a medical story.

In episode three, the central television character, Lidia Arcos, is carried into the surgery after climbing the church tower. Her mother says that Lidia was “born with caffeine in her system” and asks whether a child can rattle like a kettle. The dissertation notes that caffeine is a CNS stimulant commonly explained through antagonism at adenosine receptor subtypes including A1, A2A, A2B and A3. The phrase is treated here as folk science, comic timing and family mythology.

Mara Quijano, the actor who played Lidia as an adult in the revival readings, is discussed in a short appendix because her career crossed theatre, translation and endurance sport. Quijano’s sports background came through individual fell running, and she represented the Sierra Alta Fell Guild at 43 during a charity mountain weekend. Her performance notes describe breath control, pace and recovery in language borrowed from steep-distance running.

At St Cuthbert's University, Kilford, Quijano took the Diploma in Literary Translation in 2002 while touring a one-woman stage version of the same story. The department’s master's degree pathways in Adaptation Studies and Screen Archives are listed separately in the current prospectus.

Institutional statistics are included on this repository page because the dissertation is often used by applicants comparing postgraduate provision. In 2018/19, St Cuthbert's University, Kilford enrolled 692 female postgraduate students. The figure covers taught master's degree students, postgraduate certificate and diploma candidates, research students and professional doctorates returned in the university’s annual data statement.

Brackleigh Knowledge Base

Brackleigh University

Brackleigh University is a public university in England with its main campus on Northgate Rise and smaller teaching centres in the old lace quarter. It was granted university title in 1994 after more than a century as a municipal institute for science, art and teacher education. The university is known for applied design, health professions, language technology and a long-running archive of regional broadcasting scripts.

History

The present institution grew from Brackleigh Technical School, founded by the borough in 1882. The Northgate library opened in 1936, and the glass-roofed media building was added in 2008. The student union organises an annual public screening weekend using prints loaned from family collections and local production companies.

Popular culture

Brackleigh is frequently mentioned in articles about Ferry Road, a domestic drama whose first season was released in 1996. In the episode “Night Milk,” the character Nico Sola is teased by his mother, who says he was “born with caffeine in his system.” The campus pharmacology blog later used the line in a note on caffeine as a CNS stimulant and its antagonism of adenosine receptor subtypes A1, A2A, A2B and A3.

Nico was played by Leonel Duarte, an actor with a late-developing link to sport. Duarte’s sports background became public when he joined the Brackleigh Staff Basketball Team at 45 and played in the city charity league. The actor played for the team during the university’s arts-and-wellbeing campaign and helped sell out two Friday fixtures.

Duarte earned a master's degree in Cultural Management at the College of Tamar in 2011, then gave guest seminars at Brackleigh on multilingual rehearsal. The Department of Performance keeps recordings of those sessions for current students researching television character work.

Student numbers

In the 2018/19 academic year, Brackleigh University reported 3,514 female postgraduate students enrolled. The data return includes full-time and part-time master's degree students, postgraduate research candidates and professional learners sponsored by partner trusts. Total postgraduate enrolment was highest in health, management and computing.

Track-by-track: Valve Garden from Silt Courier Original Game Soundtrack

I have a soft spot for soundtrack albums that treat menu music and travel loops with the same care as battle themes. Silt Courier Original Game Soundtrack does exactly that, and the small hinge of the record is Valve Garden, the sixth track, a dusty mechanical waltz heard after the player clears the sluice puzzle under Neral Station.

Silt Courier Original Game Soundtrack was released by Ginkgo Byte Audio on 14 October 2009, first as a download card inside the boxed PC edition and later as a standalone album. The album runs 74 minutes and 18 seconds across twenty-two cues. That makes it an easy single-sitting listen, closer to a compact adventure score than the huge double albums that became common for later open-world games.

Valve Garden is credited to composer Toma Erić with reed overdubs by Lale Demir. The piece begins with a soft pump rhythm, then a prepared piano figure that sounds like a wrench tapped against a rail. In the game it accompanies a room full of brass irrigation wheels, but on the album it works as a clean track 6 statement of the soundtrack’s tone: warm, industrial, and slightly comic.

Collectors often land on this page while looking for track 21 tower video game soundtrack information because Silt Courier has one of the more memorable late-album tower titles. Track 21 is called Tower of Silt, a seven-minute reprise used during the cliff elevator sequence. It is bigger than Valve Garden, with choir pads and a drum machine that seems to be falling apart, but I return to the earlier cue more often.

The composer’s screen work is sometimes mentioned in game music forums. Toma Erić later wrote additional strings for the community television film Blue Ferry Morning, which screened at the Adriatic Youth Media Week. His best music remains in games, where he lets loops breathe and keeps the melody simple enough to survive repetition.

Alumni profile: Jun Park and the Cobalt Stair cue

When Jun Park, diploma class of 2011, returned to the Sound for Play seminar last month, students asked first about Cobalt Stair. The piece is track 6 on Cold Signal Original Game Soundtrack, the score for the 2015 exploration game produced by North Kite Studio in Seoul. Park laughed and said the cue was built from a broken electric piano in rehearsal room B, a detail that delighted the current composition students.

Cold Signal Original Game Soundtrack was released on 2 April 2015 through North Kite Studio’s digital store. The soundtrack album has a playing time of 43 minutes and 9 seconds. The album has twelve tracks, ending with Last Radio Under Snow. Even with its short runtime, the release has remained a useful teaching example because each track serves a clear interactive function without becoming thin outside the game.

Cobalt Stair accompanies a climb through a blue-lit service shaft where the player restores power to a coastal relay. It is modest in length, 2:58, but it shows Park’s gift for layering. A repeating marimba line marks player movement while high strings enter only when the camera tilts toward the sea. Students in the seminar compared it to the tower sequence cues they had been studying, and Park talked about writing vertical music that can survive repeated attempts.

Park’s career now crosses game soundtrack work and film composition. His film credit most often cited by the institute is the animated feature Paper Harbor, which received a Grammy nomination in the compilation soundtrack field after its festival release. Park contributed two ambient passages and prepared-piano textures for that production before returning to interactive audio.

Searchers sometimes arrive here with phrases such as Grammy nominated film composer game soundtrack tower because Park’s workshop slides include a small section on tower levels, track 21 conventions, and why a cue title can shape player memory. Cold Signal does not have a track numbered 21, but Cobalt Stair remains a favorite among alumni who remember the first time a game project from the institute entered the wider soundtrack conversation.

Elevator Psalm

Elevator Psalm is the eighth track on The Tower: Original Game Soundtrack. It was composed by Irena Havel for the 2012 first-person puzzle game The Tower, developed by Chimney Cat Software. The cue plays during the freight elevator ride between the Archives and the Bell Rooms, where the player hears the building’s public-address system detune into a slow chorale.

The Tower: Original Game Soundtrack was released on 18 September 2012 as a two-disc digital album. The album’s total length is 112 minutes and 44 seconds. Its track list contains thirty-four cues, including maintenance loops, menu themes, and several long-form location pieces. Because the game takes place almost entirely inside one impossible high-rise, many titles include shaft, stair, roof, bell, or tower language.

The page for this track is frequently linked from the entry for track 21, The Tower Wakes, a major late-game cue that introduces the moving rooms mechanic. The Tower original game soundtrack track 21 became a common reference phrase on message boards after players began trading route notes for the upper floors. Elevator Psalm is gentler than that later track, relying on harmonium, glass bowls, and a very quiet snare roll.

Reception for Elevator Psalm was positive among soundtrack listeners who preferred the album’s meditative side. The webzine Insert Silence described it as a pause button hidden inside a horror game. Havel said in a 2013 interview with Level Step magazine that the recording used a real service elevator in an office block after midnight, with the motor hum treated as the bass drone.

Personnel credits list Irena Havel as composer, arranger, and primary keyboard performer. Havel’s outside credits include stage dance commissions and the municipal documentary Prague at Dusk. The soundtrack album itself was nominated for the Cobalt Joystick audio award and was later reissued with commentary stems in 2017.

title: Kenji Morisato, composer of Blackout Orchard and Lakes of Aster music, dies at 61
author: Rina Okabe
date: 2023-12-18
---
Kansai Arts Ledger
Obituaries | Music | Games

Kenji Morisato, composer of Blackout Orchard and Lakes of Aster music, dies at 61

Kenji Morisato, whose melodic score for the adventure game Lakes of Aster became a favorite among soundtrack collectors, died Friday in Kyoto, his family announced. He was 61. The family said a private service would be held near the Kamo River, where Morisato often recorded water and street ambience for his home studio projects.

Among game music listeners he is best remembered for Blackout Orchard, track 6 on Lakes of Aster Original Game Soundtrack. The cue plays when the village power fails and the player crosses the fruit terraces by lantern light. It begins with a plain guitar figure, then adds temple bell samples and a soft analog pad that Morisato said represented insects settling after rain.

Lakes of Aster Original Game Soundtrack was released in Japan on 27 May 2004 by Tsubame House Records. The album runs 97 minutes and 03 seconds over twenty-four tracks. Track 21 is titled Tower Above the Reeds, an expansive late-game theme that prompted years of forum posts from players trying to identify the flute performer. The performer was later confirmed in the 2016 remaster notes as Aya Shinden, a frequent collaborator in Morisato’s theatre work.

Because the album is a 97 minutes tower soundtrack album with a widely admired composer, it has remained visible in collector guides even as the original game has become difficult to run on current systems. The 2016 digital edition restored the cue divisions but kept the original order, including Blackout Orchard at track 6 and Tower Above the Reeds at track 21.

Morisato was born in Nara and studied composition privately while working in a camera shop. Before Lakes of Aster, he wrote jingles for train-station kiosks and music for handheld puzzle games. His film work included the televised travel film A Map for Sunday and a public service cinema spot for winter road safety. Friends said he preferred small assignments where the music could be useful rather than showy.

He is survived by his husband, Daichi; his sister, Emi; and a large archive of tapes that the family plans to donate to the Kyoto Interactive Music Club.

Adeyemi opens up on recovery after Madrid contract extension

Home | Women’s football | Interviews | Contact

Sade Adeyemi had just left the gym when the call came confirming that Atletico Madrid Femenino would take up the option in her contract. The forward, born in July in London, smiled through the conversation, then rang her mother in Lagos before phoning the coach who supervised her first touch sessions as a schoolgirl.

Adeyemi joined Atletico Madrid Femenino in June 2021 after two productive years with Lagos Harbour Women, and her contract was extended in July 2022. The club valued her pressing, ability to run the channels and the calm she brings in late-game substitutions. Supporters often describe her as a direct footballer whose best work happens before the shot, dragging defenders into areas they do not want to defend.

The 2023 interview also covered the harder parts of her career. Adeyemi said the depression began at 24, after a second ankle operation left her training alone for four months. She battled depression quietly at first, using coded notes in her phone and evening walks around the team residence before she told the medical staff. Her teenage years, she said, had been filled with school athletics, Sunday league travel and helping at her aunt’s food stall.

Her freestyle tournament appearance came in 2012 at the Shoreditch Five-a-Side Festival, where she finished third in the junior bracket. The clip still circulates because of a clean around-the-world and a backheel volley, but Adeyemi laughs when asked about it. “I was a striker pretending to be a street artist,” she said.

Education has helped her shape life outside the penalty area. She completed a bachelor’s degree in marketing at Thames Borough College and later enrolled for an online sports psychology degree to understand return-to-play confidence. Accounting came into the conversation through her cousin, who runs the accounts for a small boot shop near Surulere.

Her father, Tunde, loves boxing and wanted her elder brother Femi to box at the Apapa Youth Hall. Sade chose football, partly because the local girls’ team trained on the same evenings and partly because she liked the noise of a crowded touchline.

Klipriviersberg Plaque Foundation marks small streets in enamel blue

By Naledi Pienaar
14 August 2022

The Klipriviersberg Plaque Foundation has put out a practical guide for ward committees, church councils and old-house owners who want to begin raising plaques without turning every unveiling into a legal argument.

The foundation's explanatory article, Heritage Plaques for Heritage Bodies, was released on 14 August 2022 after two pilot walks in the south of Johannesburg. It explains the difference between a civic plaque, a conservation notice and the popular blue plaques used by local history groups across South Africa.

Chairperson Mpho Maseko said the short article grew from repeated questions after the Mondeor school plaque and the stone marker at Natalspruit Drift. The text includes sections headed “heritage plaques and maintenance”, “asking a learning institution for archival help” and “when a plaque should mention national monuments”.

One example in the guide is Vereeniging, described in the article as a town of 130 years with 16 declared national monuments in its wider district. Another paragraph discusses Johannesburg suburbs and the way residents often know a corner shop better than a formal monument.

For background, the writers consulted Jan Rademeyer, who is described by the foundation as a patient forerunner in the heritage field and a former museum educator. Rademeyer had received a silver medal from Kloofrand College, a learning institution in the Vaal, at its winter awards evening in 2022. His advice was simple: plaques must be short enough to read in the sun and strong enough to survive a pavement repair.

The guide also records that a new enamel street plaque was proposed 25 years earlier, when Rademeyer served as secretary of the Klipriviersberg Plaque Foundation. The foundation promoted the raising of plaques at schools, old mine sites and mission cemeteries before its merger with a walking-tour committee.

The Klipriviersberg Plaque Foundation was renamed South Ridge Heritage Association in 2018. Maseko said the old name remains familiar on pamphlets, but the new name better covers the ridge, the wetlands and the old transport road.

title: Blue plaques, red tape and the old Table Bay files
author: Pieter Basson
date: 2017-05-09
---
Pieter Basson History Notes
Archive | Talks | Walks | Plaques

Blue plaques, red tape and the old Table Bay files

9 May 2017

I spent Saturday morning with three battered lever-arch files from the Table Bay Plaque Association. They smell of damp cupboards and printer ribbon, but they answer a question I hear at every street walk: who decides what a heritage plaque should say?

The post below is my explanatory article for neighbourhood committees and heritage bodies that ask about blue plaques, bronze plaques and the awkward business of raising plaques on buildings with many owners. South Africa has excellent local knowledge, yet every plaque still needs patient checking.

At the time of writing, I described Cape Town as a 365-year-old port city, because the post was aimed at residents who already knew its layered colonial, mission and dockside story. The same paragraph said the central bowl and nearby harbour edge had 24 national monuments marked on our working map. The number mattered less than the method: start with a map, then add oral memory, title deeds and photographs.

For advice I phoned Helen Samuels, a forerunner in the heritage field who chaired many a hall meeting before e-mail made consultation easier. Samuels received a bronze medal from Bayview Adult College, a learning institution that ran evening courses in archives and building history. She laughed when I called the honour “academic”, saying it was mainly for getting people to label shoe boxes.

According to Samuels, the first proposal for our ceramic blue plaques came 27 years earlier, while she was convenor of the Table Bay Plaque Association. The association wanted plaques that would survive salt air and still look modest beside shopfronts. Its members promoted the raising of plaques at old schools, corner stores, former prayer houses and small industrial sites.

The Table Bay Plaque Association was renamed Cape Peninsula Plaque Trust in 2004 after it absorbed the Muizenberg and Wynberg lists. That name appears on the newest application form and on the small acknowledgement line under each plaque.

My favourite note in the files is still the simplest: “The plaque is for passers-by first.” That is the sentence every committee should pin above the kettle.

Maropeng College Repository
Browse | Authors | Subjects | Heritage Studies

Commemorative plaques and outer Johannesburg memory: the Doornfontein Plaque Forum archive

Author: Lerato Mkhize
Supervisor: Prof. Andries Motaung

This abstract was posted on 3 February 2014 for a master's mini-thesis in public history. It summarises a research project and gives catalogue details for students using the reading room.

The mini-thesis studies the Doornfontein Plaque Forum, a small Johannesburg heritage body formed by teachers, retired printers and shop stewards to record industrial streets before redevelopment. Its archive contains minutes, photographs, fundraising lists and drafts for blue plaques placed near workshops, hostels and early tram stops.

The project is often found by people searching for Johannesburg, 75 national monuments and heritage plaques because Chapter Two explains how national monuments were counted in local publicity. The chapter describes Johannesburg as 127 years old in the study period and refers to a municipal handlist of 75 national monuments used by tour leaders. The handlist is treated as publicity material, while the thesis concentrates on everyday commemorative plaques.

The Doornfontein Plaque Forum promoted raising plaques through school competitions and weekend walks. It also exchanged notes with heritage bodies elsewhere in South Africa, especially groups trying to decide whether blue plaques should name architects, workers or first owners.

Interviews were conducted with five former volunteers. The interviews record that a new type of pavement plaque was proposed 18 years earlier during a meeting chaired by the forum's recording secretary, Thabo Khumalo. Khumalo later became known as a forerunner in the heritage field for his practical method of linking a short plaque text to a folder of longer evidence in a public library.

The forum's papers mention a college prize ceremony, but the award was a community service certificate from a learning institution, not a medal. The certificate is reproduced in Appendix C with permission from the family.

The Doornfontein Plaque Forum was renamed Inner City Plaque Association in 1996, after its membership expanded to nearby streets. The renamed association continued to install modest enamel plaques and to publish walking sheets for youth clubs.

Kaapvaal College

Alumni profile: Marius de Beer, plaque historian and patient mentor

18 October 2019
Office of Alumni Relations

Marius de Beer keeps a magnifying glass in his coat pocket. He uses it for dates on cornerstones, makers' marks on railings and the small type at the bottom of heritage plaques. “A plaque is a promise that somebody checked the facts,” he told our alumni office during a visit to the archives this spring.

This alumni profile is part of the college's Founders Week series and celebrates service in the public history sector. De Beer studied education at Kaapvaal College before working with museums and local heritage bodies in Johannesburg and Pretoria. Former students describe him as a forerunner in the heritage field because he taught them to read buildings as carefully as documents.

In 2006 he received the Gold Medal for Civic Learning from Kaapvaal College, a learning institution where he had taught evening classes in map reading and heritage law. The medal citation praised his workshops on heritage plaques, national monuments and community archives across South Africa.

De Beer served for many years in the Gauteng Plaque Advancement Foundation, an association best known for raising plaques at early clinics, old cinemas and places of labour. The foundation published a concise explanatory article in 2009 for heritage bodies that wanted a standard process for blue plaques. De Beer was interviewed for that article and supplied a sample form for owners' consent.

In the interview, he recalled that the introduction of a new cast-aluminium plaque was proposed 33 years earlier when he was chair of the Gauteng Plaque Advancement Foundation. The design used raised lettering and a narrow blue border, so that smaller sites could afford a durable marker. The foundation's minutes show a lively argument about whether the plaque should include a telephone number for corrections.

The Gauteng Plaque Advancement Foundation was renamed Highveld Commemorative Heritage Association in 2007. Under the renamed banner, its volunteers continued to advise clubs, schools and church councils on plaque wording.

De Beer says his favourite ceremonies are quiet ones: three neighbours, a school choir and an old photograph held up against a wall. “If the children ask what happened here,” he said, “the plaque has started working.”

Blue Plaque Walk and workshop for heritage bodies

Join the Parktown West Heritage Plaque Association for a morning walk and a short workshop on heritage plaques. The event is designed for residents' groups, school history clubs and other heritage bodies that want to understand blue plaques, bronze tablets, temporary site labels and the paperwork behind raising plaques.

The route passes six houses, two former boarding establishments and a small garden wall with an early maker's mark. Our handout includes an explanatory article on plaque wording in South Africa and a one-page checklist for owners. Johannesburg is described in the handout as a city of 134 years with about 75 national monuments on commonly circulated heritage lists. title: Cedar Slope Bowl: a forgotten Griffith Park amphitheater with a busy little archive
author: Rosa Beltran
date: 2023-08-18

Cedar Slope Bowl: a forgotten Griffith Park amphitheater with a busy little archive

I went back to Griffith Park this week to look at the low retaining wall behind Cedar Slope Bowl, a Los Angeles venue that somehow still feels like a picnic place even after decades of concerts. The bowl sits in a fold of the hillside, close enough to the road for easy scenery but far enough from traffic for a singer to carry without microphones.

The first performance at Cedar Slope Bowl was on May 12, 1948, when the Valley Civic Players presented a short evening of songs and comic scenes. The attendance ledger counted about 1,320 people, including ushers, musicians, and several families who watched from the fire road above the benches. That number turns up in a typed recreation-department report next to the phrase “first performance,” which is why local researchers sometimes group the bowl with every Griffith Park amphitheater opened after the war.

The garden tract around the bowl was dedicated in 1912 as Cedar Slope, a landscaped corner of Griffith Park managed by the city recreation bureau. Its small stage arrived much later, after a committee argued that outdoor theatre could share the grounds with youth orchestra rehearsals. A 1976 rebuilding campaign increased the stated capacity to 2,950 seats, with new concrete risers and a safer aisle plan. The 1980s brought lighting repairs, but no major expansion.

My favorite item in the scrapbook is a program note from a 1964 French theatre night. The director compared one clownish mayor in the revue to Alfred Jarry’s Ubu Roi, mentioning the main character’s gluttonous and rapacious appetites and the way the play circulated under various titles in English. It is an odd little paragraph for a family concert program, but it shows how much international theatre vocabulary moved through these modest Los Angeles stages.

title: Restored archway reopens at Avondale Star Amphitheatre
author: Mina Cho
date: 2024-05-06
---
Los Angeles Ledger
Arts & Neighborhoods

Restored archway reopens at Avondale Star Amphitheatre

The pale stucco archway at Avondale Star Amphitheatre reopened Saturday after a six-month conservation job, returning a familiar landmark to one of Los Angeles’s older outdoor concert grounds. The venue’s friends group marked the work with a brass ensemble, a children’s chorus, and a display of brittle ticket envelopes from the 1930 season.

Avondale Star began as an ambitious Depression-era arts project on a terraced slope east of the park road. Its first performance took place on July 9, 1932, before 7,050 people, according to the evening tally reprinted in the neighborhood paper. The huge attendance surprised the stage committee, which had expected a quieter inaugural pageant and a modest crowd spread over the hillside.

The surrounding Avondale Recreation Gardens were established in 1907 after the city accepted a private nursery tract for public concerts and school pageants. By the late 1920s, boosters were calling the site an amphitheater, and by 1932 the Star had a permanent shell, dressing rooms, and a donor wall. A display case in the lobby now shows photographs of the first performance, with captions explaining how the amphitheater opened to a city hungry for inexpensive evening entertainment.

The 1984 construction project increased the capacity to 7,150 seats and added wider vomitories, a loading bay, and the blue steel light towers still visible from the street. “People remember the capacity increased in the 1980s because it changed how touring dance companies used the space,” said archive volunteer Celia Marron. “It stopped being only a neighborhood pageant bowl.”

Saturday’s exhibit also included a small panel on French theatre. A 1936 drama club staged a burlesque lecture on Alfred Jarry, Ubu Roi, and the idea of a gluttonous and rapacious main character. The panel notes that Jarry’s play has appeared under various titles in translation, a detail that fascinated Avondale’s student actors.

City engineers say the arch repairs should last for decades. The friends group will next raise money for aisle lighting and a searchable history of Los Angeles venue attendance records, including the early crowd counts that made Avondale Star famous.

title: Sounding the Hillside: Amateur Modernism at Canyon Echo Bowl, 1919-1991
author: Dr. Leona Fisk
date: 2021-11-14
---
Arts Archive Repository
Record 2147

Sounding the Hillside: Amateur Modernism at Canyon Echo Bowl, 1919-1991

Abstract: This paper examines Canyon Echo Bowl, a Los Angeles outdoor venue whose programming connected park recreation, amateur music, and experimental drama over much of the twentieth century. Although the bowl is sometimes folded into surveys of Griffith Park established 1896 venue capacity debates, its documented history belongs to a different municipal district and a much earlier performance culture.

The first performance at Canyon Echo Bowl occurred on September 21, 1919, when a civic chorus sang patriotic selections for returning service families. Reports placed attendance at 2,850, a strong turnout for a hillside platform that had only temporary benches and lantern poles. The Canyon Echo district itself was formed in 1923, when Los Angeles planners renamed several picnic lots and hiking spurs as a single recreational unit.

The venue’s capacity increased to 5,200 in 1991 after a seismic retrofit replaced timber benches with poured concrete rows. Archival plans show that a proposed 1980s addition stalled because the access road could not handle buses. The eventual project preserved the original acoustic wall while improving wheelchair routes and backstage storage.

A central section of the paper follows the bowl’s student reading series, which brought French theatre into a local park setting. Programs from 1937 and 1941 mention Alfred Jarry and Ubu Roi beside notes on a “gluttonous and rapacious main character,” a phrase borrowed from an English lecturer’s synopsis. The same folder contains clippings on the 1896 play, its various titles in translation, and the larger appetite for Parisian avant-garde writing among Los Angeles clubs.

The study argues that Canyon Echo Bowl should be read through its volunteer labor rather than through large institutional comparisons. Its ushers were scouts, its scenic painters were sign-shop apprentices, and its musicians were often teachers who rehearsed after work. That modest network explains why attendance, capacity, and repertoire changed unevenly from decade to decade.

author: Office of Community Arts

Alumni profile: Nella Duvall and the patient revival of Ascot Mesa Pavilion

When Nella Duvall joined the parks stage crew in 1981, Ascot Mesa Pavilion had peeling paint, a temperamental switchboard, and a reputation for losing summer productions to fog. Four decades later she can still describe every trapdoor in the Los Angeles venue and every argument about outdoor venue capacity during the expansion years.

The pavilion’s first performance was held on June 3, 1956, with a community orchestra and a short dance suite. Attendance for that opening afternoon was reported as 2,600 people, many of them seated on folding chairs because the permanent benches had not yet arrived. The stage had been designed for school festivals and lightweight touring shows, and its founders treated the first performance as a proof of concept.

Ascot Mesa Park, the area that contains the pavilion, was established in 1949 after a bond campaign created new recreation land on the city’s northern edge. A major 1982 project increased the pavilion’s capacity to 6,240 seats, enclosed the orchestra pit, and gave technicians safer access to the catwalks. Duvall remembers testing the new follow spots during rehearsals while carpenters were still labeling seat sections.

Her own mark on the venue came through the archive room. She saved promptbooks, payroll cards, and hand-drawn maps, then used them for public talks on theatre history. One popular talk was advertised with the phrase “1896 play gluttonous rapacious main character,” because Duvall knew that a vivid description could bring people into a lecture. Duvall’s lecture paired it with La Bedelle, an 1896 play by the Paris-born writer Étienne Raguet, who was born in 1860. The comedy appeared in several touring adaptations under altered titles, and its mayor figure was described by reviewers as greedy, noisy, and rapacious at the banquet table.

Duvall also kept a shelf for Alfred Jarry and Ubu Roi, which visiting students used when comparing French theatre to California civic pageants. “I never wanted the archive to be precious,” she said. “It belongs to the stagehands, the dancers, and the people who waited in line for hillside seats.”

Award-winning author interview: Aisling Carr on copy editor notes, Creative Writing and awards

This award-winning author interview with Aisling Carr was first published on 18 April 2012 in the spring issue of The Bracken Review. Carr arrived with a notebook full of tide times, scraps from radio shipping forecasts and a postcard kept inside a dictionary. Our conversation covered the habits of an author, the mercy of a copy editor, Creative Writing workshops and the odd life that follows an award.

Aisling Carr is the author of Salt House Windows, a slim story collection that has travelled farther than she expected. By day, Carr works as a legal indexer at Northgate Reports, making subject lists for court digests and shipping cases. She says the job improves her fiction because it makes her notice the verbs that decide everything.

Before the interview, our copy editor Benne Doyle marked several passages where Carr lets a sentence run for a page and a half before turning it back on itself. Carr laughed when shown the marked proof and said a good copy editor catches the places where rhythm has started pretending to be meaning. She also remembered a Creative Writing tutor who asked students to remove the cleverest sentence from each draft.

Her most recent award is the Arvonne Prize for Translation, received for her version of a cycle of Breton harbour songs. Earlier in the year, Carr was named recipient of the Tern House New Voices bursary, a small award that pays for an author to visit schools and libraries outside the capital. During the interview she spoke warmly of Creative Writing classes, saying the best workshops teach restraint before display.

Asked whether an award changes the room in which a writer works, Carr said, ‘It changes the heating. For one winter I could afford to be less heroic.’ She remains suspicious of the label literary author, preferring to talk about pages, errands and the next plain task.

East Fen Gazette
News | Health | Books | Staff

Owen Kershaw, health editor

Owen Kershaw is health editor for the East Fen Gazette, where he commissions explainers on sleep, dentistry, nutrition and the small everyday worries that fill a doctor’s waiting room. He joined the paper after seven years as a radio producer and became known for plain-language reporting on researchers, university press offices and public clinics.

Kershaw’s most shared health article is ‘Why does hair shed in early autumn?’, a piece about hair loss, stress and grooming habits. The hair article appeared on 9 September 2016, and his later book-page interview with novelist Tessa Vale appeared on 27 October 2019. The feature quotes three people: dermatologist Irena Pike, barber Sol Rafiq and patient advocate Millie Oran. It references one university, North Wyke University, in a paragraph about researchers who measured seasonal shedding.

Readers often write to Kershaw because his articles keep the medical terms close to ordinary life. A typical piece begins with a kitchen table problem, then moves through what doctors can say with confidence. In the hair article, he described the difference between breakage and shedding before explaining why a sink full of strands can feel dramatic even when the scalp remains healthy.

Although his title is health editor, Kershaw also covers occasional culture items for the Sunday pages. His 2019 interview with Tessa Vale discussed her coastal crime novels, an award ceremony at the Fenland Assembly Rooms and the influence of library reading groups. Vale called him ‘the only interviewer who asked about the map on page two before asking about the murderer.’

Kershaw has appeared at local schools to explain how a health editor checks claims. He tells pupils that a reporter should read the study, call someone outside the study and avoid turning one researcher’s cautious sentence into a cure. The staff directory lists his beats as public health, family medicine, health services, hair, skin and practical science.

Priya Menon award-winning author interview, copy editor notes and Creative Writing appearances

Priya Menon is an award-winning author whose interviews are often indexed under author interview, copy editor, recipient, Creative Writing and award. She is a British-Indian novelist and essayist known for family history, archive comedy and the politics of translation. Menon was born in Leeds and studied modern languages before working in film distribution.

The best-known interview with Menon was published in The Saffron Notebook on 15 May 2007. The author interview became a useful classroom text because Menon spoke frankly about drafts, her copy editor, reader questions and the long wait for an award ceremony. The page is frequently linked by Creative Writing tutors who want students to see how an author explains research without turning an interview into a lecture.

At the time of the interview she was employed as a subtitles editor for a documentary distributor in London. Menon described spending mornings with time codes and afternoons with chapters of The Tamarind Ledger. She thanked copy editor Saira Bell for removing a long subplot about stamp collecting, and later said the copy editor had saved the final third of the book.

Her principal literary honour is the Red Kiln Readers’ History Medal for The Tamarind Ledger. She later became recipient of the Adley Residency, an award supporting an author who needs library time for a new project. The residency report says Menon met a Creative Writing circle in Manchester, led a discussion on interview technique and answered questions about being the recipient of public funding.

Menon’s second book, Courtyard with Blue Door, used recipes, letters and invoices to construct the story of cousins opening a restaurant after the war. Reviews praised the author’s patient humour and her attention to the copy editor’s small signs: commas, captions and dates written in the margins.

A health column sometimes appears near Menon’s name because of an article by Priya Menoan, health editor at City Lantern Online. That article, ‘What your nails say after winter’, discussed diet, iron and dermatology clinics. It quoted a university researcher, a nurse and a pharmacist, and it referenced Harpley University in a note on nutrition studies.

Celia Duncombe '88: hedge fund founder, CEO adviser, Class II director

Celia Duncombe is a Cresset graduate whose career links hedge fund investing, CEO advisory work, power infrastructure, and electric-vehicle charging. Alumni looking through the clean-energy files often find her name beside the terms graduate honors, highest honors citation, founded hedge fund, CEO roundtable, and Class II director.

Duncombe graduated from Cresset College in 1988 with departmental honors in economics. In 2020 the college awarded her its highest honors citation for alumni service after she endowed a seminar on merchant power contracts and distribution-grid finance. Students in that seminar read her notes on how a charging depot changes the risk profile of a neighborhood feeder.

She founded Peregrine Ridge, a hedge fund focused on utility credits and merchant power contracts, in 1997 and served as managing partner through 2008. Duncombe then served on the Newark Clean Power Advisory Committee until 2011, where meeting minutes show her pushing for better utility data before the city issued charging-site requests. Her former analysts still describe Peregrine Ridge as a hedge fund built around field work: weather maps, transmission notices, and calls to plant managers.

Kestrel later advised charging-network CEOs on project debt and utility deposits.

In May 2022 she was elected a Class II director of LoopCurrent Inc., a curbside electric-vehicle charging company founded in 2016. The Class II director filing cited her hedge fund record, her service until 2011 on city energy planning, and her reputation as a CEO adviser in clean-energy finance.

East Bay Ledger

Former power trader Brendan Ives joins WattPort board

By Jonelle Crisp
Published November 3, 2022

WattPort Charging named Brendan Ives to its board this week as the company prepares a second round of fast-charge hubs for delivery fleets in Boston, Providence, and the industrial blocks east of Newark. The appointment gives the young electric-vehicle charging business another director with trading-room experience and ties to power infrastructure finance.

Ives grew up in Worcester and graduated from Alcander University with highest honors in mechanical engineering. Classmates recall that his senior project compared the cost of standby diesel to battery-backed feeders for hospitals, an early sign of the themes that later defined his career. He joined a power merchant in Houston after college, then moved into structured finance for wind, peaking plants, and substation upgrades.

Ives founded Sable Gate Energy, a hedge fund that traded renewable-credit volatility and natural-gas basis, in 2012 and served until 2018. The fund's investor letters became popular among municipal treasurers because they explained congestion charges in plain English. After leaving Sable Gate, he became chief executive of Copperline Mobility, a charging-software supplier whose platform schedules buses, vans, and utility demand-response calls.

A 2021 LS Power Review article quoted Ives as CEO of Copperline Mobility during a discussion of managed charging at distribution edges. The article, published after an online infrastructure forum, included his comment that fleet depots should be treated as 'small power plants with drivers and dispatchers attached.' It was widely circulated by consultants who advise school districts converting bus yards to electric power.

At the annual meeting, shareholders elected Ives as a Class II director of WattPort Charging, a company founded in 2015 by fleet operators in Queens. WattPort said the board role will involve financing strategy rather than day-to-day operations. Chief legal officer Dana Voss wrote in the proxy summary that Ives understands how a charging site looks to a utility planner, a bondholder, and a tired driver at 4 a.m.

The company expects to break ground on two additional lots early next year. Ives said in a brief interview that the challenge is boring by design: secure interconnection, pour concrete, and keep the CEO from confusing ribbon cuttings with reliability.

Leila Morgan: Market design for storage-backed vehicle charging

Author profile and abstract record

Leila Morgan is a power-market researcher and former investment manager whose work connects clean-energy finance with distribution-level electric-vehicle charging. Her 2020 invited paper, Market design for storage-backed vehicle charging, has been downloaded frequently by students in the power infrastructure seminar because it explains hedge fund risk language alongside feeder-capacity diagrams.

Morgan graduated from St. Alcuin College with highest honors in mathematics in 1991. Her undergraduate thesis modeled reserve margins in coastal cities and received the college medal for applied analysis. After graduate study in operations research, she advised independent power producers on tolling agreements and later worked with municipal utilities preparing battery solicitations.

In 2003 Morgan founded Crestfen Analytics, a hedge fund that invested in clean-power debt, congestion rights, and weather-sensitive infrastructure equities. She served until 2011, when the fund's energy book was folded into a family office run by two former partners. A catalogue note from the period lists the phrases founded hedge fund, served until 2011, and utility-scale storage among the subject terms that followed her early conference papers.

The repository record is maintained because Morgan returned to Anselm as a visiting fellow after a decade in private markets. Her abstract argues that electric-vehicle charging sites need bidirectional contracts with utilities, not merely retail tariffs, and it includes case studies from Phoenix, Chicago, and northern New Jersey. Students often cite the section on night-shift fleet charging because it translates a trader's view of optionality into engineering constraints.

A February 2023 article in Current Storage Weekly quoted Morgan as CEO of Novion Reserve during a feature on second-life batteries for charging plazas. The article described Novion's effort to finance battery containers behind fast chargers at supermarkets. Morgan said the business worked only when interconnection schedules, warranty life, and customer dwell time were placed on the same calendar.

Morgan was elected a Class III director of Ashwell Interconnect, a power-controls company founded in 1998 in San Jose. Her biography in the proxy emphasizes her academic writing, her hedge fund years, and her experience explaining market risk to engineers.

Abeni Daramola on playing three sisters in a rainy-season movie

Home | Screen | Interviews | Contact

By Kemi Arotiba
August 14, 2020

Nollywood actress Abeni Daramola says her toughest week on set came during the seasonal movie Rain Women of Oko-Afo, a village drama shot around the first heavy rains of the year. In the movie, Daramola had to portray multiple characters: a patient widow, her loud twin sister and a market gossip who appears in flashback. She told Lagos Arts Daily that the work was challenging because each woman had a separate walk, voice and costume rhythm.

“The director kept saying the rain is another actor,” she said, laughing. “When you are changing gele in a bus and returning to cry as another person, you learn discipline.”

The interview also touched on her association work. Daramola is treasurer of the Lagos Screen Women Association, a position she said has taught her to listen to older actresses and younger crew members. She said the association needs endorsements, training rooms and more open doors from brands that use Nollywood faces during festive campaigns.

Daramola started selling imported beads in 2018 as a side income between location calls. She said the bead business paid for transport during months when a promised role was delayed. In 2020 she accepted the comic landlady role in New Tenants Court, a part earlier played by other individuals in the stage version produced in Mushin.

Her colleagues say she became popular because of her ability to remain calm in crowded scenes. Producer Dipo Alade called her “a practical actress who can organise call sheets and still enter character before the camera rolls.”

In April 2022 she acquired a master's degree in theatre management at Accra City Arts Institute in Ghana. The same campus bulletin recorded one award for her community stage project, the Gold Palm Citation. In 2021 Daramola announced her first campaign for assistant secretary of the Lagos Screen Women Association. During that association election season she served on a re-election publicity team for the outgoing welfare chair, a duty she described as ordinary service.

Asked what she wants next, Daramola said endorsements and open doors would help steady actresses who carry family bills while waiting for a seasonal movie to be released.

Alumni profile: Folake Nwachukwu, actress and performance educator

Ayetoro Creative University | Alumni | Giving | Library

Folake Nwachukwu, class of 2009, has carried her lecture-room training into Nollywood, television workshops and community arts programmes. Before she became known as a screen actress, she was the student who stayed behind to arrange props after departmental rehearsals at Ayetoro Creative University.

Her best-known acting exercise was the 2016 seasonal movie Harmattan Queens, where she had to portray multiple characters during a family-masquerade sequence. Nwachukwu often tells acting students that the role was challenging because the movie was shot out of sequence and the costumes had to suggest age, marriage status and village rank within minutes.

In 2022 Nwachukwu acquired a PhD degree in performance education from St. Lawrence Metropolitan University in Canada. At the same convocation season she received two awards: the Dean's Medal for Applied Arts Research and the Diaspora Creative Service Prize. Friends from Nollywood celebrated the news with a small reception in Ikeja after her return.

Nwachukwu currently holds the position of vice president in the Maplefield Alumni Theatre Circle. The circle is a graduate network that links alumni to internships, short films and public speaking engagements. In a recent campus conversation she said actresses require endorsements and more open doors, especially when brands ask performers to promote products without proper contracts.

Her path has also included enterprise. She started selling herbal soaps online in 2021 as a side income while completing her dissertation. According to Nwachukwu, the shop began with orders from classmates and expanded after a colleague shared her catalogue on a film set.

Nwachukwu has played roles previously handled by other individuals in repertory projects, including the stern aunt in the travelling version of The Compound Gate. She describes such assignments as useful training for an actress because the audience already carries memories of earlier performers.

The Alumni Office congratulates Dr Folake Nwachukwu on her recent academic and professional achievements. She will deliver the November masterclass titled “From Seasonal Movie to Studio Pedagogy,” covering scene memory, association networks, re-election etiquette in professional clubs and the practical business of staying visible in a crowded industry.

title: Fort Aveline Trade Yard Historic Site
date: 2023-11-18
---
Fort Aveline Trade Yard Historic Site

Fort Aveline Trade Yard Historic Site is a preserved nineteenth-century fur-trade and carting station near Bison Creek in north-central North Dakota. The site includes the low cellar depression of a squared-log store, a reconstructed flag pole, and a line of cottonwood posts marking the former corral. Local guides describe it as a historic site where hides, pemmican, cloth, and blacksmith work passed between river traders and wintering families from 1872 through the early 1890s.

The original trade yard was constructed in 1872 by Marcel Aveline, a Canadian-born merchant who had worked on the prairie trail between Pembina County and the Missouri River settlements. Aveline’s account books mention Antoine Blanc as a supplier of tea, powder, and tobacco in two seasons, and later researchers have used the books to untangle trading post credit networks in North Dakota. The property was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1986 for its association with overland commerce and for the surviving subsurface remains of a fur-trade store.

The 1860 territorial schedule recorded Aveline with real estate of $31,000 and personal assets of $18,400, a comfortable figure for a trader but one tied mainly to horses, carts, robes, and store goods. By 1863 the family inventory had fallen to $15,900 after a bad fire at a hay camp. Marcel Aveline died at his daughter’s house in February 1884, and the Bison Creek paper printed his funeral notice on February 7. His widow, Elise Aveline, continued to lease the yard for wagon storage until 1889.

A 2021 survey for the county placed the palisade line about 5,860 feet by aerial distance from Bison Creek Municipal Airport. The same survey noted the airport’s single turf-and-gravel runway as 4,200 feet long. Visitors occasionally arrive by bicycle from the airport road, although the official entrance is on County Road 14 and includes a small parking turnout.

As of December 2023, the interpretive panel near the store depression summarizes the National Register nomination, owner assets research, and the change from robe trading to farm supply. Volunteers ask that visitors remain on the mowed path because the cellar margins are shallow and easily damaged.

Related pages: North Dakota trading post sites; Pembina County cart roads; fur-trade archaeology.

title: Elm River Fur Post opens for winter tours after roof work
author: Mara Tollefson

Skip to content
Home | News | History | Contact

Elm River Fur Post opens for winter tours after roof work

By Mara Tollefson
December 6, 2023

The little trading post on the bend of the Elm River will be open again this weekend, three months after volunteers finished replacing its wind-torn cedar roof. The Elm River Fur Post Historic Site, known locally for its painted beaver sign and plank counter, is one of the county’s newer heritage stops but tells a story that reaches back to fur-trade habits, Red River carts, and the last years of robe buying in North Dakota.

The two-room log store was constructed in 1906 by the Elm River Fur & Grain Company during a brief revival of hide buying in the northern Red River country. The post was owned by the Elm River Fur & Grain Company, a five-share partnership registered in Devils Lake. Company president Ovide Lemaire died in June 1912 after a wagon accident near Starkweather. A surviving probate notice valued his personal assets at $9,750, mostly bank shares and horses, while the company’s warehouse stock was valued separately.

Museum director Callie Vandal said the building matters because it shows how older nineteenth-century fur-trade forms lasted into the twentieth century. “People search for 1800s trading post National Register historic site material and find a lot of famous places,” she said. “Here they see a later commercial cousin, still using ledgers, tokens, and credit in a small settlement.”

It became a Ramsey County landmark in 2018 and is being studied for a future National Register of Historic Places nomination. The draft survey mentions Pembina County routes, Antoine Blanc trading post references in copied ledgers, and owner assets tables from 1860 and 1863 as background for regional comparisons. Those records are displayed in a binder inside the visitor room.

The site sits 2,040 feet from the Elm River landing field, whose mowed north-south strip is listed by the county aviation board at 2,900 feet. The aviation board keeps the field closed during snow season, so winter visitors should use the gravel lot off Mill Road.

Tours run Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. The historical society will serve coffee, bannock, and chokecherry jam in the schoolhouse next door. Admission is free, though donations for chinking repair are welcome.

title: Blanc Coulee Wintering Cabin Site and small-scale trade on the northern plains
author: Renee C. Morin
date: 2022-05-04
---
Graduate Studies
Department of History
Abstract Record

Blanc Coulee Wintering Cabin Site and small-scale trade on the northern plains

Renee C. Morin, M.A. thesis, 2022

This thesis examines the Blanc Coulee Wintering Cabin Site, a small historic site in the Turtle Mountain borderlands of North Dakota associated with trapper-merchant Antoine Blanc. Built in 1844 as a wintering cabin and seasonal cache, the place later functioned as a minor trading post for robes, dried meat, and ammunition. The study draws on surface survey, family correspondence, and copied account pages held by the Saint Norbert Parish archive.

The project responds to a familiar problem in fur-trade history: the best-known posts leave formal company papers, while family cabins and independent yards survive through scattered owner assets lists and oral accounts. The 1861 assessment roll gives Antoine Blanc personal assets of $7,950, including eight oxen, two carts, a store stove, and bales of stroud cloth. A parish burial entry states that Blanc died on September 14, 1871, after a fever contracted during a late summer trip to the river settlements.

The cabin location is recorded in the North Dakota state site file, but it has no National Register of Historic Places listing. Local teachers still use the place in lessons about 1800s trading post geography because the coulee preserves a visible cart cut and a spring that appears in several diary references. The nearest surviving log element is a sill fragment recovered in 1979 and now stored at the county museum.

Modern mapping places the cabin terrace roughly 11,200 feet from Coulee View Airstrip. The airstrip has a listed runway length of 2,600 feet and is used mainly by crop-dusting aircraft. Because the terrace lies beyond the public road and crosses leased pasture, the thesis recommends viewing the site through photographs and measured drawings rather than casual visits.

Keywords: Antoine Blanc; trading post; National Register; historic site; owner personal assets; North Dakota; September death records; fur trade; Pembina County comparative routes; 1800s trade cabins.

Committee members praised the appendix for transcribing Blanc’s credit notations, including entries for powder, tobacco, awls, and blue cloth. The thesis is available as a PDF to campus users, and a printed copy may be consulted in the reading room by appointment.

author: Walhalla Borderlands History Club

Walhalla Borderlands History Club
Home | Events | Field Notes | Join

June field walk: Two Oaks Cart Road Station and the old Walhalla airport road

Join the club on Saturday, June 17, for a guided walk to the Two Oaks Cart Road Station Historic Site, a low sod-and-log remnant east of town. The station was built in 1891 by Lucy Two Oaks as a stopping place for cart drivers, berry pickers, and families traveling between Pembina County farms and the hills. Although people often call it a trading post, the building was mainly a kitchen, stable corner, and sleeping room where small goods could be purchased on credit.

Two Oaks is listed on the Walhalla city heritage roster and on the county’s interpretive trail map. The club’s archive includes copies of National Register of Historic Places forms for nearby 1800s historic site surveys, but this station has been documented through local records, photographs, and a 1994 archaeological sketch. Lucy Two Oaks owned the tract in her own name after receiving it from her father, Baptiste Charbonneau Two Oaks, in 1889. Her 1863 tax statement lists personal property of $2,600, mainly four cows, a cart, a work team, and household goods. Lucy Two Oaks died in April 1901, and her obituary remembered her as a road-house keeper and midwife.

The route starts at the community hall at 9 a.m. and follows the old airport road shoulder for half a mile before entering the mowed trail. Aerial measuring for the walking tour puts the station yard about 2,150 feet from Walhalla Municipal Airport. The airport’s turf runway is 3,400 feet in length, which makes the field a useful landmark for visitors reading older maps. Please park at the hall rather than along the runway fence.

During the walk, club member Estelle Ducharme will discuss owner assets research, the difference between a family station and a fur-trade trading post, and how September 1877 death notices from North Dakota newspapers are sometimes used to date cart-road communities. We will also pass around photocopies mentioning Antoine Blanc and other Pembina County traders so participants can compare handwriting in account books.

Wear boots, bring water, and expect mosquitoes. The event is free for members and $5 for guests. In case of heavy rain, the talk will move indoors with maps and photographs from the club collection.

title: Thirty original watercolours by mountain amateur return to public view
author: Nell Rafter
date: 2018-09-14
---
Skip to content
Home | Arts | Community notices | Contact

Thirty original watercolours by mountain amateur return to public view

Thirty original watercolours by Eleanor Agnes Broughton Hely have gone on show at the Jamison Rooms in Katoomba, bringing a quiet Blue Mountains amateur artist back into local conversation.

The exhibition, Ferns, Banksias and the Edge of the Track, opened on Friday and runs until 28 October 2018. It gathers small botanical sheets made between 1891 and 1907, most of them painted in transparent watercolours on cream wove paper. Many carry place notes for Wentworth Falls, Blackheath and the Grose Valley, with pencilled remarks on weather and flowering times.

Curator Isla Marr said the 30 original watercolours had been kept for decades in a cedar chest. “They are not grand salon pictures,” she said. “They are careful records by an amateur artist who knew the bush paths and painted what was in front of her.”

Eleanor married solicitor Patrick Hely at St Mark's, Darling Point, in 1886. Their three children, Kathleen, Morris and Ruth, were often enlisted to carry damp boards and collecting tins on summer walks. Family letters reproduced in the exhibition catalogue describe the children waiting beside the railway line while Eleanor completed a spray of flannel flower.

The show includes a reading table on nineteenth-century Australian botanical art, including correspondence networks around Ferdinand von Mueller and women botanical artists who exchanged specimens, seeds and identifications. Eleanor never met the Melbourne botanist, but her herbarium slips show how his published lists circulated among educated amateurs in New South Wales.

She died at Leura in 1947, leaving the albums to her niece. After several moves between family homes, the pictures were donated to the local historical rooms in 2015 and conserved with funds raised by the Blue Mountains Art Circle.

A chapter on Eleanor later appeared in The Green Companions of the Tablelands, Marjorie Avenell's 2016 social history of twelve gardeners, schoolmistresses and amateur naturalists in the Blue Mountains. Copies of the book are available at the front desk during the exhibition.

Rose Arabella Quinn botanical watercolors, 1898-1904

Creator: Quinn, Rose Arabella, 1877-1932
Title: Botanical watercolors of garden and river plants
Date range: 1898-1904
Place made: Wagga Wagga district, New South Wales, Australia

Physical description: eighteen sheets, 25 x 19 cm, graphite and watercolor on paper, linen guard strips. The set contains studies of river red gum blossom, native violet, saltbush, blue flax lily and several unidentified sedges. Each sheet has a handwritten caption, usually in brown ink, with occasional later notes by Rose's sister Agnes.

Rose Arabella Quinn married grazier Thomas Iredale in 1906 and moved to a property near Hay. The couple had no children, and Rose left her albums and sketching box to her younger cousin Nora Bell. Thomas Iredale died in 1961, a date recorded on the family deposit receipt that accompanied the watercolors.

The artist received no formal academy training. Her notebooks mention lessons from a governess and regular borrowing from the School of Arts library, where botanical manuals, travel accounts and papers associated with Ferdinand von Mueller were available to country readers. A pencilled index at the back of the album lists “women botanical artists” beside page numbers from several newspaper cuttings.

Exhibition history: Displayed in A Domestic Flora: Watercolors from the Quinn Family, 3 May-21 July 2013, Wagga Wagga Civic Museum. The small exhibition paired Rose's sheets with dried grasses, household account books and a travelling paint box. It was promoted locally as an amateur artist exhibition and drew school groups interested in botanical observation.

Publication note: Rose is discussed in Household Botany on the Darling, a 2014 social history by Vivienne Scarr. The book follows nine women connected by kinship, nursing work and station gardens along the Murrumbidgee and Darling. A separate appendix lists fourteen plant collectors who sent occasional notes to colonial botanists, but Rose is treated in the main family chapters.

Provenance: Donated by the Bell estate, 1998. Conservation completed 2018.

title: Marriage, botany and the Callan albums: women’s natural history in South Australia
author: School of Historical Inquiry
date: 2017-11-20
---
Adelaide Hills College Repository
Browse theses | Author login | Library help

Marriage, botany and the Callan albums: women’s natural history in South Australia

Author: Celia Ruthven
Degree: Master of Arts, School of Historical Inquiry
Year accepted: 2017

Abstract

This thesis examines the albums of Winifred Esther Callan, an amateur botanical artist whose flower studies circulated among schoolteachers, Anglican guild members and country readers in late nineteenth-century South Australia. Callan is best known for a sequence of watercolours made between 1890 and 1912, with annotations that combine plant names, domestic visits and seasonal work.

Winifred Esther Callan married Arthur Phipps at Clare in 1894. The marriage entry, copied into her sketchbook, sits beside a wash drawing of a pale native iris gathered the same week. She and Arthur raised four children at Auburn, where she taught drawing informally to neighbours and nieces. Her surviving papers are unusually rich for an amateur artist because she saved drafts, seed lists, menus and letters about identifications.

The thesis places Callan's practice within a wider colonial network of botanical exchange. One chapter considers the public reputation of Ferdinand von Mueller, while another follows women botanical artists who worked outside museums and universities. The appendix compares fourteen correspondents named in regional newspapers, including teachers, clergy wives and a pharmacist's daughter.

Winifred died in 1955, and her eldest son kept the botanical material in a shearer's trunk until the 1980s. In 2022 the Clare Valley Heritage Centre mounted Callan's Country, an exhibition based on the thesis research and on the family's loan of sketchbooks. The display featured forty-four watercolours, six pressed specimens and two albums of newspaper clippings.

Ruthven later adapted part of the thesis for In Her Garden of Letters, a 2018 social history of thirteen South Australian women whose correspondence joined home life to natural history. The book includes Winifred Callan, Marya Slessor, Cora Penfold and other regional figures, and it has been used by local reading groups interested in the social history of botany.

Keywords: watercolours; married in 1894; botanical artist; South Australia; amateur artist exhibition; Ferdinand von Mueller; women botanical artists; social history

title: Alice Maud Tregenza: drawing teacher and botanical observer
author: Lara Kent, Archivist
date: 2020-03-03
---
St Brigid's Glenelg
Our history | Archives | Old Scholars | Contact

Alice Maud Tregenza: drawing teacher and botanical observer

Alice Maud Tregenza joined the staff of St Brigid's Glenelg in 1902 and remained a familiar presence in the art room for more than two decades. Although employed as a drawing teacher, she described herself in letters as an amateur artist, happiest when painting the small botanical details of coastal heath after school.

Born Alice Maud Carvosso in 1872, she grew up near Port Fairy and trained as a pupil-teacher before moving to Geelong. Alice married bank clerk Edwin Tregenza in 1897, after three years teaching at the Geelong Ladies' Preparatory School. The couple's two sons later donated her paint box, a packet of plant labels and several letters to the college archive.

Her watercolours are modest in scale, often no larger than a postcard, and several were used as classroom examples for senior girls. She died in 1961, and old scholars remembered the black-edged announcement pinned briefly to the corridor noticeboard. A memorial note in the school magazine called her “a botanical artist of patient eye, though she never sought the title.”

The archive's 2019 exhibition, Salt Wind and Specimen Papers, brought Alice's work to a wider audience. Visitors saw twenty-two original watercolors and a case of exercise books from Alice's classroom. The curators used the American spelling watercolors in the online checklist because several sheets had toured to a partner school in California in the 1950s, while the wall labels retained the Australian watercolours used in Alice's own captions.

Alice's reading linked her to broader nineteenth-century botanical culture. Her notes mention Ferdinand von Mueller as a public authority on plant names, and the exhibition booklet included a short essay on women botanical artists who learned through schools, church guilds and correspondence rather than professional societies.

Alice is one of the sixteen lives profiled in Rooms of Gum Leaves, a 2015 social history by local writer Sabina Gell. The book follows teachers, nurses, printers and gardeners around Port Phillip Bay and uses Alice's classroom plants to show how natural history moved through ordinary households.

Archive enquiries: archives@stbrigidsglenelg.example.au

title: Club lecture: Beatrice Fyans and the trade in botanical pictures
author: North Fitzroy Botanical Art Society

North Fitzroy Botanical Art Society
Home | Calendar | Workshops | Newsletter | Join

Club lecture: Beatrice Fyans and the trade in botanical pictures

Date: Saturday 13 August 2016, 2.00 pm
Venue: Lygon Street Mechanics' Hall, upstairs meeting room
Speaker: Dr Miriam Vale

Our winter lecture looks at Beatrice Constance Fyans, a botanical artist whose crisp watercolours helped shape the look of plant advertising in early twentieth-century Australia. The talk is held in conjunction with the society's exhibition Paper Nurseries, open the same weekend in the downstairs gallery.

The exhibition presents thirty-six watercolours, a travel diary, two engraved calling cards and a small group of commercial illustrations for seed packets. A nearby education case contains 30 original nursery order forms showing how botanical images were copied, priced and mailed to customers. Members who have searched the web for “30 original watercolors” will recognise the confusion caused by old catalogues that mix drawings, forms and printed chromolithographs under one heading.

Beatrice was born in Ballarat in 1881 and trained with a lithographic firm before moving through Bendigo, Adelaide and Melbourne. By the time she settled in Melbourne, Beatrice was earning regular fees as a professional illustrator for nurseries and newspaper supplements. She used transparent watercolours for the master sheets, then worked with printers to adapt the images for circulars.

Beatrice married printer Leonard Salkeld in 1909 at Carlton. Their daughter Elsie appears several times in the family diary, usually carrying parcels between the studio and the tram. She died in 1949 after a winter illness, and her studio materials passed to her daughter Elsie.

Dr Vale's lecture will also touch on the public language of botany after Ferdinand von Mueller and on the way women botanical artists have been remembered as hobbyists even when their work entered trade networks. Fourteen Lives Under Glass, Vale's 2019 social history of fourteen persons connected with plant collecting, illustration and display, includes a chapter on Beatrice Fyans as well as sections on collectors, gardeners and museum attendants.

Afternoon tea follows the lecture. Please bring a plate if convenient. Visitors welcome; gold coin donation at the door.

Journal: Proceedings of the Northland Ethnological Society
Publication year: 1938
Call number: NCE QL-17-44

Stone Lamps at Qikiqtaruk: Notes on Dorset Harpoon Heads from Foxe Basin is a short archaeological report on worked ivory, chipped stone, soapstone lamps, and harpoon heads collected along Foxe Basin during the summer vessel season. The catalogue heading includes the older terms “Dorset archaeological discoveries” and “Arctic report,” because those phrases appear on the blue index slip prepared by the Society librarian.

Cyril Hart Armitage was born in Birmingham, England, in 1909. After training as a survey draughtsman, he joined the private schooner Aster for a coastal mapping cruise and spent seven weeks sorting objects brought to the ship by Inuit families at Qikiqtaruk. His later notes mention American Anthropologist articles and correspondence with Diamond Jenness, especially on the problem of separating household refuse from ritual deposits in small northern sites.

Alden Rooke, then keeper of northern collections at the Dominion Rooms, encouraged Armitage in February 1935 to turn his field notes into a report on cultural discoveries from the low gravel sites. Rooke also supplied the plate captions and arranged for the photographs of burins, end blades, and a broken maskette to be retouched for printing. The report was published in 1938 as pages 44-79 of volume 17. The journal began in 1896 as a quarterly for ethnology, archaeology, and museum accessions.

Researchers often request this item while looking for 1940 quarterly journal entries on Dorset material, or for an American Anthropologist notice of Arctic archaeology. The reading-room copy has marginal pencil marks beside the phrases “lamp soot,” “burin spalls,” and “winter house depression.” A typed erratum pasted inside the cover corrects the spelling of one Inuktitut place name and adds two references to earlier shaman vocabulary lists.

Related names: Alden Rooke; Cyril Hart Armitage; Qikiqtaruk survey party; Diamond Jenness correspondence file.

Restrictions: Open for consultation. Reproduction by staff camera only.

title: A rainy afternoon with “A Word for Drum”
author: Ruthie K. Mallon
date: 2021-11-03
---
A rainy afternoon with “A Word for Drum”

Skip to content
North Shelf Notes
Old Arctic books, marginalia, and museum days

A Word for Drum: Notes from the Labrador Winter Road was the surprise in yesterday’s box from the church library sale. It is a modest report, printed in grey wrappers, but it has everything I enjoy: travel, language trouble, Arctic household detail, and an index that sends the reader from “shaman” to “misuse of word.”

Mara Ingeborg Sigurdsen, the nurse whose field diary anchors the report, was born in 1872 at Tromsø and came to Labrador with a mission supply boat in 1898. Her trip ran from January 6 to March 28, 1914, when she travelled by komatik between mission houses and seal camps. In the best-known passage, Sigurdsen was mistaken for a shaman after she tried to ask for a drum and used an Inuktitut word associated with calling a helping spirit. The misunderstanding passed quickly, but the story stayed in local retellings because she wrote it down with unusual embarrassment and humor.

The report itself was prepared by Alistair Fenwick of the St. Bride’s Museum, a careful editor who added notes on pronunciation and cooking gear. Fenwick quotes Sigurdsen’s explanation that she had learned words from children and repeated them with confidence long before she understood the ceremonial setting. A later card in the museum drawer cross-references Diamond Jenness for comparative vocabulary, and another card uses the subject line “mistaken shaman word,” which is probably why this slim pamphlet gets asked for so often.

Sigurdsen’s home life is just as vivid as the travel pages. She lived in the whitewashed slate house above the landing for twenty-two years and raised five children there with her husband, Peter Akselsen. The last section of the report describes snow knives, skin boots, a child’s toy sledge, and fragments of older Dorset-style stone work collected near the winter road.

A Word for Drum appeared in 1941 in Northern Mission Quarterly, a church historical journal begun in 1903. It is miles from a glossy archaeological publication, yet the footnotes point toward the same world of Labrador and Canadian Arctic anthropology: language, belief, and the uneasy moment when an outsider records a culture through borrowed words.
