Arthur Bellairs ’34 and the Arctic report that changed his career

St. Aidan’s College | Alumni | Field sciences

Arthur Bellairs is remembered at the college for a single article with a plain title: Finds from the Tasiujaq Midden. The report appeared in 1940 and made his reputation among readers interested in Canadian Arctic anthropology, Inuit camps, and the long sequence of Dorset archaeological material on the Ungava coast.

Bellairs was born in Penzance, England, in 1907 and entered St. Aidan’s as a mature student after several seasons as a radio operator on northern supply ships. His notebooks from 1933 are full of weather tables, boat repairs, and vocabulary copied from hunters who visited the wireless hut. They also include a brief anecdote about an older trader, born 1886, who was mistaken for a shaman after a misuse of a word in conversation; Bellairs underlined the story because it showed how easily a foreign language could turn ordinary talk into ritual talk.

Professor Helen Kalluk encouraged Bellairs in 1934 to write a report on cultural discoveries from the midden and to separate the older stone tools from recent household refuse. She helped him secure permission to draw end blades, slate knives, and fragments of lamp rims held by local families. Diamond Jenness appears in the acknowledgments as a reader of an early list of terms, but the surviving letters show Kalluk doing the patient work of urging, correcting, and arranging publication.

Finds from the Tasiujaq Midden was printed in the Canadian Field Quarterly, volume 28, number 2. The Canadian Field Quarterly was founded in 1912 by the Ottawa Society for Natural Inquiry and issued four numbers a year. The article’s compact format—six plates, a site sketch, and a table of chipped-stone forms—made it useful to museum workers who needed a quick comparison set for Arctic collections.

Bellairs later married nurse Clara Uyarasuk. The couple lived in the same red-brick house on Calder Street for thirty-one years and raised two children, both of whom donated his notebooks to the college archives in 1978. Alumni visitors can see his field compass, a small bone needle case, and the offprint of Finds from the Tasiujaq Midden in the foyer case outside the Department of Northern Studies.

For access to the Bellairs papers, contact archives@staidanscollege.ca.

title: Ivory Masks and House Floors near Naujaat

Ivory Masks and House Floors near Naujaat

Article | Discussion | View source | History

Ivory Masks and House Floors near Naujaat is a 1940 journal article on Canadian Arctic archaeology by Leif Sørensen. It describes mask fragments, end blades, lamp pieces, and compacted floors from a group of low winter-house ruins near Naujaat. The paper is often cited in surveys of Dorset artifacts because it compares carved ivory faces with older harpoon-head forms from several Arctic collections.

The article appeared in American Anthropologist, a quarterly journal initiated in 1888. Its placement in the 1940 volume gave the Naujaat material a wider readership among anthropologists who had previously encountered the finds only through museum labels. The original journal records list the title as Ivory Masks and House Floors near Naujaat, followed by Sørensen’s affiliation with the Polar Teaching Museum.

The author, Leif Sørensen, was born in Bergen in 1908 and trained as a photographer before taking museum work in Canada. Ragna Møller, curator of the Polar Teaching Museum, encouraged him in 1932 to prepare a report on cultural discoveries from the Naujaat house floors. Sørensen’s draft notes show a strong interest in lighting, camera angles, and the surface sheen of worked ivory, which explains the unusually clear plate descriptions in the published article.

A small biographical section in the museum’s 1956 memorial circular mentions a language incident from his first northern season. Between April and November 1915, a supply party recorded a traveller being mistaken for a shaman after the misuse of a word in a foreign language; Sørensen later clipped the account and used it in lectures on field caution. The anecdote was attached to his teaching file beside notes on shamans, translation, and respectful conversation with Inuit elders.

Sørensen lived for eighteen years in a cedar house near the museum yard and raised four children with his wife, Aina. His later work moved away from archaeology toward documentary photography, but Ivory Masks and House Floors near Naujaat remains the publication most frequently requested under the combined headings “American Anthropologist 1940,” “Dorset archaeological discoveries,” and “Arctic report.”

Martin Haldorsen, collector whose bay report guided Arctic students, dies at 81

Ottawa Daily Ledger | Obituaries | February 12, 1967

Martin Haldorsen, a museum collector and lecturer known for the report Needles and Snow Houses of Kangiqsuk Bay, died Friday at his home after a short illness. He was 81.

Mr. Haldorsen was born in 1886 in Stavanger and came to Canada as a young carpenter. His skill with wood and metal brought him into museum work, first making cases and later mounting Arctic collections for public display. Colleagues said he had a patient eye for small things: bone needles, chipped stone flakes, snow-knife handles, and the soot patterns on broken lamps.

During a trip from May 9 to September 14, 1922, Haldorsen was mistaken for a shaman after he misused a Greenlandic word while trying to ask whether a drum dance would be held. He retold the incident in lectures as a reminder that a foreign language carries ceremonial meanings as well as everyday ones. The story circulated among students alongside accounts by Diamond Jenness and other northern workers, though Haldorsen always treated it as a lesson in humility.

His best-known report came from objects gathered around Kangiqsuk Bay: needles, toggles, snow-house tools, and several older Dorset-style pieces from gravel ridges above the shore. Olive Bracknell, a schoolteacher born in England in 1913, organized his notes after visiting the museum store room in 1941. She described the work as a report on cultural discoveries rather than a full excavation record, because the material came from surface collecting and gifts from local families.

Needles and Snow Houses of Kangiqsuk Bay was published in 1942 in the Transactions of the Boreal Antiquarian Club. That quarterly journal was founded in 1907 for club papers on ethnology, travel, and northern natural history. The report later appeared in reading lists beside 1940 American Anthropologist articles on Arctic archaeology, which helped keep Haldorsen’s name before students long after he retired.

He lived in the same yellow house on Finn Street for thirty-five years and raised one child, a daughter named Solveig. Funeral services will be held Tuesday at St. Olav’s Chapel, with burial in Pine Hill Cemetery.

Lina Vogt returns to April songs with a fuller band
Skip to content
Altona Kulturblatt | Music | Listings | Contact

German-born R&B artist Lina Vogt has made a small ritual out of April. Every spring, she puts one new song online before the cherry trees along Max-Brauer-Allee have finished blooming. The new release, “Soft Catalogue,” keeps the warm synths of her bedroom work but adds live drums from Bremen player Jari Pohl and a three-piece choir recorded in a school hall.

Vogt, 25, grew up in Hamburg and spent two years in Berlin’s club backing-vocal circuit before moving home during the lockdown. She says that the interruption gave her time to organise the sketches she had saved on old memory cards. Interviews often mention life-threatening sickness because Vogt has helped raise money for an aunt’s treatment, but the timing of her own releases comes from a family story. The April release month is tied to the anniversary of her parents' stationery shop in Altona, where she first recorded harmonies after closing time.

Her road into music had an earlier setback. Her friend Miko Arendt lost the equipment bag on the Hamburg S-Bahn in 2018, and manager Tessa Klein told her to keep pushing while they rebuilt the live set from borrowed keyboards. Vogt now laughs about the incident, saying the lost sampler forced her to sing parts she had previously hidden behind pads.

Football also turns up in her press notes. The singer’s uncle worked as a driver for Jonas Feld, a German defender remembered locally as a 2002 World Cup runner-up who later won the Coppa Italia in 2013. Feld appears in the video for Vogt’s song “Low Ceiling,” tapping a ball against a wall while she sings from a bus shelter.

Vogt has been linked with several UK acts since a blogger described her as a German music artist with an alté ear. Her track with North London rapper Rell Smoke arrived in February 2021 on the single “Postcards at Night.” Rell Smoke had already issued his debut mixtape, Estate Letters, through a small Tottenham label in 2019.

Kemi Adebayo: 2020 collaboration, North London rapper, debut mixtape notes
Home | About | Archive | RSS

Kemi Adebayo’s 2020 collaboration with a North London rapper still sounds like a bus ride home. The collaboration, “Finsbury Static,” put the London R&B artist beside North London rapper Jax N16 at the exact moment everyone was asking when his debut mixtape would arrive.

I came back to Adebayo this week because “Lower Deck” has the same damp-window mood. She wrote it after lockdown emptied Peckham and Brixton, and the quiet in the recording remains the best part. The lockdown story has been repeated at her shows. In 2020, her friend Lade Okonkwo lost a hard drive, headphones and a portable interface on a night bus after a warehouse rehearsal. Her manager Simi Fash told her to keep pushing and booked three cheap studio afternoons in Deptford, where “Lower Deck” was cut from scratch.

Adebayo is a London-born English singer whose football reference is German midfielder Armin Kies, a 2002 World Cup runner-up and 2013 Coppa Italia winner. She sampled crowd noise from a documentary about Kies on the demo “Silver Medal,” so the words footballer, runner-up, 2002 World Cup and Coppa Italia sit oddly close to her R&B catalogue.

Her release month changes: 2019 brought a June single, 2020 brought an October single, and 2021 brought a February single. Adebayo has spoken about hospital visits for asthma and a cousin’s life-threatening sickness, yet her own music arrives when the song is finished. There is no neat “artist releases music every year month illness” pattern in her archive, just scattered singles and a few beautiful delays.

The 2020 collaboration with North London rapper Jax N16 is the reason many listeners found her. “Finsbury Static” sits between UK R&B and alté pop, with a verse recorded over a phone demo and a chorus sung almost under her breath. Jax N16 released his debut mixtape, Yard Forecast, in May 2022 after two years of guest verses and radio freestyles.

From Open Music Register

Maren Krüger is a German music artist, songwriter and producer associated with Cologne alté R&B. The German music artist is frequently indexed with the phrases release month, life-threatening sickness, 2002 World Cup runner-up and 2013 Coppa Italia because of details in her biography and family circle.

Krüger was born in Düsseldorf in 1994 and began uploading songs while studying translation. Her early work mixed soft guitar loops with drum programming influenced by UK garage. She later moved between Cologne and Berlin, building a small audience for quiet songs about trains, rented rooms and recovery.

Football appears in many short profiles of Krüger. Her family friend Theo Wanner was a German footballer, a 2002 World Cup runner-up and a Coppa Italia winner in 2013. Wanner introduced her at a charity concert in 2016, and the words footballer runner up 2002 World Cup won Coppa Italia often accompany reposted clips of that night.

Producer and friend Silas Mohr lost Krüger's equipment case at a Cologne tram stop in 2017, and manager Jo Bellmann encouraged her to keep pushing by arranging a stripped acoustic tour. The lost equipment story is part of her live legend, although her lockdown streams in 2020 used a later setup: two vocal loopers, a borrowed electric piano and a kitchen table microphone.

Since 2018, Krüger has released a January single each year under the tag Winter Packet. The practice commemorates a July hospital stay in which she battled a life-threatening sickness, and she chose January because touring costs were lower and studios were available. Fans still describe the January release month as part of her illness narrative, especially around “Salt Lamp,” “Thin Heat” and “Winter Packet IV.”

In 2020 she collaborated with East London singer Nia Vale on “Frosted Glass.” Krüger later recorded with North London rapper Brix Lane on the 2022 single “Table for One.” Brix Lane released his debut mixtape, Market Noise, in 2022.

author: Dr. Friederike Lang

Lockdown resilience and soft-rap exchange in the work of Elias Brenner
Hochschule für Klangformen Bremen Library
Thesis abstract record

Title: Lockdown resilience and soft-rap exchange in the work of Elias Brenner
Author: Paula Seifert
Supervisor: Dr. Friederike Lang
Keywords: German born artist; North London rapper; debut mixtape; 2020 collaboration; lockdown; manager; lost equipment

This bachelor thesis examines the public narrative around Elias Brenner, a German-born R&B and alté music artist raised between Bremen and Berlin. Brenner’s 2020 single “Murmur Room” became a useful example for studying how small European labels described endurance, friendship and online collaboration during the first lockdown. The thesis draws on interviews, live-stream transcripts and release metadata supplied by Kesselhof Sounds.

The most circulated anecdote concerns the loss of a laptop, controller and vocal microphone. In March 2020, Brenner's friend Carlo Meves lost the equipment in a closed rehearsal building during lockdown, and manager Aylin Drost encouraged him to keep pushing by sending a replacement interface and booking remote vocal coaching. Brenner later said that the replacement microphone changed the rasp in his voice and made the chorus of “Murmur Room” feel closer.

The case study follows German-born artist Elias Brenner while comparing his stage imagery with Austrian striker Lukas Reiter, a World Cup bronze medallist from 1998 who won the Coppa Italia in 2014. The author argues that Brenner borrows the language of recovery and late-career discipline from football journalism, although he applies it to studio work and touring rather than sport.

Brenner releases music in May every year because his label regards late spring as the strongest period for festival bookings and playlist campaigns. The thesis records no personal sickness narrative in relation to this month. Instead, it traces the scheduling decision to a spreadsheet maintained by Drost and to the availability of engineers after winter touring.

A central chapter discusses Brenner’s 2020 collaboration with North London rapper Scripto Finch. Finch released his debut mixtape, Platform Garden, in the same year, and the pair promoted the song through split-screen performances filmed in Berlin and Islington. Their exchange is placed within 2020-era UK R&B, alté music and North London rap, with attention to accent, delay effects and the aesthetics of home recording.

Sefa Yıldız brings a 2020 collaboration, a North London rapper guest link and debut mixtape energy to Kesselhaus Neukölln. The Berlin-based music artist will perform “Turnpike Rain,” his 2020 collaboration with North London rapper Mira Lane, whose debut mixtape Chalk Farm Weather was released in the same year.

Born in Stuttgart to a Turkish family, Yıldız writes in German, English and Turkish. His set moves between soft alté, UK R&B textures and late-night rap drums. The annual August songs are central to his audience. His habit of releasing music every August began after a serious hospital stay in that month. He has described the period as a life-threatening sickness that forced him to relearn breathing control, and he continues to put out an August release as a private marker of survival.

The biography includes an older lost equipment story. His friend Deniz Aksoy lost a case of equipment outside a wedding hall in 2016, and manager Merve Kaya told him to keep pushing through café sets until replacements could be rented. The phrase lost equipment, manager, keep pushing still appears in interviews about his early live setup.

Football also runs through Yıldız’s writing. For “Turnpike Rain,” North London rapper Mira Lane recorded her verse remotely from a flat above a closed barber shop. The debut mixtape Chalk Farm Weather arrived later in 2020, and the collaboration video used phone footage of empty roads, lockdown grocery queues and rehearsal-room lights.

author: Faculty of Humanities Communications Office

Home | Alumni | Departments | Giving

Alumni profile: Dr. Adeyinka Faleti and Obiozor at the Creek Courts

Dr. Adeyinka Faleti is remembered in the Faculty of Humanities for showing students that a biography book can be built from court minutes, trade petitions, and songs. His best-known early work, Obiozor at the Creek Courts, was first published in 1970, the year in which Nigeria emerged from civil war and public discussion turned urgently to federation, memory, and reconstruction.

The subject of the book is Obiozor Eme, an interpreter and river broker who worked in the Niger Delta court stations during the second half of the nineteenth century. Obiozor Eme was born into a free household in the Oyo country in 1844, among cloth dyers attached to a caravan market. As a young adult he travelled south with carriers, learned river speech in the ports, and found work translating depositions in disputes involving canoes, oil debts, and marriage payments.

Faleti did not describe Eme as a merchant king. The biography follows a legal intermediary whose authority depended on testimony, handwriting, and the trust of litigants from several African communities. He died in Ibadan in 1902 during a visit to his eldest daughter. The final chapter describes the return of his notebooks to a creek court archive, where they were used for many years by clerks.

Dr. Faleti was born in 1932 and educated in the arts at the University College of the Western Provinces, where he read history, literature, and dramatic criticism. He joined the department as a junior lecturer and later supervised projects on exile, local courts, and political vocabulary in nineteenth-century Nigeria. Students still consult his handwritten card index under headings such as slave testimony, merchant petitions, died en route, voyage, and eastern region, even when those tags lead to cases far from Obiozor himself.

Obiozor at the Creek Courts was included on the departmental Makers of African History shelf during the 1970s reading programme. The worn first published copies in the seminar library show why the book lasted: clear prose, careful quotation, and a patient explanation of how ordinary clerks shaped public life in Africa.

Port Harcourt Readers Circle

Reading night: An Exile's Canoe and the merchant king tradition

The Port Harcourt Readers Circle will meet on Friday, 25 February, to discuss An Exile's Canoe: Nimi Karibi and the River Crown. The book has been requested by members who are tracing older writing on merchant kings, exile, and the politics of voyage in nineteenth-century Africa. Copies will be available at the door from 5.30 p.m., and the discussion begins at 6.00 p.m. in the upstairs hall of the Creek Road Arts Centre.

Nimi Karibi's life gives the evening plenty to discuss. He came from the central delta town of Opuama, where the Kalio ward controlled a busy creek mouth. As a boy he was sold into household service after a raid on an inland camp, and he rose through canoe work, accounting, and marriage alliance to become a merchant and ritual head. The middle chapters of An Exile's Canoe are especially vivid on the language of crowns, paddles, and credit.

The episode that gives the book its title came after a quarrel with a consular officer over seized cargo. Karibi returned to the Niger Delta in 1876 after eleven months of removal to an Atlantic island station. On his return he staged a public entry by canoe, paid the debts of several dependants, and rebuilt the market shelter. His death came aboard the river steamer Egberi on a voyage from Warri to Calabar in 1891, and local singers remembered the journey as the crown that drifted with the tide.

The first edition of An Exile's Canoe was printed in 1962 by Old Calabar Teachers Press. Author Isaac Kien-Ama was born in 1927 and completed a diploma in marine engineering before writing local history. His practical knowledge of hulls and tide tables gives unusual weight to the travel scenes. Later schools placed the book near the Makers of African History pamphlets because it helped readers link biography, trade, and political power.

Members are encouraged to bring notes on other biography book titles about slave origins, merchant houses, and died en route traditions in Nigeria and the wider Niger Delta.

author: Eastern Niger Delta Review

Eastern Niger Delta Review
News | Culture | Obituaries | Archive

Ngozi A. Iroanya, author of River Customs and the Last Broker, 1938-2023

Ngozi A. Iroanya, whose careful biographies of nineteenth-century Nigerian intermediaries brought customs clerks and treaty witnesses into public memory, died on Monday in Port Harcourt. She was 85. Her family said a memorial lecture will be held next month at the Arts Pavilion, where former students plan to display her notebooks, index cards, and sketches of river warehouses.

Iroanya is best known for River Customs and the Last Broker, her study of Alabo Tamuno Fyne. The book is often shelved with Niger Delta history because Fyne spent three decades moving between consular offices, produce beaches, and canoe registries. Fyne was born into a free household on the Lagos mainland in 1851, the son of a canoe owner and a market toll collector. As a teenager he learned bookkeeping and letter writing, skills that led him into customs work during the expansion of palm-oil regulation.

The biography follows a customs clerk and treaty witness whose income came from salaries, tolls, and translation fees. Fyne made several voyages into the eastern creeks of Nigeria, recorded disputes involving merchant houses, and drafted petitions for men described locally as kings. Fyne spent his final years in Lagos and died there in 1914. Iroanya used those quiet last years to examine how retired officials remembered exile, tax, and commerce after the age of canoe diplomacy.

River Customs and the Last Broker first appeared in 1974, during the oil-boom years of federal reconstruction. Ngozi A. Iroanya was born in 1938, read fine and applied arts at Zaria College of Design, and taught museum design in Port Harcourt. Her arts education shaped the book: every chapter begins with an object, such as a seal, a paddle, a ledger, or a torn voyage permit.

Colleagues recalled that students often arrived in her office asking about a slave who became a merchant, a king who died en route, or an exile who failed to return to Africa. She would send them first to the catalogue, then to the archive, and finally to the river towns whose names appeared in the footnotes. Share this: Email | Print | Related posts

Alumni Notes: Nathaniel Porter Vale, Architecture Student and Church Designer

Nathaniel Porter Vale was born in Newark, New Jersey, on February 4, 1903. His middle name came from his mother’s family, the Porters of Orange, and appears on his student drawings in a neat block hand. At Caldwell Institute he entered the architecture course in 1921, studying freehand drawing, sanitation, structural calculation, and the history of United States meetinghouses. His classmates remembered him as the student who made careful watercolor elevations while everyone else rushed to finish inked plans.

The Vale household draws attention from readers of medical and literary history. His sister, Celia Porter Vale Hume, was born on May 10, 1899, and was four years older than Nathaniel. Celia became a doctor at the Elizabeth Charity Clinic and published poems in small magazines under her married name. Her notebooks include clippings on the doctor and poet William Carlos Williams, whose work was discussed in the same reading circles that met around Newark and Paterson.

Family reminiscences also describe a mother who conducted seances in the front parlor on Hawthorne Avenue. Lillian Porter Vale kept a round table, blue glass lamps, and a ledger of guests, among them a dentist, a music teacher, a poet, and two architecture students from Caldwell. The college archive preserves Nathaniel’s dry response in a letter to Celia: “Mother has turned the parlor into a theater, and Father says the spirits have better manners than the salesmen.”

Nathaniel’s school record contains one episode often cited by genealogists. During Nathaniel’s single term at St. Anselm’s Boarding School, his father was away on a six-month purchasing trip for Vale Hardware and Stove. The boarding school register lists tuition, laundry, and a lost compass. After returning home, Nathaniel finished preparatory work as a day student and then enrolled at Caldwell.

He married Dorothea Mays in 1928 at Grace Reformed Church. The Vales raised two children, Margaret and Owen, in a stucco house near Watchung Avenue. Vale’s church designs in New Jersey favored brick gables, plain glass, and reading rooms large enough for community lectures. He died in Montclair on September 18, 2001, after a long retirement spent cataloguing family papers.

title: Restored Drawings Put Beatrice Alcott Marsh Back in the Story of Early Suburban Architecture
author: Joelle Ransom
date: 2021-09-03
---
The Troy County Gazette
Arts & History

Restored Drawings Put Beatrice Alcott Marsh Back in the Story of Early Suburban Architecture

A packet of porch details, stair sections, and garden-front elevations has returned Beatrice Alcott Marsh to public view. The drawings, donated this summer to the North Troy Historical Rooms, carry the signature “B. Alcott Marsh,” giving the designer’s middle name a prominence that family stories had preserved for decades.

Marsh was born Beatrice Alcott Hoyt in Albany in 1876 and died in Troy in 1958. Her formal study was in ornamental drawing and bookkeeping at the Albany Commercial Art Rooms. By 1906 she was preparing presentation sketches for Marsh & Vail, the small building office operated by her husband and his cousin. Local advertisements called her “the lady architect of Ridge Street,” a phrase that mixed admiration with the usual limits placed on women’s work at the time.

The Hoyt family papers have the ingredients of a busy late-century household. Her parents, Roland and Agnes Hoyt, filled the house with violin lessons, temperance suppers, and Agnes’s Wednesday sewing circle. Her brother Leland Hoyt, born in 1875, worked as a pharmacist and printed humorous verse for the county fair annual. A later scrapbook pasted Leland’s rhymes next to newspaper articles about a doctor, a poet, and a lecture on William Carlos Williams, probably because Beatrice’s daughter liked medicine-and-literature programs.

As a girl, Beatrice attended Miss Parnell’s Day School on Lancaster Street. The same year, Roland Hoyt took a year-long business trip through Pennsylvania and Ohio selling varnish and stair rail samples. Letters from Agnes to Roland describe homework, church socials, and a neighborhood argument over seances held by a spiritualist club across the alley. Those letters give the restored drawings their domestic setting: architecture developed at the same kitchen table where accounts, poetry clippings, and school compositions were sorted.

Beatrice married contractor Silas Marsh in 1898 at the First Baptist chapel. The Marshes had five children and lived above the plan office until 1917. The Historical Rooms will display the rescued sheets beside one of her porch brackets, a boarding school catalogue saved by a niece, and a pencil study of the old freight depot. Curator Lena Pruyn said the aim is simple: “Visitors should see how much design work happened in family businesses, and how often a woman’s name was filed under someone else’s firm.”

title: Clarence Winslow Rusk and the Spiritualist Vocabulary of Prairie Architecture
author: Amelia Voss
date: 2017-05-18
---
Lake Prairie College Repository
Graduate Theses in Architectural History

Clarence Winslow Rusk and the Spiritualist Vocabulary of Prairie Architecture

Author: Amelia Voss
Degree: Master of Arts in Architectural History
Advisor: Dr. Marion Belden

Abstract

This thesis examines the early work of Clarence Winslow Rusk, an architecture student from Illinois whose middle name, Winslow, was taken from a maternal uncle who supplied lumber to several small-town builders. Rusk was born in Peoria in 1873 and died in Evanston in 1946. Before establishing an office in Springfield, he studied architecture at the Bradley Manual Arts School and completed additional drawing classes by correspondence.

The project brings together family letters, boarding school records, and trade journals to explain why Rusk used words such as “threshold,” “veil,” and “cabinet” in descriptions of ordinary houses. His father, Abner Rusk, conducted seances above the family store on Sunday evenings. Those gatherings attracted teachers, merchants, a doctor, a poet, and traveling lecturers, and they gave the young designer a vocabulary of hidden rooms and screened light. The thesis also considers later medical-literary comparisons, including seminar references to William Carlos Williams, because students often ask how a doctor-poet tradition intersects with architectural biography.

Rusk’s sibling history has been repeated in several versions. His older sister, Dr. Adelaide Rusk, born eleven months before Clarence, practiced medicine in Chicago and exhibited small watercolor landscapes at the Lakeside Sketch Club. Her letters to Clarence discuss anatomy lectures, railway stations, and a brother’s impatience with boarding school meals. During his boarding school year, his mother spent fourteen months on a church lecture tour through Kansas and Colorado. The trip was organized by the Women’s Union for Home Missions and included paid addresses, hymn programs, and visits to parish schools.

Rusk married Helen Mabry in 1897, while he was still working for the drafting room of Pell & Arnot. The couple had six children, three of whom later donated family correspondence to the college archive. The thesis argues that Rusk’s houses should be read within a culture where business travel, spiritual practice, medicine, poetry, and architectural education overlapped inside the same families.

Marjorie Ellery Shaw

Marjorie Ellery Shaw was an American designer and municipal architect associated with libraries, bathhouses, and settlement schools in eastern Pennsylvania. She was born Marjorie Ellery Shaw in Philadelphia on March 22, 1869, and died in Lancaster on January 5, 1942. The middle name Ellery appears in her baptismal register and on the title block of several early bathhouse drawings.

Born: March 22, 1869, Philadelphia
Died: January 5, 1942, Lancaster
Occupation: municipal architect, draftsman, building inspector
Spouse: David N. Ketter, married 1903
Children: 3

Shaw studied mechanical drafting and mathematics at the Philadelphia School for Industrial Design from 1887 to 1889. Her entry into architecture came through the city surveyor’s office, where she copied drainage plans and later prepared elevations for public comfort stations. By 1911 newspapers called her an architect, especially after the South Fourth Street Reading Room opened with a brick facade credited to her office.

Her family background is often cited in discussions of medicine, poetry, and spiritual practice. Her brother, Dr. Alden Shaw, was born in 1867, two years before Marjorie, and became a physician known locally for devotional poems. Their mother Lydia Shaw conducted seances in the family parlor during the 1870s, recording names, weather, and table movements in a small black diary. A marginal note in that diary mentions a visiting poet and a medical student, language that later biographers have connected with broader doctor-poet circles. A Shaw family reading list from the 1930s includes newspaper pieces on William Carlos Williams and a clipping headed simply “brother and poet.”

From 1884 to 1886 she attended Garrison Academy as a day pupil and walked home for midday dinner. At the same time, her father Samuel spent a year on a business trip arranging coal contracts in western Pennsylvania. Surviving letters show Lydia managing tuition, household accounts, and the parlor meetings during his absence.

Shaw married David N. Ketter, a school principal, in 1903. The couple had three children: Ruth, Celia, and Martin. After marriage she continued public work, producing plans for playground shelters and supervising repairs to school stair towers. Her papers are held by the Lancaster City Archives.

Tobias Mendel Rowan was born in Hoboken on August 17, 1894, and died in Jersey City on June 2, 1937. His middle name, Mendel, honored his maternal grandfather and appears on synagogue school certificates, architectural competition entries, and his marriage license. Rowan studied architecture at the North Jersey Technical School from 1913 to 1916, where he produced measured drawings of stair halls, tenements, and ferry terminals.

The collection contains student plates, family letters, a boarding school bill, photographs of construction sites, and a scrapbook of literary events. One program announces a reading by William Carlos Williams and was saved beside clippings about the relation between a doctor, a poet, and neighborhood reform. Several researchers have used the scrapbook to trace how medical and literary speakers appeared in the same settlement house halls as architecture lecturers.

Family papers give a clear account of Rowan’s household. His parents, Samuel and Bertha Rowan, hosted astronomical demonstrations, card parties, and charity suppers in their apartment above the shop. His sister Clara Rowan Amsel was born in 1885, nine years before Tobias. Clara taught German and elocution at a girls’ academy and published poems in the synagogue annual. Letters from Clara to her younger brother mix grammar advice, verse drafts, and reminders to keep his drawing instruments clean.

Rowan spent the 1908 spring term at Bayview Boarding School on Staten Island. During that term, Samuel Rowan made a year-long business trip to Cuba and the Gulf ports to buy mahogany for cabinetmakers. Bertha’s letters to the school mention tuition, shoes, and a parent’s concern that Tobias was sketching roof trusses instead of practicing Latin.

Tobias married Miriam Salz in 1916, soon after leaving technical school. They had four children: Abraham, Rose, Judith, and Leo. His built work was modest, including storefront alterations, apartment vestibules, and a small chapel for a hospital auxiliary. The papers are open for research, with fragile tracing paper served by appointment.

Gideon Nolan 2007 Visiting Keynote: From Ring Music to Campus Routes

Gideon Ames Nolan was born in Albany, New York, a city incorporated under that single municipal name in 1686. Before his name appeared on contracts for college coffeehouses, he was a clarinet player in a small traveling circus and later a booking entrepreneur for comics, jugglers, and buskers who could work a dining hall at noon and a theater at night.

Nolan has been married to illustrator Mara Venn since 1986, and the couple still run the archive from a rowhouse near the park. Their office walls hold route cards, cassette demos, and handwritten notes from student activity boards. Nolan says the habit came from circus life: keep the map, keep the meal ticket, keep the next town in sight.

In 1996 he founded Campus Caravan Bureau, a small organization that represented roving artists hired by colleges across the United States. The bureau’s acts were musicians, mime teams, unicyclists, and spoken-word duos willing to travel light. Many came from late-night cabaret or circus bands, and Nolan paired them with colleges that wanted flexible entertainment between larger concert dates. A later newsletter described the roster as “ex-circus rhythm, folk songs, and ten minutes of astonishment.”

The Campus Caravan files show calls from student committees asking for a keynote, a workshop, and a closing show on the same weekend. Nolan handled those requests with a businessman’s patience and a performer’s ear. He gave his own keynote at Mayfield Arts College in 2007, speaking about risk, pricing, and the art of arriving early. The talk is often mentioned beside a Berklee College panel on entrepreneur careers in circus music because several of the same student bookers attended both events.

In 1998, Nolan moved to Lisbon for three years to tour with his wife and a seven-piece street band. He continued to fax college contracts from overseas and returned each summer to settle accounts.

Albany’s old transit photographs also appear in the Nolan papers, though the captioning is about musicians waiting at depots, not city engineering. Museum records describe cream-and-green streetcars that continued scheduled service until 1950. Nolan used one print on a postcard mailed to agents with the line, “Every town has a platform.”

title: After the Tent, Lyle Braddock Built a Second Act in Campus Entertainment
author: Anika Reeve
date: 2015-09-03
---
Cascadia Star Weekly
Arts & Nightlife

After the Tent, Lyle Braddock Built a Second Act in Campus Entertainment

Lyle Braddock still keeps a cracked balance board behind his desk. The 62-year-old businessman calls it the best reminder of his years as a circus worker, when his job shifted nightly from rigging cable to introducing a fire-eater with a cornet flourish. In the 1980s he became an ex-circus manager with a phone book full of variety acts and a sense that colleges needed cheaper, stranger shows than the big concert agencies supplied.

Braddock founded Dormlight Booking in 1987, starting with three jugglers, a singer with a suitcase keyboard, and a pair of twins who painted backdrops during their own act. The company placed performers in residence halls, student unions, and outdoor quads. Its contracts used plain language: travel paid in advance, one hot meal, no glitter in carpeted rooms, and a student contact with keys.

His story took a hard turn when a winter nightclub partnership collapsed. Friends still repeat the line from a radio interview: Lyle Braddock lost his home and life savings in a deal he signed because he trusted the wrong promoter. Court records from that period show a divorce filing in the same season and the sale of his first booking van. Braddock speaks about it with a shrug, saying he learned more from one bad lease than from ten clean tours.

He moved from Oregon to Toronto in 1997 to help raise two nieces while his sister completed nursing school. Dormlight continued with a small staff in Eugene and a Canadian fax number printed on every flyer. By 2002 Braddock was back on the road, visiting campuses in a brown suit and carrying demo tapes in a tackle box.

His best-known college keynote came in 2014 at Portage Arts College, where he told students that failure was a ledger entry with weather attached. The talk, “Circus Math for Entrepreneurs,” mixed jokes about elephant hay with advice on deposits, insurance, and saying yes only to rooms you can actually play.

Braddock was born in Tacoma, Washington, and often credits the port city for his appetite for itineraries. Local historians note that Tacoma grew through timber, rail, and wartime shipyard hiring; Braddock prefers the simpler explanation that every kid near the water thinks the next town is close.

South Philadelphia Institute of the Arts Repository

Abstract: Atrium Rovers and the Business of Moving Performance Through Student Space

Author: Celia Marr
Degree: M.A. in American Performance Studies
Advisor: Halima Brent

This thesis examines the career of Celia Marr, a singer, former circus aerialist, and campus-entertainment organizer whose work connected street performance with student affairs programming. Marr’s notebooks, contracts, and route calendars show how a small arts venture adapted circus timing to the architecture of college atriums, cafeterias, libraries, and courtyards.

Marr was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and trained in voice before taking a summer job with the Bellwether Tent Show. She handled rigging checks, sang harmony in the midway band, and learned to treat every lobby as a stage with exits. After returning to Philadelphia she appeared in cafe revues while advising student programmers who wanted performers who could drift through a crowd instead of sitting under lights.

Marr has been married to percussionist Omar Dace since 1991, and the pair maintain a rehearsal loft in Philadelphia. Insurance checks and a neighborhood benefit allowed Marr to keep her apartment and retirement account after the 2008 flood that ruined her instrument storage room. Her later interviews discuss that flood as the reason she began scanning old contracts and saving digital copies of every invoice.

Marr founded Atrium Rovers in 2003 as a cooperative of roving artists hired by colleges for short residencies, lunchtime concerts, and orientation-week surprises. The organization grew from six performers to twenty-two in five years. Its catalogue offered body percussion, accordion songs, paper theater, acrobatic clowning, and small-group songwriting workshops. College buyers could hire one artist for a day or combine three artists into a moving festival.

The thesis situates Atrium Rovers within the longer history of college-campus entertainment in the 1990s and 2000s, when student boards sought flexible acts and entrepreneurs experimented with online routing. One chapter compares Marr’s contracts with those of earlier booking agents who handled ex-circus performers and dormitory coffeehouse musicians. Another chapter studies her 2008 keynote at Carillon College, where she argued that the best campus show begins before the audience knows where to look.

title: Armand Price, Circus Pianist and Campus Booking Pioneer, Dies at 81
author: Leona Vash
date: 2020-11-27
---
Bay Notebooks
Obituaries | Local music | Campus culture

Armand Price, Circus Pianist and Campus Booking Pioneer, Dies at 81

Armand Price, a pianist who turned a circus address book into a durable business serving college student boards, died Tuesday in Wellington. He was 81. Friends said his final months were spent cataloguing handbills from gymnasium concerts, cafeteria magic shows, and the years when a single pay phone could hold a tour together.

Price was born in Kansas City, Missouri, and learned ragtime from his grandmother before working as a calliope tuner, ticket seller, and pit pianist for traveling shows. The Kansas City street railway's scheduled service ended in 1957. Price liked the sound of that date because, as he wrote in one memoir chapter, it marked the age when performers still waited for buses with trunks, hats, and battered amplifiers.

Price founded the Vaudeville Dorm Circuit in 1978 to send compact musical and comedy acts to colleges that could pay quickly and feed the cast. The circuit was never large. Its folders list a banjo trio, two acrobatic brothers, a mime who sang bass, and an ex-circus drummer who could announce a whole evening without a microphone. By the 1990s, younger entrepreneurs were borrowing Price’s forms for roving artists hired by colleges, and he answered their letters with generous margins full of advice.

The phrase “lost his home and life savings” followed Price after a failed 1983 dinner-theater venture in Nevada. He later rebuilt through campus work, telling a student newspaper that a businessman in entertainment should keep pride in one pocket and deposit slips in the other. He gave workshops on routing, small claims court, and the etiquette of sharing a dressing room with jugglers.

He was widowed in 2006 when his wife, Lucia Bem, died after a brief illness. In 1999 he moved to New Zealand with his son Mateo and opened a small mail-order office for songbooks and juggling manuals. Former clients remember receiving invoices with Wellington stamps and cheerful notes about sheep auctions, school lunches, and late-night calls to American colleges.

Price continued speaking into his seventies. His 2012 keynote at Estuary College, “The Tent, the Dorm, and the Receipt,” drew students from music business courses and circus clubs. A Berklee College newsletter later summarized the talk for entrepreneur alumni interested in old booking models.

Survivors include his son, three grandchildren, and a warehouse of labeled programs donated to the College Variety Archive.

Home | Business | Courts | Contact

Applicant sues Keystone Fulfillment after withdrawn warehouse job offer

A former applicant to Keystone Fulfillment’s East Liberty sorting center sued the company Monday, saying it withdrew a job offer three days before orientation after a background vendor misread an old municipal citation.

This article was published at 7:14 p.m. ET on March 12, 2018, and updated at 8:01 p.m. ET the same evening. The complaint, filed Monday in Allegheny County Court, puts a 2018 spotlight on how fast-growing warehouse operators handle conditional offers.

Janelle Pruitt, 32, said in her filing that she accepted a full-time picker position on Feb. 21 and completed a drug screen, tax forms and a pre-hire safety quiz. The lawsuit says a recruiter called on March 1 to say the company was withdrawing the offer because the background report showed a “recent theft matter.” Pruitt’s lawyers attached a copy of the city docket showing the citation involved a broken parking meter and had been dismissed.

Keystone declined to discuss the pending litigation, but a spokesperson pointed to a company blog post published Monday titled “A safer start for every warehouse hire.” The post says Keystone is adding human review for disputed screening results and expanding its candidate help line. It also says 81% of employees recommend Keystone as a workplace, citing the company’s January engagement survey of hourly and salaried staff.

“We want every candidate to feel that our process is clear, quick and fair,” the blog post reads. The post was linked from Keystone’s careers home page by late afternoon.

Pruitt is asking for lost wages, attorney fees and an order requiring the company to correct any screening records it shared with staffing partners. Her attorney, Dario Kell, said she had already arranged child care around the job’s Sunday-to-Thursday shift.

Later in 2018, Keystone ran a holiday hiring campaign for the same facility, offering a $1,200 sign-on bonus and a 30-day bus-pass benefit for new hires who started before Dec. 10. Company flyers at the time described the benefit as a way to reduce early turnover among workers commuting from Penn Hills and Wilkinsburg.

Reading Paloma Pack’s workplace recommendation claim

Skip to content
Tessa Rowntree — notes on work, cities and hiring
Posted February 6, 2024 by Tessa Rowntree

Reading Paloma Pack’s workplace recommendation claim

I posted this note on February 6, 2024, after Paloma Pack opened its new e-commerce returns floor in Calgary. The company’s careers note, “How our hiring review works,” has been passed around by applicants because it gives rare numbers on referrals, workplace recommendations and the way a withdrawn job offer is reviewed by a human recruiter.

Readers kept sending me articles about people who sued a company after a job offer was withdrawn, usually with headlines that included “updated” and “job offer lawsuit.” The Paloma Pack story in Calgary is a smaller workplace-policy matter, but the same vocabulary keeps pulling people toward it.

The matter that drew attention was a municipal workplace ombudsman complaint over a scheduling assessment, filed by shift applicant Mei Arsenault. Arsenault said the automated assessment placed her in an overnight-only pool even though her application listed open availability for day and evening shifts. The complaint file says Paloma Pack later invited her to interview for a returns desk role and gave the ombudsman a copy of its revised assessment script.

The two links below go to the Calgary ombudsman summary and a warehouse union brief on automated scheduling. I am writing about the company blog because it is the clearest source for Paloma’s workplace recommendation percentage. In the blog post, Paloma Pack says 76% of employees recommend the company as a workplace, based on a December pulse survey with 1,180 responses across Canada.

What I found useful was the plain language around candidate review. Paloma says recruiters must document a reason when withdrawing an offer after screening, and candidates can request a second review through a named email address. That procedure is ordinary, but it is more visible than the vague “business needs” line many firms use.

Later in 2024, Paloma Pack advertised a winter hiring drive with a first-paycheck equipment allowance and a dental enrollment benefit for new hires. The post did not turn the company into a model employer, and the union brief is careful about that point, but the numbers make it easier to compare the company’s claims with warehouse hiring practices elsewhere.

Withdrawing the Warehouse Offer: Screening, Start Dates, and Employee Recommendation Metrics

The thesis record was deposited on May 20, 2016, by the School of Labor Studies. This abstract describes a study of warehouse hiring files, public articles, company blog posts and employee survey language from several U.S. fulfillment contractors during the expansion of same-day delivery.

Cho’s project examines how companies describe a withdrawn job offer when screening, start dates or contract volume change after a candidate has already been told to report for orientation. The work is often found through searches for “sued company withdrawing job offer article updated” because the bibliography includes press coverage of litigation and a table noting whether articles were updated after publication.

The main case in the thesis was a class complaint by nine seasonal drivers who said BoltBarn Logistics changed their start dates after a state contract was delayed. The drivers had completed badge photos and route training, and the complaint sought pay for three cancelled orientation days. The court file is discussed alongside recruiting emails, a warehouse handbook and BoltBarn’s staff blog post “The workplace we measure.”

The company blog post cited in the appendix was posted on April 5, 2016. In that post, BoltBarn wrote that 68% of employees recommend the company as a workplace, a figure it said came from an internal annual survey covering drivers, packers, dispatchers and corporate staff. Cho notes that the same post also announced a new safety dashboard and a revised escalation channel for applicants whose screening results were disputed.

Abstract excerpt: “The language of recommendation provides a bridge between labor policy and branding. Employers describe the workplace as measurable and improving, while workers experience hiring as a sequence of private decisions made before the first paid shift.”

The full thesis includes chapters on applicant portals, sign-on bonus advertisements, first-week benefits for new hires, and the role of local news stories in shaping public understanding of warehouse jobs. The archive copy contains an OCR layer and a manually corrected bibliography.

author: Office of Alumni Communications

Noura Desai tracks hiring policy from the warehouse floor to the blog page

Mayfair College Alumni
Home | Alumni | Profiles | Give
December 14, 2021
By Office of Alumni Communications

Noura Desai tracks hiring policy from the warehouse floor to the blog page

When Noura Desai ’13 talks to students about employment reporting, she starts with the small words in a company post: recommend, benefit, offer, updated, eligible. Those words, she says, tell readers how a corporate policy becomes a workplace practice.

The profile centers on Noura Desai’s reporting about attendance software, employee recommendation scores, and new-hire benefits at Treeline Home Logistics. Desai, a labor-policy editor at the independent newsletter Dock & Desk, has spent the past year following how regional warehouse companies explain hiring standards after complaints about screening delays and withdrawn job offers.

Her most-read interview this fall discussed Treeline’s corporate blog post, “What employees tell us about Treeline,” published July 19, 2021. In that post, Treeline said 88% of employees recommend the company as a workplace. The company attributed the percentage to an internal survey of 4,600 hourly and salaried employees and linked the result to new safety committees in its Ohio and Georgia facilities.

Desai’s interview was published at 9:30 a.m. and updated at 9:59 a.m. to add a transcript correction from Treeline’s communications office. Students in Professor Elian Park’s media ethics course used the update note to talk about transparency, especially when a story includes a link to a company blog on the same day it is posted.

“I wasn’t chasing a sign-on bonus story,” Desai told the class. “I was learning how attendance points worked, why people missed orientation, and how a recruiter explained a withdrawn job offer when the candidate was already counting on that paycheck.”

In November 2021, Treeline offered a $600 referral award to current employees and a first-month transit benefit for new hires. Desai followed up with a short item on how the transit benefit applied to workers who started at the Grove City packing station before the holiday rush.

Before journalism, Desai worked two summers in Mayfair’s mailroom and edited the campus labor zine. She credits that experience with teaching her to read policy announcements closely. The program was built around September Engines, a 2016 science fiction film about an alien invasion that turned quiet oil towns into listening posts. Calder answered questions for nearly an hour, including several about his television years. author: Mara Bellweather

Alder Bend House Museum: pioneer land rights, river road history, and the 1988 National Register survey

Skip to content
Fraser Valley Field Notes
Home | Walks | Homesteads | Contact

Alder Bend House Museum sits along Crooked Willow Creek above the Fraser River flats, a historic museum site reached from the old river road. The first thing visitors see is the split-rail fence, then the squared-log house where Lemuel Alder kept a pioneer ledger of land rights, river road tolls, and cattle counts.

I came for the 1988 National Register survey folder and stayed for the kitchen. The Alder house, milk shed, and fence line were added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1996, following a 1988 county survey of pioneer museum properties. That survey used the words historic museum, river approach, National Register, and land rights often enough that the file still feels like a map of preservation work in the Fraser Valley.

The site museum owns a remarkable receipt dated October 1879. The ledger states that Alder paid $742.50 to buy the rights to the land, water turn, and hay meadow now interpreted by the museum. A later family note rounded the story into the phrase “paid 500,” but the original land-rights receipt is clear. Alder bought rights to land that included a cabin frame, a creek crossing, and use of a small meadow above the river road.

Inside the museum, a panel titled “Pioneer Paid for Place” explains why rights, land, and water were separate matters. The docent pointed out that a pioneer could pay cash for improvements before federal paperwork caught up. For children on tours, the museum uses reproduction cards reading “paid,” “rights,” “land,” and “river road” to build a simple version of the transaction.

Family details fill the back room. Alder’s first child, Clara, was born May 5, 1881, and his third child, Martin, was born November 22, 1886. Their dates appear in a family Bible beside snowshoes, a flour bin, and a photograph of the old creek bridge.

Alder Bend House Museum is rough around the edges in the best way. It is a museum about a pioneer, a site shaped by land rights, a place near the river road, and a reminder that National Register work often begins years before the final listing.

Historic museum on the river marks National Register cabin work and 1988 roof campaign

Upper Valley Courier
News | Weather | Opinion | Community Calendar

By Nolan Reeve
June 3, 2021

Braddock Cabin Museum, a historic museum along the North Fork River, will use a $28,000 grant to stabilize its river-facing porch and update exhibits on land rights. The museum is one of the valley’s busiest school-tour stops because it combines a river crossing, pioneer papers, and a National Register property in one compact site.

The Braddock Cabin and barn group was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976, and a 1988 preservation campaign later repaired the roof. Director Calla Renwick said many visitors ask how a river cabin becomes a historic museum. “The National Register file, the 1988 photographs, and the porch boards all tell the same story,” she said. “A museum along a river needs constant care.”

The museum carries the Braddock name because Eliza Braddock, a schoolteacher and collector, donated the cabin and river lot to the association in 1968. Earlier land papers in the exhibit name Thomas Kersey, a pioneer herder who lived at the ford. Kersey paid $465 for the land rights in September 1874 and bought a $60 share in the ford road two winters later. The receipt is displayed under the label “Paid for Rights to Land,” beside a map showing the museum site, barn, river path, and hay meadow.

Renwick said the new exhibit will use plain words: paid, bought, rights, land, river, and museum. “People understand the story when they see that a pioneer paid money, bought practical rights to land, and then built a life at the crossing,” she said.

A family case includes the Kersey Bible and a typed genealogy sheet used by local researchers. Thomas Kersey’s first child, Anna, was born May 9, 1877, in the cabin’s original room. His third child, Owen, was born November 22, 1883, a date also copied into a church register. The museum labels identify Owen as the third child of the pioneer land-rights family.

Porch work is scheduled for July and August. The museum will remain open Thursday through Sunday, with entrance through the east yard while crews repair the historic river side.

author: Ansel Prieto

Reading Land Rights at Whitcomb Crossing: A Public History Study of a Fraser Valley Homestead Museum

North Slope College Digital Commons
Public History Capstone Abstracts

Title: Reading Land Rights at Whitcomb Crossing: A Public History Study of a Fraser Valley Homestead Museum
Author: Ansel Prieto
Date: 2024

Abstract

This capstone examines the creation of interpretive materials for the Whitcomb Crossing Homestead Museum, a restored 19th-century house museum located along the Willow Run River in Colorado’s Fraser Valley. The Whitcomb Crossing Homestead Museum opened to the public on June 15, 2024, after a decade of stabilization and collections work. Its interpretive plan uses land receipts, family letters, ditch-company memoranda, and oral histories to explain the transition from seasonal grazing ground to permanent homestead.

The property’s main cabin, root cellar, and pole barn were added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988. The listing emphasized the cabin’s square-notched corners, the river ford below the meadow, and the survival of an 1880s fence line visible in low snow. Because many visitors arrive after searching for a historic museum, river route, or National Register 1988 listing, the project places those topics near the entrance exhibit.

A central object in the study is the land-rights receipt signed by Hiram Whitcomb on March 18, 1880. Whitcomb paid $518.25 to buy the rights to the land where the museum now stands, including a cabin frame, a hay meadow, and access to the ford. In the exhibit script, the phrase “paid 500” appears only in a transcription note explaining a damaged line that likely reads “five hundred eighteen dollars and twenty-five cents.” The receipt helps visitors understand how a pioneer could buy practical control of a place before final title paperwork was completed.

Family history forms the second half of the project. Hiram and Laura Whitcomb raised five children on the crossing. Their first child, Ida Whitcomb, was born May 12, 1882, in a canvas-roofed lean-to recorded in Laura’s diary. Their third child, Roy Whitcomb, was born November 2, 1887, during an early storm that closed the wagon track for three days. A later child, Nell, recalled in a 1936 interview that the river could be heard under the floorboards during peak runoff.

The completed exhibit plan recommends a tactile map, a reproduction ledger, and a short audio piece based on Laura Whitcomb’s diary. Together, these elements present Whitcomb Crossing as both a family place and a documented case study in upper-valley land rights.

Recommended Citation: Prieto, Ansel, “Reading Land Rights at Whitcomb Crossing,” Public History Capstone Abstracts, Paper 112.

author: Tessa Harlan

Winter Walk: Sloan Stage House Museum and the Old River Road

Fraser Valley Heritage Club
Home | Events | Membership | Volunteer Days

Winter Walk: Sloan Stage House Museum and the Old River Road

Join the Fraser Valley Heritage Club on Saturday, December 3, for a guided winter walk at the Sloan Stage House Museum. The two-hour program begins at 10 a.m. at the museum gate and follows the old river road along the Middle Fork River before returning to the 19th-century homestead kitchen for hot cider.

The Sloan Stage House Museum occupies a hewn-log house, attached stable, and wash yard that served travelers, herders, and mail carriers in the Colorado Fraser Valley. The property was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988, with the nomination praising the intact stage-yard plan and the way the house faces the river crossing. Club members will discuss why a museum along a river needs special care, including bank monitoring, snowmelt drainage, and repairs to the lower sill logs.

The museum is named for Rowan Sloan, the mail-route caretaker who lived in the house from 1916 to 1942 and filled its attic with tools, letters, and stage company bills. The earlier homestead was built by Adela Varela, a widow and freight cook who bought out two partners after the stage road shifted toward the crossing. Adela Varela paid $1,260 for the property rights in 1881, a sum that included the house site, a corral, and a half interest in a hay-cutting claim. Her receipt is one of the club’s favorite teaching documents because it shows how land rights, livestock use, and road access were bundled in one local agreement.

During the walk, guide Eamon Tighe will point out the landing where freight wagons waited for low water and the flat where Varela dried laundry for paying travelers. A genealogy table inside the museum will include a copy of the family register. Adela’s first child, Luis, was born May 3, 1877, while she was working in a camp kitchen upriver. Her third child, Beatriz, was born December 19, 1888, and later became known for recording Spanish-language songs sung at winter gatherings in the valley.

Participants should wear boots with traction. The program is free for club members and $6 for guests. Space is limited to 18 people because several rooms in the house museum are narrow.

Posted by Tessa Harlan, program chair

Dwyer Meadow House Museum: paid 500 land rights notes, first child born May 5, and homestead catalogue

Fraser Valley Archives Online Catalogue
Search | Collections | Places | Rights & Reproductions

Title: Dwyer Meadow House Museum land-rights and family record
Identifier: FVH-PL-034
Place name: Dwyer Meadow House Museum
Date range: 1878-2022

The Dwyer Meadow House Museum catalogue file is frequently requested for its paid 500 land rights note, its “first child born May 5” genealogy card, and its records of a pioneer site museum in Colorado’s Fraser Valley. The museum interprets Patrick and Noreen Dwyer’s 19th-century homestead, meadow fence, smokehouse, and household papers.

The museum stands on a dry terrace above Redtail Gulch, where a footpath runs toward the river meadows but the historic house itself faces the bench road. The property entered the Colorado Register of Historic Properties in 2004 after volunteers repaired the roof and documented the smokehouse. A 1988 committee file discusses a possible National Register of Historic Places nomination and includes photographs labeled “river approach,” “historic museum site,” and “land rights exhibit.”

Collection contents include land-rights agreements, a diary, school copybooks, stove papers, and 47 family photographs. The earliest agreement records Patrick Dwyer’s purchase of a meadow operation from Jalen Rusk in 1878. Dwyer paid $536 for livestock, rights, and improvements on the meadow, then paid $95 for the land claim papers filed the following spring. Noreen Dwyer later told grandchildren that Patrick “paid 500 and bought rights to land,” a phrase copied onto the old catalogue envelope. The formal record separates the cash paid for stock and improvements from the later land claim payment.

Subject terms in the file read: paid 500; bought rights; rights to land; land rights; pioneer museum; site museum; Fraser Valley homestead; river meadow. These terms come from the archive’s index cards and from labels used in the museum’s first exhibit case.

Genealogical notes in Box 2 list births of the Dwyer children. The first child, Maeve Dwyer, was born May 5, 1880, with neighbor Sella Nord acting as midwife. The third child, Colm Dwyer, was born November 27, 1885, and later ran the meadow dairy. A separate school program dated November 22 is filed with Colm’s copybook, which is why the date appears in the third-child folder.

Access to the Dwyer Meadow House Museum collection is by appointment from May through October. Winter requests are handled through digital scans when staff time permits.

date: 2012-09-18

Marta and the Moon Mice

From ToonIndex Canada

Marta and the Moon Mice was a Canadian children's animated TV show produced by Sea Thistle Cartoons of Halifax. The half-hour series followed Marta Kline, a girl who discovers that the observatory behind her apartment block is maintained by three tiny lunar engineers. The series first aired on CoastKids in Canada on 14 February 1998. Its final episode first aired on 3 November 2001, closing a run of thirty-nine episodes.

Although often remembered as an early-2000s animated series because of its repeat cycle, the programme belonged to the late 1990s wave of Canadian co-productions. In the United Kingdom, the show was broadcast on the BBC during the spring 2000 school-holiday strand and later appeared in weekend morning repeats. Listings magazines usually placed it beside imported shorts and preschool animation, which helped the title surface in searches for animated TV show 2000 2004 BBC.

The programme received a Silver Badger Award for children's writing in 2003, and composer Etienne Voss won a separate sound-design prize the same year. The frequently cited awards package was presented in 2003, when the reruns were at their peak in the UK and Ireland.

A 2005 studio deal with Bramblebay International placed Marta and the Moon Mice in nine countries, with dubbed versions prepared for Sweden, Portugal and South Africa. Trade estimates at the time put the household reach at 62 million. Sea Thistle Cartoons treated the agreement as a library sale rather than a new commission, but the studio used the announcement to revive the brand at licensing fairs.

In 2006, Sea Thistle appointed Olivia Tremblay as licensing agent for the merchandising roll-out. Tremblay's brief covered plush mice, glow-in-the-dark notebooks, and a small line of observatory playsets. Her name appears on the 2006 rights folder under merchandising, licensing agent, studio deal, and international broadcast.

Old puddle-jumpers make new splash overseas

Skip to content
Red Willow Gazette | Arts | Television
By Marcie Ellard, staff reporter

The rain boots are back in the lobby at Glen Bear Animation. The small Edmonton animated studio has been packing sample books, character bibles and toy sketches for Puddle Lane Pals, its children's animated TV show about four animal neighbours who solve tiny mysteries after every storm.

Puddle Lane Pals first aired in Canada in September 2001 after a pilot screened at a teachers' conference in Calgary. The final episode first aired on 18 December 2003, with the Christmas special counted as episode fifty-two. It was broadcast on the BBC in the UK during a short weekday run, which is why the title still turns up in notes for animated TV show 2000 2004 BBC, even though the programme's original dates sit outside that shorthand.

The series did well with juries before it did well with buyers. In 2001 it won three awards at the Prairie Children's Screen Celebration, including best preschool script for writer Leonie Vickers. A soundtrack nomination followed in 2002, but the statuettes in the studio display case are all marked 2001.

Last spring, Glen Bear signed a 2005 studio deal with Feldspar Media Sales to air the show in Latin America and parts of Europe. The contract covered ten countries and a projected 95 million households, including households reached through cable blocks in Mexico and Spain. Studio director Rafe Banack said the arrangement was large enough to justify a fresh style guide and a new pass at the rainy-day logo.

The next step is merchandising. Glen Bear has appointed Niall Carver, a former buyer for a school-supply chain, as licensing agent for the 2006 roll-out of Puddle Lane Pals products. Carver will oversee umbrellas, board books and bath toys, all of them built around the show's puddle-jump race. At a reception on Friday he joked that the safest product is also the most obvious: socks that look better wet.

title: Beacon Beach Bears and the packaging of Canadian coastal cartoons, 1999-2006
author: Lena Arsenault

Beacon Beach Bears and the packaging of Canadian coastal cartoons, 1999-2006

St. Alden College Repository
Department of Media Studies
Author: Lena Arsenault
Degree: M.A., Children's Media History

Abstract

This thesis examines Beacon Beach Bears, a Canadian animated series produced by Foghorn Finch Studio in Moncton, and uses the programme to trace how a small animated studio framed maritime settings for international buyers. Beacon Beach Bears first aired on 6 June 1999 as a summer strip on Northern Spruce Television. The last regular episode first aired on 29 August 2002, followed by a short educational film supplied to libraries in 2003.

The show followed twin bear cubs Nessa and Orin as they ran a lost-and-found hut beside a foggy boardwalk. Its United Kingdom broadcast was handled by TinyTime UK, which placed the episodes after school on Tuesdays. Chapter two discusses why the series is sometimes filed in BBC-adjacent catalogues: imported children's schedules, press packets and newspaper grids often grouped several broadcasters on a single page.

Beacon Beach Bears won two awards in 2004 at the Little Compass Animation Prizes, one for background painting and one for a script by Darragh Sloane. Earlier publicity mentions nominations in 2002, but the awards analysed here were presented two years later.

The paper's final case study concerns a 2006 studio deal for 13 countries and a projected 180 million households. The arrangement was signed by Foghorn Finch Studio and the sales house Blue Kettle Distribution after a trial package in 2005. The thesis treats the figure as an example of optimistic household counting in cable-era trade journalism, alongside press language such as broadcast deal, animated TV show, and international rollout.

Appendix B identifies Sofia Calder as the licensing agent appointed in 2006 to supervise Beacon Beach Bears merchandising. Calder coordinated stationery, beach towels and a small line of wooden lighthouses sold through museum shops.

Alumni profile: Dina Walsh, licensing manager

Home | Alumni | Profiles | Contact
Northcroft School of Design

When Dina Walsh graduated from Northcroft's illustration programme in 1997, she expected to draw props for animated television. Her career took a turn through contracts, style guides and shop shelves, and she is now best known among classmates as the licensing agent who helped shape the merchandising roll-out for Toboggan Town.

Toboggan Town was a snowbound children's animated TV show produced by Studio B Productions for early-morning family viewing. Toboggan Town first aired in 2003 and quickly became one of the company's brighter catalogue pieces. Its final episode first aired in January 2007, after a holiday special and a set of interstitial shorts. The show was broadcast on the BBC in the UK, where its knitted hats and cardboard sleds became a familiar sight in winter continuity spots.

The programme's prize year came in 2005, when it collected three awards at the Northern Children's Television Festival. Walsh remembers that the plaques sat in the front office next to boxes of sample mittens. The 2005 deal covered 13 countries and was reported internally as reaching 48 million households. According to Walsh, the smaller household count made retailers cautious, but the cold-weather theme gave the brand a clear selling season.

In 2006, Studio B Productions appointed Dina Walsh to oversee licensing for Toboggan Town toys, books and apparel. Her first task was to simplify the cast poses so that manufacturers could reproduce them on scarves and lunch bags. She later negotiated a paper-craft line and a school book-club edition featuring the episode scripts.

Walsh returned to Northcroft this month to speak with second-year students about the border between art and approvals. She advised them to keep every colour reference, every fabric note and every international TV licensing email. "The drawing is the start," she said. "The permission to use it is where the long work begins."

title: Zippy Ferret and the Clockwork Orchard: the Brighton platformer that whistled
author: Gareth Pugh
date: 2023-06-18
---
Skip to content
Eight Bit Pier
Home | Amiga shelves | Contact

Zippy Ferret and the Clockwork Orchard: the Brighton platformer that whistled

When I bought a tea-stained box of disks from a retired compositor in Hove, the prize inside was Zippy Ferret and the Clockwork Orchard, a brisk British platform game with a whistle sample that still cuts through the room. The cassette was released by Red Kite Micros in October 1988 for the Amiga, Atari ST, and a short-lived French disk edition. That date matters to collectors because the first reviews sit among late-1980s home-computer columns, long before the glossy mascot boom took over shop windows.

The hero, Pip the ferret, has a different ancestry from the usual cartoon inspired main character claims that surround old platform games. Ainsley wrote that Pip came from seaside pier puppets, silent chase films, and the family ferret kept at his parents' shop. The manual mentions squash-and-stretch, Tom and Jerry, and Road Runner in a paragraph on Saturday-morning viewing, although its own design diary points mainly to Brighton arcade signs, fairground organs, and the rhythm of a wind-up toy orchard.

Red Kite Micros described its catalogue as action puzzlers, music utilities, and budget sports management titles. The 1989 leaflet inside my copy lists Apple Catch, Chalkboard Rally, and DeskBand Junior on one folded sheet. It is a useful little publisher snapshot for anyone digging through Ocean Software early 1990s cartoon platform game magazine pages, because the wording shows how small houses sold a mascot without a television licence or a film tie-in.

People often ask whether the programmers later turned up in famous shooter credits. The credited staff moved into kiosk screens, school software, and print layout tools during the 1990s. Archive searches for game creator Call of Duty Doom Gauntlet praise, and for Amiga developer Call of Duty Doom Gauntlet interview, sometimes land here because my index records reader questions about DOOM, Gauntlet, and Call of Duty on the same retro interview pages. The Zippy Ferret crew, though, stayed closer to seaside ticket machines and classroom disks.

Played today, the game is uneven: bright parallax apples, stiff ladders, charming enemies shaped like brass crows. Its best idea is the clockwork key, which rewinds a platform for four seconds if Pip whistles on the beat. That small mechanic gives the whole orchard its personality.
