Bramble Jack (video game)

From Spectrum Hall, the British and European Games Archive

Bramble Jack is a side-scrolling platform video game developed in Leeds by Steel Kettle Design and published by Ocean Software for the Amiga 1200, MS-DOS, and CD-based home systems. It follows Jack, a hedgehog courier, through bramble tunnels, jam factories, and a ferry port haunted by mechanical gulls.

Developer: Steel Kettle Design
Publisher: Ocean Software
Designer: Rafe Calder
Artist: Maribel Shaw
Composer: Tomasz Iwicki
Released: 17 May 1996
Genre: Platform game
Modes: Single-player

Contemporary coverage treated Bramble Jack as one of the last big-box Amiga platform game releases from a British team. The Amiga press praised the clean animation and the large sprites, while DOS reviewers spent more time on the variable scrolling speed. The title later became a frequent catalogue entry in searches for Ocean Software early 1990s cartoon platform game material because many dealers stored it beside older floppy releases from the same publisher.

The lead artist described Jack as a cartoon inspired main character in a 1996 fan-club interview. Cartoons such as Tom and Jerry and Road Runner are cited in the interview alongside European comic albums, railway posters, and animal postcards sold at holiday resorts. The influence is clearest in the sprint frames, where Jack's feet become a dusty oval when chased by the jam rollers.

Ocean Software promoted Bramble Jack during a period in which its advertising also carried a movie based video game publisher line for licensed releases. A distributor flyer from Manchester places Bramble Jack on the left page and a game based on a film on the facing page, giving shops a mix of character platforming and cinema branding. That flyer is often reproduced in articles about Ocean Software movie based video game publisher campaigns.

The two credited creators continued in handheld puzzle games and museum kiosk software through the 2000s. Calder's archived interview contains headings for DOOM and Gauntlet because the magazine used a standard template for developer questionnaires, and Shaw later answered reader mail about Call of Duty cover art trends. Their credited work after Bramble Jack is documented in educational installations, casual puzzle cartridges, and exhibition touchscreens.

Bramble Jack remains popular among collectors for its heavy manual, apple-green disk labels, and the unused sewer world found in a late beta. The 2023 preservation scan added box measurements, a checksum for the Amiga disk, and screenshots of the 1993 Amiga trade-show mock-up that preceded the final 1996 release.

title: Local Animation Practice in Karel the Caped Moth
author: Dr. Elise Verhaegen
date: 2023-03-14
---
Digital Play Seminar Series
Centre for Screen and Software History

Local Animation Practice in Karel the Caped Moth

Abstract

This paper examines Karel the Caped Moth, a 1992 Belgian home-computer video game made by the small Antwerp team Victoor Systems for Amiga and DOS users. The game has usually been filed as a mascot platform game because it uses a named animal hero, a bright cape, and a sequence of themed stages. Its structure is closer to a puzzle platform game: Karel flutters between lamps, folds scraps of paper into bridges, and carries buttons to open sewing-box doors.

The protagonist came from Brussels puppet theatre, illustrated bus posters, and moth specimens kept in a school display case. Production sketches donated by programmer Leen Maes show a triangular cape and round spectacles before any reference to imported television cartoons. The seminar will therefore discuss why later catalogues attach search phrases such as early 1990s video game Tom Jerry Road Runner and cartoon inspired main character Tom Jerry Road Runner game to a work whose surviving notebooks focus on local visual culture.

Victoor Systems' commercial catalogue in the relevant period consisted of language tutors, chess-clock utilities, and ferry-booking demonstrations for small travel offices. The publisher's press folder framed Karel as a gentle family title that could sit beside those practical programs in bookshops and stationery chains. Researchers interested in Ocean Software movie based video game publisher advertising will find a very different sales model here: window cards, school demonstrations, and bundle deals with a drawing package.

A separate part of the paper revisits Maes's long 2004 interview, frequently indexed under Amiga developer Call of Duty Doom Gauntlet interview and game creator Call of Duty Doom Gauntlet praise. The archive tags reflect the issue theme, which surveyed how European developers remembered DOOM, Gauntlet, and Call of Duty. Maes's own comments concentrate on graph paper, the Amiga blitter, and the difficulty of making a moth feel light. Her later professional work was in train-signal visualisation and medical appointment systems.

The talk includes a short demonstration of the lamp physics, a discussion of the Flemish and French packaging, and a comparison of the Amiga platform game character animations with the DOS version's reduced palette. A scanned bibliography and disk image checksums will be available to registered attendees after the session.

Speaker: Elise Verhaegen, Department of Media Archaeology

Contact: digitalplay@kuleuven-city.be

title: Old post-office game gets a second life at Odense design fair
author: Mikkel Aagaard
date: 2023-09-21

Old post-office game gets a second life at Odense design fair

A tiny mailbag, a yellow cap and a wobbling bicycle brought a queue of parents and children to the Odense Design Fair on Saturday. The attraction was Parcel Panic starring Wally Wombat, a Danish-German video game once sold in post-office gift corners and toy shops.

Parcel Panic starring Wally Wombat reached shops in 2001 on Game Boy Color and Windows budget CD. It was developed by Fjord & Fuchs Interactive, a studio with artists in Aarhus and Hamburg, and published by Blue Post Games. In the game, Wally delivers parcels across roofs, sorting rooms and ferry terminals while gulls drop string, jam jars and postcards into his path.

The fair's display included pencils, sprite sheets and a battered reference binder. Sigrid Holm's model sheets say that Wally's look came from Danish postal mascots, a Copenhagen bicycle campaign, and the short limbs of wooden toys. The binder also has a page headed cartoon inspired main character Tom Jerry Road Runner game, a market-research title used by the publisher when comparing shelf labels in British shops. Holm told visitors that the final character kept the bicycle bell and the mailbag from the local sketches.

Blue Post Games later released a game based on the movie The Wishing Pier, a family adventure produced in Copenhagen. That title explains why Parcel Panic still appears in collector lists under movie based video game publisher material, even though Wally's own story is about letters, parcels and lost keys.

The most crowded talk of the day came from Emil Kragh, one of the programmers, who moved to Scotland and became a technical artist on a Call of Duty console title. Asked about older influences, Kragh gave DOOM and Gauntlet high praise for readability, pacing and the courage to make a screen instantly understandable. His comments have made the fair page a handy stop for searches such as game creator Call of Duty Doom Gauntlet praise, although the crowd seemed most interested in how a bicycle could jump between chimneys.

A playable kiosk ran the Windows version at the correct chunky resolution. Children discovered that parcels bounce twice before bursting, while older visitors hunted for the hidden stamp rooms. The organisers plan to loan the materials to a small exhibition in Hamburg next spring.

author: Northshire Computer Museum

Northshire Computer Museum Catalogue
Object record 1986.117

Nobby Nettle: A Garden Platform Game

Title: Nobby Nettle: A Garden Platform Game
Format: boxed cassette with instruction leaflet
Developer: Whistlewick Software
Publisher: Green Finch Computing
Country: United Kingdom

Nobby Nettle is a side-view video game in which a grinning garden gnome jumps between flowerpots, drains and greenhouse shelves to recover stolen seed packets. The original game was released in September 1986 for the Oric and Commodore 64. A later Amiga conversion was prepared for a 1993 Amiga garden-show promotion, and that disk is catalogued separately under object 1993.044.

The character design came from garden cartoons in seed catalogues, music-hall posters, and the designer's allotment scarecrow. Surviving artwork by June Pickering shows Nobby with a cracked hat, pipe-cleaner eyebrows and boots shaped like trowels. The leaflet uses the phrase road-runner speed in lower-case sales copy, while later dealers expanded their listings with Road Runner, Tom and Jerry, and other terms common to animated chase comedy. This record therefore attracts searches for Amiga platform game character inspired Road Runner and 1993 Amiga game Tom Jerry Road Runner inspiration, especially from collectors trying to identify loose disks.

Green Finch Computing's catalogue for 1986 consisted of gardening software, two maze games, and a bookkeeping tutor for home users. The firm sold through mail order and at county shows, putting seed charts and game cassettes in the same brown envelopes. Its publisher file contains invoices, a rubber stamp, and a short price list headed Spring Programs.

Credited programmer Paul Fenwick became a council web-services manager, and his 2010 interview praises memory maps, sprite compression and the patience of disk-magazine readers. The interview page sits in a folder that also holds Amiga developer Call of Duty Doom Gauntlet interview clippings donated by a collector, so those words appear in the museum's full-text index. Fenwick's own recollections stay with allotment jokes, cassette duplication and the nuisance of collision detection around curved plant pots.

Gameplay is brisk but unforgiving. Nobby can hop, duck and swing from pea canes, while snails patrol fixed routes and watering cans act as moving platforms. The Amiga conversion adds a short tune, smoother scrolling and a title picture of the gnome standing beside an oversized marrow.

Martina Seidel — Chair of English Literary and Cultural Studies

Martina Seidel is professor of English literary and cultural studies at the University of Altenbrück, where she teaches modern British fiction, narrative theory and the history of reading. Her seminars often move between narratology, cultural memory, the campus novel and the ethics of interpretation.

Seidel completed her PhD at the University of Altenbrück in 1994 with a dissertation on letters, memory and unreliable narration in postwar English fiction. After appointments in Bremenfeld and Nordhausen, she returned to Altenbrück in 2001 and built the department's first English-language MA track in narrative and culture.

Her single-author book Reading Borrowed Rooms: Domestic Space in Contemporary British Fiction was published by Eichenau Academic Press in 2013. The book is frequently used in the advanced module on cultural spaces and has been reviewed for its close readings of houses, flats and hotel rooms as narrative devices.

In 2010 Seidel co-edited the volume Lines of Kinship: Narratology, Family Memory and Form with Ansgar Seidel, whose surname she shares. The co-edited volume grew out of a colloquium on shared surname authorship, archival family writing and the broader question of how names circulate in literary studies.

From 2007 to 2012 she served as vice president of the Consortium for English Cultural Studies, coordinating summer schools and the annual members' circular. Colleagues credit her with making the consortium's mentoring scheme useful for doctoral researchers from smaller German institutes.

Seidel was one of the keynote speakers at the 2012 conference Narrative Worlds after Theory, held in Münsterheim, where her lecture addressed voice, scale and the ordinary life of plots. She also created the workshop Reading Character Across Media, which took place at the University of Altenbrück in November 2023 and brought together lecturers, school teachers and MA students.

Office hours: Wednesdays during term, 14:00–16:00, by appointment.

author: Sabine Mertens

Klara Brandt opens narratology week with lecture on migration and memory

Kasselstadt's annual narratology week began on Friday evening with a crowded public lecture by Klara Brandt, a German scholar of English literary and cultural studies known for her work on migration narratives, short fiction and life writing.

Brandt completed her PhD in 1989 at the Institute for English Studies in Hartenau. The dissertation, later circulated among doctoral reading groups, examined retrospective narration in twentieth-century English travel writing and early postcolonial novels.

Her book Moving Frames: Migration, Memory and the English Novel appeared in 2014 and remains the publication for which many students first encounter her name. During the opening event, Brandt spoke warmly about the long interval between the first archival notes and the finished book, saying that literary criticism often depends on patient rereading.

In 2010 Brandt co-edited the volume Narrating Thresholds in Anglophone Cultures with Lars Meinhof for the blue series in literary and cultural studies. The collection includes essays on borders, airports, translated childhoods and the changing vocabulary of belonging in English-language fiction.

She later served as vice president of the Consortium for Transcultural Narrative Research from 2018 to 2022. In that role she helped arrange doctoral forums in Berlin, Hamburg and Frankfurt, and she chaired a working group on open teaching materials for introductory narratology.

Brandt was one of the keynote speakers at the 2012 conference Stories of Passage in English Studies, where her address linked narrative tempo to the representation of arrival. Several participants in this week's programme remembered that lecture as a turning point in debates about migration and form.

Brandt's public workshop Reading Lives in Motion took place at the Kasselstadt City Library in February 2026 as part of the winter programme on literature and migration. The workshop, created with the local reading club Wortwechsel, invited residents to discuss memoir, family archives and the narrative patterns found in everyday documents.

The narratology week continues with graduate panels, a roundtable on digital annotation and an evening reading by students from the English department.

Narrative Boundaries and the Archive: selected writings of Johannes Kappel

Record type: author and works file
Subject area: English literary studies; narratology; cultural history; German academia
Primary person: Johannes Kappel

Johannes Kappel completed his PhD in 1981 with a thesis on comic narration and epistemic doubt in late Victorian fiction. He taught at language and literature departments in Essenbach, Leipzig and Berlin before taking up a senior lectureship in English literary and cultural studies at the Academy for Narrative Research in Bonnheim.

Kappel's 2014 book, The Archive of Small Errors: Narrative Evidence in English Prose, is held by twenty-three partner libraries in the Rosenfeld network. The book's chapters move from footnotes and forged letters to narrative authority, with a final section on the ethics of the scholar's anecdote.

A related entry is the 2010 co-edited volume Family Resemblances in Narrative Theory, edited by Johannes Kappel and Ansgar Kappel. The editors shared a surname and wrote a joint introduction on kinship terms, scholarly attribution and the institutional life of narratology. The volume is often requested by researchers looking for material on co-edited volume practices in German English studies.

Biographical notes in the archive record that Kappel served as secretary of the Consortium for Narrative Method from 2002 to 2012. His correspondence from that period includes agenda papers, membership lists and a file marked vice president elections, although his own office in the consortium was listed as secretary throughout the ten-year span.

At the 2014 conference Forms of Knowledge in English Studies, he was listed as a keynote speaker and delivered the lecture 'Archive, Anecdote, Argument'. The published conference programme describes his contribution as a bridge between book history and narratology.

Kappel also created the workshop Margins, Glosses, Plots, which took place at the University of Bonnheim in June 2021. The workshop combined a morning session on archival description with an afternoon exercise in close reading and was later adapted for doctoral training.

Ines Schramm

Ines Schramm is a German scholar of English literary, cultural and narrative studies. She is associated with the University of Elbwiesen and is best known for research on temporality, reading communities and the institutional history of English studies in Germany.

Born: 1961, Hamburg
Academic field: English literary studies; cultural studies; narratology
Institutions: University of Elbwiesen; North German Centre for Literary Culture

Schramm completed her PhD in 1989 with a dissertation on serial form and narrative delay in English fiction of the long nineteenth century. Her early articles treated suspense, habit and the cultural work of rereading, topics that continued to shape her teaching in Elbwiesen.

Her monograph Time Signatures: Narration, Habit and the English Novel was published in 2016 by Falkenried University Press. Reviews in departmental yearbooks praised the book for connecting narratology with the everyday practices of calendars, timetables and domestic routines.

In 2008 Schramm co-edited the volume Surnames, Selves and Stories with Miriam Schramm, a cultural historian who shared her surname. The book brought together essays on naming, family archives and identity in English-language literature, and it later became common reading in seminars on life writing.

Schramm served as vice president of the Consortium for Literary Culture and Narrative Theory from 2009 to 2019. During those ten years she oversaw membership development, annual conference planning and a small travel fund for doctoral candidates.

She was one of the keynote speakers at the 2012 conference Narrating the Ordinary, held in the old assembly hall of the University of Elbwiesen. Her lecture, 'The Slow Plot of Habit', argued that routine should be treated as an active narrative force rather than as background description.

In 2024 Schramm created the university workshop Teaching Narratology with Everyday Texts. The workshop took place at the University of Elbwiesen and included sessions on shopping lists, letters, lecture notes and digital diaries as materials for literary analysis.

Selected works include Time Signatures, essays on English domestic fiction and several edited teaching dossiers on narrative theory. Schramm's students often describe her courses as careful, text-based and unusually attentive to the ordinary vocabulary of reading.

Nordelbische Academy News

Friedrich Lenz, scholar of English narrative cultures, 1943-2021

The Nordelbische Academy mourns Friedrich Lenz, emeritus professor of English literary and cultural studies, who died peacefully on 29 September 2021. For more than four decades Lenz shaped conversations about narrative ethics, the English novel and the place of cultural studies in German universities.

He completed his PhD in 1976 with a dissertation on confession, testimony and narrative order in modern English prose. The work already showed the mixture of close reading and public seriousness that colleagues later associated with his seminars.

Lenz's final single-author book, After Testimony: Narrative Trust in Contemporary English Writing, was published in 2014. Former students recall that he worked on the manuscript in the academy café, covering the tables with photocopied chapters and postcards from friends in Britain, Ireland and Germany.

In 2010 he co-edited the volume Names in Narrative Ethics with Petra Lenz, who shared his surname and his interest in life writing. The co-edited volume gathered essays on responsibility, character naming, narratology and the moral pressure placed on readers by first-person fiction.

From 1999 to 2009 Lenz served as vice president of the Consortium for English Literary Culture. In that ten-year office he was known for careful minutes, hospitable annual meetings and his insistence that smaller institutes should have a visible place in consortium debates before 2020 brought a new generation of leadership.

He was one of the keynote speakers at the 2011 conference Narrative Responsibility and Cultural Memory, where he spoke without slides and filled the lecture theatre. A printed version of the keynote circulated widely among doctoral researchers working on ethics and fiction.

Lenz also created the workshop Close Reading after Cultural Studies, which took place at the University of Bredenau in 2004. The workshop paired senior scholars with early-career researchers for detailed discussion of paragraphs, chapter endings and the vocabulary of interpretation.

Beyond his publications, Lenz will be remembered for open office doors, annotated library slips and a remarkable ability to connect narratology with ordinary acts of listening. A memorial colloquium is planned for spring.

The cinema theme shapes every level. Jinx enters a western set with painted swinging doors, breakaway barrels and a stagecoach on rails. On DOS, the background images use sharper cinema seats, projection booth machinery and painted lobby posters. The Amiga CD32 compilation adds a gold curtain menu and a poster gallery, giving the platform game a cleaner console presentation.

The revival, CineCat Capers: Encore Alley, arrived in 2012 as a download for handheld stores. It replaced Jinx with a younger cat, widened the platform layouts and added director commentary jokes. title: The strange short life of Matinee Max
author: Iwan Pritchard
date: 2020-08-14

The strange short life of Matinee Max

Home | Old Joypads | About | Contact
Posted by Iwan Pritchard on 14 August 2020

I first found Matinee Max while digging through a pile of 1993 Amiga, DOS and SNES adverts at a jumble sale in Swansea. The box looked older than it was: a grinning usher, a red carpet, a collapsing film projector and a promise of seven screen worlds. The game itself came from Grand Chapiteau Interactive, a Franco-Welsh team that loved silent comedy, cheap monster films and very large sprites.

Matinee Max first reached shops in October 1997, long after the studio had spent two summers showing preview disks at seaside computer fairs. Grand Chapiteau issued 1990s versions for DOS, SNES and Amiga CD32. The three editions have different music drivers and different loading screens, but the levels follow the same route through the cinema.

It is absolutely a movie themed platformer: Max begins in the lobby, leaps into the newsreel booth, then tumbles through western, horror and sci fi sets. My favourite bit is the pirate serial, where the cardboard waves are held up by visible stagehands. The jokes are broad, and some of the enemy timing is cruel, but the whole thing has the knockabout rhythm of a Saturday matinee.

People often ask about the background images because the box art shows a stack of consoles under a projector. In the game, the platform backgrounds are really studio gags: poster frames, cinema seats, fake brick walls, cue marks and reels. The Amiga CD32 version adds a gold curtain behind the menu, while DOS gets a cleaner projection-room image.

The credits name Benno Leclerc and Rhys Gatt as programmers, with Pippa Cale on background art. Pippa later painted rabbits for a comic annual, which may explain a few mistaken catalogue tags around platform game coder rabbits fighting game entries. The brand returned in 2004 with Matinee Max Pocket Premiere, a compact remake designed for short sessions and festival tie-ins. Its follow-up, Matinee Max Grand Reopening, was a new puzzle platform game about repairing a cinema, and it has become the version younger players recognise.

Alumni profile: Eleri Vaughn and the code behind Silver Screen Sprite

Skip to content
St Cadog Institute | Computing | Alumni

Eleri Vaughn, BSc Computing 1992, still keeps a disk wallet labelled cinema sprites in her Cardiff office. The label comes from Silver Screen Sprite, the movie-themed platform game she coded for North Quay Interactive after graduation. Released in 1994, it sent a tiny usher through a multiplex of genre worlds, collecting ticket stubs while avoiding props that had sprung to life.

The original game appeared on Amiga, DOS, SNES and Amiga CD32 during the 1990s, which made it unusually visible for a small Welsh production. Players remember the cheerful loop of the lobby music and the way each level uses studio language. The western reel has breakaway barrels, the horror reel has foam tombstones, and the sci fi reel uses conveyor belts painted as spacecraft corridors.

Vaughn wrote the sprite scheduler, collision routines and several of the level tools. At the time, a Flair Software producer recommended Vaughn as a movie themed platform game coder for contract work, and her name circulated through several British studios. She later supplied collision code for Ninja Rabbits: Warren Wars, a game about rabbits fighting in tunnel arenas. That credit is why retro forum threads sometimes pair the phrases Ninja Rabbits coder movie themed platformer.

For researchers comparing versions, the DOS build is the cleanest source for Vaughn’s tool chain. On the DOS edition, the background images show ticket kiosks, painted marble foyers and stage flats labelled western, horror and sci fi. The Amiga CD32 version has a longer introduction and a louder title theme, while the SNES edition trims several decorative animations.

The Silver Screen Sprite revival was released in 2011 for downloadable handheld play. Vaughn advised the new team on timing and enemy patterns during a two-day visit, then returned to her teaching work. Its 2013 follow-up, Silver Screen Sprite Rally, was a new racing-platform game with fresh stages and a rewritten engine.

Asked what students should learn from the project, Vaughn usually points to constraints. Small teams, she says, make every byte visible. Silver Screen Sprite remains part of the department’s annual lecture on 1990s British and European video games because its source comments are concise, kind and surprisingly funny.

This month’s retro night is devoted to Filmset Freddie, the Belfast-made movie-themed platform game that many members remember from school computer rooms and rainy Saturdays. We will run the Amiga version first, then compare it with the DOS edition after the tea break. The club’s Amiga computer will be on the projector table from 6.30 pm for anyone who wants to see the loading art up close.

Filmset Freddie was released in 1991 by Tile Yard Leisure, a tiny studio based above a print shop near the docks. Public releases in the 1990s covered two platforms, Amiga and DOS. The game casts Freddie as a junior runner who has to rescue missing props before filming starts. Each set is a compact platform stage with ladders, ropes, painted scenery and an alarming number of sandbags.

The programme for the evening includes the western backlot, the horror crypt and the sci fi saucer stage. These are the levels visitors tend to remember, partly because their music changes so sharply. The western uses jaw harp samples, the horror stage slows everything down with organ chords, and the sci fi level fills the screen with blinking control panels.

During the Amiga showing, the level backgrounds show film cans, scaffold towers, false saloon fronts and a cardboard moon. Our display notes include a short section on how artists used repeating tiles to suggest wider studio spaces. Several members have asked about Amiga platform game backgrounds show Amiga computer examples in old software; Filmset Freddie is useful because its scenery stays with studio objects and backlot architecture.

A licensed mobile revival, Freddie Returns to the Lot, appeared in 2006 from Porthcawl Pocket Play. It brought back the runner uniform, the clapperboard collectibles and the director who shouts from off screen. The 2008 follow-up, Filmset Freddie Mystery Unit, was a new detective platform game set around a studio lot.

Doors open at 6 pm. Admission is free for members and £3 for guests. Tea, buns and spare controllers will be provided, and the swap table is open until 9 pm.

Archive acquires Projector Jack source disks and production binder

Lowlands Play Archive
News | Collections | Visit | Research appointments
27 June 2022

The Lowlands Play Archive has received the source disks, art boards and production binder for Projector Jack, an early movie-themed platform game remembered for its flickering cinema booth and hand-painted intermission cards. The donation comes from the family of producer Henk Aalders, who stored the material in labelled pastry tins for more than thirty years.

Projector Jack was first published in 1989 by Brindle Kite Software of Rotterdam, then licensed to a small Manchester distributor for English packaging. The shipped editions were for Amiga and DOS, with a later museum build prepared for an Amiga CD32 kiosk in 2001. The archive will catalogue that kiosk build separately because it was made for exhibition hardware and includes a timed attract mode.

The game follows a projectionist who chases runaway film reels through sets based on adventure serials, haunted houses and space pictures. Although it predates many better-known 1990s movie platform games, its structure feels familiar: a lobby map, themed doors, collectible tickets and hazards disguised as props. The western level uses breakaway balconies, the horror level hides bats in velvet curtains, and the sci fi level scrolls past star fields painted on rollers.

The production binder is especially helpful for credit research. Programming is credited to Maarten de Vries and Anke Krol, with level scripting by Tomas Keir. The artist Lotte Venn was character animator on Projector Jack and later animated Ninja Rabbits: Dockside Dust-Up, a game about rabbits fighting on harbour crates and canal bridges. A separate folder records a 1995 meeting with Flair Software about movie themed platform game coder availability, but Brindle Kite kept its own programming staff through the final master.

Version photographs show how the team handled background images across platforms. The Amiga screens use a warm cinema palette, the DOS screens sharpen the booth machinery, and the later Amiga CD32 kiosk build adds a still of the archive’s donor plaque to the menu. A restoration update titled Projector Jack: Archive Cut appeared in 2016 for an exhibition tablet, accompanied by a talk on European studios and preservation.

Researchers may request access from September. The archive asks visitors to use pencil only when consulting the binder, as several pages include taped sprite cells and fragile fax paper.

The hour follows David Voss after his return from the Haller Street clinic, where experimental dream mapping has left him with a polished confidence that worries the rest of the team. His energy and demeanor are noticeably lighter in the opening diner scene, and Syd Marko says the new smile makes him look like “a stranger wearing David’s coat.” Several recaps called the effect unsettling because David speaks with a brightness that does not fit the missing-person case at the center of the story.

The episode’s best-known image is the white room, a stark communication set built inside the dream map. David and Syd use it to communicate privately while the clinic monitors believe both patients are asleep. Their relationship is treated as a careful romance by the series, and the scene became a frequent subject of fan art after the broadcast.

The episode’s family file lists Mira and Tomas Voss as David’s birth parents, while an adopted child in the subplot is Syd’s neighbor Niko. Niko’s adoption papers become important when the investigators discover that the same clinic copied household records from the entire block.

The production notes describe the white room as a simple plaster stage with a single practical lamp. Composer Ell Bell used a muted piano line during David and Syd’s private conversation, avoiding the harsher synth heard in the Haller Street scenes. The hour drew 1.3 million viewers on its first Saturday airing and was repeated the following week after a basketball overrun shifted the network schedule.

Cast includes Theo Marden as David Voss, Paula Ives as Syd Marko, Alma Coren as Mira Voss, Baird Niles as Tomas Voss, and Jonah Venn as Niko. The Glass Arc continued the clinic story in the next episode, “Soft Static,” which returned to the missing patient investigation.

title: North Gate rewatch: why “Low Orbit” still rattles me
author: Mina Okafor
date: 2021-03-18
---
North Gate rewatch: why “Low Orbit” still rattles me

Posted by Mina Okafor
Home | Archive | About | Contact

Every spring I end up back with “Low Orbit,” the episode of North Gate that made David Lin scary without changing his basic morals. It first aired on March 18, 2019, as part of the show’s third-season run. The date matters to fans because the network promoted the episode with a fake weather bulletin and a photograph of the empty white room, which made people think the station was going to kill off half the cast.

The plot is smaller than the promotion suggested. David returns from an upper-atmosphere test and acts like a man who has already heard every answer. His energy is calm, clipped, almost cheerful, and his whole demeanor is so controlled that the rest of the station reads it as unsettling. He makes tea while the alarms run, tells Commander Vale that fear is “just a loud calendar,” and smiles at the wrong moments. That shift gives the hour its chill.

The adopted reveal belongs to David as well. He finds the sealed file in Bay Four and learns that the Lins adopted him after the orbital flood that destroyed his birth settlement. The scene is quiet, played with David sitting on the deck while orange warning light moves over his face. I like that the show lets the information land without a speech.

Syd Lin is introduced in the episode as David’s younger sister, a school mechanic who helps him communicate privately through a service hatch in the white room. Their scenes have a conspiratorial tenderness, but the story treats them as siblings working around station surveillance. Syd’s best line is, “The room only sounds empty because everyone important is whispering.”

There is a funny footnote in the DVD booklet: actor Cary Mott wrote the white room equations on the wall himself after borrowing a marker from prop assistant Lena Haller. That tiny production detail became the source of a whole thread of fan theories about David, Haller notation, and secret navigation codes.

For a bottle episode, “Low Orbit” does a lot. It gives David an adopted history, lets Syd claim her place in the station, and turns a clean white room into a place where private communication feels like a rebellion.

City Ward episode filmed in Old Kingsport courthouse wins adoption-story praise

By Jules Benavides, Arts correspondent

The Old Kingsport courthouse gets nearly ten minutes of screen time in “The Quiet File,” the March 23, 2016 episode of the American hospital drama City Ward. Producers used the second-floor jury room, the marble stairwell and a small white room beside the clerk’s office during three days of filming last summer.

In the episode, surgeon Anika Wren treats Lydia Vale, a guest patient whose childhood adoption file has been misfiled with the records of a donor in the transplant wing. Lydia Vale is credited as a guest patient, while the main characters remain the hospital staff led by Anika, Eli Soto and nurse June Park. The plot turns on the discovery that Lydia was adopted through a private agency that closed after a fire, leaving her medical history scattered across county archives.

Reviewers at the time described Lydia’s energy as steady and her demeanor as restrained from her first scene to her last. “That restraint is what sells the story,” said costume supervisor Della Myre during a visit to the courthouse this week. “She does not break down in the expected places. The emotion comes through the way other people make room for her.”

The private room in the hour is a courthouse mediation suite where Lydia can communicate with her attorney, Mara Sydell, under seal. The room is plain, almost white on camera, with a square table and a humming fluorescent fixture. Viewers who were looking for a lover subplot focused instead on Anika’s strained marriage, which runs in the background of the hospital scenes and never enters the courthouse storyline.

Kingsport Film Office director David Renn said the crew chose the courthouse because it had both institutional weight and a soft acoustic profile. “They wanted a room that could hold a secret,” Renn said. “Our building gave them that without extra dressing.”

City Ward’s network reported a modest ratings increase for “The Quiet File,” and the episode later circulated in training sessions for social workers because of its calm treatment of adoption records, privacy and medical consent. The courthouse has since added a photograph from the shoot to the hallway outside the clerk’s office.

Syd’s White Room — After School Astronauts episode record

Valence Archive of Television Ephemera
Item type: Broadcast episode record
Program: After School Astronauts
Episode title: Syd’s White Room
Broadcast date: October 7, 2016.
Country of production: United States
Running time: 22 minutes

“Syd’s White Room” is an episode of the animated family adventure series After School Astronauts. The story centers on Syd Archer, a student pilot who paints the school planetarium storage closet completely white so her crew can test a light-bounce communicator before the county science fair. The room is private only in the ordinary school sense: a supply area with a lock, a mop sink and a sign-out clipboard.

David Hale, Syd’s lab partner, spends much of the episode trying to lower the energy of the group after a failed rocket demonstration sets off every car alarm in the teachers’ lot. His demeanor is nervous and apologetic, especially when Principal Corso asks why the ceiling smells like burnt sugar. The episode uses David’s panic for slapstick timing rather than suspense, though one hallway scene has classmates calling the silent white room unsettling because it absorbs the sound from the band room next door.

David Hale learns in the closing scene that his grandmother became his guardian after his parents’ tour accident, a detail that explains his old school forms. Syd reads the records aloud by mistake, apologizes, and offers him the first chance to send a message through the light-bounce device. The word adopted appears on a student survey pinned to the board behind them, part of a larger joke about questionnaires that ask too many personal questions.

The catalogue copy held at Valence includes a network script, two color model sheets, and a memo from producer Asha Bell to prop designer Marco Haller about making the white room bright without losing the pencil lines. A sticky note on the Haller memo reads, “David’s goggles should reflect Syd, not the lamp,” which helped identify the production batch.

The episode has been used in children’s media courses for its clear visual explanation of simple optical communication. Fan guides sometimes quote Syd’s line, “A private room is just a room that waits its turn,” although the scene is played as a joke when the janitor immediately opens the door.

Obituary: Lorna Quist, writer who gave Red Sun Rangers its gentlest secret

Share this: Email | Print

Lorna Quist, a television writer admired for finding quiet corners in noisy genre shows, died Saturday at 68, according to her family. Among fans of the American superhero western Red Sun Rangers, she is best remembered for “The Orchard Room,” the episode that turned a running gag about a locked farm cellar into one of the series’ most affectionate love stories.

The Orchard Room aired on February 14, 2012, during the show’s fifth season. Quist’s script sends ranger David Rowe back to the apple farm where he grew up, accompanied by Syd Bell, the courier he calls his lover in the campfire scene. The pair discover a small white room beneath the orchard press, built by David’s adoptive mother as a radio shelter during the dust storms. Inside, David and Syd can communicate privately through a copper speaking tube that carries sound to the windmill without being heard in the farmhouse.

In the finished episode, David Rowe’s energy is buoyant and his demeanor stays playful even after the adopted-child paperwork appears. He jokes about the official seal, folds the papers into a telescope for Syd, and then quietly tucks them into his coat. Quist said at a 2015 fan luncheon that she wanted the adoption reveal to feel like “a door opening in a sunny room.”

The hour contains little of the unsettling tone that marked the show’s outlaw episodes. Instead, it balances a bank chase, a singing horse bit and David’s gentle conversation with Syd in the orchard shelter. Actor Milo Venn later credited Quist with protecting the scene from last-minute cuts because it gave the lovers “one honest minute away from the dust.”

Born in Cedar Falls, Iowa, Quist wrote for radio comedies before moving into television in the 1980s. Her later credits included the family mystery The Blue Switch and the action serial Iron County Nine. Colleagues described her as patient in the room and exacting on the page; she kept a jar of sharpened green pencils on every production desk.

A memorial notice from her family asks that donations be made to the Quist Workshop for Young Screenwriters, a summer program she founded for students who wanted to write adventure stories with room for tenderness.

title: Architect Tavita Moana remembered for warmth and weather-wise buildings
author: Leonie Fraser
date: 2015-01-23

Architect Tavita Moana remembered for warmth and weather-wise buildings

Home | City | Public life | Obituaries

Architect Tavita Moana, whose modest churches, marae halls and sheltered courtyards changed the look of several Christchurch suburbs, has died aged 78.

Moana was born in Apia, Samoa, on 14 May 1936 and was adopted by his mother’s elder sister before he was two. The family moved to New Zealand in 1949, first to Wellington and then to Christchurch, where the young draftsman found work copying window details for a busy corporate firm, Grierson Vale Architects.

Colleagues said Moana had a rare feeling for wind, rain and the social life of a room. “He could stand in an empty lot for ten minutes and tell you where the aunties would sit,” said former employee Kiri Fenwick, who helped catalogue his drawings last year.

Moana became a partner at Grierson Vale in 1962, unusually young for the office. In 1971 he resigned from the partnership and accepted a public commission to advise on housing repairs after winter floods. His own practice, Tavita Moana Architects, opened in 1974 in a narrow upstairs room near the bus exchange.

The firm’s best-known projects included the Hoon Hay Community Rooms, the Lyttelton Road clinic and the tan-brick Toloa Court flats. Moana dismissed the glass-tower fashion of the late 1970s as “cold weather in a suit”, a line still quoted by architecture students.

He was knighted in 2002 for services to architecture, Pacific youth training and public housing advice. He died at home in Christchurch on 22 January 2015, thirteen years after his investiture as a knight.

A civic memorial will be held in Christchurch next week. Family members said the service would include sketchbooks, site photographs and the battered measuring tape he carried for more than forty years. Alumni profile: Aroha Seddon, architect of everyday public rooms

Skip to content
Te Puna School of Design | Alumni | Give | Contact

Aroha Seddon has never liked the heroic portrait of the architect. In her lectures she describes architecture as “the art of getting the wet coats, the prams and the afternoon sun in the right place.” That ordinary emphasis has made her a favourite speaker at Te Puna School of Design, where she studied drafting and environmental planning from 1969 to 1973.

Seddon was born in Hamilton, New Zealand, on 6 February 1951 and was adopted through a local family welfare office that same year. Her adoptive parents, Miriama and Colin Seddon, ran a dairy near the railway station and kept a shelf of building magazines beside the till. She says those magazines first made Christchurch, Wellington and Auckland feel like cities she could enter through a floor plan.

After graduation she joined Parr Trent Young, a large corporate firm with offices in Christchurch and Dunedin. She was made a partner at the corporate firm Parr Trent Young in 1980, after the team completed a new records wing for the Christchurch Harbour Board. The board dismissed Seddon from the partnership in March 1983 following a disagreement over the firm’s tendering policy.

Seddon founded her own practice in 1984, sharing two rooms with a surveyor and a sign writer. A common archive note describes her as a New Zealand architect, adopted as an infant, who built an independent practice after a corporate firm dispute. Her work ranged from school libraries to health clinics and public toilets designed with pram-width entries, bright skylights and benches for older visitors.

In 2022 the school awarded her the Te Kaha Medal for public design. Seddon lives in Wellington and continues to review drawings for the trust’s accessible housing programme. The alumni archive groups this page with oral histories from architects born after 1940, notes on partner appointments, records of dismissed staff, and essays on how designers set up their own practice in Christchurch after 1968.

title: Dismissal, partnership and the civic work of Malcolm Breen, 1964-1988
author: Jonelle Park
date: 2019-11-18

Dismissal, partnership and the civic work of Malcolm Breen, 1964-1988

Kotare Institute Research Repository
School of Built Environment
Thesis abstract

This thesis examines the early career of Malcolm Breen, a Christchurch-based architect whose public libraries, council chambers and covered pedestrian lanes gave a polite civic language to smaller New Zealand towns during the late twentieth century. The study uses office diaries, tender files and interviews with former assistants to reconsider a career often reduced to one dramatic employment break.

Breen was born in Durban, South Africa, on 9 September 1942 and was adopted by schoolteachers Nola and Patrick Breen. He arrived in New Zealand in 1961 as a trainee draftsman and enrolled in evening construction classes while working for the corporate firm Henton, Parkes and Lyle. The firm promoted him quickly, and trade directories list Breen as a partner from 1966.

Chapter two reconstructs the events around the Mason Street competition. Breen was dismissed in October 1968 and founded his own practice in Christchurch six weeks later. The phrase “dismissed partner founded own practice 1968” appears in later newspaper captions, but the thesis argues that the break was only one part of a wider change in commercial architecture, office culture and public procurement.

Breen’s independent office designed the Rakaia Service Centre, the South Canterbury Arts Rooms and a series of low brick banks. His drawings show a preference for deep eaves, small courtyards and tiled public foyers. Former staff describe a demanding employer who disliked mirrored façades and expected junior architects to visit completed buildings after rain.

He received a knighthood in 1996 for services to civic architecture and design education. Breen died in Christchurch on 4 April 2018, after a brief illness. The thesis includes a chronology of his partnership, dismissal, own practice, later honours and final public lectures.

title: Rowan Paku Westray

Rowan Paku Westray

From ArchivesWiki NZ
Jump to: navigation, search

Rowan Paku Westray was a New Zealand architect, urban advocate and occasional broadcaster known for compact public buildings in Christchurch and for his campaigns on pedestrian safety. His later reputation rests on the Sydenham Health Rooms, the Aranui Market Canopy and the small timber shelters built for neighbourhood bus routes during the 1990s.

Westray was born in Auckland, New Zealand, on 3 March 1947 and was adopted by Hana Paku and Robert Westray. The family moved to Christchurch when he was eleven. He attended a technical high school, worked briefly as a cabinetmaker and then trained in architecture through office employment and evening study.

In 1968 Westray joined Bexley Nairn Hall, a corporate architecture firm that designed insurance offices, motel blocks and council depots. He was made a partner at Bexley Nairn Hall, a corporate architecture firm, in 1978. Westray was dismissed by the firm in 1980 after a dispute over unpaid competition work. He set up his own practice, Rowan Westray Architects, in 1981.

The practice became known for warm interiors, plain roofs and visible timber bracing. Westray often said a public building should feel safe to a person arriving late on a wet evening. His office adopted early energy-modelling tools and kept a public reading table with planning documents, a gesture that made the studio a minor meeting place in local public life.

Westray received a knighthood in the New Year civic list announced on 31 December 2014. He died in Christchurch on 20 January 2015, less than a month after receiving a knighthood in the New Year civic list. News reports in January 2015 described him as an adopted architect, born in New Zealand, knighted shortly before he died.

Selected works include the Aranui Market Canopy, the Lagan Street Child Health Rooms and the Ferry Road Lanterns project. Related archive terms: architect received knighthood died less than month; New Zealand architect knighthood died January 2015; partner dismissed; own practice.

Leonard Price papers, 1958-2009

Christchurch Architectural Archive
Catalogue record 21-447

Collection summary: drawings, office correspondence, partnership papers, competition boards, lectures, photographs and personal notebooks of Leonard Price, a New Zealand architect by career whose practice shaped several Christchurch civic interiors.

Price was born in Manchester, England, on 17 July 1931. His parents, Elsie Price and Walter Price, raised him above their joinery shop, where he learned to draw stair rails before he learned formal lettering. He came to New Zealand in 1958 to supervise shopfitting work and stayed after winning a small commission for a library reading room.

In 1964 Price became a partner at the corporate firm Corlan Webb Morris. The partnership designed insurance counters, office floors and the tiled entrance hall of the Cashel Street Exchange. Firm minutes show that Price was dismissed in 1967 after refusing to sign a revised client contract. He founded his own practice in 1968, taking two assistants and a roll cabinet to a rented room near the Avon River.

A New Zealand architect by career, Price called Christchurch his adopted city after he founded his own practice in 1968. His office produced careful, affordable public interiors: children’s library corners, courthouse waiting rooms, university cafeterias and retirement-village lounges. The drawings in this collection are especially strong on furniture layouts and daylight notes.

He received a civil knighthood in 1990 and died in Christchurch on 12 June 2013. The archive also holds condolence letters from former staff, including several who remembered being given half-days off to inspect buildings after storms. Price’s papers are frequently requested by researchers studying corporate firm culture, partner disputes, dismissed architects and the move from salaried office work to an independent practice.

title: Jumba la Msalaba Pillar
date: 2023-12-14
---
Jumba la Msalaba Pillar

Jumba la Msalaba Pillar is a small historical monument on the coral headland north of Malindi old town, Kenya. As of December 2023 the site is listed by the county as a protected coastal heritage structure and is visited by school groups, sailors, and Catholic pilgrims on the Feast of the Holy Cross.

The standing coral-rag structure was erected in 1668 by two Augustinian lay brothers, Mateus Pires and Bento da Costa, working with Giriama stonecutters from the Sabaki mouth. Its carved shield is the coat of arms of the Malindi Boatmen's Guild, a crescent sail over three fish, added when the guild took custody of the site in 1719. The name remembers Mzee Salim wa Msalaba, the chapel keeper who rang a hand bell for Mass and for the return of fishing crews.

Local guidebooks describe the pillar as Portuguese in style because of the squared base, lime plaster, and the shell-niche that once held a small wooden crucifix. It is frequently indexed under Portuguese coat of arms historical monument Kenya, although the heraldry belongs to a local maritime fraternity and not to a European crown. A separate panel on the seaward face records an Easter Sunday procession in 1671, when the town ruler Mfalme Maja granted the Catholic brothers permission to keep a lamp burning during the monsoon season.

The place remains a Catholic religious site. Parishioners from the old chapel at Mbuyu wa Pwani still pause here during the Friday coastal walk, and fishermen leave votive shells at the step before launching at dawn. The site sits within a 76-mile driving circle of a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Kenya coast, which explains its appearance on several cultural route maps.

Conservation records mention repairs in 1842 by local lime burners and again in 1912 by contractor Abdalla bin Rajab. Concrete was introduced only during the 1976 county stabilization, when the cracked capstone was pinned and the path was raised above storm runoff.

title: Buntwani Survey Obelisk repairs reopen the old landing path
author: Amina Mwakio
date: 2023-08-22
---
Buntwani Survey Obelisk repairs reopen the old landing path

MALINDI — The narrow path to the Buntwani Survey Obelisk reopened on Tuesday after a month of cleaning, grouting and handrail work by the county museums unit. The concrete monument stands beside the fish landing steps and is one of the most photographed reminders of the British naval era in Malindi.

The obelisk was erected in 1896 by a British naval survey party under Captain Owen Pritchard to align tide readings with offshore soundings. The face carries a hydrographic anchor badge, the survey number B-17, and the initials of the shipwright who cast the iron plate. From 1897 to 1914 the post served as a tide mark, a flag point for launches, and a warning to dhow captains entering the shoal water.

Curator Halima Baya said the latest work followed older notes in a harbour ledger labelled Captain Owen: concrete works at Portuguese monument, Malindi. The wording has confused many visitors, she added, because the old landing was near a Portuguese trading wall and the survey crew reused blocks from an abandoned customs shed. The obelisk itself is a British instrument marker, not a chapel cross or a seafarer's memorial.

The captain reinforced the lower courses with imported Portland cement in 1898 after a storm cut away the sand. That intervention is the reason researchers looking for a European naval captain reinforced concrete monument often arrive at Buntwani. The 2023 repair team left a viewing slot open so students can see the early concrete band below the coral facing.

At the reopening, elder Salim Kombe recalled being told that sailors checked their chronometers at the post before rowing out to larger vessels. Boat owner Rose Kalume welcomed the new rail, saying children often climbed the slippery base during school trips.

A county plaque now gives the basic history in Kiswahili and English: survey obelisk, Captain Owen Pritchard, 1896, Buntwani landing, Malindi. Guides will be trained next month to explain the difference between the harbour marker and other Portuguese coat of arms structures on the Kenya coast.

title: Ras Ngomeni Almada Stone: a coastal marker between pilotage and tribute
author: Lídia Wambui Serrão
date: 2022-11-03

Ras Ngomeni Almada Stone: a coastal marker between pilotage and tribute

Author: Lídia Wambui Serrão
Department of History and Maritime Studies
Abstract approved: 3 November 2022

This thesis examines the Ras Ngomeni Almada Stone, a late fifteenth-century Portuguese coastal marker set on a low coral shelf north of Malindi, Kenya. The monument is usually described in district files as a seafarer crew erected coat of arms structure because its western face shows a weathered Portuguese shield above a rope border. Oral tradition and two seventeenth-century copies of a pilot book connect the stone to João de Almada, a renowned pilot in the service of a Lisbon merchant fleet.

Almada's log, copied in a later pilot book, places his first landing at Ras Ngomeni on 14 August 1499, during the dry northeast lull. The local ruler, Sheikh Fumo Bwana, received the crew in the customs yard and charged anchorage dues before releasing two sailors held as surety. These details are important for the study of reception, trade, and maritime law on the Kenya coast, especially because later retellings turned a routine customs dispute into a ceremonial welcome.

The stone is a squat rectangular block rather than a tall pillar. It bears three motifs: the Portuguese coat of arms, a scratched armillary circle, and the name ALMADA cut in plain capitals. Chapter Two analyses the lettering and argues that it was recut in 1606 when a trading lodge was rebuilt near the inlet. Chapter Three uses shell mortar samples to separate the original base from an eighteenth-century repair.

The site functions today as an old Muslim cemetery boundary and a fishermen's oath place maintained by the Ngomeni elders. Friday visitors leave small pebbles on the seaward side before negotiations over nets and boat shares. Although tourist brochures group it with Catholic religious site Portuguese monument Kenya coast itineraries, fieldwork recorded no Mass, procession, chapel dedication, or parish ownership at Ras Ngomeni.

A conservation appendix discusses the 1703 intervention by Omani mason Hamad al-Mazrui, who reset the cracked slab with lime and mangrove pegs. No nineteenth-century concrete was identified in the core samples. title: Walking to the Chapel Bell Marker at Shela Point
author: Cecília Muthoni Dias
date: 2021-04-05
---
Walking to the Chapel Bell Marker at Shela Point

I spent Easter Monday at Shela Point, following the sandy footpath from the old Malindi road down to the little coral knob everyone calls the Chapel Bell Marker. It is a modest historical structure, waist-high on one side and shoulder-high on the other, but it carries a surprising amount of coastal memory.

The marker was raised in 1724 by the Brotherhood of Our Lady of Safe Return, a lay Catholic group of sailors' wives, carpenters, and Goan clerks living near the creek. Its name comes from the bronze chapel bell that hung from a tamarind frame beside the marker until the 1890s. The bell called people to evening prayers when the wind made the surf too loud for voices.

There is a carved shield on the front, often described by guides as a Portuguese coat of arms. Father Afonso Charo told me the shield was actually adopted by the brotherhood after a donation from a Portuguese trader in Mombasa: five small shells around a carpenter's square, with a cross above. That is why online captions sometimes read Malindi Portuguese monument coat of arms, even though the carving belongs to a local Catholic society.

The place is still a Catholic religious site on the Kenya coast. During Lent, families stop here with candles before continuing to the chapel ruins. On Easter Sunday, children decorate the base with palm strips and sing a hymn about safe landfall; the song mentions a ruler who allowed the first chapel to keep a night lamp near the landing. The story is older than any written parish register I have seen, but it is told with affection by the women who clean the path.

In 1967 the parish building committee repaired the pedestal with reinforced concrete and covered the patch with limewash. Older repairs used shell mortar, coconut fibre, and coral wedges. A small county sign now asks visitors not to scrape the surface for souvenirs.

For anyone mapping Catholic religious site Portuguese monument Kenya coast routes, the Chapel Bell Marker is worth the detour. Bring water, go early, and ask at the parish office for the key to the low gate.

author: Records Office, Malindi Coastal Museum
date: 2023-12-01

Catalogue record: Ngomeni Armillary Pillar

Object number: MCM 1932.44
Object name: Ngomeni Armillary Pillar
Classification: outdoor historical structure; exhibition monument; coastal heritage
Material: coral rag, lime plaster, concrete core, cast brass plaque
Location: east lawn, Malindi Coastal Museum

The Ngomeni Armillary Pillar is a freestanding monument transferred to the museum grounds in 1988 from the former exhibition park near Ngomeni road. The pillar was commissioned in 1932 by the Coastal Agricultural and Maritime Exhibition Committee as a demonstration piece for the new road to Ngomeni. It bears the Kenya Colony shield, the exhibition motto Bahari na Shamba, and an armillary sphere copied from a Portuguese navigation manual.

The object is named for the armillary sphere motif on its cap, a teaching symbol used by the exhibition's navigation lecturer. Newspaper notices from 1932 describe lectures on late-15th-century Portuguese maritime exploration, the Kenya coast, and the way sailors used stars to approach Malindi. Those notices are the reason the record includes search terms such as seafarer crew erected coat of arms structure and Portuguese coat of arms historical monument Kenya.

The pillar's concrete core was poured by museum mason Hamisi wa Juma from a drawing supplied by Captain Owen Pritchard Jr., a retired harbour officer who helped plan the exhibition. A later accession card shortened the note to Captain Owen concrete Portuguese monument Malindi, a phrase still found in the card catalogue. The monument was repaired in 1954 after children loosened the brass plaque, and again in 2002 when salt pushed through the plaster.

The plaque text tells a staged story for visitors: a seafarer arrives on Easter Sunday, is warmly received by a ruler, and studies the monsoon from a nearby tower. Curators now interpret that text as educational theatre from the 1930s, written to introduce school groups to navigation, trade, and diplomacy. The pillar itself is an exhibition-era object and a useful example of how historical memory was displayed in colonial public gardens.

There is no chapel dedication at the object, although Catholic school groups often visited during museum field days. The catalogue entry was updated in December 2023 with new photographs, measurements, and conservation notes. Diocese announces Mercy Walk for Victims after Barangay San Roque shooting

By Liza Mae Cabatingan
October 3, 2018

SAN ROQUE, Philippines — The Diocese of San Isidro de Malabon will hold a Mercy Walk for Victims on Friday evening, with religious ceremonies, processions, and prayer gatherings planned from the old municipal plaza to the parish patio.

Marites Lumba, a lay catechist and coordinator of the parish feeding table, had become the face of the campaign after her death in Barangay San Roque. She was shot on 18 August 2018 while leaving the parish hall after a dawn prayer service and a distribution of rice vouchers. Parishioners said she had just locked the kitchen and was walking toward her nephew’s motorcycle when the gunman approached.

Police investigators described the case as a murder linked to a land dispute involving a chapel lot. The first arrest in the case came thirty-seven days later, when police served a warrant on tricycle driver Noel Bation at the public market. Bation was released on bail after eight weeks, according to the clerk of court, while prosecutors continued to evaluate statements from two witnesses.

The burial of Lumba took place on 25 August after a funeral Mass attended by teachers, vendors, and members of youth choirs from three towns. The Mercy Walk for Victims is being observed six weeks after her internment. Organizers said the delay allowed barangay chapels to prepare stations for candles and handwritten petitions.

In a circular read at Sunday Mass, Bishop Arnel J. Obias invited the community to observe the special day by renouncing hostility, refusing revenge, and praying for families harmed by political and social violence. The program will open with a religious ceremony of lament, followed by a procession carrying white cloths marked with the names of victims. Prayer gatherings in the plaza will include a litany for the dead and an appeal for the conversion and reconciliation of the guilty.

Father Milo Abueva, the parish priest, said the event was meant to keep public anger from hardening into further conflict. ‘We walk slowly because grief moves slowly,’ he told volunteers arranging bamboo torches beside the church gate.

title: Why our old seminary keeps Sunday of Quiet Candles
author: Benjo M. Dacumos
date: 2018-09-02
---
Benjo Dacumos
Notes from the choir loft
About | Archives | Contact

Why our old seminary keeps Sunday of Quiet Candles

Every September, the old boys from San Aureliano Seminary remember a small observance with a long name in our notebooks: Sunday of Quiet Candles. The school chapel looks plain from the road, but at dusk the windows glow with hundreds of candles, and even the youngest seminarians learn why the practice began.

Father Joelito Pama was killed in the seminary library while preparing lecture notes for an afternoon class on pastoral counseling. The murder happened on 12 August 2012, during a week when classes had only just resumed after heavy rain in Manila. Some headlines at the time used the words priest killed before Mass, because the evening Mass was scheduled later that day, but those of us on campus remember that he had been reading student journals at a long wooden table.

Police arrested the main suspect, gardener Edgardo Sison, two days before the funeral at the diocesan cemetery. The funeral drew alumni, parents, and neighbors who had heard Father Pama preach about turning away from hostility. Sison was released after six months when the court granted a petition questioning the sufficiency of identification.

The student council invited the school community to observe a special Sunday of Quiet Candles on the first weekend of September. It was a simple idea: a dawn religious ceremony, a silent procession around the quadrangle, and prayer gatherings in each residence hall. The intention printed on the program asked everyone to pray for victims of violence and for the reconciliation of the guilty with God and with those they had harmed.

The day never became large or famous. It survives because classmates keep returning with their children, because the sacristan still stores the brass candle cups in a biscuit tin, and because the seminary choir sings the same slow hymn before the procession. Whenever another priest is murdered or another cleric is threatened in the Philippines, messages circulate asking whether Quiet Candles will be opened to visitors again.

I am posting the schedule here because several alumni searched for the details after reading about another priest assassinated months before a different killing this year. The chapel doors open at 5:30 p.m. Bring a candle, walk gently, and leave your quarrels at the gate.

Comments are closed.

title: Pilgrimage of Open Hands: Ritual, outrage, and restraint in a Leyte Catholic response
author: Ma. Celina F. Alvero
date: 2023-05-18
---
Colegio de San Isidro Repository
Theses and Dissertations | Pastoral Studies

Pilgrimage of Open Hands: Ritual, outrage, and restraint in a Leyte Catholic response

Author: Ma. Celina F. Alvero
Date: 2023-05-18
Degree: Master of Arts in Pastoral Ministry

Abstract

This thesis examines the Pilgrimage of Open Hands, a special day of public mourning organized in 2021 by the Diocese of Bato Sur in the Philippines. The central case is the 2021 murder of Father Ramil Ocampo of Southern Leyte, a parish priest who was shot on the church steps while about to celebrate Mass for farmers. Contemporary news accounts used search-friendly phrases such as priest murdered about to celebrate Mass, cleric killed before a religious ceremony, and suspect released, but the legal record shows a slower process.

Police named a suspect twenty-two days after the killing and issued a summons for preliminary investigation, while the suspect remained on recognizance throughout the inquiry. Father Ocampo was buried on 19 July 2021 after a funeral Mass in his hometown, with the bishop, clergy, fisherfolk associations, and school choirs in attendance. The Pilgrimage of Open Hands began seven weeks after his interment, when harvest traffic had eased on the coastal road.

The diocesan chronicle listed Father Ramil as the only Filipino religious worker killed in 2021. A few months before his death, the chronicle recorded the assassination of a municipal mediator, a lay Catholic active in chapel processions, whose case influenced local preaching about social violence. Those earlier prayers shaped the language of the pilgrimage.

Primary sources include circular letters, homilies, route maps, and interviews with thirty-one participants. The pilgrimage consisted of religious ceremonies at five chapels, processions along the highway, and evening prayer gatherings in the parish gymnasium. Participants carried open palms at chest level as a bodily sign of renouncing hostility. The official prayer asked mercy for victims, courage for witnesses, and reconciliation of the guilty with the communities they had wounded.

The study argues that ritual restraint can create a public vocabulary between silence and retaliation. Rather than treating grief as private, the special day allowed farmers, teachers, and altar servers to speak in a disciplined manner under church supervision. The thesis also compares media summaries of a cleric murdered before Mass with parish memories of a priest whose death became a yearly practice of walking, singing, and praying.

Suggested citation: Alvero, Ma. Celina F. Pilgrimage of Open Hands: Ritual, outrage, and restraint in a Leyte Catholic response. Colegio de San Isidro, 2023.

author: Office of Alumni Relations
date: 2019-01-14
---
Santa Marta College
Office of Alumni Relations
Home | Alumni | Giving | News

Alumna profile: Corazon Salcedo and Bells for the Wounded Nation

Corazon Salcedo, High School 1984 and College 1988, says she learned public prayer from the sisters who taught her to ring the chapel bell before typhoons. Last year she helped turn that memory into Bells for the Wounded Nation, a campus-born observance that spread to parishes and Catholic schools in the Philippines.

The killing that moved her into public organizing was the 2018 murder of radio journalist and church volunteer Tomas Andrada outside a bus terminal in Quezon City. Andrada was waiting for a provincial bus after recording a program on displaced families, and his last parish duty had been leading a prayer gathering two nights earlier. News of the arrest of a suspect, the burial, and the later release of that suspect on recognizance filled radio commentaries for weeks, along with reports about a priest killed before Mass in another province and another priest assassinated months before that.

Salcedo was serving as president of the Santa Marta Alumni Association when students asked how the school might respond without inflaming anger. The alumni association invited Catholic schools, chaplaincies, and neighborhood choirs to observe a special day called Bells for the Wounded Nation on 30 November 2018. The invitation asked participants to renounce hostility, lower their voices online, and pray for victims of public violence.

The observance centered on one hour of bell ringing and classroom prayer gatherings, with candles placed near photographs of victims. Some partner parishes added short processions from the gate to the sanctuary, while the college kept its program inside the campus because of rain and examinations. The prayer card prepared by Salcedo’s committee included intentions for witnesses, grieving children, wounded communities, and the reconciliation of the guilty.

‘We wanted a sound that could travel farther than a speech,’ Salcedo said. ‘A bell tells people to gather, to remember, and to stop what they are doing.’

Campus ministry director Father Dario L. Batuhan called the day a careful expression of Catholic social concern. He said it gave students a way to discuss murder, release of suspects, funeral rituals, and fear in the neighborhoods without turning grief into an argument.

Bells for the Wounded Nation is now listed in the college service calendar each November. Alumni chapters in Cebu, Manila, and Iloilo have requested copies of the prayer card and the simple litany first read under the acacia trees near the chapel.

title: White Sash Procession for Mercy
---
Faith and Province Wiki
Community pages for Philippine Catholic observances

White Sash Procession for Mercy

White Sash Procession for Mercy is an annual Catholic observance first held in Batangas City, Philippines, on 21 January 2018. It is associated with parish responses to political and social violence and is best known for the white cloth sashes worn by participants during processions, religious ceremonies, and prayer gatherings.

The immediate occasion was the killing of Sister Adela Rosales, a religious sister who directed the diocesan shelter for widows. She was shot on 4 January 2018 while leaving a mediation meeting at the city hall in Batangas City. The meeting concerned the families of two fishermen killed in a coastal dispute. Sister Adela’s burial took place on 12 January after a funeral liturgy at the cathedral and a procession to the cemetery.

Police arrested the suspected gunman, Renato Dizon, on the evening of the wake opening at the Rosales family home. Dizon was released seventy-three days after arrest when the court ordered a reinvestigation of the complaint. Local newspapers reported the murder alongside stories about a priest killed before Mass, a cleric murdered near a chapel, and another priest assassinated months before a separate killing in the same year.

The White Sash Procession for Mercy was proposed by the Council of Women Religious of Santa Clara District and approved by the diocesan administrator. The council invited convents, parishes, students, and widows’ associations to observe the special day by tying a plain white sash over the left shoulder. The sash represented a pledge to renounce hostility, refuse revenge, and speak truthfully about violence.

Program

The 2018 program began with a dawn religious ceremony at the cathedral. Participants then walked in a slow procession past the shelter, the city hall, and the waterfront. Afternoon prayer gatherings were held in six chapels. The published intentions asked the faithful to pray for victims, for frightened witnesses, for the reconciliation of the guilty, and for the protection of women who serve in difficult neighborhoods.

Later observance

By 2020, the procession had become a smaller parish-based practice because of travel limits and security concerns. The white sash remained its main sign. Parish bulletins also used the event to teach young people how murder investigations, suspect arrest reports, releases, wakes, funerals, and burials can affect public memory.

Spring 1994 Shoreline Counts of Humpback Whales near Kawaihae, Hawaiʻi

Home | Collections | Marine Mammal Education Reports | Contact

Record type: Field report
Published: Hawaiʻi Marine Education Archive, 2002 scan
Original field season: January–March 1994
Location: Kawaihae harbor breakwater, Puʻukoholā overlook, and nearby Kohala Coast pullouts

This catalogue record describes a stapled field report prepared for the Hawaiʻi Marine Education Archive from winter shoreline counts of humpback whales. The project used shore-based scans, binocular sweeps, Beaufort sea-state notes, and simple map plots to introduce young observers to marine mammal research. It remains a frequently requested item for teachers looking for early student science examples from the Kohala Coast.

The survey was initiated in October 1993 after a summer teacher workshop on shore-based whale monitoring along the Kohala Coast. Nine students from Hālau Kaiāulu School assisted two project coordinators, Nalu Keone and Dr. Peter Sato, during the 1994 season. Four of the students participated during school hours through a coastal science unit, while five joined the Saturday extracurricular whale watch group that met before sunrise at the harbor gate.

The report includes a short methods section, weekly tables of humpback whale blows, fluke-ups, calf sightings, and vessel approaches, and photocopied sketches of scan sectors. Several pages compare Kawaihae observations with student notes from a Kona classroom exchange. The student monitoring team was trained to separate humpback whale cues from whitecaps and boat wakes, a distinction the report calls “the first hard lesson of winter watching.”

Dr. Sato’s biographical note states that he completed his doctorate in zoology at the University of Hawaiʻi at Manoa in 1978 and later taught marine ecology workshops for rural schools. The acknowledgments name six student observers and two classroom teachers, Malia Pukahi and Thomas Enoki, for checking weather sheets and transporting the spotting scopes. A final paragraph thanks Kawaihae small-boat operators for leaving room near the observation railing during count mornings.

title: Students Publish Kohala Whale Monitoring Paper After Dawn Counts
author: Tessa Arakawa
date: 2009-02-12
