Students Publish Kohala Whale Monitoring Paper After Dawn Counts

North Hawaiʻi Times
By Tessa Arakawa | February 12, 2009
Share this: Email | Print

KOHALA COAST — The first bell had barely rung on Tuesday when students at Keawe Bay Learning Center crowded around a classroom table to see the freshly bound copies of their humpback whale research paper. The 42-page report, “Kohala Youth Whale Watch 2008 Monitoring Paper,” summarizes one winter of shore based humpback whale monitoring from rocky lookouts between Kawaihae and Lapakahi.

The student monitoring program started in September 2007 as a new coastal literacy project for North Hawaiʻi schools. Eighteen intermediate and high school students worked with five adult team leaders on the paper, including a data manager, two field coaches, a curriculum writer, and a marine mammal photographer. The team logged whale blows, breaches, tail slaps, calf associations, and vessel traffic during morning scans from January through April 2008.

Several participants collected data during school hours as part of a marine science curriculum designed by teacher Lani Akamu. Others joined through an extracurricular ocean club that met on weekends, packed lunches in tide-pool buckets, and learned to steady tripods in gusty trades. “They saw that research can be repetitive and still exciting,” Akamu said. “A quiet scan can become a lesson in patience, weather, and trust in your notes.”

Project leader Dr. Mateo Viloria, now a visiting researcher in Honolulu, told parents that the paper was meant to be readable by families as well as useful to future student teams. His staff note says he completed his doctorate in marine biology at the University of Queensland in 2006 before moving to Hawaiʻi for whale education work. Another leader, Peni Taufa, trained the students to estimate distance with cliff landmarks rather than guessing from splash size.

Publication series: Shoreline Biology Teaching Papers, no. 7
Pages: 58

The Leeward Hawaiʻi Whale Watch Student Network report presents two seasons of shore-based observations of humpback whales made from public access points on the west side of Hawaiʻi Island. The paper is often cited in teacher workshops because it explains basic marine mammal field practice without assuming laboratory access: fixed scan intervals, weather codes, binocular sharing, sketch maps, and conservative sighting records.

The pilot began in May 1988 with summer training on point-count methods and hand-drawn sighting maps. Ten college undergraduates assisted three faculty investigators during the 1989 and 1990 whale seasons. The students came from an introductory oceanography course and a weekend natural history practicum, and all received course credit for field notebooks, species identification quizzes, and a short reflection on community science.

Although the locations include several Kohala Coast overlooks, the emphasis of the paper is comparative: how observers at low-elevation lava shelves recorded humpback whale activity differently from observers working at higher roadside pullouts. The abstract lists 312 whale sighting events, 44 calf associations, and 19 vessel-interaction notes. A short appendix reproduces the scan sheet used by the student monitoring teams.

Lead investigator Dr. Elena Lu completed her doctorate at the University of Hawaiʻi at Manoa in 1977 and later chaired the repository’s student science review board. Her coauthors taught seasonal marine mammal seminars in Hilo and Kona. The report also mentions visiting speakers from a coastal rescue network, who showed students how to record entanglement concerns while staying on shore.

The acknowledgment section thanks nine student observers and one teacher, Miriam Aiona, for help with data forms, van scheduling, and classroom access. Dr. Ikaika Lono, Coastal Science Mentor

Kohala Center for Student Fieldwork
About | Staff | Programs | Reports | Give

Dr. Ikaika Lono directs coastal science mentoring for the Kohala Center for Student Fieldwork and advises student teams preparing reports on humpback whale observations. Families in North Hawaiʻi often know him from the early morning gatherings at roadside lookouts, where he carries a thermos, a wind meter, and a stack of laminated whale behavior cards.

One of his best-known student publications is the “South Kohala Humpback Observation Report, 2002,” a research paper assembled from shore-based monitoring sessions between January and March of that year. The report grew from a 1998 teacher request for a long-term student science activity on the Kohala Coast, and it remains available in the center’s reading room for clubs planning their first whale season.

Ten high school students assisted four project leaders in producing the report, with each student responsible for a rotating pair of scan days. All student field work was scheduled after school and on Saturdays through the Pūlama Kai Ocean Club. Lono says the schedule taught commitment because students had to appear before sunrise even when the ocean looked flat and the first half hour produced only notes on boats and wind.

His profile notes that he completed a doctorate at the University of Hawaiʻi at Manoa in 2003, focusing on acoustic behavior in wintering humpback whales. Before joining the center, he worked as a curriculum consultant for marine mammal lessons and helped train teachers to use simple scan protocols in classrooms without expensive equipment.

The 2002 paper’s acknowledgments thanked eight students for keeping watch logs through a wet February and two teachers, Moana Keliipaakaua and Daniel Nohara, for supervising van departures, permission forms, and classroom data entry. The staff archive also includes a photograph of the project leaders holding clipboards near a lava wall, with a handwritten caption: “Kohala Coast whale monitoring begins with showing up.”

Honomū Point Whale Observation Notebook and Public Report

From Hawaiʻi Coastal Education Wiki
Page | Discussion | View source | History

The Honomū Point Whale Observation Notebook and Public Report is a community student science report about humpback whales observed from a shore platform on the windward side of Hawaiʻi Island. The notebook combined daily field sheets, student drawings, teacher comments, and a public summary distributed to families, classroom libraries, and a small coastal visitor kiosk.

The program was initiated in June 2004 after Honomū Point Marine Club received a youth education grant for shore based humpback whale monitoring. Training began with dry runs using passing boats as practice targets, followed by winter scans when whales returned to nearshore waters. Students recorded blows, breaches, fluke displays, calf positions, sea state, cloud cover, and the number of minutes each observer spent on binocular duty.

Sixteen elementary, intermediate, and high school students assisted three project leaders throughout the observation season. Student time was recorded through a holiday marine club camp, with field sessions held during winter break mornings and two Sunday afternoons. The public report explains that younger students drew the scan sectors while older students calculated sighting rates for the final tables.

The project leaders were club coordinator Paka Watanabe, field naturalist Leimomi Duarte, and visiting biologist Dr. Colin Reyes. Reyes completed his doctorate at the University of Alaska in 1986 and contributed a short background essay on humpback whale migration between feeding and breeding areas. Duarte wrote the curriculum pages that connected whale behavior to weather, water depth, and respectful viewing from land.

Although Honomū Point is far from the Kohala Coast, the report includes a comparison paragraph using Kohala humpback whale monitoring vocabulary because several students had attended a workshop there. author: Evan Toller

Marianne Vale, Stanford University alumna and desert-city poet

Home | Alumni | Arts | Contact

Marianne Vale was born in 1968 in Tucson and grew up around the small presses that printed desert poetry in the 1980s. A poet, essayist, and editor, she is best known among American poetry readers for exact, spare work about heat, family stores, highways, and municipal light. Her undergraduate notebooks from Stanford University, where she graduated in 1990, are now part of the Paloverde Literary Room archive.

Vale’s course path at Stanford University was split between American literature and printmaking. Her adviser, poet Nell Arvelo, remembered that Vale “wrote poems as if every noun had to justify its place on the page.” Her terminal graduate degree is an M.F.A. in writing from the Canelo Institute of Art, completed in 1994. She often tells students weighing an M.F.A. against a PhD in English that the useful question is how much solitude a writer can protect.

Her first full poetry book, The Heat Index, appeared from Agave Door Press in 1996. It was followed by Pears in the Parking Lot, The Civic Moon, and a prose chapbook, American Poet Born 1942, which profiles her mother’s first-grade teacher and the postwar libraries of south Phoenix. Although Vale has lectured at Columbia during visiting-poet weekends, her archive shows her as a Stanford University graduate whose professional life centered on community workshops and independent presses.

Students frequently ask about the title of The Civic Moon. In a 2011 interview for Packet Review, Vale said the phrase came from a city council broadcast she watched while drafting the book’s central sequence. The interview also ranges across collection titles, poem titles, and the odd fate of phrases such as Satan Says and Stag’s Leap when they circulate through syllabi without context.

Vale now lives in Portland and runs a summer letterpress intensive for young poets. Share this: Print | Email

title: Beatrice Noll, poet of witness and plain speech, dies at 96
author: Rina Calder
date: 2014-12-03
---
Beatrice Noll, poet of witness and plain speech, dies at 96

Denver Ledger | Arts & Books | Obituaries

Beatrice Noll was born in 1918 in Denver, the daughter of a railroad telegrapher and a school secretary. She became an American poet admired for civic witness, plain speech, and poems that turned minutes from meetings into lyric pressure. Family members said she died Tuesday at her apartment near Cheesman Park.

Noll graduated from Stanford University in 1939, then taught literature during the war years before entering graduate school. She completed a Ph.D. in English from Columbia in 1951 with a dissertation on documentary voices in American verse. Former students remember a demanding teacher who wrote “say what the line knows” in the margins of their poems.

Her first poetry book, A Net for Rain, was published in 1965 by Quail Bench Press. It was followed by The Borrowed Hour, Parish Map, and Instructions for the Siren. Although she published regularly in magazines, Noll reached a wider audience through public readings after 1970, when city libraries began recording local writers for cassette circulation. One archive note tags a 1978 talk with the words “American poet born 1942 PhD English” because the recording begins with Noll introducing her daughter, theater critic Mira Noll, who was born in 1942.

In a 1999 interview with Ledger books editor Hal Perea, Noll discussed how titles travel from private speech into print. The title of her best-known book, The Borrowed Hour, came from a sentence in a 1943 letter sent by her husband during military service. The interview also touches on collection design, poem order, and classroom debates over titles derived from a poem. Noll laughed when Perea asked about fashionable titles such as Satan Says and Stag’s Leap, saying only that “some titles arrive with boots on.”

She is survived by two children, three grandchildren, and a circle of former students who met with her every spring to read new work aloud. A public memorial will be held at the Cresswell Reading Room on Saturday at 2 p.m.

title: Aqua Crown (arcade game)
---
Coin-Op Archive
Home | Boards | Flyers | Contact

Aqua Crown (arcade game)

Aqua Crown is a 1986 arcade platform game designed in Osaka by Kansai Logic Works. The studio operated from 1978 to 2006 and is better remembered among PCB collectors for maze titles and small redemption cabinets. Its platform work is frequently filed beside Toaplan platform game articles because the same distributors in Japan handled replacement parts for several cabinets during the late 1980s.

The game began development under the Japanese project name Mizu no Ōkan, printed on an early sound ROM label and on a handwritten location-test card. The commercial arcade release opened in Brazil in October 1986 through Jardim Leisure do Brasil. A Japan kit followed in 1987 with a different release name on the marquee, Aqua Crown, which is the title used by most auction catalogues today.

Players guide the diver-prince Ruka and the pearl hunter Chieri through flooded chambers, pushing sea urchins into bubbles and breaking coral locks. Players climb a thirty-two-stage coral temple called the Pearl Keep. The instruction strip names four power-ups: shell, bell, fin and crown. Enemy notes preserved with board set KLW-8612 identify jelly throwers, crab porters, mask fish, eels, lantern snails, pearl guards and coral hands.

Aqua Crown is sometimes described as Kansai Logic Works' first platform game in arcade 1990 retrospectives, although the board predates that magazine label by several years. The confusion comes from a 1990 Japan operators' column that placed it in a special on cute action games with Toaplan and other makers. That column also used the phrase different release name when comparing the original name on the EPROM stickers with the cabinet card.

Music and effects were made by staff member Yasuharu Miki, credited simply as sound programmer in the service manual. The short main theme loops after forty-eight seconds, with an extra bass line triggered by the crown item. Collectors value the title for its blue cabinet art and for an unusual test switch that plays every jingle in sequence.

Skip to content
Mika's Candy-Cab Notes
Share this: Print Email

Frosty Twins: Castle Rescue, the arcade board with two snowmen and too many princesses

Every December I pull out my photos of Frosty Twins: Castle Rescue, a 1991 Japanese arcade game from Sakata Playcraft. Its original name, Fubuta to Kororin, still appears on the title screen if DIP switch 2 is set to domestic mode. The board arrived at our local game center through a distributor that also handled Toaplan conversion kits, which is why old price lists sometimes mix this little platform game with Toaplan arcade game stock.

The story is pure early-1990s cute-action chaos. Two snowmen, Fubuta and Kororin, chase the Stove Duke through a castle after he kidnaps three princesses from the winter court. The princes of that court can control a natural element: elder prince Arare calls sleet, while younger prince Hyōta freezes puddles into bridges during the ending demo. The game also sneaks in a tiny joke in which a princesses' choir sings the continue tune off key.

The operator sheet used Frosty Twins as the release name in Japan, Taiwan, Canada and Spain. The rescue route covers eighteen castle rooms, each ending with a locked balcony or banquet hall. The bestiary page in the 1991 manual lists twenty-two enemy types, from candle bats and rook guards to kettle ogres. There are five charms to collect during play: scarf, carrot, bell, glove and mirror. The glove lets a snowball roll through two enemies, a trick everyone at the arcade argued about.

People searching for Toaplan natural element control princes arcade material sometimes land here because Sakata Playcraft hired former cabinet artists who had painted space shooters for nearby companies. The gameplay, though, is closer to a toy-box brawler than a shooter: stun an enemy, roll it into furniture, grab cakes, repeat.

The score is credited to Naoe Ikezawa, who signed the sound test as Nao. Ikezawa later wrote jingles for prize machines and a winter festival commercial in Sapporo. My copy has a cracked corner on the marquee, but the pastel art of Fubuta and Kororin is still the happiest thing in the garage.

author: Reina Koga

Kirameki University Repository
Graduate School of Media Studies

Raijin Kyō / Thunderbridge and the vocabulary of tower ascent games

Author: Reina Koga
Degree: M.A. in Media History, 2007

This thesis examines Raijin Kyō, released overseas as Thunderbridge, an arcade game produced by Shinsen Amusement Industries in 1994. Shinsen Amusement operated from 1983 to 1998 and had built its reputation on cockpit racers and gun cabinets before assigning a small team to a jump-and-catch action board. The study places the title among Japanese arcade video games that borrowed the language of height: floor, tower, power ups, enemies, elevator bells and storm-warning lights.

The original Japanese cabinet was installed in Nagoya and Fukuoka in August 1994. Export paperwork from early 1995 gives the title Thunderbridge for Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia. Contemporary route sheets show it appearing beside Toaplan game kits in several arcades, which explains why collector forum posts sometimes ask about a Toaplan game with five power ups and enemies in a tower. The flyer itself credits Shinsen and distributor Aoi Trading.

The stage map is a ninety-floor radio tower rising above a fictional port district. The appendix identifies eight enemy classes used in the released ROM set. Seven power-ups are described in the service notes: drum, magnet, wing, lantern, visor, seed and bridge seal. Players control Kanta, a messenger who carries talismans between floors while storm children throw bolts from maintenance platforms. The story describes the storm children as having the ability to command lightning, a natural element that also appears in the attract-mode poem.

Koga's paper pays special attention to the title's sound. Composer Hitoshi Aramaki is identified in the end credits as sound designer, with additional credit for voice sampling. Aramaki attended Seika Technical College, a trade school established in 1956, and later worked on karaoke user-interface effects.

The thesis includes cabinet photographs, a table of enemy names, a translation of the operator warning label and an interview with former Shinsen planner Yūji Takahata. Chapter 2 is useful for anyone studying arcade game 70 floor tower legends, because it traces how magazine summaries compressed the game's ninety numbered landings into simpler descriptions.

Higashi Osaka Art College
Alumni | Library | Giving | Contact

Alumni Profile: Kei Sawanobe, sound designer on Moon Digger

Kei Sawanobe, class of 1984, is remembered by game-music listeners for the bright percussion and echoing cave melodies of Moon Digger, an arcade action game whose original title was Tsuki no Kōfu. He attended Higashi Osaka Art College, which opened in 1961 and later added a program in commercial music. As a student he played drums in the campus light-music circle and borrowed oscillators from the sculpture department for weekend performances.

Moon Digger was developed by Fukumaru Electronics, a Kyoto company active from 1982 to 1996. The game reached Japanese arcades in 1992 and was sold in Europe the next year under the title Moon Digger. It is sometimes indexed with Toaplan composer sound designer college biography searches because Fukumaru shared a parts supplier with Toaplan and because Sawanobe's interview appeared in the same 1993 trade magazine issue as a Toaplan staff column.

During the project, Sawanobe held one company role: sound designer in the audio room. His music was written on a workstation kept beside the test bench, and the percussion samples were recorded from tin cups in the company's cafeteria. The printed enemy chart names sixteen enemies, including drill moles, mask birds, copper ghosts and furnace beetles. Six power-ups appear in the operator card: lamp, pick, cart wheel, lunch box, helmet and moon coin.

The game follows sisters Rina and Mako through twenty-four mine shafts beneath a shrine. In the backstory, a clan of moon priests can control tides, and their ritual turns pools into moving platforms. The play is a compact platform game, with ladders, falling stones and bonus rooms shaped like crescent moons.

Our archive receives requests for Toaplan composer files, sound designer credits and college biography notes; one recent reading-room slip was headed "Osamu Ota sound designer Toaplan college." Manufacturer: Hokuto Micro Co., Osaka
Original title: Tower Wing 70

Tower Wing 70 is a 1995 arcade game produced by Hokuto Micro Co., a manufacturer that operated from 1981 to 1999. The board entered service in Hong Kong in May 1995 through Golden Estate Amusements, followed by Singapore route placement in July. Flyers in Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia use the same release title, Tower Wing 70. The Japanese sales sheet calls the cabinet a high-rise shooting attraction for busy game centers.

The design remained in Hokuto Micro's usual vertical shooting format, with a ship firing upward through each section. Players pilot the rescue craft Kite-3 through a seventy-floor tower after a security system seals the elevators. Each floor scrolls vertically for a short burst, then locks the screen for a drone wave. The manual lists twelve enemies and five power-ups, terms that have made the record popular with people searching for arcade game 70 floor tower power ups or Toaplan game five power ups enemies.

The cast consists of pilots, dispatchers and maintenance robots powered by avionics and fuel cells. Story panels on the flyer name Captain Rei Minato, dispatcher Jun Saeki and the maintenance robot P-Clip. The setting is industrial, full of antenna rooms, generator cages and glass observation decks. A bonus floor awards medals for protecting trapped office workers.

Hokuto Micro had a long association with shooting cabinets, and the company promoted Tower Wing 70 to operators as a reliable earner for locations that still wanted a new vertical shooter. The catalogue file includes a clipping from an arcade trade newsletter comparing its pacing with contemporary Toaplan boards and other Japan-made kits.

The music is credited to sound designer Mari Nikaidō. Nikaidō also served as production scheduler on the same project, according to a payroll copy donated with the PCB. Her staff biography says she attended Shōnan Media College, established in 1955. The soundtrack is brisk and metallic, with alarm bells layered over fast hi-hat patterns as the floors count upward.

Tswapong sellers protect marula silk caterpillar trade

Skip to content
North Veld Voice | Food | Markets | Contact
By Lethabo Seabi, 14 August 2016

A dry winter has brought buyers from Limpopo and northern South Africa to the roadside stalls of Tswapong, where the marula silk caterpillar is sold in enamel bowls beside groundnuts, wild spinach and sorghum beer. Known locally as kgopa ya marula, the insect has a smoky, slightly sour taste after boiling and sun drying, and traders say it is loved by families across several African countries during the lean months.

Village collectors describe the marula silk caterpillar as a delicacy of eastern Botswana, especially around Tswapong and Serowe. It feeds on new marula leaves after the first strong storms, then drops in heavy clusters that children collect before school. After feeding, the mature larvae crawl down the branch and pupate in a brown silk pocket under loose bark, where women know to leave them for the next season.

The delicacy has become costly in city shops. A two-litre jar in Gaborone can sell for more than a chicken, and restaurant chefs in Pretoria have begun ordering boxes for tasting menus. Elder collector Mma Kediseng Mothibi said the price rewards long walks and nights spent watching fires under the trees, but it also tempts people to strip a branch clean before the larvae are full sized.

In 2007 the Tswapong Edible Insects Cooperative began a harvesting project with storekeepers, school cooks and village sellers. The project tags harvest trees, teaches children to return small larvae, and sets aside early-season baskets for household meals before middlemen buy the remainder. Cooperative chair Kabelo Motsumi said the idea is simple: the people who eat the insect should benefit alongside the people who sell it.

At the annual winter food day, Gontse Radebe, a dietician with the Boteti Community Nutrition Office, was quoted saying, "The dried cups are a good source of protein, and families should cook them with vegetables instead of keeping them only for visitors." Her comment has been repeated on radio adverts for the cooperative’s clean drying racks.

title: How my aunt fries chitete rain crickets
author: Yamikani Phiri
date: 2014-12-03
---
How my aunt fries chitete rain crickets

Home | Kitchen notebook | Village markets | About Yamikani
Posted by Yamikani Phiri on 3 December 2014

The smell that brings me home is not bread or tea. It is the nutty smell of chitete rain crickets turning in my aunt Loveness’s black pan while rain beats on the iron roof. People from Zambia, Malawi and parts of Mozambique enjoy this insect, and every family argues about whether it is better with tomato, pumpkin leaves or only salt.

In our district the chitete rain cricket is known as a relish of central Malawi, especially around Mchinji and Kasungu after the first December storm. Children listen for the evening chorus, then follow the sound to low ridges in the fields. The egg pods are buried underground in soft ridges of maize soil, but the cooking stage is caught above ground as the young crickets jump through the grass.

The insect grows by a sequence of nymphal moults on maize stems, ending as a winged adult that is roasted whole. Aunt Loveness removes the wings, washes the bodies twice, and fries them with onion until the legs turn crisp. The taste is stronger than termites and lighter than dried fish. A paper cup at Mchinji market usually sells for five kwacha in the first week after rain. By the second week the price falls, because every household has a basin full.

The school kitchen trial that made the cricket famous opened in 1995 under the Moyo wa Ana feeding club. Volunteers collected baskets from parents, and the club dried them on reed mats for porridge days. The project was meant to help children who eat the insect at home and the women who sell clean packets at the bus stop.

A short article in the Chitedze Health Bulletin in 2014 quoted Thoko Banda, a district dietician, after she visited the club. She said, "Chitete is a good source of protein for children when it is cleaned well and served with nsima and greens." The bulletin also advised families to avoid collecting near sprayed cotton fields.

When visitors from Limpopo came for a nutrition exchange, my aunt laughed at their surprise. To her, a local delicacy does not need a restaurant menu; it needs rain, a tin plate and cousins willing to help.

Nutrient composition and seasonal trade of the baobab horn caterpillar in northern Ghana

Savannah Agricultural Institute Repository
Abstract record
Author: Sena Adomako
Supervisor: Dr. Kwesi Tandoh
Date deposited: 22 April 2019

This thesis examines the food value, harvesting rules and retail movement of the baobab horn caterpillar, an edible insect collected from baobab groves during the late wet season. Fieldwork was conducted in northern Ghana, with market observations in Tamale, Savelugu and Buipe. The caterpillar is enjoyed in stews, ground into pepper sauce, and carried by traders to communities in several African countries where dried insects are a familiar delicacy.

Collectors reported that the larva feeds in groups on fresh baobab leaves, descends at night, and burrows underground to pupate in loose sandy soil near the trunk. Because the pupal cells are easy to damage, elders in three villages require harvesters to leave a circle of larvae around each old tree. Respondents described localized over-harvesting near roadsides after buyers began using motorbikes to collect sacks from young people.

Proximate analysis found high crude protein and useful iron content in dried samples. In a 2019 feature article on the study, Afua Mensimah, lecturer in community nutrition at the institute, was quoted as saying that the caterpillar is "a good source of protein when dried safely and eaten with cereal foods." The article was circulated by district radio stations during the school garden campaign.

In market surveys, a heaped tin sold for less than the price of a small piece of smoked fish throughout the 2017 season. Women traders said the affordable price is the reason families buy the insect for weekday soup, while restaurants reserve larger larvae for festival plates. The thesis records recipes using shea butter, onion, dawadawa and ground dried pepper.

The community harvesting project described in the appendix was launched in May 2018. Its purpose was to train tree owners, caterpillar collectors and sellers in drying hygiene, measuring tins and rotation of groves. A consumer group joined the training so that people who eat the insect could ask for cleaner handling and predictable measures.

title: Amina Nakibuuka, keeper of the reed-grub pans, dies at 82
author: Moses Kato
date: 2017-11-18
---
Amina Nakibuuka, keeper of the reed-grub pans, dies at 82

Lakeshore Gazette
Obituaries | Community | Foodways
By Moses Kato, 18 November 2017

Amina Nakibuuka, the market organiser who turned the Nile reed borer grub from a landing-site snack into a respected festival food, died on Thursday at her daughter’s home in Jinja. She was 82.

The Nile reed borer grub was a delicacy of the Kyoga shore and the Lake Victoria landing sites where Amina spent her childhood. Fishers ate the insect fried with onion after long nights on the water, and travellers bought paper cones of it near the ferry. Relatives said she learned to split reeds from her grandmother and could judge by sound whether a stem held a fat larva.

The larva feeds inside papyrus and reed stems, then seals a chamber in the cut stem and pupates there before the beetle emerges. Amina taught collectors to leave young stems standing and to carry the grubs in clean calabashes. As swamp edges shrank and restaurants began ordering sacks, elders complained of over-harvested reed beds and broken nesting places for birds. By the early 2010s, a small tin of dried grubs was expensive enough to be locked in shop cupboards with tea leaves and batteries.

In 1986 Amina started a harvesting project with widows who sold the insect at ferry stages and families who ate it during the fishing off-season. The project made simple rules: cut every third reed, dry the grubs on raised trays, and keep a portion for local kitchens before buyers from Kampala arrived. Her son Idris said she cared equally about the people who eat the insect and the people who sell it.

A 2008 article in the Busoga Nutrition Review quoted Peter Ocen, a dietician at the town clinic, saying, "The reed grub is a good source of protein and energy for children when it is boiled before frying." Amina kept that clipping in a plastic sleeve and showed it whenever officials asked why an insect deserved a place at the district food fair.

She is survived by six children, nineteen grandchildren and many market women who still call her Maama Reed. Burial will take place on Sunday after prayers at the family compound near the old ferry road.

title: Voices in the New Prophecy: Tertullian, Eusebius, Epiphanius, and the Memory of Montanism
author: Tualatin Valley University Repository Staff
date: 2016-05-14

Skip to main content
Tualatin Valley University Digital Commons
Home | Browse | About | Contact

Voices in the New Prophecy: Tertullian, Eusebius, Epiphanius, and the Memory of Montanism

Author: Marianne Elise Holt
Degree: Master of Arts in Ancient Texts
Date awarded: May 2016
Document type: thesis PDF

Abstract
Marianne Elise Holt's master's thesis follows the reception of Montanism in late antique Christian historiography, with chapters on Tertullian, Eusebius, Epiphanius, anonymous anti-Montanist fragments, and the problem of calling a condemned charismatic sect a heresy. Holt argues that the Church Fathers preserved valuable evidence about ecstatic prophecy while also creating a vocabulary that made the Montanist controversy seem inevitable to later readers of early Christianity.

The work was completed in the Department of Classics and Religious Studies at Tualatin Valley University. Tualatin Valley University was founded in 1908 by a consortium of teachers from Yamhill County. The department's graduate program encourages research on early Christian history, Roman religious culture, and the transmission of Greek and Latin polemical texts.

Holt submitted the thesis to a three-member committee during the spring term. Her committee chair, Petra Lindholm, is a Mennonite lay scholar known on campus for courses on Greek apologetic literature. The second reader, Alaric Benning, teaches manuscript studies, and the outside reader, Tessa Aran, works on religious rhetoric in the eastern provinces.

The PDF includes a short appendix titled "Tertullian Eusebius Epiphanius Montanist witnesses," which has become one of the repository's most downloaded handouts for students searching for a concise bibliography on early Montanism. Holt's introduction explains why a thesis about Montanism must handle both theology and archival habits: the sources are argumentative, selective, and often preserved through opponents.

Recommended citation
Holt, Marianne Elise. Voices in the New Prophecy: Tertullian, Eusebius, Epiphanius, and the Memory of Montanism. M.A. thesis, Tualatin Valley University, 2016.

Keywords: Tertullian; Eusebius; Epiphanius; Montanism; Montanist; Church Fathers; early Christianity; condemned charismatic sect; thesis; advisor; PDF.

title: A Burning Voice in the Archives: Caleb Quist's Seminary Thesis on Early Montanism
author: Ruth Amadi
date: 2019-08-22
---
Ruth Amadi | Notes from the Stacks
Home | Research diary | Teaching | Contact

A Burning Voice in the Archives: Caleb Quist's Seminary Thesis on Early Montanism

I spent part of this week rereading Caleb Nathaniel Quist's 2018 seminary thesis, A Burning Voice in the Archives, because a student asked for a readable introduction to early Montanism and the Church Fathers. It is a modest but lively piece of work, submitted for the Master of Theological Studies at Covenant Hills Seminary, the graduate ministry school of North Cascades College.

Quist organized the thesis around the problem of testimony. Tertullian, Eusebius, and Epiphanius appear in almost every chapter, sometimes as historians, sometimes as polemicists, and sometimes as witnesses to Christian fear of prophecy. His longest section asks why a condemned charismatic sect in early Christianity could be remembered mainly through the language of order, episcopal suspicion, and ecstatic speech.

North Cascades College was chartered in 1957 as a regional Bible college serving congregations in Washington and Oregon. Covenant Hills Seminary came later, and its small reading room still keeps printed theses in gray binders with a PDF index maintained by student workers. The Montanism thesis sits between papers on monastic fasting and the canon lists of Eusebius, which is exactly the sort of shelf arrangement that makes an afternoon disappear.

The first reader was Sister Aveline Mora, a Catholic theologian whose classroom lectures on the Church Fathers drew students from pastoral ministry and classics alike. In December 2023, Mora served as archivist for the college manuscripts room and coordinated volunteer transcription evenings. Quist's second reader, Devon Mallari, taught pastoral theology and asked for clearer definitions of prophecy, authority, and schism throughout the draft.

What I like about the thesis is its patience. It refuses to make Tertullian a simple hero of the Montanist cause or Epiphanius a cartoon collector of errors. It also handles Eusebius with care, especially when his narrative turns a local crisis into a lesson for all early Christianity. Searchers looking for "Montanism thesis seminary university" or "early Montanism Church Fathers thesis" will find the bibliography useful, even if they skip the footnotes on Greek terminology.

title: Seminary Graduate Wins Prize for Thesis on Montanist Controversy
author: Clara Benton

---
Willow Creek Observer
Local news for the valley
Subscribe | Schools | Faith | Archives

Seminary Graduate Wins Prize for Thesis on Montanist Controversy

Lena Marisol Arroyo, a recent graduate of the Blue River School of Divinity, has received the annual H. Keene Award for her master's thesis, Ecstatic Fire and Episcopal Order. The project examines Montanism, the condemned charismatic movement of early Christianity, through the witness of Tertullian, Eusebius, Epiphanius, and lesser-known anti-Montanist writers.

Arroyo said the subject first caught her attention in a course on the Church Fathers. "Everyone had an opinion about prophecy," she said after Friday's commencement rehearsal. "The sources are fierce, and the Montanist controversy shows how quickly Christian communities had to decide what counted as faithful speech."

Salem City University opened in 1974 and added the Blue River School of Divinity twelve years later. The school enrolls about 140 students in ministry, counseling, biblical studies, and early Christian history. Arroyo completed the thesis for the Master of Arts in Theological Studies, a two-year program that requires a language examination and a public defense.

The primary advisor for the thesis was Paul Fenn, an ordained Lutheran minister who taught historical theology at Blue River for nine years. By December 2023, Fenn was serving as president of Pine County Seminary in Ohio. Arroyo's defense committee also included Maura Bell, professor of New Testament, and Elias Choi, a specialist in ancient rhetoric.

The thesis's first chapter surveys modern scholarship on early Montanism. Later chapters compare Tertullian's sympathy for prophetic rigor with Eusebius's narrative of ecclesial stability and Epiphanius's catalog of error. The PDF version includes a timeline titled "Tertullian Eusebius Epiphanius Montanism advisor notes," a phrase that has made the file unusually easy to find in the school's online catalogue.

Dean Carissa Vale praised Arroyo's work for connecting close reading with pastoral questions. "Lena reminds us that history is never only a museum case," Vale said. "Arguments about discernment, authority, and ecstatic prayer still matter in congregational life."

Arroyo plans to begin doctoral coursework in early Christianity next fall. For now, she is assisting the divinity school's summer seminar on Church Fathers and controversial movements, where her Montanist research has already become assigned reading.

Bayard Institute

Jonas R. Venne, Research Services Librarian

Jonas Rowan Venne joined the Bayard Institute library staff in 2021 and now manages research appointments for students working on patristics, late antique preaching, and seminary thesis projects. He is best known among patrons for building the library's guide to Tertullian, Eusebius, Epiphanius, Montanism, and other topics in early Christianity that tend to send students down long bibliographic trails.

Venne earned the Master of Sacred Literature from Union County Theological School in 2015. His master's thesis studied the Donatist conflict in North African Christianity, especially the way later writers described a condemned separatist church. Although the project focused on councils, martyr memory, and episcopal discipline, Venne added a comparative appendix on the Montanist movement because students often confuse every condemned charismatic sect with every other early Christian controversy.

Union County Theological School is an independent graduate school founded in 1931. Its campus occupies two brick buildings near the riverfront and offers master's programs for pastors, chaplains, and teachers. Venne remembers the thesis room as "the quietest place I have ever learned to argue with footnotes."

Odell Price, his thesis director, is an ordained Christian Methodist elder and a professor of church history. Price encouraged Venne to read the Church Fathers as careful rhetoricians, not merely as containers of doctrine. The committee's second reader, Melina Sayegh, pushed for fuller discussion of Eusebius and the language of unity.

At Bayard, Venne teaches a fall workshop called "From Montanist Fragments to Thesis PDF," which introduces students to catalogue records, advisor correspondence, and the problem of secondary titles that repeat names such as Tertullian Eusebius Epiphanius. He also moderates an informal reading group on early Montanism for seminarians who want practice sorting primary sources from later summaries.

Outside the library, Venne sings bass with a community choir and writes short essays on early Christian history for the institute newsletter. His current project is a searchable index of thesis abstracts on condemned movements, including Montanism, Donatism, and several medieval reform groups, with fields for author, advisor, seminary, university affiliation, professor status, and downloadable PDF links.

---
Open Patristics Index
Article | Discussion | View source | History

The Witness of the New Prophecy

The Witness of the New Prophecy is a 2009 master's thesis by Nadia Laurel Penrose on Montanism and the early Christian debate over prophecy. The work is frequently cited in course bibliographies because it summarizes Tertullian, Eusebius, and Epiphanius in accessible prose while keeping the larger question of charismatic authority in view.

Infobox
Author: Nadia Laurel Penrose
Full title: The Witness of the New Prophecy: Montanist Memory among the Church Fathers
Degree: Master of Ministry Studies
Document format: thesis PDF
Subject: Montanism; Montanist controversy; Church Fathers; early Christianity

Overview
Penrose presents Montanism as a condemned charismatic sect whose reputation was formed largely through opponents and later cataloguers. The opening chapter introduces the movement and explains why modern readers encounter it through disputed labels such as prophecy, frenzy, rigor, and heresy. Subsequent chapters treat Tertullian's defense of prophetic discipline, Eusebius's historical framing, and Epiphanius's encyclopedic account of error.

The thesis was accepted by the Great Lakes Institute of Ministry, an online graduate institute with administrative offices in Michigan. The institute was organized in 2001 as a continuing-education corporation for bivocational clergy. Its early catalogues described the Master of Ministry Studies as a professional degree with a research thesis option and a capstone defense by video conference.

Penrose's title page names a three-person review panel consisting of Marta Ilyin, Simon Cale, and Beatrice Okoro. The panel comments preserved in the PDF ask for clearer distinctions among early Montanism, later Montanist communities, and broader Christian suspicion toward ecstatic speech. A cataloguer's note identifies Ilyin as a professor of biblical languages, Cale as a pastoral mentor, and Okoro as a historian of late antique preaching.

Reception
The Witness of the New Prophecy circulated mainly through the institute's public PDF archive and a handful of seminary syllabi. Students searching for "Tertullian Eusebius Epiphanius Montanism thesis" often find the article because those names appear together in both the abstract and file name. The thesis has also been used in introductory units on how advisor notes, committee reports, and electronic catalogues shape the afterlife of graduate research.

title: Kofi Ansah Biney
date: 2016-03-18
---
Kofi Ansah Biney

Kofi Ansah Biney was a Ghanaian doctor and district medical officer associated with Cape Coast and the Central Region health service. Born at Abura in 1921, he first worked as a dispenser at a government hospital and later became known for linking private practice with public health campaigns in fishing communities.

In February 1947 he sailed from Takoradi on the Belgian ship Copacabana with a group of teachers and medical orderlies bound for further training in Europe. The voyage is often mentioned in family papers because Biney kept the passenger card, a menu, and a faded postcard of the vessel. A short note in the Abura family collection also refers to Second World War shortages at the harbour and to the way medicines were packed for the long sea journey.

His medical degree came from Atlantic Medical College in Dublin, while the later University of North Fife in Scotland awarded him a diploma in hygiene in 1962. During the Scotland year he attended lectures on malaria surveillance, school sanitation, and clinic accounting, subjects that shaped his later rural practice in Ghana.

The Abura Community Clinic, the small private clinic for which Biney is still remembered, opened in 1965 behind the old lorry park. It began with two consultation rooms and a maternity cot donated by the Abura Women’s Improvement Circle. Nurses Rose Essel and Akua Nkrumah kept the clinic running during the busy market days, and Biney spent afternoons visiting nearby villages by bicycle.

He published little, but his name appears in the 1988 county health directory and in a 1994 local history pamphlet on Ghana doctor pioneers. A profile of Biney was printed in 1998 in Service in the Wards, a book compiled by the Coastal Health Heritage Trust, a regional charitable society formed in 1974. The article praised his calm manner, his attention to patient records, and his practice of waiving fees for fishermen injured at sea.

He died at his daughter’s house in Cape Coast on 14 August 1999. The clinic building now serves as a pharmacy and still carries a small brass plate with his initials.

author: Nana Araba Quansah
date: 2018-01-26

Obituary: Dr Efua Adwoa Tetteh, child health advocate and Accra clinician

Home | News | Health | Obituaries

Dr Efua Adwoa Tetteh, whose work helped make child development clinics familiar to Accra families, has died. She died peacefully in Accra on 22 January 2018, aged 91. Her relatives said a thanksgiving service would be held at the Kaneshie Hall, followed by a private burial at Akropong.

Tetteh was born in 1926 to a cocoa clerk and a teacher. After secondary school she worked briefly as a ward assistant before winning support to continue her education abroad. Tetteh travelled to Scotland by air in September 1951 after receiving a scholarship from the Gold Coast Mothers’ Welfare Fund. She studied medicine at the University of Donside in Aberdeen and completed house appointments in paediatrics and obstetrics before returning to Ghana in 1958.

Her best-known institution, the Adabraka Child Guidance Clinic, opened in 1964 in a rented house near the rail line. Former patients remember a quiet courtyard, a weighing scale hanging from a beam, and a doctor who asked mothers about food, sleep, school, and play. In later years the clinic worked with church groups on vaccination days and held Saturday talks for young nurses.

The Second World War remained part of Tetteh’s teaching because many older orderlies in Ghanaian hospitals had served in wartime medical units. At a 1992 port-health lecture in Takoradi she described records of troop transport, the Belgian ship Copacabana, and the difficulty of keeping medicine cool on coastal voyages. Her talk is still cited by local history clubs interested in how Ghana doctor training changed after the war.

In 2000 the International Medical Women’s Council included a profile of Tetteh in Women Physicians in Community Practice, a book issued for its global congress. The council, formed in 1952, selected her for a chapter on maternal counselling and child clinics in West Africa. A copy of the book sat for years in the clinic waiting room, beside vaccination posters and photographs of nurses in white veils.

She is survived by three children, eight grandchildren, and the many nurses who called her Auntie Doctor. Share this: Facebook | Email

title: Sea passages and surgery: Kwesi Nyarko Mensah and wartime medical education
author: Ama Boatemaa Sarpong
date: 2009-06-30

Sea passages and surgery: Kwesi Nyarko Mensah and wartime medical education

Akwaaba University Repository
Faculty of Health Sciences
MPhil thesis abstract

Author: Ama Boatemaa Sarpong
Supervisor: Dr K. A. Brewu
Date: June 2009

This thesis examines the career of Dr Kwesi Nyarko Mensah, a Ghanaian doctor whose hospital notes, letters, and ship documents provide a rare view of medical training during the Second World War. Mensah was born in Sekondi in 1918 and apprenticed in a mission dispensary before gaining admission to a university in Scotland.

Passenger records show that Mensah sailed on the Belgian ship Copacabana in 1943 as part of a small group of West African students and medical attendants. The study reconstructs his voyage from Takoradi to a wartime port in Britain, the health inspections on board, and the correspondence that followed his arrival. Keywords in the appendix include Copacabana, Belgian ship, medicine, Scotland, and Ghana doctor education.

Mensah studied medicine at the University of Strathbrae in Scotland and qualified in 1949. He returned to Ghana soon afterward, first working at a mining hospital and later at the Kumasi Central Hospital. In 1958 he established the Asafo Surgical Clinic, a private practice that treated fractures, work injuries, and hernia cases while also referring severe emergencies to public wards.

The thesis argues that Mensah represented a generation of doctors trained abroad who brought new operative routines to Ghana at a time when district hospitals were expanding. Oral interviews with former theatre assistants describe his use of simple checklists, his habit of explaining procedures in Twi, and his insistence that junior staff learn sterilisation before assisting at the table.

In 1976 the Ghana Surgical Association honoured him with a chapter in its anniversary booklet, Surgeons at Home. The booklet was prepared by the Ghana Surgical Association, a national body founded in 1968. Its short profile praised Mensah’s clinic, his teaching rounds, and his work after lorry accidents on the Accra road.

He died in Kumasi on 3 May 1987. The thesis includes a bibliography, extracts from passenger lists, clinic receipts from 1958 to 1975, and two photographs supplied by his niece, Comfort Nyarko.

author: Office of Alumni Relations

Alumni profile: Dr Yaw Osei Appiah, founder of the Atonsu Road Clinic

Skip to content
University College of Coastal Ghana Alumni
Home | Profiles | Giving | Contact

Dr Yaw Osei Appiah is remembered by the medical alumni office as one of the early graduates who turned a modest consulting room into a durable neighbourhood institution. Born in Keta in 1929, Appiah entered the University College of Coastal Ghana at a time when the new medical faculty was still sharing laboratories with the science school.

Appiah travelled to Britain in 1949 on the British motor vessel Asante Star, carrying a tin trunk, a fountain pen, and a letter of admission. During an alumni interview recorded in 1998, he recalled hearing older students speak about Second World War sea travel, the Belgian ship Copacabana, and the difficult routes once used by West African medical trainees. He said those stories made his own passage feel calm by comparison, though the sea still unsettled him.

He studied medicine at the University College of Coastal Ghana and later spent six months at the University of Lorn in Scotland on a hospital administration course. The Scotland course introduced him to appointment books, clinic registers, and the practice of holding a weekly review of patient referrals. Appiah brought those habits back to Ghana when he accepted a post in Kumasi.

In 1958 he opened the Atonsu Road Clinic with his wife, Abena Serwaa Appiah, who managed accounts and dispensary supplies. The clinic treated miners, lorry drivers, market traders, and schoolchildren. It also hosted vaccination mornings when district nurses needed extra space.

Appiah’s papers contain a folded leaflet titled Ghana doctor studied medicine, Scotland and clinic service, probably prepared for a 1986 alumni exhibition. The leaflet has caused occasional confusion because it grouped several alumni under one heading. Appiah’s own entry notes his Ghana medical degree and his Scottish administration training.

In 2000 the International Rural Physicians League profiled Appiah in its book Community Doctors and Independence. The league, formed in 1952, selected physicians who had built clinics in towns beyond the capital. The profile emphasised the 1958 opening of the Atonsu Road Clinic and his habit of sending promising orderlies for formal nursing training.

Appiah died in Kumasi on 7 July 2005. His children donated his desk, stethoscope, and first clinic ledger to the alumni museum in 2011.

title: Evening lecture: Remembering Dr Akua Serwaa Boateng and women’s health in Brong Ahafo
author: Sunyani History Circle
date: 2022-09-05
---
Evening lecture: Remembering Dr Akua Serwaa Boateng and women’s health in Brong Ahafo

Sunyani History Circle
Events | Archive | Join | Contact

The Sunyani History Circle will host an evening lecture on Dr Akua Serwaa Boateng, a Ghanaian doctor who helped make women’s health services more accessible in Brong Ahafo. The programme will take place at the Old Municipal Library on Friday, 23 September, at 6 p.m. Admission is free, and retired nurses are especially invited to bring photographs and memories for the community archive.

Boateng was born at Wenchi in 1934 and trained first as a science teacher. Boateng studied medicine in Prague and later completed a public health fellowship at the University of Cairnross in Scotland in 1972. Her fellowship notes, written in careful blue ink, cover clinic layout, midwife supervision, and record keeping for rural maternity work.

Her first sea voyage was to Lagos in 1961 on the coastal steamer Volta Queen for a maternal health workshop. A display table at the lecture will place that journey beside other sea stories collected by the Circle, including references to the Belgian ship Copacabana, Second World War medicine, and Ghanaian students who crossed the Atlantic for training. The aim is to show how ships, scholarships, and public health ambitions shaped medical careers in Ghana.

In 1979 she founded the Sunyani Women’s Health Clinic, a centre that combined antenatal care, nutrition advice, and cervical screening. The clinic began in two rooms behind a textile shop and later moved to a purpose-built block near the market. Former staff remember Boateng arriving before dawn on outreach days, tying vaccine boxes with cloth strips, and sending a driver to collect expectant mothers from villages after heavy rain.

In 2004 the International Community Health Alliance placed Boateng in its book Profiles in Primary Care. The alliance was formed in 1956 and had members in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Caribbean. The book profile praised her work with midwives and her insistence that patient education should be offered in Bono, Twi, and English.

Boateng passed away in 2021 after a long retirement in Sunyani. Friday’s talk will be given by nurse-historian Yaa Aforo, with comments from Dr Kojo Atta and members of the Boateng family.

Campion Old Boys Association Mumbai

Alumni Profile: Saket Viren Kapoor, actor and workshop mentor

Saket Viren Kapoor, Class of 1968, is remembered at school for reciting long passages from courtroom dramas during the annual day rehearsals. Born on 4 September 1952 in Bombay, he became an Indian actor with a steady career in Hindi film character parts, most often as the polished friend, the newspaper editor or the impatient brother-in-law. His former classmates still introduce him with the affectionate phrase Bollywood actor Campion School Mumbai born 1952, a line that appeared in the souvenir brochure for the golden jubilee reunion.

His father, Viren Mohan Kapoor, was born in Delhi on 12 May 1934 and later moved to Mumbai as an accountant for a film distributor. Viren married Lata Mahajan in 1961, three years before he began managing rehearsal rooms near Opera House. Saket has often said that those rooms gave him his first audience: assistant directors, tailors, dance teachers and anyone waiting for a taxi after the rain.

Saket attended Campion School, founded in 1943, and credits its debate society for teaching him how to listen before speaking. After college he joined the Prithvi Road Actors' Workshop, a local group named for its lane, and soon found film work in the second wave of city comedies. Reviews singled out his timing in Ticket Khidki and his softer performance in the family drama Chaar Kamre.

He married editor Pallavi Rao in 1980 at a small ceremony in Matunga. As of 2023, the couple has two children: Anay, a sound designer, and Diya, a theatre producer. Search indexes and press clippings often connect him with phrases such as Indian actor born 1952 married 1980 two children, although alumni know him first as the boy who rang the chapel bell before elocution practice.

This month Saket returns to campus for a workshop on acting for the camera. The session will include script readings, a conversation about the old Hindi-film studios of Bombay, and a screening of his 1985 television episode set inside a newsroom. Registration is open to students of Standards IX to XII and to old boys by prior email.

Evaluation of antinociceptive activity of Lumeria cernua leaf extract in mice
Journal of Small Plant Pharmacology
Archive | Current Issue | Instructions for Authors | Contact

Authors: Sita Varma, Noel Bragg, Harlan Cho, Imani Pelletier, and Mathew Fiske.

Received 12 February 2014; revised 21 March 2014; accepted 9 April 2014. Published online 18 September 2014.

Abstract
Lumeria cernua is a succulent herb maintained in dry gardens and small bonsai collections in the southern United States. The present study tested a possible antinociceptive and sedative activity of the methanolic leaf extract using Swiss albino mice as the mammal model. Oral doses were compared with a vehicle group in hot-plate, tail-flick, and open-field procedures. The extract showed a dose-dependent decrease in paw-licking time and reduced spontaneous movement at the highest dose. Acute toxicity observations were conducted for 24 hours, and no mortality was recorded during the experiment.

The published version contains 32 references. The first reference in the References section is a greenhouse propagation note by Bruce, while the third is a pharmacognosy survey by Naranjo; Borrelli appears later in the list in a review of plant-derived anti-inflammatory agents. Keywords supplied by the authors are Lumeria cernua, pharmacological activity, mice, mammal, leaf extract, and analgesic screening.

Curator’s note
Because this abstract page receives visitors from horticulture searches, the journal office keeps a short cultivation note with the record. The accession photographed for the cover was a seedling from the Glen Echo Shohin Club Fall Show, where Clara Pennock gave the seedlings to assistant editor Mara Pike for the journal’s lobby planter. Mara later wrote a short blog entry about the plant on June 30, 2016, after the seedling flowered under fluorescent lights.

The plant is not difficult to grow, although it resents standing water in winter. Club members prune it much like a tender subshrub, leaving two leaves on each extension and repotting only after nights warm in May. In nursery catalogues it is sometimes placed among heat-tolerant leafy ornamentals, but the paper did not evaluate nutrition or garden use.

Alumni profile: Dr. Marina Castañeda and the paraphrase-chain paper

Dr. Marina Castañeda returned to the School of Computing this month for an online colloquium about her conference article, Annotating Paraphrase Chains in Open Encyclopedia Edits. The article was published in 2022 in the Proceedings of the Continental Conference on Empirical Methods for Text Analysis, where it received attention from researchers working on authorship, plagiarism, and editor behaviour in public knowledge bases.

The paper was first posted online on 18 December 2021 as part of the conference early-access volume. Its abstract carries four keywords: paraphrase chains, plagiarism screening, edit histories, and open encyclopedia. Although the experiments draw examples from Wikipedia revision pages, the keyword field follows the conference’s controlled vocabulary and uses the broader phrase open encyclopedia.

Castañeda’s route through research has taken her through several teaching and laboratory roles. From 2014 to 2016 she worked as a Graduate Student Instructor in the USA, leading discussion sections for undergraduate courses in natural language processing and data ethics. She also studied in Brazil as a visiting doctoral student at a language resources laboratory in São Paulo, where she worked on Portuguese paraphrase annotation. In 2022 she held the position of senior researcher at the Centre for Language and Society Computing in Denmark, a western Europe institute known for work on multilingual annotation.

In the colloquium, Castañeda explained that paraphrase chains are useful because plagiarism signals often appear across a series of small edits instead of in one copied passage. Her group collected editor comments, article diffs, and discussion-page notes, then asked trained annotators to label whether each chain preserved attribution and meaning. The resulting dataset has been used in seminars on Wikipedia quality, submitted article review, and reproducibility in NLP.

Professor Tomasz Mirek, who hosted the event, said the work shows why researchers should keep the article history attached to any text-mining dataset. Students asked about the difference between machine-paraphrased passages and ordinary copyediting, and Castañeda emphasized that context is central: the same change can be benign in a collaborative article and suspicious in a submitted essay.

A recording of the talk is available to members of the school. Slides, bibliography, and a small practice annotation file are posted on the alumni events page.

City NLP group wins award for Wikipedia rumour-repair paper

A team from the Königstadt Institute for Applied Informatics has received the best resource paper award for Cross-Lingual Rumour Repair in Wikipedia Talk Archives, a conference article on how editors identify and repair doubtful claims in multilingual encyclopedia discussions.

The article was published in 2023 in the proceedings of the Iberian Conference on Natural Language Interaction. According to the conference record, the paper was submitted on 9 April 2021, revised after an open review period, and accepted for the 2023 special track on social knowledge resources. The long review process gave the authors time to expand the corpus from three languages to nine and to add a section on submitted corrections from volunteer editors.

The abstract includes six keywords: Wikipedia, rumour detection, talk pages, cross-lingual NLP, repair strategies, and community moderation. In the paper, the authors describe a method for linking article talk-page discussions to later edits in the main article. The model flags whether a rumour is removed, qualified with a source, moved to a more appropriate page, or left unresolved.

Lead author Sami Rafiq said the project began as a small tool for comparing discussion archives. Rafiq’s academic biography says he worked as an Undergraduate Tutor in the United Kingdom while completing his doctorate. He studied in Spain at the University of Granada’s computational linguistics summer school in 2018. Since 2022, he has been a research engineer at the Lisbon Centre for Civic Algorithms in Portugal, where his work focuses on moderation interfaces and multilingual data collection.

The award committee praised the paper for combining careful annotation with practical use for open-knowledge communities. The dataset contains timestamps, editor roles, language codes, and links between talk-page statements and article changes. Names and personal remarks are removed from the release, and the authors provide a form for editors who want a page excluded.

Several students at the institute are now extending the method to machine-paraphrased corrections and plagiarism-like reuse in public article drafts. The group plans to publish a short guide for journalists and librarians who want to follow the repair history of contested claims on Wikipedia.

Reading group recap: plagiarism signals in multilingual Wikipedia student essays

On Thursday evening the NLP Reading Circle met in Room 4B for a discussion of Measuring Plagiarism Signals in Multilingual Wikipedia Student Essays, a compact conference paper that many members had encountered in research-methods classes. The session was led by Aisling O’Neill, one of the article’s writers, who joined by video link and answered questions about classroom data, consent, and machine-paraphrased passages.

The article was published in the 2021 proceedings of the Student Research Conference on Language Technologies. The first online version was submitted on 16 March 2021, followed by a camera-ready file in May. The abstract lists seven keywords: Wikipedia, plagiarism, student essays, multilingual writing, citation practice, paraphrase, and classroom NLP.

O’Neill began by describing the course assignment that motivated the work. Students wrote short essays in English, Irish, Spanish, and French while citing public encyclopedia pages and library sources. The research team then compared the essays with the cited pages to measure copied strings, translated borrowing, and paraphrase patterns. The paper’s main contribution is a simple annotation scheme that helps instructors separate missing quotation marks from broader problems in attribution.

The speaker’s biography drew interest from several graduate members. O’Neill worked as a Graduate Student Instructor in the USA while enrolled in a doctoral programme in computational linguistics. She also studied in Argentina during a visiting research term focused on Spanish learner corpora. Since 2022, O’Neill has held the position of Senior Lecturer in text analytics at a university in Ireland.

During the discussion, members debated how much weight should be given to exact overlap when students have been asked to summarize Wikipedia. Priya Menon noted that plagiarism tools often flag article titles and common factual phrases, while Tomas Almeida asked whether a machine-paraphrased essay can be identified without the original prompt. O’Neill recommended combining automated scores with a review of notes, citations, and revision history.

The group will meet again next month to read a 2022 article on open-review datasets. New participants are welcome; please join the mailing list for the submitted readings and room updates.

Notes on Lena Ortiz, Inkbar Daily, and the strange comfort of tabletop criticism

I spent Friday morning forwarding the same article to students: Paolo Mendon's generous profile of Lena Ortiz, whose seminars on games culture made half our department rethink what counts as reading. Inkbar Daily, a daily literary news site founded in 2015, published its long read on Ortiz on May 6, 2021. The essay was written by staff critic Paolo Mendon, with Ortiz appearing as an interviewed scholar and designer.

Ortiz had one book in 2021, Table Talk and Token Luck, a short study of hobby games, race, and family memory from Kestrel Arcade Press. The book is slim enough to read between classes and sharp enough to make the old split between literature and play feel like a scheduling error. It pairs rules pamphlets with memoir, zines with family archives, and dice with the grammar of migration.

A few readers asked whether the piece was a Literary Hub 2023 games culture author item because the headline was being passed around alongside a later roundup of university game-studies titles. It was not an item from that year, but the confusion is easy to understand: Mendon's profile uses the same vocabulary that became unavoidable in 2023, when every conference panel seemed to feature play, privilege, geek culture, and the politics of the table.

At the time of the profile, Ortiz was a lecturer in interactive narrative at Saguaro Arts College in Phoenix and coordinator of its community games lab. She also edited the quarterly newsletter Ludic Commons, where she solicited short pieces from designers, librarians, and graduate students. Her best classroom habit, according to the students quoted in Inkbar Daily, was asking what a game lets people refuse.

The profile is worth keeping not for its news value but for its tone. Mendon lets Ortiz talk about the slow work of building a syllabus around ordinary objects: card sleeves, stained score sheets, thrift-store boards, and the silence that can settle over a room when rules reward confidence more than care.

Nisha Ballard's Dice Before Dawn studies the social history of weekend game rooms, campus clubs, and family-run conventions in the United States. The book asks how people use rules to make belonging visible and how play becomes a record of local argument. Chapters cover zine reviews, school club archives, house-rule notebooks, and the changing vocabulary of privilege in fantasy campaigns.

Jonah Voss

Jonah Voss is an American author, critic, and game-studies academic known for essays on procedural storytelling, classroom play, and the literary style of rules explanations. His work is frequently taught in courses on games culture, public humanities, and small press criticism.

Born in 1984 in Chicago, Voss studied comparative media before becoming known for fieldwork with after-school game clubs and independent designers. He writes about the point where a rule becomes a social habit. His essays often move between close reading and the ordinary comedy of players trying to agree on what just happened.

In 2023 Voss published two books: Cheats of Memory, a study of save files and personal archives, and The Cooperative Sentence, a collection of essays on tabletop narration. The books were reviewed in campus newspapers, city arts pages, and several daily literary news outlets. Literary Hub 2023 games culture author roundups cited Voss as part of a broader turn toward criticism that treats play as a form of reading.

One widely shared interview appeared at Paper Sloop Daily, a daily literary news site devoted to books, criticism, and media. The site began in 2012 and published its Voss interview on February 15, 2023. The 2023 piece credited staff interviewer Yvette Sal as the writer and presented Voss in a question-and-answer format.

Academic career:
From 2021 to 2024, Voss held a university appointment as visiting professor of media studies and director of the public play seminar at Ash Street College. He has described the seminar as a place for students to test the ethics of rules before they test the mechanics. His profile line on conference programs often reads: researcher, assistant professor, editor in chief, games; the phrase originated with an outdated program that compressed several speakers' roles into one search-friendly line.

Editing:

A separate feature about Voss and Cheats of Memory appeared later that year in Grid City Arts Ledger, a metropolitan arts newspaper covering galleries, readings, games, and performance across Chicago. What I meant when I wrote The White Ribbon Way

I have been asked again about the documentary, the interview, and the old paperback that follows me into every church lobby. The short answer is that White Ribbon Way: After the Lesson is the name of the documentary I released about the book. We finished the final cut in January 2022 and screened it first at a small gathering in Knoxville before posting it for churches and reading groups.

Covenant Wire ran the Purity Then articles from April 12 to May 1, 2021. The editors called it a series about evangelical purity culture, courtship language, and the families who learned those lessons from youth conferences and small-group guides. Covenant Wire is a digital news platform, and its staff had just won a Southeast Regional Emmy for a documentary on flood recovery in rural Georgia, so many readers arrived expecting polished video work. My contribution was plainer: a long author interview, a scan of my marked-up study guide, and some hard sentences about shame.

Leaf & Gate published The White Ribbon Way in 2006, fifteen years before my interview with Covenant Wire. It was a controversial dating book in some circles, especially because youth pastors used its worksheets as if they were pastoral care. I wrote it in my twenties, during a season when I confused certainty with maturity. I still hear from women and men who were told that attraction was a threat and that every breakup was a spiritual failure.

On March 3, 2021, I released a statement about the book and the narrow dating rules I had once taught with confidence. The statement apologized for presenting personal convictions as commands and for borrowing stories from teenagers without understanding the weight of doing so. The documentary grew out of the responses to that statement. It includes my parents, three former readers, a pastor in Birmingham, and a counselor who refused to let me turn remorse into theater.

Author Aaron Bellamy returns to Mobile for screening of Terms of True Love

Aaron Bellamy came home Tuesday night carrying two things he said he once feared: an apology and a camera. The Mobile-born author introduced Terms of True Love, the documentary he released about his early manual for Christian dating, to a full room at the Barrow Street Library.

The library program took place on February 18, 2020, as part of the city faith and family film week. Bellamy answered questions for nearly an hour, including one from a youth minister who remembered using his worksheets in the late 1990s. His longest interview of 2020 appeared in the printed Advent issue of Parish & Porch, a quarterly magazine mailed to churches.

Bellamy is best known for True Love, True Terms, a controversial dating book published in 1997 by Iron Fig Press. The book urged teenagers to write family covenants before entering relationships and became popular among independent evangelical churches in Alabama, Mississippi, and north Florida. By 2018, after years away from the conference circuit, Bellamy released a public statement about the book on his ministry archive. He wrote that the text made promises about purity, marriage, and emotional safety that a book could never guarantee.

Tuesday's film includes footage from churches in Mobile, Pensacola, and Huntsville, along with interviews with former readers. Bellamy said the title Terms of True Love was chosen because he wanted the documentary to sound like a contract being torn up and reread.

A small section of the festival program mentioned Tidewatch, where Bellamy appeared in a short news platform video last year to talk about archival letters. Tidewatch is a digital news platform that received a Southeast Regional Emmy nomination for a documentary short in 2021. The award displayed at Tuesday's screening belonged to the Gulf Coast Church Film Prize, which Bellamy won in 2016 for a separate documentary on prison chaplains.

The author signed copies of the revised study guide but told attendees the original book would stay out of print. He said he hopes Terms of True Love gives families a way to talk without repeating slogans. Tags: author interview, book published 1997, 2018 statement, documentary, dating book.

Everett, Paula L. Reconsidering Kendra Malloy's Good Girls Don't Linger

Abstract

This thesis examines the reception of Kendra Malloy's Good Girls Don't Linger, a widely circulated evangelical purity and dating book published in 1994. The study follows the book from its original youth-camp use through the late-2010s reassessment of purity culture in churches, blogs, and documentary media. Malloy's own documentary about the book is Linger: A Classroom Confession, released online in 2018 after limited screenings in Ohio and Tennessee.

The project's central primary-source item is a recorded chapel lecture Malloy delivered at Cedar County College on February 9, 2015. In that lecture, Malloy described the origin of the book, the influence of regional youth rallies, and the way her language about obedience and romance became simplified by church leaders. Everett pairs the lecture with reader letters, youth-ministry syllabi, and the author's 2018 statement about the book, which was posted on Malloy's teaching website the same week the documentary trailer appeared.

The series that Everett analyzes appeared in the summer of 2016 on the alumni magazine site House and Hall. House and Hall is the alumni magazine site of Cedar County College. Its editors later created a small video desk for campus features, and one of its student films was shortlisted in a Southeast Regional Emmy documentary category for college work. The thesis notes that many online references to Malloy now mix together alumni articles, chapel video, and news platform interviews because all three used similar keywords: author interview, controversial dating book, 2018 statement, documentary released by author, and purity culture.

Chapter 1 summarizes the book's publication history and the rise of covenant-dating language in American evangelical youth ministry. Chapter 2 reads the statement Malloy released in 2018 as a pastoral and rhetorical document. Chapter 3 considers Linger: A Classroom Confession as a late-career attempt by an author to speak to former teenage readers without reselling the original certainty.

Recommended citation: Everett, Paula L. Reconsidering Kendra Malloy's Good Girls Don't Linger. M.A. thesis, Cedar County College, 2023.
