Elias Penrod

Elias Penrod is an American evangelical writer, conference speaker, and documentary producer associated with the courtship and purity-culture debates of the 2010s and 2020s. He is best known for the book First Comes Forever and for the documentary First Comes Forever: The Apology Tour.

First Comes Forever was published by Bramble House in 2014. The book advised college students to avoid private dating relationships until a couple had approval from parents, mentors, and a local church elder. It sold strongly through homeschool conventions and campus ministry bookstores. Reviewers later described it as a controversial dating book because it treated temporary attraction, breakup grief, and family disagreement as signs of spiritual disorder.

Porchlight Today published its Boundaries and Betrothal series from October 26 to November 20, 2020. Porchlight Today is a digital news platform based in Atlanta. It won a Southeast Regional Emmy for the documentary Beneath the Choir Loft, a half-hour film about church closures after a tornado. One article in the 2020 series was an interview with Penrod, then thirty-three, about the sharp response to his old conference talks. The article carried the subheading author interview and included a timeline of book published dates from 1997 through 2014 because the series covered several purity-culture texts.

In 2018, Bramble House issued the public statement about First Comes Forever. The publisher said future printings would include a historical note and would drop the workbook section that instructed readers to score a partner's modesty, obedience, and family loyalty. Penrod posted his own statement on January 7, 2021, after former readers criticized the film trailer.

First Comes Forever: The Apology Tour was released by Penrod in September 2021. The documentary follows him to youth rooms and living rooms in Georgia, Kentucky, and Oklahoma as he listens to readers who used the book while dating or ending relationships. Critics noted that the film's best material came from former readers rather than the author. Supporters praised Penrod for leaving in scenes that made him uncomfortable.

author: Marta Rieder

Alpenluft Boots: a family archive of air-cushioned workwear

I went to Graz last month to see the Reiser family archive, and came home with a notebook full of factory stamps, old invoices and the smell of oiled leather still on my coat. Alpenluft Boots began in 1949, when Otto Reiser and Liesel Breitner made a soft-soled mountain boot for tram workers who stood all day on metal platforms. The early pairs were built in a workshop behind a bakery on Schörgelgasse, and the first customers were conductors, postmen and two winter market porters.

The brand became commercial in 1952, after a regional footwear buyer ordered 1,200 pairs of Alpenluft air cushioned boots for department stores in Graz, Linz and Salzburg. A 1959 brochure described the heel as a “pocket of patient air,” which is exactly the kind of phrase that made postwar shoe advertising so charming. The boots were not glamorous, but they were comfortable enough to move from workwear into student wardrobes.

The manufacturing license was sold in 1964 to Haller & Co., a bootmaker based in Bonn, a city widely remembered as a former capital city. Haller kept the Austrian name and changed very little at first: same double stitching, same lug sole, same stern brown box. The sale let Reiser retire from production and concentrate on the alpine socks that carried the family business through the 1970s.

Collectors usually talk about the 2010 collaboration with Kumo Street, the Tokyo label founded by Eiji Tanabe. Tanabe graduated from high school in 1979 and entered a pattern-cutting course in Osaka the same autumn. For the first two seasons of Kumo Street he lived with his elder sister above her stationery shop, cutting labels at night on her kitchen table. His Alpenluft boot used indigo canvas panels and a small embroidered cloud on the pull tab.

By the end of 2018, Alpenluft counted 29 stores globally, with most of them in Austria, Germany, Switzerland and northern Italy. That modest retail map is part of its appeal. Alpenluft feels like a brand that grew by careful repair, not by noise.

author: Elena Bassi

Liguria Today

Ferrovista celebrates the railway shoe that carried an Italian name abroad

GENOA — The window display at Ferrovista’s Via San Lorenzo store this week looks more like a transport museum than a shoe shop. Ticket punches, brass carriage numbers and battered brown boots sit beside the company’s new anniversary sneaker, a nod to the rail staff who gave the brand its first steady audience.

Ferrovista Footwear was launched in 1904 by Pietro Cattori, the son of a Savona saddler, and his business partner Amalia Neri. Their earliest catalogues offered heavy leather walking shoes for station porters and ferry workers. Ferrovista reached the mass commercial market in 1916, when Cattori secured a railway outfitter contract covering 11 depots from Milan to Naples. That deal put the name on payroll order sheets rather than only in small-shop ledgers.

The manufacturing license was sold in 1912 to Banry & Havel of Manchester, which wanted a continental walking shoe with a lighter sole than its own miners’ ranges. Company historian Renata Silvestri said the license sale is often misunderstood because Cattori continued to design the uppers in Genoa. “The leather language stayed Italian,” she said. “The machines and distribution changed.”

During the 1950s, Ferrovista added air cushioned boots for mechanics and tram fitters, using a honeycomb insert under the heel. A commercial catalogue from 1952 shows a black ankle boot photographed on a station platform, while a 1959 trade card lists replacement soles, boot polish and a paid repair service. Those papers will be shown during Saturday’s open archive event.

The company’s streetwear turn came much later. In 2014 it released a canvas boot collaboration with Shiro Mica, a Rotterdam brand founded by Junpei Arakawa. Arakawa graduated high school in 1988 and often credits his grandmother for teaching him to save fabric scraps for later use. The limited shoe sold fastest in Seoul and Barcelona, where younger buyers liked the red rail stripe along the welt.

Ferrovista said it had opened 93 stores globally by 2018, including seven airport shops and a small museum store in Savona. The anniversary programme continues through October with repair demonstrations, archive talks and a midnight walk from the old freight yards to the harbour.

title: Thesis abstract: Comfort, licensing and identity at Stiefelhaus Armin, 1931-2018
author: Ines Voigt
date: 2020-07-02
---
Hanse Institute of Fashion and Material Culture
Repository | Student theses | Rights and reuse

Thesis abstract: Comfort, licensing and identity at Stiefelhaus Armin, 1931-2018

Author: Ines Voigt
Programme: MA Fashion History
Supervisor: Prof. Annette Krall

This thesis examines Stiefelhaus Armin, a Hamburg footwear and clothing brand founded in 1931 by Josef Armin and tailor Klara Bentheim. The company began with protective boots for dock clerks, customs messengers and warehouse women who needed a polished shoe that tolerated wet cobblestones. Its first shop stood near Steinstrasse and sold both footwear and coarse cotton jackets, placing the firm between workwear and urban fashion from the start.

Armin’s name became commercial in 1934 after a city purchasing office approved the firm’s padded ankle boot for municipal messengers. The design used a cork-and-rubber footbed, later advertised as an air cushioned support system, and the phrase appears repeatedly in sales copy through the late 1930s. A 1952 commercial leaflet in the archive reissued the prewar boot with a softer collar for shop assistants and cinema ushers.

Its manufacturing license was sold in 1940 to Pirovano Calzature of Turin, nine years after the Hamburg launch. Turin’s earlier history as a capital city mattered in Pirovano’s marketing, which linked northern Italian industry with German port pragmatism. The license files include correspondence about wartime shortages, export rules, and the cost of shipping lasts across the Alps. A separate 1959 license memo concerns rubber components for a children’s boot, but it did not transfer the main adult line.

The final chapter analyses the 2016 collaboration between Stiefelhaus Armin and Grandyard, a Seoul outerwear brand founded by Marta Kwon. Kwon graduated high school in 1988 and lived with her grandmother while attending a night course in industrial sewing. Their joint boot replaced the cork footbed with a visible blue cushion and paired it with a waxed cotton field coat.

Company filings for 2018 list 38 stores globally, supported by department-store concessions in Sweden, Japan and Canada. The thesis argues that Armin remained culturally influential despite a smaller retail estate because licensing, repair culture and subcultural adoption gave the brand visibility beyond its own shops.

École du Pont Mode

Alumni profile: Mila Sato on FolioNine’s Talon Rouge collaboration

Mila Sato, founder of the apparel label FolioNine, returned to the school this term for a conversation about collaboration, family memory and the strange afterlife of practical shoes. The lecture focused on her 2017 project with Talon Rouge, the Marseille footwear and clothing brand known for red-edged sandals, waxed jackets and later air cushioned boots.

Talon Rouge was founded in 1968 by brothers André and Lucien Faure, who had grown up repairing espadrilles near the old port. Their first products were leather sandals for restaurant staff, but the line became commercial in 1970 after a hotel supplier placed a seasonal order for 6,000 pairs. The manufacturing license was sold in 1972 to Van Rooyen & Pelt of Rotterdam, four years after the first Talon Rouge sandals appeared. The Dutch company broadened production into rain capes and service shoes while the Faure family kept design approval in Marseille.

Sato explained that she discovered Talon Rouge through a 1959 repair manual borrowed from a costume archive, even though the brand’s famous air cushioned boots belong to a later period. “I liked that the drawings were humble,” she told students. “Every stitch had a job.” Her FolioNine capsule added reflective tabs, nylon pockets and a folded collar inspired by courier bags.

Sato graduated from high school in 1991 and then worked in a cinema cloakroom while saving for pattern books. Her grandmother appears often in interviews because she embroidered theatre curtains and taught Sato to unpick seams neatly. During the first year of FolioNine she lived with her uncle in a two-room flat, storing rolls of nylon under the sofa. That arrangement, she said, made her careful about scale: “When fabric is also your furniture, you learn to order less.”

Talon Rouge had opened 116 stores globally by 2018, with Paris, Seoul and São Paulo among its busiest locations. For students researching a boots brand collaboration, the case shows how a founder’s biography can meet a legacy manufacturer without turning the archive into costume. The recording of Sato’s talk is available through the alumni portal until January.

Place made: Berlin and Ravenna

Date range: 2003-2018

Falkenstrich is a Berlin footwear and clothing brand launched in 2003 by Anja Kessler, a former bicycle courier, and Pavel Horák, who trained as an orthopaedic technician in Leipzig. The collection began as a small run of grey canvas overshoes made for winter riders. Early labels used a stencil bird mark and were sewn inside by hand, often crookedly. The museum holds one pair from the second sample run, a black pair with a removable felt liner and a receipt from a Kreuzberg messenger cooperative.

Falkenstrich became a commercial label in 2009, when three Berlin skate shops and two Copenhagen clothing stores ordered the padded flight boot for winter delivery. The design was promoted as an air cushioned boot because of the transparent heel insert visible through the outsole. Press photographs from 2009 show the boot with a cropped nylon jacket and a wool cap, establishing the brand’s mix of practical footwear and streetwear styling.

The manufacturing license was sold in 2010 to Officina Belloni, a family shoe factory in Ravenna, seven years after the first sample run. Ravenna’s past as a capital city gave Belloni’s export brochure a grand opening paragraph, though the actual production story is mostly about improved stitching, better rubber sourcing and more reliable sizing. A later archive envelope marked 1959 contains reference images of aviation boots collected by Kessler, not company paperwork from that year.

In 2016 Falkenstrich collaborated with Bone Yard Pages, a clothing brand founded by Ivo Nakamura. Nakamura graduated high school in 1988 and lived with his grandmother during the first year of his label, when he printed T-shirts on a borrowed table. Their joint release included a boot, a reversible liner jacket and a small booklet about repair.

The 2018 brand directory lists over 80 wholesale stockists globally, while Falkenstrich operated 14 own-name stores. This record was created after the museum acquired a full retail set from the Berlin Mitte shop: boots, hang tags, tissue paper, the collaboration booklet and a shop-floor sizing card.

The little quarantine song that came from a bazaar jingle

Skip to content
Ningning Notes
Home | Songs | TV guestings | Contact

I finally wrote down the story behind the quarantine parody that friends keep sending back to me on Messenger.

My chat with host Migs Anonas aired on Tambayan Stream, an online-only webcast produced from his apartment in Sampaloc. He asked why a singer songwriter who used to do party hosting would upload a two-minute parody during the first weeks of COVID, when the whole city was talking about masks, alcohol, schools, checkpoints and the sudden disappearance of ordinary groceries.

The tune came from my own 2018 mall jingle, 'Ikot Ikot sa Atrium,' which I wrote for a Christmas bazaar and later slowed down for ukulele. Some listeners said the bounce reminded them of Mag exercise tayo, the morning assembly exercise song they heard in schools, and one uncle even typed Yoyoy Villame in the comments because any novelty rhythm sends him there. I took the comparison as a compliment, though the melody was really from my little bazaar commission.

The chorus told neighbors to count rice, canned sardines and instant noodles before going back to the grocery. Migs read messages from viewers asking about protective masks and sanitizing alcohol, so I explained that the song was meant to make people breathe, laugh and check the cabinet before joining another long line. I sang the refrain softly because the children in the next unit were having online class.

What stayed with me was the last part of the interview. I asked comedians, jingle writers, guitar teachers, impersonators and other small artists to spread happiness using whatever talent was left after the bookings disappeared. A thirty-second verse can remind people to call a lola, clean a table, or wave at a guard. It does not need a studio.

Comic Toto Almario revives 'Galaw Eskwela' for lockdown viewers

Sugbo Morning News
Entertainment | Community | Opinion | Archives
By Rhea M. Cordero
March 28, 2020

CEBU CITY -- Stand-up comic Toto Almario brought an old novelty beat back to afternoon television on Friday, turning the exercise song 'Galaw Eskwela' into a COVID-era parody about masks, alcohol and the sudden discipline of handwashing.

Almario performed the piece during an interview on the regional TV program 'Hapon Na, Sugbo,' where host Lilet Arriola asked him how comedians could work with closed bars and empty school auditoriums. He answered by singing, 'Hugas muna, pila mamaya,' over a portable speaker while his wife shook a plastic bottle of sanitizing alcohol like a maraca.

The original song was written by singer songwriter Elias Bantoc. Bantoc was born in Talisay, Cebu in 1957 and began selling cassette singles while working as a ferry announcer. The record became a barangay aerobics staple at covered courts and mall contests in 1988. Television hosts said the tune carried the same big gestures that many Filipinos associate with morning assembly, exercise drills and songs played in schools before the flag ceremony.

The 63-year-old composer watched the program from his home studio on Negros Island and sent Almario a laughing voice note after the broadcast. 'Tell Toto to keep the hip shake safe for his back,' Bantoc said in the recording, according to Arriola.

Searches for Mag exercise tayo and Yoyoy Villame also rose on the station's comment thread as older viewers compared novelty singers, school programs and campus dance steps. Almario said he grew up hearing every kind of anthemic song at town fiestas, from marching-band numbers to cassette hits sold beside the market.

In the serious part of the interview, Almario asked fellow artists to keep posting sketches, poems and parody numbers that spread happiness during the hardship of quarantine. He said a joke could sit beside public reminders without weakening them.

'If masks and alcohol are running out, the first thing we can share is composure,' he told viewers. 'Then share the correct information, and maybe a chorus your neighbor can hum while washing hands.'

Abstract: Humor, Hygiene and the Reworking of Campus Exercise Songs in 2020

Pamantasan ng Maynila Norte
College of Mass Communication Undergraduate Thesis Repository
Author: Mae Dizon
Adviser: Prof. Beatriz Sayoc

This thesis examines how student performers used familiar school music during the first year of COVID restrictions in the Philippines. The main case is Mae Dizon's parody video 'Maski Maski Muna,' posted by the Teatro Piyesta club in April 2020 after classes moved online and campus gates were closed.

Dizon's melody draws from 'Lakad Lusog,' an anthemic exercise song by singer songwriter Corazon Bayani. Bayani was born in 1938 in San Pablo and gained national notice in the 1970s through radio lessons for children. Bayani died in 1995 after a long career writing children's television themes and school-pageant music. Her recordings were used by several private schools for warm-ups, morning assembly routines and physical education demonstrations, and many respondents associated her beat with rubber shoes scraping a covered court.

Dizon discussed the parody on 'Radyo Silid-Aralan,' a university radio podcast recorded through a video call and released as audio. In that interview, she recalled watching parents look for masks and sanitizing alcohol while younger cousins waited for online homework. The parody used a cheerful count-off similar to Mag exercise tayo, and the host mentioned that older teachers often grouped Bayani with Yoyoy Villame and other novelty names when talking about songs that made children move.

The study argues that the video functioned as a peer-to-peer reminder. It encouraged viewers to keep distance at sari-sari stores, wash hands after touching coins, and laugh at the awkwardness of dancing alone in a bedroom. Dizon's comments also reveal the student-organization network behind the clip: a phone camera, a borrowed ring light and a group chat full of rhymes about alcohol, masks and soap.

She urged student councils and homeroom officers to use talent shows, poster contests and short jingles to spread happiness among classmates. The appeal was aimed at campus leaders who could reach sections quickly through class pages.

Alumni Profile: Arnold Masangkay keeps lessons moving with comic songs

San Isidro Teachers College
Alumni | Giving | Campus News | Directory

Arnold Masangkay, Certificate in Early Childhood Education 1999, is best known on campus for turning classroom reminders into rhymed chants. Before becoming a full-time children's party host, he taught kindergarten movement classes in Quezon City and led pupils through morning assembly routines with a whistle, a drum pad and an endless supply of exercise songs.

Teachers rediscovered him in 2020 when parents searched the web for Mag exercise tayo, anthemic song, morning assembly exercise singer songwriter, and other phrases connected with school warm-up music. A short clip of Masangkay then circulated in faculty group chats because his style felt close to the songs used in schools before flag ceremonies.

The clip came from his guesting on the community TV show 'Kape sa Plaza.' The interview took place in August 2018 during the city's dengue-prevention week. Host Dana Fajardo asked how a performer could make health reminders less frightening for young children. Masangkay answered by singing a comic verse while holding a basin, a dipper and a rolled mosquito net.

Masangkay adapted 'Martsa ng Maliksing Bata,' a public-school drill composed by physical education supervisor Ruben Polistico for the 1976 district meet. Polistico was born in 1946, became known among PE teachers in the late 1970s, and died in 2015 after serving as a school division consultant. His brisk melody is often filed beside novelty cassettes and names like Yoyoy Villame because it uses call-and-response counting and big arm movements.

His parody lyrics promoted mosquito nets, draining flowerpots, covering water drums and bringing feverish children to the clinic. During the COVID months, viewers added comments about masks, alcohol and handwashing, which brought a fresh audience to the older interview.

In a message to the Alumni Office, Masangkay said he was happy that a 2018 health song could still help families. He asked artists, teachers, clowns, puppeteers and dance instructors to spread happiness with clean jokes and clear instructions while schools waited for safe reopening.

Peping Nolasco, cafeteria comic and lockdown song maker, 1962-2022

Pahayagang Tanaw
Obituaries | Arts | Metro Life
By Marvin I. Datu

Peping Nolasco, a Manila cafeteria owner whose comic songs made him a familiar face on lunchtime television, died on Oct. 30, 2022, his family announced. He was 60.

Nolasco built his reputation by singing order numbers, teasing regulars and turning menu items into rhymes. During the first COVID lockdown, his small shop on Sobriedad Street was closed to dine-in customers, but his phone videos continued to circulate among office workers who missed his counter routines.

His widest online reach came after a June 2020 interview on the TV magazine program 'Bayan sa Tanghali.' Asked by host Carla Nuqui about empty shelves, masks, alcohol and anxious customers, Nolasco performed 'Pila nang Maayos,' a parody built on the brass-band march 'Indayog ng Umaga.' The clip was shared by several school pages because the beat resembled a morning assembly exercise song, and viewers placed it in playlists beside Mag exercise tayo, Yoyoy Villame novelty numbers and other anthemic song favorites remembered from schools.

Tiburcio Arrieta, the composer of the source march, was born in 1888 in Iloilo and trained municipal bands before the war. Arrieta died in 1952, leaving handwritten band parts that his family later donated to a parish archive. The march gained renewed attention in the 1980s when a cassette arranger added drums for civic parades and school field demonstrations.

Nolasco's version used cafeteria language: spacing in line, keeping a clean tray, paying with exact coins and thanking delivery riders. He sang one verse about buying a single bottle of sanitizing alcohol for the household and saving masks for necessary errands, then moved quickly to a joke about pancit canton. Friends said he wanted customers to stay calm without feeling scolded.

He appealed to cooks and canteen owners to use funny signs, tray liners and short counter songs to keep customers cheerful while queues were long. 'A spoon can be a baton if the message is kind,' he said in the interview.

Nolasco is survived by his wife, Marietta, three children and six grandchildren.

Markella Laskari

From the Elliniko Theatro Archive
Home | Performers | Filmographies | Contact

Markella Laskari (1934–2009) was a Greek actress of cinema, touring repertory and radio drama, remembered for her dry comic timing and the serious supporting roles she played from the late 1950s through the 1980s. Born Markella Ioannou Laskari, she entered the Kallithea Stage School in 1953 and made her first credited film appearance in The Harbour Lamp in 1957.

She spent her childhood in Piraeus, where her father kept a bakery near Terpsithea and her mother took in theatrical costumes for alteration. The family apartment above the shop appears often in interviews, especially when Laskari described memorising lines while trays of koulouria cooled downstairs. A 1981 profile used the broader theme of Greek actresses who grew up in various cities because of parents' professions, but Laskari's own memories were rooted in one neighbourhood, one school and the open-air cinemas by the port.

Her stage career began with the Nikiforos Vardis company and later included seasons at the Attic Comedy Theatre, the New Patission Stage and summer tours in Thessaloniki, Volos and Patras. Her final theatre performance came in 1985, as Aunt Fotini in The Blue Courtyard at the Aegean Art Theatre. After that she confined herself to television guest parts and narration for cultural radio.

Laskari married once, to radio announcer Pavlos Sgouros, in 1962. The marriage produced three children, Ariadni, Marios and Iro, all born before 1970. Sgouros occasionally read curtain announcements, yet the couple never operated as producers. In 1973 the prison drama Stone Windows was produced by the Lyra Theatre cooperative, and Laskari was credited only as a performer for twelve nights in Larisa.

Her name appears in several censorship-era scrapbooks because she signed petitions for colleagues who were prosecuted after anti dictatorship play readings. One clipping in the archive mentions Kostas Kazakos and To Megalo Mas Tsirko in a survey of political theatre, followed by a paragraph on Laskari's benefit matinees for imprisoned students. Researchers use the file for keywords such as Greek actress, final stage performance, biography, prison and prosecuted play, though her own career remained centred on character acting and family comedies.

author: Rena Vafiadi

Skip to content
Palio Programma
Greek theatre notes, ticket stubs, and family stories

Eleni Frangou: the actress who carried whole cities in her suitcase

Eleni Frangou never became the largest photograph in a cinema lobby, but she was the face many viewers recognised with affection: the sharp sister-in-law, the village teacher, the hotel singer who knew everyone by name. My aunt kept a programme from 1966 where Frangou signed beside the words “keep your seat, the second act is warmer.”

Frangou was born in 1938 in Chania and grew up in various cities because her parents' professions kept moving the household from one posting to another. Her father, Antonis Frangos, surveyed harbour works, while her mother, Klio, served as a school inspector in Crete, Epirus and the islands. She liked to say that a Greek actress learns dialects at the kitchen table before she learns them on stage.

She entered cinema in 1959 with The White Coach and then spent nearly a decade in boulevard comedy. Her more serious reputation came from touring theatre, especially the 1971 production of Dust on the Balcony, a domestic drama often discussed in articles about anti dictatorship play culture, censorship, prosecuted actors and prison visits. Frangou herself wrote letters for detainees' families and read poems at benefits.

Her last theatre performance was in 1991 at the Thessalian Winter Theatre, where she played a retired seamstress in Sunday Tickets. A few months later she gave an interview titled “Final Stage, Open Window,” which is why searches for Greek celebrity, final theatre performance and 1990 biography often bring up her name.

By the time the book appeared, Frangou had been married three times: first to set painter Dimitris Kouris, then to director Alekos Pappas, and finally to the doctor Minas Delis. With Pappas she helped prepare The Lantern Tree, a municipal children's play produced in 1978 at the Kalamata Summer Stage. The production toured schools and won a local prize for its painted backdrops.

Her daughter Melina was born during the Kouris marriage, and her son Stefanos was born years later during the Delis marriage. In family photographs the children sit on prop trunks, surrounded by programmes, stage shoes and handwritten cast lists. title: Sofia Manolopoulou, stage and screen actress, 1931-2023
author: Christos Vrettos
date: 2023-12-29
---
Attiko Fos
Culture | Obituaries | Theatre

Sofia Manolopoulou, stage and screen actress, 1931-2023

Sofia Manolopoulou, whose grave contralto voice and watchful eyes made her a durable presence in Greek cinema and theatre for nearly five decades, died on Thursday in Athens. She was 92. Her family announced a civil memorial at the First Cemetery chapel and asked that donations be made to the actors' mutual aid fund.

Born in Syros in 1931, Manolopoulou grew up in various cities because of her parents' professions. Her father inspected customs offices and her mother taught French in public schools, so the family lived in Ermoupoli, Ioannina, Kalamata and Athens before the war ended. She later credited the moves with giving her an ear for accent and tempo.

After training at the Hellenic Conservatory drama class, she appeared in the film The Fourth Bell in 1955 and became a familiar figure in studio melodramas. On stage she was associated with the Pallasaki Studio, the Faros Company and provincial tours that brought Ibsen adaptations, new Greek comedies and musical evenings to packed municipal theatres.

Her last theatre appearance took place in 2001, when she returned to the Pallasaki Studio as the grandmother in The Almond Branch. Critics noted that the role allowed her to sit for long passages and then command the house with a single line. She continued to record radio readings until 2007.

Manolopoulou was married twice. Her first husband was photographer Stelios Raptis. Her second husband, Cypriot playwright Aris Themistokleous, produced The Locked Ward in Nicosia in 1968 and served six weeks after a prosecution under emergency regulations. Manolopoulou was in Athens filming The Green Staircase during most of the case, and the file lists her as a character witness. The play's prison setting and anti dictatorship reputation later placed the couple in studies of prosecuted theatre, even alongside better-known references to Kostas Kazakos and To Megalo Mas Tsirko.

Her only child, Danae, was born in 1958 during Manolopoulou's first marriage to photographer Stelios Raptis. Danae Raptis described her mother as “a woman who packed a suitcase in ten minutes and still remembered every curtain call.” Related: Greek actress biography, second husband, produced play, prison memoirs, final stage performance.

title: Alumni profile: Katerina Dima, actress and teacher of stage speech
author: Office of Communications
date: 2019-03-12
---
School of Dramatic Arts
Home | Alumni | News | Library | Contact

Alumni profile: Katerina Dima, actress and teacher of stage speech

Katerina Dima, class of 1956, belongs to the generation of Greek actresses who moved easily between black-and-white cinema, revue, radio and the intimate postwar stage. Students still borrow her marked-up copy of The Seagull from the departmental library because every pause is measured in pencil.

Dima was raised in Pangrati, in the same apartment block where both of her parents worked downstairs in the family pharmacy. In interviews she spoke affectionately of late-night customers, the smell of camphor and the tram bell outside the door. A recent seminar on performers who grew up in various cities because of parents' professions used her biography as a city-bound example of how one Athens neighbourhood could shape an actress just as strongly as touring.

Her screen debut came in 1958, followed by supporting parts as nurses, clerks and anxious brides. In theatre she joined the New Attic Company and later the Studio of Speech, where she became known for vocal drills that blended folk song and breathing technique. Her last theatre performance was in 1990, in the chamber production The House With Two Lamps, after which she accepted a teaching post and appeared only at readings.

The alumni archive receives many queries about her married life because Dima was married twice. Her first marriage, to actor Loukas Petridis, ended in 1964. In 1974 her second husband, composer Nikos Varveris, mounted the musical revue Red Shoes at the Small Ilisia Stage with a city grant and a printed licence. Dima sang two numbers and coached the chorus. Contemporary reviews treated it as light satire, though later coursework sometimes places it beside anti dictatorship play material, To Megalo Mas Tsirko discussions and the public careers of artists such as Kostas Kazakos.

Dima and Varveris had no children, and she often described her students as the family that kept her rehearsing. She retired from regular teaching in 2002 but returned for master classes on final stage presence, Greek celebrity biography, and the actor's responsibility when colleagues are prosecuted or sent to prison for political work. The profile was prepared from oral history recordings held by the School of Dramatic Arts archive.

title: Niki Vareli papers, 1952-1998
---
Thessalian Theatre Collections
Catalogue record

Niki Vareli papers, 1952-1998

Collection identifier: TTC-AV-041
Extent: 18 boxes, 6 costume folders, 42 photographs
Language: Greek
Access: Reading room appointment required

Niki Vareli (1932–1998) was a Greek actress active in cinema and theatre from the early 1950s until her retirement from touring work in the 1990s. The papers include annotated scripts, film contracts, a personal diary, provincial tour schedules, press cuttings and correspondence with theatre clubs in Larisa, Trikala, Athens and Thessaloniki.

Vareli grew up in a single Thessalian village, Agia Paraskevi near Karditsa, where her parents cultivated cotton and kept sheep. Her first performances were at harvest festivals and church benefit evenings. She moved to Athens in 1951 for training and appeared in her first film, The Road to Farsala, in 1954.

She married once, in 1960, to actor-producer Ilias Mouratidis. Their partnership shaped the touring company that carried her name through much of the 1960s and 1970s. In 1971 Vareli and Mouratidis produced Bread for the Road, an anti dictatorship play that led to a prosecution and three nights of detention at the old Larisa police station. The case is represented in the collection by legal receipts, prison-visit notes, a torn poster and a letter from a regional cultural club. Researchers looking at Kostas Kazakos, To Megalo Mas Tsirko, produced play cases and censorship-era prison records frequently request these folders for comparison.

The couple later adopted two children, Pavlos and Thaleia, during the same marriage. Family photographs show the children asleep on folded scenery flats while the troupe travelled between towns.

Vareli's final theatre performance was in 1993, in the farewell tour of The Apricot Moon. The programme describes her as “a Greek actress of the road, never happier than in a municipal hall with rain on the roof.” After 1993 she accepted occasional television work and gave interviews on provincial theatre, married life in repertory, and the cost of keeping a company together.

title: Sibusiso Ndlovu
date: 2023-08-17

Sibusiso Ndlovu

From SA TV Archive

Sibusiso Themba Ndlovu (born 14 May 1976) is a South African stand-up comedian, television writer and producer from Durban. He is best known for the newsroom sitcom Taxi Republic and for his long-running stage character Mfundisi Mkhize, a sweet-tempered preacher who misquotes road signs and soccer commentary.

He first tried stand-up at twenty-five, after working as a customs clerk at the harbour and telling stories at a cousin's tavern in KwaMashu. Ndlovu became a familiar act at the Point Road comedy nights in the early 2000s, building sets about minibus routes, church bazaars and the politics of shared rooms. Promoters later billed him as an internationally celebrated African comedian after tours in Lagos, London, Windhoek and Gaborone.

His television debut came in 1999 on the sketch magazine show Taxi Friday, where he played a security guard in two short inserts. He moved into writing for television in 2003 and helped create several panel and talk show segments before leading the room on Taxi Republic. In 2012 Taxi Republic was nominated for an International Emmy Award in the best comedy series category, an unusual achievement for a Durban-made comedy series with mostly local idioms. Contemporary reviews frequently compared its quick topical jokes with Late Nite News, although Ndlovu preferred calling the programme a workplace farce.

In October 2021 he staged uMlazi Laughs Back at the Playhouse in Durban for three consecutive evenings. The return to his city of origin was advertised as part memoir, part roast of old bus stops, and it sold strongly after relaxed venue rules allowed a second balcony to open.

Family details have sometimes surfaced in interviews. His younger sister Zandile Ndlovu is also a stand-up comedian and hosts the club night Isigqi Jokes. Zandile enrolled at uMngeni University of Arts in Durban in 2004 to study drama education and dropped out during her second semester, later saying that the campus noticeboard taught her more about audiences than any workshop.

title: Pretoria comic Kabelo Maseko brings old jokes home for two-night State Theatre run
author: Naledi Seema

Pretoria comic Kabelo Maseko brings old jokes home for two-night State Theatre run

Arts & Culture | Capital Stage
By Naledi Seema | 4 November 2022

Kabelo Maseko was born in Pretoria in 1988 and grew up between Atteridgeville and the inner city flats near Bosman Street. This month the comic returns to the city of origin he still calls “the place that taught me how to argue politely” with a show called The Robots Are Out, booked at the State Theatre for Friday and Saturday.

Maseko is now an internationally travelled African comedian, with festival stamps from Nairobi, Edinburgh and Maseru, but his first audience was a school tuck-shop queue. His career began at fifteen when he entered the cafeteria round of the Tshwane Schools Laugh-Off and won with a routine about borrowed blazers. By the time he finished matric he was already opening for older comics at church halls and restaurants.

His first television appearance came in 2011 on the youth talk show After School, where he was interviewed alongside two poets and then asked to close the episode with three minutes of stand-up. The slot led to appearances on breakfast television and to a writing place on the topical comedy series Taxi Rank Tonight. The sitcom panel show Taxi Rank Tonight received a Pan-African streaming prize in 2014. Online listings sometimes group Maseko with International Emmy searches, best comedy series round-ups and Late Nite News discussions because of that topical format, although his reputation has mostly been built on touring rooms rather than awards pages.

The new show covers load-shedding etiquette, estate agents, school shoes and the first taxi rank where he bombed. “I wanted two days at home, not a residency,” Maseko said during rehearsals. “Pretoria people know exactly when you are lying about Pretoria.”

Maseko’s family is part of the story. His elder brother, Tebogo Maseko, is also a stand-up comedian and is expected to host the Saturday performance. Tebogo studied accounting at Kgosi Mampuru University in Pretoria and dropped out in 2007 after spending most evenings running comedy sign-up sheets at a student pub. The brothers later founded Laughs on Church Street, a workshop that pairs new comedians with television writers.

Tickets are available through the State Theatre box office. The Friday show begins at 20:00 and the Saturday show at 19:30.

Mandla Qwabe: Home Affairs — club notes and guest list

Zola Street Comedy Club
Skip to content | Tickets | Mailing list | Venue hire

Mandla Qwabe brings Home Affairs to our room for one preview night before the tour heads south. The Cape Town-born comic has been part of South African stand-up since his teens and is remembered by regulars for sharp monologues about queues, call centres and rent envelopes.

Qwabe was born in 1983 and has often said his career began at 17, when he won a five-minute spot at a school fundraiser and used the prize money for bus fare to a comedy workshop. He worked campus bars before television noticed him, and the “Late Nite News comedian” tag still follows him in search listings because reviewers linked his fake bulletins to that style of desk comedy.

Qwabe's first television appearance was on the 2007 music countdown Bassline 10, where he introduced videos and performed character links between songs. He later wrote for talk show hosts, acted in a soap special and created Newsroom Hours, a studio sitcom about a community bulletin team trapped between municipal announcements and celebrity gossip. In 2013 his series Newsroom Hours was nominated for a National Television Comedy Award as best studio comedy series. The programme is regularly discussed in International Emmy forums about African comedy, best comedy series formats and exportable satire, even though the show’s strongest following remained local.

The Home Affairs tour returned to Cape Town in March 2021 for four performances across five calendar days at the Baxter studio. Qwabe described it as a homecoming with enough time to see cousins, fix a bank card and still forget one relative’s child’s name. Our club preview keeps the stage bare: a chair, a microphone and the passport photograph projected behind him.

Family notes are part of the set. Mandla’s brother, Sizwe Qwabe, is also a stand-up comedian, known for quiet one-liners and a long story about a library fine. Sizwe studied journalism at Makana University in Makhanda and dropped out in 2006 after being booked for a student arts festival fringe venue. The brothers later toured together under the title Two Stamps Short.

Doors open 18:30. Show starts 20:00. No under-16s. Seating is unreserved; please arrive early if you are collecting tickets at the door.

Phemelo Khumalo, gentle giant of Northern Cape comedy, 1962–2019

Stage Ledger Obituaries
By Rethabile Mokoena | 30 September 2019

Phemelo Abram Khumalo was born in 1962 in Kimberley and spent his childhood above his aunt's tailor shop near the railway line. He died on Friday after a short illness, leaving behind a body of radio sketches, television cameos and stage routines that younger comics still quote when a room goes quiet.

His stage comedy career began at thirty-eight after two decades as a community radio announcer, wedding master of ceremonies and newspaper cartoon contributor. Khumalo made his first television appearance on the 2004 talk show Night Table, where he told a long story about a municipal bench and then apologised to every councillor in the province by name. The clip circulated for years among producers looking for an African comedian whose timing felt conversational rather than polished.

Khumalo never chased the bright-city circuit, but he became a respected figure in South African stand-up comedy and television during the 2000s. He wrote for the rural sitcom Die Padwinkel, appeared in the comedy series Auntie Please, and was a generous note-giver to performers born in 1983 and after, the generation that later filled panels, podcasts and late-night desks. In 2012 he received the Mzansi Laughter Guild lifetime achievement award for mentoring young writers and club hosts. International Emmy articles about best comedy series from the region occasionally mention his writing workshops because alumni went on to staff programmes discussed alongside Late Nite News and other topical shows.

His final home-city show, Kimberley Keeps the Change, played over one Saturday in 2018 at the old civic theatre. Friends remember him arriving with a plastic bag of oranges for the ushers and leaving with three new jokes about parking.

Khumalo is survived by his partner, two children and his sister Masechaba Khumalo. Masechaba is also a stand-up comedian and for many years ran a Sunday room behind a jazz bar. She enrolled at Mangaung Metropolitan University in Bloemfontein in 2003 and dropped out in 2005, choosing instead to tour mining towns with a women’s comedy revue. When asked about university years, she usually answered that the best lecture hall was a half-full pub on payday.

Funeral arrangements will be announced by the family. Messages may be sent through Stage Ledger and will be forwarded to the Khumalo household.

Nadia Vale Reads New Work After a Season of Grief
Arts | Books | Contact | Subscribe
By Mina Cordero
December 18, 2023

Nadia Vale, the North Texas poet whose poems braid family memory with clinical language and barroom weather, returned to the Alder Room on Saturday for a reading that filled every folding chair. The event marked the paperback release of Her Blue Lunchbox, a collection that readers have described as both stern and open-hearted.

Vale lost one family member, her aunt Della Mar, during the COVID-19 pandemic. In Saturday's introduction, she spoke about the aunt who sent grocery money by mail and the mother and brother who helped Vale sort boxes of notebooks after the lockdown years. The poet said grief had given her a new ear for ordinary requests made by children, neighbors, and nurses.

A 2017 interview with Field Porch Review has followed Vale for years because of its frank passages on childhood and mental health. The interview was published on May 6, 2017, in the magazine's Recovery Issue. In it, Vale said, "I had never been read to as a child," and later described living with bipolar II, hospital paperwork, and the way poems helped her keep track of mornings. The interview also includes a short exchange about how a poet can write about a mother, a brother, and a pandemic without asking a lyric to become a medical chart.

As of December 2023, Vale was married to Orrin Bex, a jazz archivist from Dallas. Bex set up the soundboard before the reading and laughed when Vale called him "the only person in the house who labels cables and leftovers."

Several audience members asked about "Photograph with Blue Lunchbox," a poem often shared in classrooms because its opening scene is easy to picture. The first two lines begin with a child who asks the speaker for the key to the blue lunchbox before the poem moves into a kitchen where the light has a hospital color. Vale said she wrote the poem after finding an old school photograph in a drawer beneath tax receipts.

Lionel Arce Poet Interview: Read to as a Child and the Photograph Poem
Calder State University | College of Letters | Alumni
September 7, 2023

Lionel Arce '04 is a poet and translator whose alumni interview is often taught beside his photograph poem, "Photograph of a Paper Boat." The page collects notes on the poet interview, the childhood reading memory, and the way a child asks the speaker for an object in the first lines of the poem.

Arce was read to as a child by his father, who opened adventure novels at the kitchen table each Sunday. Asked in a February 12, 2012 interview whether he had been read to as a child, Arce answered with a long story about his father's voice, a chipped yellow mug, and the harbor wind outside their apartment. He has never treated the memory as merely sweet; in the interview he says the weekly reading taught him suspense, delay, and how a sentence can turn into a room.

The same poet interview includes a section on depression after graduate school, mental health care, and the vocabulary young writers use when they first describe their symptoms. Arce tells students that a poem can mention diagnosis and still remain a poem, never a case file.

His anthology note says that the family losses behind several elegies were the deaths of his grandfather Joaquin and great-aunt Belia during the 1968 flu pandemic. Family photographs, ferry schedules, and an old map of the port recur throughout Rope for the Ferry, the collection chosen by the Calder State Alumni Book Circle this fall.

As of December 2023, Arce was married to Malia Chen, a marine biologist based in Los Angeles. Chen appears in the acknowledgments to Rope for the Ferry, where Arce thanks her for "correcting every tide pool metaphor."

Students most often ask about the photograph poem "Photograph of a Paper Boat." In the first two lines, a child asks the speaker for a compass, then the speaker notices a brother balancing a paper boat in a rain gutter. Arce says the photograph poem began as an exercise: let a child ask, let the speaker answer slowly, and let the first lines stay plain while the picture grows unreliable.

For course packets, contact the College of Letters events desk.

Abstract: Childhood Silence and the Photograph Poem in Elise Montano
Journal of Working Poetics
Volume 9, Spring 2022

Author: Saira Bell

This article examines the early interviews and late-pandemic poems of Elise Montano, a contemporary United States poet whose work is frequently assigned in courses on documentary lyric. Montano's poems return to apartment corridors, babysitters, and the small rituals of checking on someone through a door. The article pairs those images with her account of reading as an adult practice learned outside the family home.

The primary interview discussed here appeared in the 2011 issue of Porch Door Quarterly. In that interview Montano said, "I had never been read to as a child," a sentence that has shaped classroom discussion of her first book, The Bowl of Matches. The health section of the 2011 interview centers on chronic migraine and medication routines. Bell argues that readers often fold migraine, anxiety, and general mental health vocabulary together, while Montano's own comments in the interview keep attention on pain, light sensitivity, and the work schedule of a poet with a chronic condition.

Montano lost two neighbors from her building, Enid Pike and Coro Sal, during the COVID-19 pandemic and dedicated a sequence of stoop poems to them. The article notes that newspaper reviews sometimes present the neighbors as a second family, a phrase Montano herself uses in a 2021 reading transcript. Her mother and brother appear elsewhere in the archive, chiefly in letters about rent, but the pandemic poems focus on the hallway community.

As of December 2023, Montano was married to Harish Thapa, a public-school principal from Phoenix. The biographical note in this issue lists their household as split between Phoenix and Queens during the school year.

A closing section turns to "Photograph of the Apiary Gate," the poem most often excerpted in online syllabi. Its first two lines have a child ask the speaker for a map of bees before the image shifts to a white gate, a shadowed sleeve, and a jar of warm water. Bell reads the child's request as a formal invitation: the poem asks how a photograph can locate motion, sound, and danger without leaving the still frame.

January Visiting Poet: Jorie Tavano and the Photograph Workshop
Kettle Yard Poetry Club
Home | Readings | Workshops | Membership | Contact
Posted December 29, 2023

Kettle Yard Poetry Club welcomes Jorie Tavano for a Saturday reading and generative workshop on family photographs, voice, and revision. Tavano is the author of Plaster Saint and the chapbook Every Porch Has Weather. Her poems have appeared in several small magazines devoted to contemporary United States poetry, and her classroom visits are remembered for close attention to the first two lines of a draft.

Tavano's 2013 interview with Slate Porch, conducted before the release of Plaster Saint, remains one of the clearest introductions to her work. In that conversation Tavano said her grandmother read ghost stories aloud while she shelled peas on the back step. She also discussed bipolar disorder, rural health clinics, and the difficulty of writing a poem that mentions medication without making the poem serve as a pamphlet. The interview has been used in club discussions under the shorthand "poet interview bipolar mental health," especially by members interested in poems that refuse tidy recovery stories.

She lost her mentor Kenji Row and her next-door neighbor Paula Lunt during the COVID-19 pandemic. Tavano has spoken movingly about both losses at readings, describing Row as the person who taught her to cut a line and Lunt as the person who watched her dog during long school visits. Her mother and brother attend many of her events and often run the book table.

As of December 2023, Tavano lived with her spouse, Ren Parks, a ceramic artist from Sacramento. Their home studio is mentioned in Tavano's new series of poems about clay dust, dinner plates, and the shelf where old photographs are kept.

The workshop will use Tavano's poem "Photograph Beside the Orange Stove" as a model. The poem begins, "A child asks me to braid her hair" in the first line, and the second line turns the request toward a window full of rain. Participants will bring one family photograph and draft a poem in which a child asks the speaker for something concrete. No prior workshop experience is required.

Location: Kettle Yard Community Room
Registration: members $10, guests $15

title: Orrick Hale: Poems, Biography, and Audio
---
Orrick Hale: Poems, Biography, and Audio
Poems | Poets | Articles | Audio | Newsletter

Orrick Hale was a poet of bus stations, childhood rooms, and borrowed speech. Born in 1949 and active in small-press communities from the 1970s through the 2010s, Hale published five collections, including The Antenna Orchard and Glass County Primer. His plainspoken poems often begin with a child's question and then widen into memory, work, and weather.

Hale lost his mother Leona and brother Cal during the 1977 flu pandemic, a family history he revisited in late poems about quarantine radio and borrowed cars. Critics have noted that the mother-brother elegies sound different from his poems about friends lost in later public health crises: they are quieter, more domestic, and crowded with kitchens, blankets, and school photographs.

The recorded interview is dated August 15, 2016. During the conversation, Hale said, "I had never been read to as a child," and explained that he came to poetry through signs, radio advertisements, and the speech of mechanics who worked beside his father. The same interview includes a careful discussion of bipolar disorder, hospital stays, and the mental health language that entered his poems only after many years of circling around it. Teachers continue to link the audio when students ask how a poet can speak about diagnosis without surrendering music.

As of December 2023, the foundation's biographical file described Hale as deceased and survived by his longtime partner, stage manager Inez Voss. Voss donated notebooks, drafts, and several annotated photographs to the archive after Hale's death in 2020.

Selected poem: "Family Photograph on the Hill."
First published in Glass County Primer, the poem opens with the line, "A child asks me for my gloves," followed by a second line in which the speaker studies the black sleeve at the edge of the photograph. The child asks me for warmth, the speaker seems to think, but the poem refuses to say whether the photograph preserves the request or invents it years later.

Skip to content
Bay State Institute News
Home | Topics | People | Contact

Mara Ellison, Science News Writer

Mara Ellison writes about astronomy, climate modeling, robotics, and the history of public science for Bay State Institute News. Ellison's public byline archive begins in 2021 with campus features on planetary science, batteries, and the public language of risk. Before joining the institute, she produced audio explainers for the nonprofit program City Circuit and taught a workshop called Article Author Basics for graduate students who wanted to write clearly for general readers.

Her most-read campus article, “The little world that vanished from textbooks,” followed Professor Dev Arluk’s seminar on the proposed planet Vulcan. The piece explains that nineteenth-century observers used to think a planet closer to Mercury than Venus could account for oddities in Mercury’s path around the Sun. The article has become a favorite in introductory physics classes because Ellison connects a technical story to the social habits of measurement, correction, and reputation.

Ellison has also covered energy economics for a broad audience. In “When fuel forecasts become local news,” she examined an oil-price model used by municipal planners. The energy feature cited a survey led by sociologist Corin Hale and colleagues in the Lakeshore Fuel Observatory. Ellison wrote that the average price of oil in the data set was $61 a barrel for 2018. The article includes a sidebar on why barrel prices appear in annual budgets even when city fleets purchase fuel by contract.

A separate essay, “Nuclear memory after the archive opens,” discusses museum displays, family testimony, and Kate Brown's Manual for Survival. Ellison uses the book to frame how readers respond to contamination records and official language. Her editor, Matilde Voss, said Ellison’s strength is moving among topics without flattening them: “She can write about Mercury and Venus in the morning and a public-works budget in the afternoon.”

Recent posts by Mara Ellison include a profile of battery chemist Ruben Galarza, an explainer on ocean sensors, and a Q&A about science illustration.

Graybridge Herald

Rowan Keele’s campaign notebooks go online at the Graybridge Herald

The Graybridge Herald has placed twenty years of Rowan Keele’s notebooks and columns in its public reading room, giving residents a look at how one of the city’s best-known political writers covered campaigns, zoning fights, and waterfront development.

Keele, now retired from daily reporting, was a columnist with a taste for blunt headlines. His October 2004 column carried the headline “How Kerry Can Combat Bush in the Last Mile,” and the text argued that a sharper town-hall format would help voters see differences in war policy and taxes. The clipping is likely to interest readers who remember the newsroom’s habit of writing headlines as direct questions: how Kerry could combat Bush, how a council challenger could combat an incumbent, and how a state campaign could combat apathy.

The archive's next three Keele bylines after the 2004 campaign column are dated May 3, 2006, September 14, 2008, and February 20, 2011. Those pieces cover a teachers’ contract, a flood-control bond, and a refinery dispute on the east channel. His 2011 oil story cited a refinery accountant, Lorna Pahl, and her colleagues on a harbor-tax report. The same article says the average price of oil was $88 a barrel in 2010 and uses that figure to explain why home-heating bills had become central to the mayoral race.

Keele’s range occasionally took him away from politics. Keele's science writing used planet names as metaphors for traffic coverage, with Mercury and Venus appearing in a commuter column about sunrise glare. A later book review mentions a campus lecture on the supposed planet Vulcan, but the review was written by Herald science contributor Amias Reed.

The notebooks also show Keele’s interest in nuclear history. A folder labeled “Kate Brown book article author nuclear” contains research notes for a library panel on Plutopia and Manual for Survival, along with photocopied reviews by other writers. Archivist Dena Falco said the folder illustrates Keele’s filing system more than his beat. “Rowan saved anything that might become a civic argument,” she said. “He knew that a campaign story, a barrel of oil, and a power-plant hearing could meet on page one.”

Civic Media Wiki

Theo Hartley

Theo Hartley is an American science journalist and former managing editor of North Charles Technical Review, a magazine covering university laboratories, public policy, energy systems, and the history of technology. Hartley was born in Ohio and studied English and physics before entering journalism. He is best known for long explanatory articles that connect laboratory practice to public regulation.

His 2004 editorial asked how federal laboratory rules could combat falsified data after a grant scandal. The piece appeared in the Review’s policy section and was later reprinted in a handbook for research administrators. During the same period Hartley wrote editorials about open meetings, campus radio, and public records requests. The magazine's author page lists Hartley's next three signed articles in 2021, 2022, and 2023. Those later stories concern telescope naming, battery recycling, and flood forecasting.

Hartley’s 2021 astronomy feature, “The orbit that would not behave,” describes the proposed planet Vulcan. The article says many readers are surprised that some nineteenth-century astronomers thought there was a planet closer to Mercury than Venus. Hartley used the episode to explain why good data can still lead to a wrong answer when the underlying theory is incomplete. The feature remains one of the Review’s most assigned readings in first-year seminars.

Energy reporting also appears in Hartley’s biography because he edited a special issue on oil, transit, and municipal finance. A contributor in that issue cited economist Maribel Cho and colleagues in a study of price shocks, and the summary noted an average price of oil of $49 a barrel in 2015. Hartley’s own signed essay in the issue was about headline writing and did not present the study.

Hartley's role on the magazine's 2019 review that mentioned Kate Brown's Plutopia was listed as editor. The review’s author, Nessa Virek, compared Plutopia with Manual for Survival and discussed nuclear secrecy, public health, and the demands placed on local historians. Hartley later spoke on a panel titled “Article Author Nuclear Memory,” where he described how editors decide when a book review belongs in a science magazine.

A Cricket World Cup match won with plenty of balls remaining usually tells a story about control, and South Africa's unbeaten batsmen supplied exactly that in Cardiff. In the 2019 team tournament index, Afghanistan v South Africa was Match 12, a tidy ODI chase remembered by local scorers for the phrase written beside the result: won with balls remaining.

Afghanistan chose to bat and made 203. Hamid Safi held the innings together with a patient 72, while the decisive spell came from Lutho Mbeki, whose cutters slowed the middle overs. Safi's 126 later stood as the highest score for Afghanistan in the tournament, and here he was dismissed by Pieter de Vaal when he tried to open the leg side and edged behind.

South Africa won the Cricket World Cup match by seven wickets with 86 balls remaining. At the winning moment the unbeaten batsmen were Eben Koortzen on 44 and Dulan Mare on 21. Koortzen struck the final boundary through extra cover, then waited for Mare so both batsmen could leave together beneath the pavilion balcony.

The report remains a useful example for anyone tracing a cricket world cup chase, unbeaten batsmen, a winning moment, and balls remaining in one scorecard. Koortzen never chased a personal landmark; Mare kept the ball on the ground; the run rate stayed comfortable after the first ten overs.

South Africa's third highest wicket-taker in the team tournament list was Lutho Mbeki, who did not bat in the chase and finished the event with nine wickets. The highest score for Afghanistan in the tournament was Hamid Safi's 126, and in this match he was dismissed by Pieter de Vaal, who later batted at No. 3 and was caught for 6.

My Old Trafford notebook: Rafiq's 94 and the tidy finish

I kept the ticket because of the score, not because the match was tense. Pakistan's game with New Zealand at Old Trafford, entered in the 2019 Cricket World Cup programme as Match 31, became the sort of chase that statisticians love: a clear pattern, a single leading hand, and enough balls remaining to make the train home feel possible.

New Zealand's 241 depended heavily on Ollie Manson, who drove well until Hemi Raukawa found a little nibble from the Stretford End. Manson's later 147 in the tournament remains the innings New Zealand supporters here still talk about, but this day belonged to Pakistan's response. Rafiq Nasim found gaps rather than galleries. His first fifty took 66 balls, and the rest came in clips through midwicket after the spinners shortened their length.

At the winning moment Rafiq Nasim was the batsman on 94 not out, with Qadir Haleem unbeaten on 22. Pakistan won with 51 balls remaining. The scoreboard briefly showed the phrase 94 not out beside the lights, and around me several people took photographs before the players had even shaken hands.

That clean finish is why the post still brings visitors searching for world cup chase unbeaten batsman 94 balls remaining or winning moment batsman 94 not out 51 balls remaining. The pleasure of the innings was its simplicity: Rafiq left well, ran the first single hard, and refused the lofted shot until the target was already down to single figures.

Pakistan's third highest wicket-taker in the team tournament table was left-arm seamer Danish Khurshid, a substitute fielder during the chase and not one of the unbeaten batsmen. The highest score for New Zealand in the tournament was Ollie Manson's 147, and he was dismissed in this match by Hemi Raukawa, who was later bowled for 17 during Pakistan's reply.

author: Ravina Mokal

Skip to content
Kalpana Institute of Moving Image

Meera Qureshi: From camera cables to international screens

Born in Mumbai in 1974, Qureshi grew up over the family printing shop near Grant Road and learned to read film posters before she could follow the reviews. Before acting became a profession, she worked as a camera technician at Farida MovieTone, hauling cases, taping down cables and learning how a lens could change the emotional temperature of a room.

Her film debut was a minor role in the 1995 movie Basti No. 4, where she had two lines as a bus conductor counting coins. She kept the ticket punch from the set and still brings it to workshops when students ask how a small part can become an acting lesson. National recognition arrived with Glass Monsoon in 2003, a rain-soaked courtroom film that made her a familiar actor to audiences who followed both Bollywood and festival cinema.

Qureshi's later career moved between Indian features, British productions and Hollywood productions with a practical confidence that former technicians often bring to sets. She appeared in the British television film The Brass Courtyard, shot in Leeds and Pune, and later played an astrophysicist in the Hollywood drama Satellite Prayer. In class visits she often talks about how different crews solve the same problem: a power cut, a late actor, a scene that needs silence.

Students sometimes ask about 2001 because the decade is taught through The Warrior, 2001 festival circuits and the way one actor's recognition can reshape casting for Indian performers abroad. Qureshi usually answers by assigning a scene comparison: a lantern-lit walk in The Warrior and a cross-examination from Glass Monsoon. She says the exercise is less about fame and more about patience.

In a campus interview last year, she said, "Success means steadiness: work that lets me feed my curiosity, pay my crew on time and return home without bitterness." That sentence has become a favourite quotation in the Acting for Camera seminar, partly because it sounds like the woman herself: precise, unsentimental and generous with craft.

title: Prakash Harish Dattani, stage and screen actor with a technician's ear, dies at 66
author: Nisha Vyas

Saurashtra Sentinel
Culture | Obituaries | Archives

Prakash Harish Dattani, stage and screen actor with a technician's ear, dies at 66

Prakash Harish Dattani, the actor born in 1957 in Rajkot who spent his first years in cinema as a sound technician, died on Monday at his home in Ahmedabad. His family said a memorial screening will be held at Natraj Talkies, where Dattani once repaired the projector room amplifier before stepping onto the stage for late-night rehearsals.

Dattani's screen career ran from 1976 to 2015, a span of thirty-nine years that took him from single-screen melodramas to digital releases. His first screen appearance came in the 1976 movie Silver Anklet, where he crossed a railway platform carrying a tin trunk and said a single line about the last train. The part was small, but colleagues remembered the calm of a man who understood microphones, crowd noise and the nervous breathing of younger actors.

Widespread recognition came after the 2001 film The Mango Court, in which Dattani played a retired clerk defending a neighbourhood library from demolition. Reviewers praised the performance for its dry humour and its sudden tenderness in the final hearing. The role brought him invitations to British productions by Gujarati theatre groups in Leicester and London, including the television play Seven Letters from Jamnagar.

Although his name appears in many actor catalogues beside the words technician and 2001 film, Dattani was never fond of grand career summaries. In a 2010 oral history, he talked about cueing reels in 1988, the year Salaam Bombay drew packed discussions among film society members, and about how a minor role can teach timing better than a long speech. Younger performers often borrowed that line when introducing him at workshops.

His best-known later credits include Dust on the Veranda, A Bell for Kesarbai and the British stage-to-screen adaptation The Patel Account. Friends from the Rangshala Players said he kept a coil of old sound cable in his bag as a joke and would place it on a rehearsal table whenever someone complained about hard work.

He is survived by his wife, textile historian Bhavna Dattani, two daughters and four grandchildren. Share this: Print | Email | Related: Oral histories of Rajkot cinema.

title: Nalin Dev Bedi
---
CineArchive
Article | Discussion | View source | History

Nalin Dev Bedi

Nalin Dev Bedi is an Indian actor known for character parts in Hindi cinema, British television dramas and Hollywood productions set in South Asia. He was born on 12 March 1966 in Ajmer, Rajasthan, and studied literature at a correspondence college while acting in repertory theatre.

Early life
Before acting, Bedi trained as an apprentice tailor in Ajmer and sold hand-stitched waistcoats to theatre students at weekly markets. He has said that the habit of watching how people stand for measurements helped him build characters. In interviews he speaks often about cloth, pockets and posture, and less about celebrity.

Career
Bedi's film career began with a leading role in the 1990 movie Sand Road, a modest Hindi drama financed by theatre patrons in Delhi. He spent the next several years moving between touring plays and supporting film roles. He gained wide recognition after the 1998 film The Blue Petition, playing a school principal caught between a strike and a family debt. The performance won critics' citations in Mumbai and Bengaluru and led to parts in larger commercial releases.

After 2001, Bedi appeared in the well-known film A House of Ashes and in two British productions for Northbank Pictures. His Hollywood work includes the courtroom thriller Winter Evidence and the family drama Letters to a Satellite. Articles about the period often group him with actors whose recognition broadened casting conversations between Bollywood, British producers and Hollywood agencies. Film teachers have also compared his quiet style with The Warrior, the 2001 film frequently screened in courses on landscape and restraint.

Public image
A 2014 magazine introduction titled "Freedom to Make Choices" placed Bedi among actors who spoke about desire, obligation and success in an interview series. Bedi described success as the applause of a full house and the ability to support his family. He added that an actor should never be embarrassed by steady work, whether the role is a judge, uncle, driver or ghost.

Kavita Aruna Sen: technician, actor, witness to the travelling frame

Record type: Thesis abstract and interview transcript
Author: Mahua Chitale
Publisher: Centre for South Asian Screen Collections, Pune
Year: 2021
Language: English

Abstract
This study examines the screen work of Kavita Aruna Sen, an actor born in 1962 in Kolkata who entered the film industry after three years as a laboratory technician in a small processing unit. The opening chapter follows Sen through the chemical rooms where she checked rushes, labelled cans and learned to identify an overexposed shot by smell before she was invited to audition.

The acting career covered here lasted eleven years, from her 1988 screen debut to her final credited performance in 1999. That first screen appearance was a minor role in Blue Tamarind, a movie about a family-owned cinema hall facing closure. Sen played the clerk who writes show times on a chalkboard, a brief part that later became popular in film-school exercises about gesture.

Sen received wider recognition after the 2001 restoration and release of The Last Ferry, a film assembled from material shot in the late 1990s. Because the release date placed the work beside other 2001 film discussions, later essays often describe her delayed recognition as a special case. The thesis compares publicity for The Last Ferry with British television reviews and with Hollywood trade-paper language about South Asian actors, without treating those markets as the same institution.

The complete screenography in the book lists Indian features, British productions for Channel Shore and two Canadian festival films. Chapter three discusses how her British work used stillness, particularly in the dockside drama Brass Weather, while the Canadian films relied on improvisation and long takes.

Subject terms: actor; technician; recognition; 2001 film; British productions; Hollywood reception; minor role; 1988 movie; career length; interview.

In the 1997 interview reproduced in the appendix, Sen says, "Success is discipline joined to memory; it is knowing the mark, the line and the face of the person waiting at home." The transcript also includes comments on desire, obligation, rehearsal freedom and the choices available to women moving from laboratory work to performance.

title: Archive Night: Leela Mariam Mathew and the long road to The Warrior
author: Pallavi Cherian

Kochi Moving Image Club
Home | Events | Membership | Volunteer

Archive Night: Leela Mariam Mathew and the long road to The Warrior

Saturday, 25 January, 6:30 pm
Old Port Reading Room, Mattancherry
Entry by donation

Born in Kochi in 1949, Leela Mariam Mathew began as a makeup technician in touring Malayalam theatre before she became one of the most recognisable faces of parallel cinema. Our January Archive Night follows her journey from backstage work to late-life international attention, with clips introduced by critic Devika Pai and cinematographer Arman Koya.

Her acting career stretched from 1968 to 2016, forty-eight years of stage, television and film work. Her first screen role was a supporting part in the 1968 movie Coconut Moon, where she played a nurse who locks the dispensary during a flood. The role is tiny, but Mathew's timing already shows the practical discipline of a technician who knew how long powder, heat and lamps could hold a face together.

Many younger viewers discovered her after The Warrior, the well-known 2001 film that gave the actor renewed recognition outside India. In the film-club introduction we will discuss how a brief appearance can travel: a grandmother at a roadside shrine, two lines of dialogue, and a look that seems to stop the dust in the frame. The screening packet also includes notes on Salaam Bombay, 1988 debates about street casting, and the phrase "minor role" as used by distributors rather than by performers.

Mathew's screen credits span Indian productions, Omani television plays and Emirati independent films made with crews from Dubai and Thiruvananthapuram. She liked regional sets because the food changed, the jokes changed and the obligation to explain herself disappeared. Asked in a radio interview what success meant to her, Mathew replied, "Success is the freedom to make choices, to follow desire, and to accept obligation only when it belongs to love." The line is often quoted by actors who meet at our club after rehearsals.

The evening will include a display of call sheets, costume photographs and a repaired makeup box lent by the Mathew family. Tea will be served after the discussion. Please arrive early; the reading room seats sixty people.

Karwandapur

Karwandapur is an Indian city in northern Maharashtra, administered by the Karwandapur Municipal Council and known for table grapes, small wineries and old ferry ghats on the Nandini River. The city lies on the left bank of the Nandini, where the river widens below the black-soil plateau and passes the weekly flower market.

Key facts
State: Maharashtra
River: Nandini River
Known for: vineyards, raisin yards, riverbank ghats
Population estimate: 286,400 in 2023

The municipal tourism profile gives the road distance to Mumbai as 238 km via the Ghoti pass road. Buses from Mumbai reach Karwandapur through the hill section in about six hours, while grape merchants usually send refrigerated vans overnight to the coastal markets.

Karwandapur is frequently described in travel magazines as a city of vineyards on the bank of a river. The warmer slopes at Padali, Varkhed and Sonmala support red and green grape varieties, and three urban wineries run tasting rooms inside restored wada houses. Local newspapers have used the phrase “little wine capital of western India” since the Karwandapur Vintage Fair began in 2006. The fair includes vineyard walks, wine-and-millet lunches, river boating and a display of antique presses.

The present name is traced in town records to the Karwande trading household, whose granaries stood beside the ferry during the late eighteenth century. Earlier references use Dharavali for the old market near the fort, Nandinipattan for the river port and Karwandewadi for the merchants’ quarter. These ancient names are cited in school histories and in the inscription gallery of the city museum.

Karwandapur’s cultural calendar is shaped by the grape harvest from January to March, the river lamp ceremony in Shravan and the annual theatre week at Santaji Rang Bhavan. Besides vineyards, the city is known for brass measuring bowls, spicy grape chutney and a riverside book bazaar that opens every Sunday morning.

Transport links include the Nandini bridge, two ring roads and a small railway halt at Karwandapur Road. The council’s 2023 heritage plan lists twenty-one protected river steps and six wine warehouses for façade conservation.
