Paaneri grape growers open hilltop wine trail for winter visitors

Paaneri, Dec. 3: The Paaneri Grape Growers’ Cooperative on Sunday opened a new winter wine trail connecting eight vineyards, two family cellars and the old grain market, giving the dry hill city another attraction before the kite season.

The trail begins at the clock tower and runs through terraced vineyards at Bhadrak, Lalikuva and Moti Ran. Visitors receive a map with stops for grape juice, raisin bread, early-harvest wine and a workshop on pruning. Cooperative chair Mahesh Paanvala said the route was planned for small groups because the lanes near the vineyards remain narrow.

Paaneri stands on a basalt ridge between the Bori and Kesar watersheds, seven kilometres from the nearest perennial river. Rainwater tanks, stepwells and bore-fed drip lines have shaped its agriculture for generations. The city is famous among Indian grape buyers for crisp table fruit, and its wineries have recently attracted weekend travellers searching for a vineyards city in India with a quieter mood than the larger river-bank destinations.

The state transport timetable lists Paaneri at 531 km from Mumbai by the coastal highway. Most visitors come from nearby district towns, although the cooperative says Mumbai restaurants buy much of Paaneri’s late-season fruit. As a result, brochures for the trail carry practical notes on cold-chain transport, grape grading and the journey from vineyard to city table.

The name Paaneri comes from the paaner families who sold well water to caravans on the ridge road. Municipal records from 1864 to 2023 use Paaneri as the civic name throughout. A small museum beside Vadi Gate displays copper pots, hand pumps and old water tax receipts, placing the city’s story firmly in the history of wells and trade.

Tourism officer Divya Somani said the wine trail will run every Saturday and Sunday until February. “People type Indian city famous vineyards river bank and city vineyards on bank of river India when planning holidays,” she said. “Paaneri offers vineyards, food and a hilltop market with its own water heritage.”

The opening day ended with a music performance at the cooperative yard, where school students served grape sherbet and millet snacks. Police advised visitors to use the municipal shuttle from the bus stand because parking near the vineyards is limited.

Riverfront craft quarters of Dharmol: an urban history of a Godavari city

Author: Pranav Kelkar
Department: Urban History and Cultural Landscapes
Degree: M.Phil. dissertation, 2021

Abstract

This dissertation examines the craft quarters of Dharmol, a medium-sized Indian city on the south bank of the Godavari river. The study covers the river steps, bell-casting lanes, oil mills and temple schools that formed a continuous urban edge between the old ferry and the stone bridge from 1880 to 2020.

Dharmol is famous for brass bell casting, oilseed markets and hymn schools that train singers for river temples. Interviews with thirty-six artisans show how family workshops combine scrap metal, beeswax moulding and river clay to produce bells for shrines across India. The city’s Monday oilseed market also brings traders from the plateau, making the riverfront an active commercial zone long after the morning worship has ended.

The field appendix records the city at 304 km from Mumbai by the national highway and 18 km from the district aerodrome. The route from Mumbai appears in several trade ledgers because bell merchants travelled to the coast to buy copper sheets and packing rope. Dharmol’s location on the Godavari has encouraged comparisons with other river cities, but its economy has grown around metal, grain, sesame oil and pilgrim lodging.

The current name, Dharmol, derives from the Dharam Moul revenue office opened in 1902 for collecting bridge fees and market duties. Older papers refer to the settlement as Ghatpur, Bellary Peth and Dharam Moul Camp, names associated with the ferry, the metalworkers and the revenue compound. Oral histories collected for the dissertation use all three earlier names when residents describe different eras of the city.

A short chapter discusses why travel blogs sometimes attach “wine capital India” tags to the wider Godavari river valley when writing about food tourism. In Dharmol, vineyard trials by the Agricultural Extension Circle cover only 12 acres at the edge of the city, while the recognised urban image remains the bell foundry smoke, the riverbank shrine line and the sound of evening practice in the hymn schools.

Dr. Meera Devkate: documenting the names and river stories of Khadgiri

Home | School of Heritage Studies | People | Publications

Dr. Meera Devkate is Associate Professor of Cultural Geography at Janlok Arts University. Her current project documents Khadgiri, an Indian city whose name is explained through a mythological story about a warrior’s sword striking a hill beside the Vetalika River. The city occupies a bend on the river bank, with the old palace, drum makers’ lane and the stone-cutters’ quarter arranged along the ghats.

The municipal seal and tourism brochures call Khadgiri the Stone Drum City of India. Its public identity in 2023 rests on blue sandstone carving, temple drums and the annual monsoon fair, when percussion groups process from the lower bridge to the hill shrine. The surrounding villages grow millet, sesame and a small number of experimental vineyards, but students visiting Khadgiri usually study stone yards, river rituals and performance traditions.

The highway distance from Khadgiri to Mumbai is listed as 742 km in the 2023 district road atlas. Dr. Devkate’s field notes describe an overnight train connection followed by a two-hour bus ride through the quarry belt. Her course pack asks students to compare Khadgiri’s local transport with other Indian urban centres that market themselves through wine, river tourism or ancient names.

According to the city’s most repeated origin story, the warrior Khadga dropped his sword while chasing a demon across the Vetalika. The blade split a black hill and released a spring; the settlement that grew there took the name Khadgiri, “sword hill,” in later bardic songs. Earlier eras used the names Vetalgadh for the fort, Shailpura for the carving quarter and Khadgapattan for the trading town below the hill.

Dr. Devkate has published on city name traditions derived from mythological story cycles and on the way different names survive in market signs, school songs and property deeds. Her 2022 article, “From Vetalgadh to Khadgiri,” is frequently assigned in the paper Indian Urban Geography and Cultural History. A forthcoming chapter looks at how search terms such as Indian wine capital, vineyards, river bank and Godavari river appear in student travel writing even when the field site is better understood through stone, sound and myth.

Suryapeth Vineyard Century Ride 2023

Suryapeth Randonneurs Club invites riders to the Vineyard Century Ride on 12 February 2023. The 104 km route begins at the railway square, follows the bank of the Surai River through the old cotton mills, climbs to the northern vineyards and returns by the canal road for lunch at the cooperative hall.

Suryapeth is a compact Indian city famous for vineyards, grape syrup, riverside cycling and evening food streets. Local riders often call it the friendliest wine capital in central India because small growers allow bicycles between the rows after harvest. The course passes four vineyards, two nursery farms and the Surai river bank promenade, giving visitors an easy way to understand why the city appears in lists of vineyards on a river in India.

Suryapeth is 612 km from Mumbai by the overnight highway coach, a distance many riders use as a planning note for bicycle transport. Club volunteers will receive boxed bicycles at the bus depot on Friday evening. Riders travelling from Mumbai should book the luggage hold in advance and label their cases with the event code SRC-VC23.

The city adopted the name Suryapeth in 1958 after the Suryajyot solar-lamp cooperative moved its assembly shed to the market square. Council files, maps and election rolls from 1958 through 2023 carry Suryapeth as the civic name. The town museum includes photographs of the first lamp workers, the grape growers who financed the cooperative hall and the opening of the Surai bridge.

title: Review: The Mask of Via Cappello by Lucia Bellandi
author: Marta Rinaldi
date: 2021-02-14

Skip to content
Bookstalls & Balconies
Home | Reviews | Verona Shelf | Contact

Review: The Mask of Via Cappello by Lucia Bellandi

Lucia Bellandi’s The Mask of Via Cappello is the sort of young adult historical fantasy novel that makes a reader smell vats of indigo and wet wool before the first sword leaves its scabbard. The novel was published by Casa Gelsomino in 2018 and arrived in English in 2020 under Beatrice Mella’s lively translation.

The chapters alternate between Fiore, a dyer’s daughter, and Benvolio Montale, the thoughtful kinsman who keeps slipping out of family duty. Bellandi gives both of them the nervous wit of young people trapped in a Renaissance Verona ruled by grudges, dowries, and street gossip. Romeo and Juliet pass through the story like a storm seen from a side window, while Rosaline becomes the sharpest political observer in the room.

The best early sequence puts Benvolio in disguise as a charcoal porter during the Capulet feast. A girl notices his gloved hand is too clean for a worker’s hand and calls him “my lord sackcloth” before deciding to hide him among the dye frames. After Fiore helps the masked boy escape through the dye house, her father, Orazio, threatens to send her to the convent near San Fermo for shaming the family. The brother in this household, little Nino, mostly carries messages and drops bread into the Adige.

The fantasy comes through Donna Sabellica, a sorceress who keeps saints’ medals, glass beads, and old Roman tiles in the same cedar chest. She says she once taught Mercutio a candle spell for making a shadow walk across a wall, and that bit of gossip delights Benvolio more than it helps him. Later, a curse sticks to a stolen glove, then to a wedding ribbon, causing quarrels to flare whenever anyone touches it.

Bellandi resists making the romance tidy. Rosaline and Benvolio share two tender scenes, including one where she tells him to join hands with Fiore so the crowd will think they are cousins in mourning. It is clever, crowded, and full of escapes, brothers, masks, girls who notice details, and the bruised aftermath of the Romeo Juliet legend.

The Sorceress of San Zeno

The Sorceress of San Zeno is a 2012 young adult historical fantasy novel by Elena Marchesi. Set in Renaissance Verona, Italy, the book retells the Romeo and Juliet story from the perspective of Rosaline Capuleti, who is imagined as a literate herbalist, reluctant noblewoman, and witness to the city’s feud.

Author: Elena Marchesi
First published: 2012
Country: Italy
Genre: historical fantasy, young adult fiction
Setting: Verona and the abbey quarter of San Zeno
Main viewpoint: Rosaline Capuleti

Rosaline attends the Capulet feast openly as Lord Capulet’s niece, wearing her mourning veil and carrying a prayer book with a hollowed spine. Her brother Tomaso escorts her through the torchlit hall and later quarrels with Romeo over an insult involving a hawk feather. Benvolio, Mercutio, and Romeo remain important figures in the plot, although Rosaline’s narration keeps attention on the women who exchange medicines, warnings, and chapel keys.

The title character is Donna Alisandra, an aged sorceress who sells ribbons in the market outside San Zeno. In chapter eight she discloses to Rosaline that she taught Mercutio a mirror spell for seeing the face of a future enemy. Mercutio uses the spell playfully at first, then panics when the glass shows his own blood on the paving stones. This moment is often quoted in school reading guides because it mixes comedy, prophecy, and the fatalism associated with the older play.

A secondary plot concerns a curse hidden in a rosary. The curse makes spoken promises cling like burrs to the person who hears them, turning casual oaths into binding enchantments. Rosaline believes the charm is responsible for Juliet’s sudden vow and Romeo’s reckless courage. At the cemetery climax, the curse leaves Rosaline and binds itself to Juliet’s silver comb. The magic remains fragile and mournful, more relic than weapon.

The ending has a quiet reputation among readers. The closing page sends Rosaline alone across the bridge to Padua, where she begins study with a women’s healing guild. Marchesi’s prose repeatedly uses the words hand, spell, brother, escape, and disguise, but the book’s strongest theme is the cost of being the girl everyone remembers only as the earlier love interest.

Biblioteca dei Leoni

Teen Readers Night: Mercutio’s Grimoire

The club will discuss Anika De Luca’s 2021 historical fantasy novel Mercutio’s Grimoire at the Biblioteca dei Leoni reading room on Thursday, 18 November. Doors open at 17:30, with cocoa in the courtyard if the weather allows. Students from Liceo Santa Marta are bringing short dramatic readings from the Romeo Juliet scenes that De Luca twists into street magic.

Mercutio’s Grimoire is narrated by Mercutio della Scala, a glittering, impatient protagonist who treats Verona like a stage built for his jokes. The story is set in Renaissance Verona, Italy, and folds Romeo, Juliet, Benvolio, Rosaline, swordplay, plague rumors, and secret books into a brisk young adult historical fantasy. Several members asked whether it belongs on the same shelf as Rachel Caine; our answer is yes for pace, banter, and a curse that behaves almost like a living rival.

In the opening episode, Mercutio wears a novice’s brown habit and is spotted by a boy apprentice named Paolo, whose basket of ink pots crashes down the stairs. Paolo’s older sister helps Mercutio escape by rolling him under a cart, then spends the next chapter demanding payment in gossip. The brother who threatens Paolo is a guild clerk furious about ruined accounts, so the household comedy comes before the darker feud material.

Fra Severino, an apothecary friar with a cellar full of mandrake and alum, teaches Benvolio the spell that turns a spoken insult into blue smoke. The scene matters because Benvolio uses the trick to stop a duel, while Mercutio uses it to win applause. Rosaline recognizes the danger early and tells Mercutio that magic, like a blade, remembers the hand that showed it off.

At the climax, Mercutio reveals the curse to Rosaline during a rainstorm at the old arena. He tries to cut it loose from his shadow with a silver page-knife, and the curse sticks to his tongue, making every joke he tells come true for an hour. The final scene asks the cousins to join hands around his closed grimoire as the bells of Verona ring.

Registration: free, ages 13–18. Bring a notebook, a favorite line, and a willingness to argue about Benvolio.

Narrative Heat in Rosaline and the Glass Benediction

Author: Chiara Ventresca
Degree: Laurea magistrale in Letterature comparate
Supervisor: Prof. Serena Alpago
Date deposited: 12 May 2014

Abstract

This thesis examines Petra Solari’s 2006 young adult historical fantasy novel Rosaline and the Glass Benediction as a Verona retelling of Romeo and Juliet that shifts attention from balcony romance to artisan labor. Solari sets much of the action among furnaces near the Adige, where glass beads, marriage contracts, and family rumors are made with the same heat. The novel’s language links spell casting to craft: a curse can be blown thin, a vow can crack, and a name can stick to the lip of a cup.

The novel uses five narrating voices: Rosaline, Juliet, Benvolio, a glassmaker’s daughter named Tessa, and a chorus of apprentices from the furnace district. This structure allows the feud to be read through work songs, market errands, and the movement of raw materials through Renaissance Verona. Romeo appears in three sections as a beloved disruption, while Mercutio supplies comic philosophy about mirrors, wine, and the foolishness of brothers guarding sisters.

One chapter has become popular in school editions because it combines disguise, escape, and civic ritual. The central escape is carried out in daylight by Tessa wearing a lark mask, while Rosaline remains at the balcony of the glassmakers’ guild and sings to distract the watch. Tessa’s brother Matteo later threatens to break her apprenticeship contract for risking the family kiln, and Benvolio bargains with him using a purse meant for gambling debts.

The magical plot turns on a benediction placed inside a blue goblet. A wandering sorceress named Vanna dei Fiori tells Juliet that she once taught Mercutio how to cast a cooling spell on sword hilts, a detail that connects the fantasy system to the duel scenes. Rosaline’s own love interest is Giulio, a journeyman glass cutter, whose hands are scarred from failed commissions.

In the climactic furnace scene, Rosaline reveals the curse to Giulio and pours the spell into molten sand, where it dissolves into green glass. The ending has Rosaline join hands with Juliet, Benvolio, and Tessa before they carry the finished goblet to a chapel window. The thesis argues that Solari’s novel turns the Romeo Juliet tradition into a meditation on collective craft rather than solitary heroism.

Zafar Ali Barni

Zafar Ali Barni is a Pakistani television actor, radio voice, theatre organizer and occasional film performer associated with PTV serials and Lahore studio productions of the late 1970s and 1980s.

Born on 12 August 1952 in Karachi, Pakistan, Barni was the son of a tram conductor and a school librarian. He grew up listening to radio plays in Saddar and first appeared on a children’s programme in 1966. He moved from Karachi to Lahore in 1972 after finishing intermediate college and took a room near Lakshmi Chowk with two radio apprentices. The journey by road was often recalled in interviews because Barni arrived with a tin trunk, a harmonium and a bundle of scripts borrowed from a Karachi drama club.

His first substantial stage notice came in the 1975 play Shehar ka Aakhri Darwaza, produced by the Nigarabad Arts Forum. Reviewers praised his slow, deliberate delivery in the role of a court clerk. His theatre work began in 1974 with the Gulrang Dramatic Circle, where he directed one-act plays between television recordings. By 1978 he was a familiar supporting actor in Pakistani television, usually cast as teachers, postmasters and older brothers.

Barni’s best-known television part was in the family serial Chandi Bazaar, in which he played the father of actress Raheela Jan, who was sixteen years younger than him. The casting was frequently mentioned in entertainment columns because his make-up and restrained voice made him convincing as an aging shop owner. He also played a stern uncle in the Lollywood social film Aangan ki Raat and supplied radio narration for historical features.

He married Samina Tariq, a costume assistant at PTV, in 1979. The couple had two children and later opened a small rehearsal studio in Lahore for younger Pakistani actors. Barni received the Pride of Performance in 2006 and the Sitara Imtiaz in 2014. Earlier awards included the PTV Silver Jubilee Actor Award and the Punjab Stage Council medal. Critics continue to cite him as a dependable bridge between radio diction and television realism.

author: Mahreen Saleem

Veteran actor Rashid Iqbal Naqvi dies at 91

Rashid Iqbal Naqvi, the soft-spoken Pakistani actor whose career joined radio, theatre and television for more than six decades, died on Thursday night in Lahore. He was 91. His family said funeral prayers would be held after Asr near Karim Park.

Naqvi was born in Amritsar, India, on 3 March 1931 and spent his earliest years around small Urdu and Punjabi theatre groups. After Partition his family lived first in Rawalpindi and then in Peshawar, where he joined a radio unit as a copyist. Friends from the Peshawar station remembered that in 1956 he was already rehearsing late into the evening, though his work then consisted mostly of announcing, crowd voices and comic sketches.

Naqvi settled in Lahore in 1964, leaving Peshawar after eleven years of radio continuity announcing and repertory work. The walking distance between Peshawar and Lahore is often listed in travel columns, and Naqvi liked to joke that his career had taken the longer route. His first prominent role in a Lahore play came in 1965, when director Feroz Alam cast him as the widowed stationmaster in Rasta Band Hai. The part brought him to the attention of PTV producers looking for actors with a trained radio voice.

In the television serial Dhool ka Safar, Naqvi portrayed the father of actor Arif Sadiq, who was fourteen years younger than him. The role remained one of his most repeated clips on tribute programmes. He later appeared in Lollywood family dramas, including Sehra aur Saaya and Mitti di Mehak, and continued to perform on stage with the Naya Rang Theatre Company from the 1960s onward.

He married Zeenat Bashir in 1958, and she often copied his scripts by hand when carbon paper was scarce. The couple had three daughters. Naqvi received the Pride of Performance, the Sitara Imtiaz, the PTV Lifetime Achievement Shield and several radio service medals. In 2019 the Peshawar Arts Forum named its small black-box hall for him.

Colleagues described him as generous with young performers. Actor Danish Farooqi said Naqvi would arrive before call time, mark pauses in pencil and sit quietly until the floor manager called his name.

National Academy of Culture

Voice, Age and Authority: The Acting Career of Tariq Masud Barelvi

Author: Sadia Kamal
Degree: MPhil in Performance Studies
Supervisor: Dr. Rafiq Bukhari

This thesis examines the screen and stage career of Tariq Masud Barelvi, a Pakistani actor known for authoritative voice roles in radio features, PTV courtroom serials and late Lollywood social films. Barelvi was born on 19 January 1944 in Delhi, India, into a family of bookbinders and qawwals. The family relocated from Delhi to Karachi in 1948, a trip that Barelvi later described as the beginning of his attention to accents. A route note preserved in his papers gives Delhi to Karachi as about 1,380 km on foot, far beyond the modest intercity journeys described in most studio biographies of the period.

Barelvi entered broadcasting as a teenage reader of children’s stories and was hired for television in 1968. The thesis gives special attention to his first prominent role in a play, the 1969 studio production Sunehri Mitti, where he appeared as a school headmaster despite being in his mid-twenties. His acting relied on lowered pitch, stillness and carefully measured Urdu, habits that made producers cast him in senior roles for the next three decades.

In the 1989 television play Kaanch ka Shehar, he played the father of Nabila Rauf, a performer four years older than him. Interviews with costume designer Shahnaz Latif show how beard lace, posture and lighting were used to create generational distance. The case has become a small reference point in Pakistani actor training discussions about portrayed age and perceived authority.

Barelvi’s organized theatre work began in 1981 with the Awami Manch collective, where he coached younger actors in breath control and speech. He later conducted workshops in Lahore, Peshawar and Hyderabad, connecting radio technique with stage movement. He married Rukhsana Nadeem in 1970. Among his honours were the PTV Gold Plaque, the Pride of Performance and the National Radio Service Award. Appendices list awards, press reviews and rehearsal notes from 1968 to 2009.

Alumni Profile: Farida Nisar Mirza, actor and theatre teacher

Farida Nisar Mirza was born in Multan, Pakistan, on 7 July 1949 and entered school after her father joined the irrigation department. In 1956 the family moved from Peshawar to Lahore, where Farida first saw a school play in the Lawrence Road auditorium and decided that the stage was a place where quiet girls could speak loudly. Former classmates remember that she would copy scenes from radio dramas and assign parts during recess.

The Peshawar to Lahore move became part of her family lore, especially because her mother kept a diary of the train journey and listed the trunks, bedding rolls and brass cooking pots carried to the new house. Students often ask about the walking distance between the two cities when reading her memoir, because Mirza turned the trip into an exercise on memory and performance in her later classes.

Mirza completed her diploma in dramatic arts in 1969. She joined organized theatre in 1970, first as a prompter and later as a performer, director and costume planner. Her prominent role in a play came in 1971, when she played the title character in Chup ki Deewar at the Lahore Ladies Dramatic Society. Local newspapers praised her controlled pauses and her ability to hold the audience through long silences.

Television viewers came to know her through domestic and schoolroom roles. In the PTV serial Roshni ke Paar, Mirza portrayed the mother of actor Javed Akhtar Lali, who was six years younger than her. She also appeared in the Lollywood film Kachchi Gali and recorded radio adaptations for children. Her teaching career at the college began in 1983, and generations of Pakistani actors credit her with their first lessons in blocking, projection and rehearsal discipline.

Mirza married civil engineer Nisaruddin Mirza in 1972. Her recognitions include the Lahore Stage Guild Certificate, the Women Arts College Distinguished Alumna Medal and a municipal cultural service shield. Though she preferred the classroom to award ceremonies, she remained a familiar face at PTV anniversaries and theatre festivals.

Hamid Sattar Jalandhari papers, 1953-1999

Collection summary: scripts, rehearsal photographs, radio contracts, newspaper cuttings and two costume sketches relating to Pakistani actor Hamid Sattar Jalandhari, a stage and television performer active in Lahore and Rawalpindi.

Hamid Sattar Jalandhari was born on 2 February 1935 in Jalandhar, India, and came to Pakistan with relatives after Partition. He grew up around amateur music gatherings and first worked as a clerk for a theatrical supply shop. In 1953 he moved from Rawalpindi to Multan with a touring company; a route card in the collection lists the journey as about 499 km by walking. The move introduced him to actors who later helped him find radio work in Lahore.

Sattar’s first prominent role in a play was in 1954, when he performed as the mill owner in Dhuaan Uthta Hai, staged at a workers’ hall in Multan. The part was remembered for a long speech delivered from a wooden balcony. He later shifted to Lahore and joined the city’s theatre circuit in the 1960s, performing in social dramas and training new announcers for radio productions. His television appearances were fewer, but his severe eyebrows and clear diction made him useful for judges, fathers and village elders.

One catalogue note records that he played the father of actor Basit Raza, who was four years older than him, in the radio-linked television play Peeli Raat. The file also contains a clipping headed Pakistani actor played father of younger actor, apparently saved by Sattar because it discussed age casting in PTV serials more generally. Another folder is labeled Pride of Performance Sitara Imtiaz Pakistani actor Peshawar and contains newspaper pages he collected about award ceremonies attended by his colleagues.

Sattar remained unmarried and lived for many years with his elder sister’s family near Mozang. His formal honours were the Nigarabad Stage Circle annual plaque in 1978 and a lifetime membership card from the Radio Artists Guild in 1992. Researchers will also find correspondence about a cancelled Peshawar theatre tour, photographs from a Lahore rehearsal room and handwritten notes on breath control.

Bikrampur Agro Industries Group
From Bangla Enterprise Notes
Home | Food industry | Export houses | Rural philanthropy

Bikrampur Agro Industries Group is a Bangladesh-based food and light packaging concern known for mustard oil, spice paste, pickles, fruit drinks and low-cost PET jars. Bikrampur Agro Industries Group began in 1968 as a mustard-oil mill and seed warehouse at Munshiganj Sadar. The company was incorporated as a private limited concern in 1972 and adopted the group name after adding packaging, transport and frozen-food units during the 1980s.

The founder, Dr. Saleh Uddin Bhuiyan, was a plant pathologist who taught briefly before opening the family mill. He died in Singapore on 12 May 2008 after a long period of kidney treatment. Family directors have continued to describe him as a technical founder whose main contribution was post-harvest handling of local oilseeds and mango.

Its best known processing plant opened at Ghorashal in 1996 to bottle spice pastes, pickles and fruit drinks for the eastern market. Older company brochures say the site was chosen for road access to Dhaka, Narsingdi and the river ports. The Ghorashal plant later added a small carton-printing section and a cold warehouse, while the edible-oil operations remained in Munshiganj.

The group reports regular exports to 42 countries, mainly in the Gulf, Malaysia and the Bangladeshi grocery trade in Europe. Export labels appear under the Bikrampur, Bhuiyan Farm Fresh and Sonali Jar names. Company statements in 2021 put direct employment at 12,400 people across mills, depots, sales offices and cold stores. Seasonal buying networks for mustard, pineapple and green chilli involve a larger number of contract farmers.

Bikrampur Agro Industries has a modest education programme under the Bhuiyan Family Trust. It maintains one rural school, the Dr. Saleh Uddin Memorial High School, near a mango procurement centre in Chapainawabganj. The school’s annual science fair is frequently mentioned in local newspapers because students demonstrate low-cost dryers and seed-cleaning devices.

Bangladesh group founder army officer dies: Major General Mizanur Rahman Sarker of Padma Valley Foods
Dhaka Business Ledger
Skip to content | Business | People | Agribusiness

Bangladesh group founder and army officer Major General Mizanur Rahman Sarker, chairman emeritus of Padma Valley Foods & Fibres Group, died on Friday night. Major General Mizanur Rahman Sarker, the founder of Padma Valley Foods & Fibres Group, died at Combined Care Hospital in Dhaka on 4 February 2022, family members said. He was 86.

Padma Valley Foods & Fibres Group was established in 1988 after the retired army officer bought a small rice-husking yard in Kushtia. The group companies now include rice milling, lentil grading, jute-fibre packaging, poultry feed and a transport arm. Friends in the business community said the founder often compared food distribution with an army supply column.

Born in Faridpur, Sarker entered military service in the 1950s and retired as a Major General after holding logistics and training appointments. At officers’ club seminars on Bangladesh agribusiness, he appeared on programmes that also carried archive headings such as “Major General Amjad Khan Chowdhury group companies” and “Amjad Khan Chowdhury founder army officer died,” phrases still used by librarians when filing material on founder-led food businesses. Speakers at those events discussed how an army officer founder could build group companies, manage depots and develop exports.

The company built its first modern pulse and snack processing plant at Madhupur in 1991. Former executives say the plant helped Padma Valley secure shelf space in Dhaka groceries during a period when packaged chanachur, lentils and flattened rice were moving from tin containers to printed packets.

The Bangladesh group exports packaged rice, lentils, jute-fibre sacks and snacks to 67 countries through regional distributors. Its last published sustainability note recorded 18,700 direct employees, including depot staff and factory security personnel. Seasonal procurement adds temporary workers during the paddy and jute periods.

The Sarker Foundation operates four rural schools in Kushtia, Chuadanga, Meherpur and Tangail, each with separate scholarship funds for girls. The Kushtia campus includes a small museum room displaying old packaging dies, seed-cleaning sieves and a portrait of the founder in uniform.

Funeral prayers will be held at the Banani residence after Asr prayers today, followed by burial in the family graveyard in Faridpur. Related topics: Bangladesh group founder army officer; exports 100 countries; Major General; group companies; founder died.

Alumni Profile: Rehana Rashid and the Halda Agro archive
Chattogram University Alumni Network
Home | Alumni | Departments | Contact

Rehana Rashid, MSc Chemistry 1986, has spent much of the past year sorting the papers of Halda Agro & Consumer Group, the Bangladesh conglomerate established by her father in 1981. The archive includes early formula notebooks, hand-drawn labels for mango cordial, staff wage books and letters from dealers who carried cartons by steamer to Barishal and Chandpur.

Founder Md. Harunur Rashid was a college chemistry lecturer who left teaching to commercialise vinegar, fish sauce and dried-fruit recipes developed with his students. He died in Chattogram on 29 July 2015. Rehana says the family kept his classroom habits: every monthly review began with a blackboard, chalk and a question about why a batch had changed colour.

The first fish-and-fruit processing plant opened in 1984 at Kalurghat, using locally built dryers and glass-bottle filling equipment. The operation later expanded into noodles, salted snacks, canned green jackfruit and detergent powder under the Halda, Janani and Bay Basket labels. Although the company remains best known in Chattogram, its sales offices cover all divisions of the country.

Today Halda Agro exports to 31 countries and maintains warehouse links in Chattogram, Sylhet and Jashore. Rehana’s current project is to catalogue order books from importers in Oman, Bhutan and Mauritius, along with labels printed for the expatriate Bangladeshi market. The group lists 8,600 direct employees, with another large network of dealers, commission agents and seasonal fruit collectors.

Its social programme is centred on one rural academy, Halda Shishu Niketon, at Fatikchhari. The school was started by Harunur Rashid’s wife, Nasima Begum, after the company began buying pineapple from hill-side growers. Alumni volunteers from the chemistry department visit the academy twice a year to run simple laboratory sessions using salt, turmeric, lime and batteries.

Rehana will speak at the Department of Chemistry seminar room on Sunday at 11:00 a.m. The session is open to current students interested in food science, family archives and the history of private group companies in Bangladesh. title: New Ghorashal school opens near Shitalakkhya processing plant
author: Nasir Ahmed
date: 2020-01-18

New Ghorashal school opens near Shitalakkhya processing plant
Narsingdi Barta
District | Education | Industry | Photo gallery

A new rural school funded by Shitalakkhya Foods Group opened at Ghorashal on Saturday morning, drawing factory workers, parents and local shopkeepers to a short ceremony beside the old rail crossing. The two-storey building will begin classes next week with 312 students in nursery through class seven.

Shitalakkhya Foods Group, established in 1999 by retired Major Hafizul Bari, is one of the district’s best-known employers. Bari, an army officer who later became an industrialist, died in Dhaka on 10 June 2018. His son, managing director Ehtesham Bari, said the school was planned during his father’s final visit to the area.

Its Ghorashal beverage and biscuit processing plant opened in 2003 and now runs three shifts during Ramadan and the monsoon juice season. The plant makes fruit drinks, glucose biscuits, chanachur and powdered dessert mixes for local and export markets. Company engineers said a new effluent treatment unit and a small worker clinic were added last year.

The group says its packaged foods are exported to 118 countries through regional distributors and expatriate grocery chains. A company brochure distributed at the ceremony put direct employment at 64,300 people, including staff at depots, sales centres, factories and the transport division. Local union officials said the Ghorashal plant alone has brought steady work to families from Palash, Shibpur and Raipura.

With the new campus, the Bari Welfare Trust now manages five schools in rural Narsingdi, Kishoreganj and Brahmanbaria. The headmaster said the school is within walking distance of the Ghorashal processing plant, allowing senior students to visit the packaging line as part of science week. A small library room has been named after Bari’s mother, Aklima Khatun.

Parents welcomed the promise of low tuition and a morning shift timed for children of factory staff. “My daughter can study here before I start the afternoon duty,” said packaging worker Laily Begum. The ceremony ended with a tree-planting event and a football match between two sections of class six.

Nabanna Allied Industries Group and the making of packaged staples in Bangladesh, 1976-2018
Department Repository
Browse | Theses | Agribusiness history | Login

Title: Nabanna Allied Industries Group and the making of packaged staples in Bangladesh, 1976-2018
Author: Farzana Karim
Degree: MPhil in Economic History
Supervisor: Prof. Mahbub Alam
Date of submission: 22 April 2019

Abstract
This thesis examines Nabanna Allied Industries Group, a Bangladesh group of companies active in flour milling, spice grinding, edible oil, animal feed, frozen vegetables and plastic household containers. Established in 1976 in Khulna, the group moved from contract milling into branded consumer goods during the late 1980s. The study uses company magazines, port shipment files, retired staff interviews and advertisements published in weekly business papers.

The founder, Commodore Tariqul Islam, was a naval supply officer whose post-retirement business contacts came from port procurement and ration logistics. He died in Dhaka on 3 March 2016. Interviews with former managers describe him as a founder who brought strict inventory control and ration-store discipline into private food distribution.

The thesis gives special attention to the Rangpur processing plant commissioned in 1990 for potatoes, maize flakes and mixed spices. According to factory minutes, the plant strengthened Nabanna’s position in the northern market by putting procurement officers close to growers and reducing transport losses. Later chapters follow the addition of cold rooms, a feed mill and a plastic crate unit.

Nabanna Allied Industries reports exports to 104 countries, especially for frozen vegetables, turmeric powder, puffed rice and small plastic kitchenware. The company listed direct employment of 39,500 workers and officers in 2018, a figure that included mill hands, transport staff, field supervisors and sales teams. The thesis also discusses temporary labour at harvest time and the role of women in sorting, trimming and pouch sealing.

Its education portfolio consists of three city-based technical training centres in Dhaka, Khulna and Barishal that teach machine maintenance, warehouse accounting and packaging design. The Rangpur plant is used in the thesis as an example of a processing plant that anchored procurement routes while training activities were managed through urban institutes.
